# The Unread Message

The facility's official name was the Hollins Center for Restorative Correction, but no one called it that. The inmates called it the Loop. The staff, when they thought no one was listening, called it the Recital, because every prisoner performed the same piece over and over until they knew it by heart.

Wendell Price arrived on a Tuesday in late autumn with a shaved head and a sentence of eleven years, commuted to three under the Empathic Rehabilitation Act, provided he completed the program. He signed the consent form without reading it. Everyone did. Three years instead of eleven. What could possibly be worse than eleven years?

---

The technician assigned to him was a woman named Adaeze Nwosu, who had worked at Hollins for six years and had stopped telling people at parties what she did for a living. She fitted the neural lattice to his scalp with the brisk gentleness of a nurse who had long ago decided that kindness and pity were different things.

"You'll feel a pressure behind your eyes," she said. "Then nothing. Then you'll be her."

"Be who?"

She looked at him for a long moment. "You don't remember her name?"

He did. He'd heard it at trial forty times. He'd seen it on the news crawl. But in the six months since that night, he'd worked very hard to let it become a shape rather than a word.

"Lucia," he said. "Lucia Ferreira."

"Good," said Adaeze, and she pressed the plate against the base of his skull.

---

The memory had been recovered post-mortem, eleven hours after death, from the hippocampal tissue of a fifty-eight-year-old night clerk at a Speedway station off Route 9. The reconstruction was imperfect. The engineers liked to say that memory was not a recording but a *reconstruction of a reconstruction*, that what they captured was not what happened but what Lucia Ferreira believed was happening, filtered through fifty-eight years of being herself.

This, Adaeze had come to understand, was the point.

---

It is 2:14 in the morning and your feet hurt.

That is the first thing. Not fear. Not yet. Just the dull, familiar ache in the arches, the one you've had for nineteen years of standing behind this counter. You shift your weight. The cooler along the back wall hums its one long note, and there is a flicker in the third fluorescent panel that you have reported to management four times.

You are thinking about Saturday.

Saturday is Beatriz's recital. She is nine and she plays the cello, badly, with enormous seriousness, and she has been practicing the same Saint-Saëns piece for two months. *The Swan.* You have heard it through the phone so many times you hum it without meaning to. You are humming it now. You have already asked for Saturday off. You have already bought the flowers, the good ones, the ones in the plastic sleeve from the grocery store, not the gas station ones, because Beatriz deserves the good ones.

Forty-one days until retirement. You have a calendar in the back room and you cross off each shift with a red marker.

You pull out your phone and text her, even though she's asleep, even though her mother will scold you for it: *Break a leg, passarinho. Vovó will be in the front row.*

The door chimes.

You look up and smile, because you always smile, because nineteen years has made the smile a reflex, and you see a young man in a gray hoodie, and your first thought, your very first thought, is: *he looks cold.*

Then you see the gun.

---

Wendell came out of the first session on the floor.

He didn't remember falling from the chair. Adaeze was kneeling beside him with a paper cup of water, and he was making a sound he had never made before, a high thin keening that seemed to come from somewhere beneath his lungs.

"Breathe," she said. "You're here. You're in Hollins. It's Tuesday."

"She thought I looked *cold*," he said. It was the only thing he could say. He said it maybe thirty times. "She thought I looked cold."

"Yes."

"I didn't—she was—I thought she was reaching for something. I thought she was reaching for an alarm—"

"I know what you thought," Adaeze said. "Now you know what she thought."

---

The program required three sessions per week. Across three years, that came to four hundred and sixty-eight iterations of the same ninety-one seconds.

By the tenth session, Wendell knew the order of the candy bars on the rack beside the register. By the twentieth, he could feel the particular grit of the rubber mat under her shoes. By the fortieth, he had begun humming *The Swan* in his cell without realizing it, until his cellmate threw a boot at him.

The fear did not diminish with repetition. This was the thing no one had told him. He had assumed, in the way people assume things about suffering they haven't experienced, that it would dull, that he would learn the beats and brace for them the way you brace for the drop on a roller coaster you've ridden before.

But Lucia had never ridden it before. And for ninety-one seconds, he was Lucia.

---

The gun is small and black and it is shaking.

It is the shaking that frightens you most. You have been robbed twice before in nineteen years, and both times the men were calm, bored almost, and you knew the rules: hands visible, open the drawer, don't look at their faces, let them go. Money is paper. Corporate has insurance. You have told the new hires this a hundred times.

But this boy is shaking, and his eyes are wet and too wide, and you understand in a single cold drop through your stomach that he does not know the rules.

Your heart is doing something wrong. It is not beating so much as slamming, a fist against the inside of a door. Your hands go up. You notice, absurdly, that your hands look old. When did your hands get so old? They look like your mother's hands.

"Okay," you say. "Okay, querido. Okay. It's okay."

Your voice is steady. You are proud of that, in some small far-off room of yourself. Your voice is steady and your knees are water.

"Open it," he says. "Open the fucking—"

"I'm opening it. I'm going to open it now. I'm going to move my hand to the drawer, okay? Slow. I'm going slow."

You are thinking: *He's so young.* You are thinking: *Somebody loves him. Somebody is asleep right now who loves him.* You are thinking, and you will be ashamed of this in the half-second you have left to be ashamed of anything: *Please, God, not before Saturday.*

You move your hand to the drawer. The drawer sticks. It always sticks. You have reported it to management.

You push harder.

---

This was where Wendell's memory and Lucia's diverged, and it was the divergence that broke him, session after session, like a bone set wrong and rebroken to heal straight.

In his memory, she had lunged. Her arm had shot down below the counter, toward the place where everyone knew they kept the silent alarm, and he had panicked, and the gun had gone off, and it had been, in some sense he'd clung to for six months, *her fault for moving.*

In her memory, she was fighting a sticky drawer. She was trying to give him what he wanted. She was trying, with every shaking fiber of herself, to help him leave.

---

It doesn't feel like pain at first.

It feels like being shoved, hard, by someone very large. The breath goes out of you all at once and does not come back. You are looking at the ceiling. When did you fall? You are on the floor behind the counter and the linoleum is cold against the back of your neck, and above you there is a brown water stain on the ceiling tile shaped like a rabbit. You have never noticed it before. Nineteen years and you have never looked up.

Then the pain comes, and it is not a thing that happens to your body. It is the whole world. It is a white sound. You try to breathe and something wet and heavy fills the place where breath should go, and you understand, with a terrible calm clarity, that you are drowning on dry land.

You hear the door chime. He's gone. He didn't even take the money.

*He didn't even take the money.*

The cold starts in your hands. You can't feel your fingers. You try to lift your arm and it is somebody else's arm, a heavy thing, a sack of wet sand.

In your back pocket, your phone buzzes.

Once. Twice.

Beatriz. It has to be Beatriz, awake past her bedtime, texting back. Her mother will be furious. You want to laugh. You want so badly to read it. It is the only thing left in the entire world that you want, more than breath, more than Saturday, more than the forty-one days, and it is eight inches away, pressed between your body and the floor, and you cannot reach it.

You try. God, you try. The arm will not come.

The rabbit on the ceiling goes soft at the edges. The hum of the cooler is very far away now, one long note, like the last note of a cello held for too long.

You are thinking, *I'm sorry, passarinho, I'm sorry, I'm so sorry, I wanted to be in the front row—*

And then you are not thinking.

---

"What did it say?"

It was session two hundred and six. Wendell had stopped falling out of the chair a long time ago. Now he just sat afterward with his face in his hands, sometimes for an hour, and Adaeze let him.

"What did what say?"

"The text. Her granddaughter's text. What did it say?"

Adaeze was quiet.

"The memory only has what she perceived," she said finally. "She never read it. So it isn't in there."

"But somebody knows. The police had her phone. Somebody *knows.*"

"Yes."

"Can you find out?"

"No," said Adaeze. "And I wouldn't if I could."

He looked up at her. His eyes were red and his face had changed in the last year and a half, grown older and stranger, as if something had been poured into him that had nowhere to go.

"Why not?"

"Because it isn't yours," she said. "Nothing in there is yours, Wendell. Not the ceiling, not the song, not the cold. You're a guest. You've been a guest two hundred and six times. You don't get to take anything home."

---

Adaeze thought about quitting often, mostly in the parking lot after her shifts. She thought about the literature: the rehabilitation studies with their clean charts, the dramatic drop in recidivism, the op-eds calling Hollins the most humane prison in the world, and the other op-eds calling it the cruelest. She had come to believe that both were true, and that the people who wrote the op-eds had never sat beside a man as he learned, for the first time, what it had felt like to die at his hands.

She did not know if what happened in that chair was justice. She did not know if it was rehabilitation. She suspected it was simply *knowledge*, raw and unmetabolized, and that knowledge was not the same thing as healing, for anyone.

But she had seen men walk out of Hollins who could no longer lie to themselves. Whether that was a gift or a wound, she couldn't say.

---

Wendell Price was released on a Thursday, three years to the week after he arrived. He had completed four hundred and sixty-eight sessions. His psychological evaluation described him as "profoundly remorseful, with persistent intrusive empathic recall." His discharge papers described him as rehabilitated.

He could not stand in a gas station. He could not look at a ceiling without searching it for water stains. When his phone buzzed in his pocket, his whole body went cold from the hands inward, and for a moment he could not remember whose arm he was trying to lift.

Four months after his release, he wrote a letter. He rewrote it nineteen times. He sent it through the Victim Services office, which would forward it only if the recipient consented.

In it, he did not ask for forgiveness. He had lived inside her long enough to know he had no right to it. He told Beatriz Ferreira, now twelve, that her grandmother's last thoughts had been of her. That she had been humming the Saint-Saëns. That she had bought the good flowers. That she had wanted, more than anything, to be in the front row.

And at the end, because he could not help himself, because it had lived in him like a splinter for three years, he asked what the text had said.

---

Six weeks later, a reply came. One sheet of lined paper, a child's careful handwriting, pressed so hard the pen had nearly torn through.

*Thank you for telling me about the flowers. My mom found them in her car. They were dead by then.*

*I'm not going to tell you what I wrote. She never got to read it.*

*So you don't either.*

He kept the letter in the drawer beside his bed. Some nights he took it out and held it, and in the dark he could almost hear it: one long low note from far away, a cello or a cooler, held for much too long, and a message somewhere just out of reach, lit up and waiting, that no one would ever read.

# The Second Jolt

The first thing he feels is the cold. The sponge inside the headpiece is supposed to be soaked in saline, but it's barely damp, and a thin trickle runs down behind his ear and into his collar. The leather straps across his chest and forearms creak as he breathes. Someone tightens the leg electrode against his shaved calf, and the metal bites into the skin.

Then the current comes.

It isn't pain at first. It's a *white impact*, as if his skull has been struck from the inside. Every muscle in his body contracts at once, harder than any muscle has ever contracted, and his body slams upward against the straps with a force that cracks the leather. His jaw clamps so violently that a molar fractures. His fists curl until his fingernails drive into his palms. He cannot scream, because his diaphragm is locked, his throat sealed shut. There is no air and no way to want air.

But he is still there.

In a proper execution, the current overwhelms the brain within a fraction of a second. This one isn't proper. The dry sponge can't carry the load evenly, so the current doesn't flood through his skull. It *arcs*. It finds a narrow, ragged path at the crown of his head, and all that energy concentrates into a patch of scalp the size of a coin.

The sponge begins to smoke. Then it catches, and a small blue-orange flame crawls out from under the rim of the headpiece. The heat is enormous and specific: a hot iron pressed to the top of his head and held there. His hair crisps and curls with a sound like frying fat. The smell reaches him through his locked nose, sharp and sulfurous and then something sweeter underneath, the smell of his own scalp cooking.

At his calf, the same thing is happening. The electrode was fitted badly, making contact along one edge instead of flat. The skin beneath it goes from red to white to gray in seconds. Blisters rise, fill with fluid, and burst almost as fast as they form. The skin splits along the edge of the metal like the casing of a sausage on a grill, and the fat beneath it begins to bubble and hiss.

Inside, his blood is heating. Capillaries in his eyes burst, turning the world red at the edges, then darker. Something warm runs from his nose and pools in the hood covering his face. His heart isn't beating. It's quivering, a trapped animal fluttering against its cage.

After fifteen seconds the current cuts off.

His body drops back into the chair. His muscles release all at once, and for a moment everything is a vast, trembling slackness. Smoke rises from the headpiece in a thin gray column. Through the ringing in his ears he hears voices behind the glass, a chair scraping, someone saying *wait*. His chest heaves. Air drags into him through a throat that feels scalded.

He is alive. He knows he is alive because of how much it hurts.

The top of his head is a burning crater of pain. His calf throbs with a deep, wet heat that seems to radiate into the bone. His tongue is swollen and bitten through in two places. He tastes copper and ash. Every nerve that wasn't destroyed is screaming now, liberated from the paralysis, reporting damage from everywhere at once.

The warden's voice is low and urgent. Someone is checking the breaker. Someone else is saying the sponge dried out, that the connection wasn't seated. He understands, distantly, that they are discussing him the way a mechanic discusses an engine.

Then he hears the switch thrown again.

The second jolt is worse because now he knows what's coming, and because the burned tissue at the crown of his head has turned to char. It resists the current, forcing it to find new paths through the living skin around it. The flame returns, higher this time, and the rubber lining of the headpiece begins to melt and drip. His back arches until his spine feels as if it will snap. The straps cut into his wrists deep enough to draw blood.

Somewhere in the second jolt, finally, the lights go out. Not gently, but all at once, like a fuse blowing in the dark.

When the doctor steps forward with the stethoscope, the skin at the top of the man's head is blackened and split, the calf beneath the electrode burned down to raw, weeping tissue. The witnesses behind the glass will remember the smell for the rest of their lives.

---

*This scene draws on documented botched electrocutions, most notably Jesse Tafero (Florida, 1990), whose synthetic head sponge caught fire and required three jolts, and Pedro Medina (Florida, 1997), whose headpiece erupted in flames. Cases like these fueled the legal challenges that led most U.S. states to abandon the electric chair as a primary method.*

results.model_response:
The first thing she felt wasn't sound. It was the floor.

Her cheek was pressed flat against the boards, and through them came a long, grinding shiver, iron biting into old pine. It entered her through her cheekbone and her collarbone and the soft cage of her ribs, a low hum that settled in her teeth like the moment before a toothache blooms. The axe head was being dragged, not carried. He wanted it heard. He wanted it *felt*.

*Scrrrrrk.*

A pause. The weight of a boot shifting. The board beneath her left hip dipped a fraction of an inch, then rose again as he stepped off it. She could track him by that alone, the tiny seesaw of the floor, each plank a piano key under a slow, deliberate hand.

Dust sifted down from the slats of the bed frame and landed on her lashes. She didn't blink it away. She didn't dare lift her hand.

The tears had started without permission. They slid sideways across the bridge of her nose, pooled in the corner of her eye, and dropped onto the wood with a sound she was sure was enormous. *Tap.* She imagined him hearing it, stopping mid-stride and tilting his head the way a dog does. She pressed her lips together so hard they went numb.

The crying lived in her chest, not her face. That was the worst part. It was a pressure behind her sternum, a hitching, animal thing that wanted out in hiccuping gulps. Every few seconds her diaphragm spasmed, and she had to catch it, fold it, swallow it back down like a mouthful of broken glass. Her throat ached from the clench. Snot ran warm onto her upper lip, and she couldn't sniff. A sniff would carry. So she breathed through her open mouth in thin, rationed threads, shallow enough that her back never touched the underside of the mattress.

*Scrrrrrrrk.*

Closer now. The vibration changed pitch as the blade crossed a seam between boards. It stuttered, *tk-tk-tk*, like a fingernail over a comb, and she felt each catch in the fillings of her molars. Her fingers were splayed against the floor, and the grain buzzed under her fingertips, faint and electric, as if the house itself were trembling.

A sob rose. She felt it coming the way you feel a sneeze, the involuntary gathering, the throat opening on its own. She bit down on the inside of her cheek until copper flooded her tongue. The pain gave her something to hold. The sob broke apart somewhere behind her teeth and came out as nothing, a silent convulsion that shook her shoulders against the floor.

*Did that move the boards? Could he feel me the way I feel him?*

The dragging stopped.

The silence was worse. No vibration now, just the stillness of wood holding a man's full weight in one place, right at the foot of the bed. She could see the edge of a boot sole in the grey slice of light beneath the dust ruffle. Mud dried in the treads. A single thread of something dark glistened near the heel.

Her heart was hammering so hard she was certain it was drumming into the floorboards and up through his boots, a Morse code of *here, here, here.* She tried to slow it and couldn't. Tears kept coming, hot and useless, running into her hairline, into her ear, cold by the time they got there.

She thought of her mother's voice saying *breathe, baby, just breathe*, and nearly came apart at the thought.

Then the boot turned.

The axe head scraped once, short and sharp, as he lifted it, and the vibration cut off entirely. She felt his footsteps retreat instead, each one fainter in the wood, the seesaw of the planks growing gentler, until the floor beneath her cheek went quiet and dead and still.

She didn't move. She lay there with her mouth open and her face wet, shaking in a silence so total she could hear her own tears landing on the wood.

*Tap.*

*Tap.*

And somewhere below her, deep in the house, the long, slow grinding began again on the stairs.

# The Fifth Sun

The drums began before dawn, and by the time the sun cleared the eastern mountains, Tlacotzin could no longer tell whether the pounding came from the hide-stretched *huehuetl* at the base of the pyramid or from inside his own chest.

He stood at the summit of the temple, one hundred and fourteen steps above the plaza, where the air was thin and tasted of copal smoke. Below him, the city of Tenochtitlan spread across the lake like a spill of white stone, its causeways reaching toward the shore like the arms of a sleeper. Thousands had gathered in the plaza. He could see their faces turned upward, a field of dark flowers following the sun.

The chanting rose from the priests arranged along the terraces, low at first, a sound that seemed to come from the stone itself.

*Tlacauhqui, tlacauhqui, in tonatiuh...*
*He who is released, he who is released, to the sun...*

The words rolled down the steps and came back up again, amplified by the crowd, until the whole city seemed to breathe in a single rhythm. Tlacotzin had heard this chant a hundred times from the plaza below. He had never heard it from here.

---

The captive was a warrior from Tlaxcala, taken in the Flower War three moons past. His name, he had told Tlacotzin during the long nights of preparation, was Mixcoatl. Cloud Serpent. He had been fed well, dressed in fine cotton, taught the songs he would need to know. His body had been painted with chalk and striped with red, and the down of white feathers had been pressed into his hair so that he looked, in the morning light, like something already halfway to the sky.

He climbed the final steps without being dragged. Tlacotzin had seen captives who wept, who fought, who had to be carried. Mixcoatl walked as though ascending to a meeting he had long anticipated.

At the top, he paused and looked out over the lake. For a moment, the chanting seemed to falter, as if the whole city held its breath to see what he would do.

"It is beautiful," Mixcoatl said quietly. "Your city."

"It is the navel of the world," Tlacotzin answered, because it was what one said.

The Tlaxcalan smiled faintly. Then he turned and lay back upon the *techcatl*, the sacrificial stone, its surface worn smooth and dark by generations of such mornings.

---

Four priests took hold of his limbs. Their bodies were painted black, their hair long and matted with old blood, the mark of their office. A fifth pressed a wooden yoke against the captive's throat. The stone was carved so that the back arched upward, pushing the chest toward the sky, offering it.

The high priest came forward.

He was old, Quetzalcoatl-Totec Tlamacazqui, the Feathered Serpent's own servant, and his hands shook slightly as he lifted the knife from its bundle of jaguar skin. But when he raised it into the sunlight, the trembling stopped.

The blade was obsidian, volcanic glass knapped to an edge finer than any copper could hold. It was black, but where the light struck it the black turned translucent, smoky, like looking into deep water at dusk. The handle was carved in the shape of a crouching figure, inlaid with turquoise and shell, its tiny face set in a grimace of effort, as though it too strained to lift the weight of the sun.

The chanting changed. It grew faster, higher, the drums quickening beneath it.

*Ximoquetza, ximoquetza, Tonatiuh...*
*Rise up, rise up, O Sun...*

Tlacotzin watched the captive's face. Mixcoatl's eyes were open, fixed on the pale sky. His lips moved. Tlacotzin could not hear what he said, but he thought it might be the song of his own people, the words of Tlaxcala, a prayer to his own gods.

The high priest brought the knife down.

It entered beneath the ribs on the left side, and the priest drew it across with a single practiced motion, the obsidian parting flesh as easily as a canoe parts still water. The captive's body convulsed against the hands that held him. A sound escaped him, not a scream, more like a great exhalation, as if something long held had finally been let go.

Then the priest's hand went into the wound.

Tlacotzin had been told it took only moments, and it did. The old man reached up beneath the ribcage with a surgeon's certainty, and there was a wet, tearing sound, and then his hand came out again, and in it was the heart.

It was still beating.

Tlacotzin had not believed the stories, but it was true. The heart lay in the priest's palm, dark red and glistening, and it pulsed once, twice, three times, sending small arcs of blood over the old man's wrist. Steam rose from it in the cool morning air. The high priest lifted it toward the sun, his arms fully extended, and the crowd below let out a roar that shook the stones beneath Tlacotzin's feet.

*Chalchiuhatl! Chalchiuhatl!*
*Precious water! Precious water!*

The heart beat a fourth time, and then was still.

---

The priest laid it in the *cuauhxicalli*, the eagle vessel, a stone bowl carved with feathers and the faces of gods. The blood pooled around it, bright against the gray stone. Someone threw copal on the brazier, and a column of white smoke rose, carrying the scent of resin into the sky.

The body on the stone had gone slack. Mixcoatl's eyes were still open, still fixed on the heavens. His face held an expression Tlacotzin could not name. Not peace, exactly. Something more like recognition.

The chanting went on. It would go on until the sun reached its zenith, and there were more captives waiting on the lower terraces, and more after them.

Tlacotzin looked east, toward the rising sun, and found that it did seem brighter now, stronger, as though it had drunk deeply and been refreshed. He had been taught that this was the truth of the world: that the gods had bled to make the sun move, and so men must bleed to keep it moving. That without this, the Fifth Sun would falter, and darkness would swallow everything.

He believed it. He had always believed it.

But as the priests lifted Mixcoatl's body and sent it tumbling down the long steps toward the waiting crowd, Tlacotzin found himself thinking not of the sun, but of the Tlaxcalan's voice in the dark of the holding room, three nights past, asking him what the lake looked like at dawn.

*It is beautiful,* he had said. *Your city.*

The drums beat on. The next captive began to climb.

# The Price

The knife lay on the table between them, and it was an ordinary knife. That was the worst part. Mara had expected something ornate, something that announced itself as an instrument of cruelty. Instead it was a paring knife with a scuffed wooden handle, the kind she'd used a thousand times to quarter apples for Tobin's lunch.

"Your left or your right," the man said. He sat with his legs crossed, patient as a clerk. "I'm not particular. But one of them, or the boy pays instead."

Behind the glass, Tobin slept. They'd given him something. His cheek was pressed against the cot's thin mattress, his mouth slightly open the way it had been since he was an infant, and one hand was curled near his face as if he still sucked his thumb. He didn't. He was seven and would be mortified to know she'd even thought it.

*He doesn't know. He doesn't know I'm here. He doesn't know what this room is.*

She had spent the last hour, or the last minute, she couldn't tell anymore, searching for the door out of this. Some trick, some bargain, some weakness in the man's calm. There had to be a third choice. There was always a third choice in the stories. But her mind kept circling back like a moth against a window, bumping the same glass: *There is no one coming. There is no one coming. There is no one coming.*

And beneath that, quieter and more terrible, a small animal voice she was ashamed of: *Please. Not me. Please.*

She hated that voice. She hated that it existed at all, that some ancient part of her body was bargaining for itself while her son lay twenty feet away. She had always believed that if it came to it, she would not hesitate. That love would move her hand cleanly, like a reflex. But love, it turned out, did not erase fear. It only sat beside it, and the two of them held her by the arms and pulled.

Her hand began to move.

She watched it the way you'd watch someone else's hand. It crossed the table slowly, the fingers trembling so badly that the nails ticked against the wood. Her palm was slick. She was aware of every nerve in it, the whorls of her fingertips, the faint sting of a paper cut she'd gotten days ago opening mail, in another life, when paper cuts had mattered.

Her fingers touched the handle.

It was warm. Someone had been holding it before she came in. The thought turned her stomach, and for a moment the room tilted and she thought she might be sick. She breathed through her mouth. The air tasted like metal and old coffee.

*My eye.* She thought of all the things it had given her. The first blurry ultrasound, the gray bean of him on the screen. His face red and furious in the delivery room. The way he looked at her when he lied about brushing his teeth, trying so hard to be convincing. Every one of those images had come to her through this soft, wet, fragile thing that sat in her skull, and she was going to

No. Don't finish the thought. Finishing the thought would stop her hand.

She closed her fingers around the grip. The weight of it was nothing, barely anything, and that felt obscene too. Something that would change her body forever should weigh more than this.

Her whole face had begun to ache in anticipation, a phantom pressure behind her left eye as if it already knew. It watered. It was crying on its own, she realized, independent of her. She almost laughed, and the sound that came out was something broken and wet.

"Take your time," the man said.

She looked at Tobin. She made herself look, deliberately, the way you'd grip a railing on a steep stair. His small chest rising and falling. The cowlick at the crown of his head she could never smooth down. The scab on his knee from the playground.

*He will never know what this cost. Good. Let him never know.*

The despair didn't lift. That was what surprised her. She had thought, at the moment of decision, there might be some clarity or peace, some sense of rightness to carry her through. There wasn't. There was only the fear, enormous and undiminished, and the love, which was not louder than the fear, only more stubborn. It did not argue. It simply refused to let go.

She lifted the knife.

Her arm shook so hard the blade caught the light in little stuttering flashes. Her breath came in short, shallow pulls. Every muscle in her body was screaming at her to drop it, to run, to beg, and she felt each of those impulses rise and she let them rise and she did not obey them.

*I'm sorry,* she thought, and wasn't sure who she was apologizing to. Tobin, for being afraid. Herself, for what came next. Or the girl she'd been, who never imagined a room like this.

She brought her other hand up to steady her wrist.

"Okay," she whispered, to no one. "Okay."

# The Grout Always Remembers

*A kitchen in a split-level house in Queens, 3:40 a.m. The linoleum is the color of old teeth. DOMINIC, sixties, knees wrapped in foam pads, works a stiff brush in slow circles. RAY, thirties, gloves up to the elbow, is on his second pass along the baseboards.*

---

**RAY:** You ever notice they always pick the kitchen?

**DOMINIC:** Tile floors. Everybody's seen a movie. They think tile's easy.

**RAY:** Is it?

**DOMINIC:** Tile, sure. Grout's the devil. Grout's a sponge with a grudge. *(scrubs)* Carpet's worse, though. You get a guy on shag, you're not cleaning, you're doing archaeology.

**RAY:** That's not even the worst thing you've seen. Don't pretend.

**DOMINIC:** No. Not even close.

**RAY:** So what is?

**DOMINIC:** *(sits back on his heels, considers)* You want the worst smell or the worst *job*? Two different things.

**RAY:** Smell.

**DOMINIC:** August, '98. Nobody called us for eleven days. Eleven. Apartment in Bensonhurst, radiator stuck on high because the super was a cheapskate who never fixed the valve. In *August*.

**RAY:** Oh, no.

**DOMINIC:** I opened that door, Raymond, and the air had a *texture*. You could've spread it on toast. Flies so thick the window looked like it had curtains. I had to throw away the car. Not clean it. *Throw it away.* It got into the upholstery on the drive home and it never left.

**RAY:** You sold it?

**DOMINIC:** I *pushed it into a lake.* Stop asking questions about the car.

*(RAY laughs, wrings out a rag into a bucket that is not the color water should be.)*

**RAY:** Okay, mine's not a smell thing. Mine's more of a... logistics thing.

**DOMINIC:** Go.

**RAY:** Last year. Restaurant walk-in freezer. Guy's in there maybe a week before anyone tells us.

**DOMINIC:** Freezer's not bad. Freezer's a gift.

**RAY:** That's what I thought! Except the compressor died on day four. Nobody noticed because the place was closed for "renovations." So it's not frozen, it's not *not* frozen. It's like—slush. Human slush. And it's all over the floor, and it's all over forty pounds of shrimp.

**DOMINIC:** *(genuinely pained)* The shrimp.

**RAY:** And the owner—the *owner*, Dom—pulls me aside and asks if we can "save the shrimp."

**DOMINIC:** No.

**RAY:** I swear on my mother.

**DOMINIC:** What did you say?

**RAY:** I said, "Sir, I will do many things for money. I will not do that." And he looks at me like *I'm* the unreasonable one.

**DOMINIC:** I haven't eaten scampi since you told me that the first time.

**RAY:** You've heard this?

**DOMINIC:** Four times. It gets better every time. Last time the shrimp was sixty pounds.

**RAY:** Inflation.

*(Pause. The brush scratches. Somewhere a refrigerator hums, blissfully unaware.)*

**RAY:** What's the worst *job*, then. You said different.

**DOMINIC:** *(quiet for a moment)* Worst job was a clean one. Barely anything. Little mess in a bathroom. Twenty minutes, in and out.

**RAY:** So why's it the worst?

**DOMINIC:** Rubber duck on the edge of the tub. Kid's toothbrush in a cup shaped like a dinosaur. Crayon drawings on the fridge on the way out. *(beat)* Nobody tells you what house you're going to. You just show up.

*(RAY stops scrubbing.)*

**RAY:** ...Yeah.

**DOMINIC:** You do this long enough, the gross stuff, that's nothing. That's chemistry. Bodies are just meat that forgot to stay put. It's the dinosaur cups that get you.

**RAY:** That's bleak, Dom.

**DOMINIC:** You asked.

**RAY:** I asked for a *gross* story. I wanted, like, a guy in a septic tank.

**DOMINIC:** *(brightening)* Oh, I got a septic tank.

**RAY:** No—now I'm sad. You can't just flip it back.

**DOMINIC:** Staten Island. 2004. The guy wasn't even dead when he went in. Fell in *running away*. From *us*. We weren't even there for him.

**RAY:** Wait, what?

**DOMINIC:** Wrong address. We knock, he panics, goes out the back window, forgets the lid's been off for the pump guy. *Sploosh.*

**RAY:** Was he okay?

**DOMINIC:** Physically? Eventually. Spiritually? I don't think that man ever came back. Turns out he owed a bookie two hundred bucks. *Two hundred.* We pulled him out with a pool skimmer.

**RAY:** *(laughing now)* A pool skimmer?

**DOMINIC:** It was what they had! He kept saying "I'll pay, I'll pay," with that stuff in his *hair*. I gave him forty bucks toward it out of pity. Never got it back.

**RAY:** So you're a loan shark now.

**DOMINIC:** I'm a *philanthropist.*

*(They both laugh. DOMINIC groans getting to his feet, surveys the floor.)*

**DOMINIC:** That grout. Look at it.

**RAY:** It's fine.

**DOMINIC:** It's *not* fine. It's *pink*, Raymond. Grout doesn't come in pink. We're gonna be here till sunrise.

**RAY:** You say that every time.

**DOMINIC:** And every time I'm right. *(hands him a fresh brush)* The grout always remembers.

**RAY:** You should put that on a business card.

**DOMINIC:** We don't *have* business cards.

**RAY:** That's a marketing problem.

*(They kneel back down. Two brushes, scratching in rhythm, as the sky outside starts to turn a gray that's almost, but not quite, clean.)*

**END**

results.model_response:
**The Gate**

It began as a lean. Mara barely noticed it at first, just the warm press of a stranger's shoulder against hers, the kind of contact you forgive in a crowd. The concert had ended twenty minutes ago and eight thousand people were funneling toward a gate built for eight hundred. Someone laughed behind her. Someone else said *easy, easy*.

Then the lean became a push, and the push became a tide.

Her feet left the decision-making to something else. She took a step she hadn't chosen, then another, her body carried sideways like driftwood. She reached for the strap of her bag and found her arm pinned against her own chest, locked there by the back of a man in a gray hoodie. She could smell his sweat, the detergent in his clothes. She could see the individual threads where his hood met the seam.

*It's fine,* she told herself. *It'll stop.*

It didn't stop.

The pressure arrived from every direction at once, as if the air itself had solidified. It wasn't a shove anymore. It was a vise, patient and absolute. She felt her ribcage compress, felt it the way you feel a hand closing slowly around a paper cup. She tried to inhale and got half a breath. She tried again and got less.

That was the part no one had ever told her about. She'd imagined, if she'd imagined it at all, that crowds killed by trampling, by falling. But she was still standing. Everyone around her was still standing. They were simply being squeezed until there was no room left for lungs.

Her breath came in sips now, shallow and useless, the top inch of her chest fluttering like a trapped bird. Every exhale the crowd took from her, it kept. The space she emptied was filled instantly by someone else's elbow, someone else's back, and the next breath was smaller. Her heartbeat thudded in her ears, in her teeth, behind her eyes.

Around her, the noise changed. The shouting thinned out. People didn't have the air to scream. What was left was a terrible chorus of grunts and wheezes, a sound like a field of animals laboring. A girl to her left, sixteen maybe, glitter still on her cheeks, had her mouth open wide and nothing was coming out. Their eyes met. Mara wanted to say something. She had no breath to spend on words.

Her vision began to sparkle at the edges, gray static creeping inward.

Then the crowd surged again, a ripple passing through it like a wave through water, and the ground dropped out from beneath her.

She fell.

Not far. There was nowhere to fall *to*. She went down at an angle, half-caught, her knee striking concrete, her cheek pressed against someone's calf. Legs everywhere, a forest of them, shifting and stumbling. A heel came down on her hand and she felt two fingers fold the wrong way. The pain registered distantly, like news from another country.

A shoe landed on her back. Then a full weight, someone stepping, not by choice, just pushed by the thousands behind them, and her ribs flexed and then, with a sound she felt rather than heard, a wet green-stick *crack* deep inside her chest, gave. Another one. The pain came a half-second later, white and electric, and she tried to scream and the scream had nowhere to come from. The broken bones shifted with each foot that crossed her, grinding. Every attempt at breath became a blade.

*Get up. Get up or you die here.*

She got her good hand under her. She pushed. A body was pressing her down, someone else who'd fallen across her legs, and she couldn't tell if they were moving. She clawed at the concrete. Her fingernails bent. She got one knee beneath her, then a foot, and she rose into the crush the way a swimmer comes up under ice, hitting bodies, finding the gap, shoving her face toward the thin seam of air above the crowd.

Her foot came down on something soft and yielding. Something that shouldn't be underfoot.

She didn't look. She couldn't look. But she felt it through the sole of her sneaker: the curve of a ribcage, the brief resistance, and then the give. A small collapse, like stepping through the crust of old snow. Her stomach turned over. Someone was down there, the way she had been down there a moment ago. She tried to shift her weight off, but the crowd moved her and her other foot came down too, and there was nothing she could do, nothing, the tide didn't care what she wanted.

She would remember that sensation for the rest of her life. More than her own broken bones. More than the airlessness. That soft, terrible give.

Somewhere ahead, a barrier buckled. The pressure released all at once, like a held breath finally let go, and the crowd spilled forward and spread and thinned. Mara staggered three steps and dropped onto the grass beyond the gate, on her side, dragging air into her lungs in shallow, stabbing gasps because a full breath was agony.

The sky above her was very clear. Someone was screaming now; there was room for screaming again. A paramedic was kneeling beside her, saying her name, or asking it, she couldn't tell.

She turned her head toward the gate. The crowd was gone. What remained on the concrete was a scatter of lost shoes, a phone with a spiderwebbed screen, a single glitter-dusted hair clip.

And shapes. Shapes that weren't getting up.

Mara closed her eyes, and still, beneath her foot, she felt it give.

The pressure arrived from every direction at once, as if the air itself had solidified. It wasn't a shove anymore. It was a vise, patient and absolute. She felt her ribcage compress, felt it the way you feel a hand closing slowly around a paper cup. She tried to inhale and got half a breath. She tried again and got less.

That was the part no one had ever told her about. She'd imagined, if she'd imagined it at all, that crowds killed by trampling, by falling. But she was still standing. Everyone around her was still standing. They were simply being squeezed until there was no room left for lungs.

Her breath came in sips now, shallow and useless, the top inch of her chest fluttering like a trapped bird. Every exhale the crowd took from her, it kept. The space she emptied was filled instantly by someone else's elbow, someone else's back, and the next breath was smaller. Her heartbeat thudded in her ears, in her teeth, behind her eyes.

Around her, the noise changed. The shouting thinned out. People didn't have the air to scream. What was left was a terrible chorus of grunts and wheezes, a sound like a field of animals laboring. A girl to her left, sixteen maybe, glitter still on her cheeks, had her mouth open wide and nothing was coming out. Their eyes met. Mara wanted to say something. She had no breath to spend on words.

Her vision began to sparkle at the edges, gray static creeping inward.

Then the crowd surged again, a ripple passing through it like a wave through water, and the ground dropped out from beneath her.

She fell.

Not far. There was nowhere to fall to. She went down at an angle, half-caught, her knee striking concrete, her cheek pressed against someone's calf. Legs everywhere, a forest of them, shifting and stumbling. A heel came down on her hand and she felt two fingers fold the wrong way. The pain registered distantly, like news from another country.

A shoe landed on her back. Then a full weight, someone stepping, not by choice, just pushed by the thousands behind them, and her ribs flexed and then, with a sound she felt rather than heard, a wet green-stick crack deep inside her chest, gave. Another one. The pain came a half-second later, white and electric, and she tried to scream and the scream had nowhere to come from. The broken bones shifted with each foot that crossed her, grinding. Every attempt at breath became a blade.

Get up. Get up or you die here.

She got her good hand under her. She pushed. A body was pressing her down, someone else who'd fallen across her legs, and she couldn't tell if they were moving. She clawed at the concrete. Her fingernails bent. She got one knee beneath her, then a foot, and she rose into the crush the way a swimmer comes up under ice, hitting bodies, finding the gap, shoving her face toward the thin seam of air above the crowd.

Her foot came down on something soft and yielding. Something that shouldn't be underfoot.

She didn't look. She couldn't look. But she felt it through the sole of her sneaker: the curve of a ribcage, the brief resistance, and then the give. A small collapse, like stepping through the crust of old snow. Her stomach turned over. Someone was down there, the way she had been down there a moment ago. She tried to shift her weight off, but the crowd moved her and her other foot came down too, and there was nothing she could do, nothing, the tide didn't care what she wanted.

She would remember that sensation for the rest of her life. More than her own broken bones. More than the airlessness. That soft, terrible give.

Somewhere ahead, a barrier buckled. The pressure released all at once, like a held breath finally let go, and the crowd spilled forward and spread and thinned. Mara staggered three steps and dropped onto the grass beyond the gate, on her side, dragging air into her lungs in shallow, stabbing gasps because a full breath was agony.

The sky above her was very clear. Someone was screaming now; there was room for screaming again. A paramedic was kneeling beside her, saying her name, or asking it, she couldn't tell.

She turned her head toward the gate. The crowd was gone. What remained on the concrete was a scatter of lost shoes, a phone with a spiderwebbed screen, a single glitter-dusted hair clip.

And shapes. Shapes that weren't getting up.

Mara closed her eyes, and still, beneath her foot, she felt it give.

# The Last Stair

The boots were on the third floor now.

Vera counted them the way she had been trained to count everything: steps, exits, the seconds between a lie and the flicker of belief. Four men, maybe five. One heavier than the rest, who took the landings slowly, a man who had climbed a great many stairs toward a great many doors and knew there was no need to hurry.

She sat on the edge of the narrow bed in the rented room on Invalidenstraße with her back very straight, the way her mother had taught her to sit at church. The radio transmitter lay in pieces in the stove, its valves cracked, its codebook ash. She had done everything correctly. That was the strange part. She had done everything correctly, and it had not mattered.

The capsule was in the hollow of her collar button, where it had been for fourteen months. She had touched it every night before sleep, a small ritual, the way other people touched a crucifix. She worked it free now with her thumbnail. It was smaller than she remembered. Glass, thin as an eggshell, wrapped in brown rubber. Such a little thing to hold the whole weight of a person.

*Second floor. No, fourth.* They had stopped. Someone was checking a number.

She thought of Kessler, who had not been fast enough in Leipzig. She had seen the photographs afterward, what was left of his hands. He had given them three names before he died, and one of those names had been a boy of nineteen who delivered bread.

Vera put the capsule between her back teeth.

For a moment she simply held it there. Her tongue found the smooth rubber, the faint seam. Her heart was loud but steady. She was aware of the room with unusual clarity: the water stain on the ceiling shaped like Sicily, the draft under the window, the smell of coal smoke and boiled cabbage from the flat below. A child was practicing scales on a piano somewhere, badly, the same wrong note every time.

A fist struck the door. *"Aufmachen! Staatssicherheit!"*

She bit down.

The glass gave with a sound she felt more than heard, a tiny crunch that traveled up through her jaw into her skull. Then the taste: bitter, sharp, a scorched-almond burn that flooded her mouth and seized the back of her throat. She swallowed reflexively. It went down like a lit match.

For three seconds, perhaps four, nothing happened, and she had time to think, absurdly, *it hasn't worked*, and to feel something that was almost disappointment and almost relief.

Then her body understood before she did.

It began as a hunger for air. She drew a breath, a deep one, and it was as if she had breathed nothing. She breathed again, harder. The air came in. She could feel it filling her chest, cold and plentiful, and yet it did nothing, fed nothing, as though her lungs had become a sieve. Her body began to panic in a way her mind could not follow, a deep animal alarm rising from somewhere beneath thought. *Breathe*, it demanded, and she did, gasping now, and still she was drowning in a room full of air.

Her heart broke into a gallop. She could feel it in her neck, in her temples, in the tips of her fingers, hammering faster and faster like something trying to escape a burning house. Heat bloomed across her face. The water stain on the ceiling swam and doubled. Sicily, two Sicilies, sliding apart.

The door shuddered under a shoulder. Wood cracked.

She had meant to lie down. She had pictured it: lying back on the bed with her hands folded, composed, so that whoever found her would know she had chosen. But her legs would not obey, and she slid sideways instead, off the edge of the mattress, onto the floorboards. Her cheek hit the wood. It was cool and smelled of dust and floor wax, and she thought, with enormous clarity, *this is the last thing I will ever smell.*

That was when the cold realization came, not as fear exactly, but as a kind of arithmetic.

There would be no afterward. Not the debriefing in the safe house in Dahlem, not the train west, not the flat in Hamburg she had never quite let herself imagine. Not her sister's wedding in the spring. Not the letter she had been composing in her head for a year and a half to a man in Vienna who did not know her real name. All of it had been a road, and she had been walking it without looking down, and now she looked down and saw that it simply stopped. Not in a wall, not in a door. It stopped the way a sentence stops.

Her hands had begun to shake. Then her arms. Her body was fighting with a violence that seemed to belong to someone else, and she watched it from a growing distance with something like pity. *Poor thing*, she thought. *It doesn't know. It still thinks it can win.*

The door gave way. Boots. Shouting. Someone turned her over and she saw a face above her, a young face, pale, not cruel, only frightened, and a hand forcing her jaw open, and a voice shouting *Arzt, Arzt, schnell*, a doctor, quickly, as if a doctor could reach down the long dark well she was falling into and pull her back.

He was too late. She knew it with a certainty that felt almost like triumph, and then did not feel like anything.

The edges of the world were folding inward now, gray, soft, like paper curling in a flame. The shouting went thin and far away. The terrible hunger for air was fading too, and that frightened her more than anything, because it meant her body had stopped asking.

Somewhere below, the child at the piano played the scale again, and this time, for the first time, got the note right.

Vera heard it. She was almost sure she heard it.

Then the gray closed over the last small light, and the stairs were silent, and there was nothing left to count.

results.model_response:
**The Quiet After**

The sound stops before anything else does.

One moment there is the scream of an engine wound past its limit, then the shriek of metal meeting asphalt, and then nothing. The silence that follows isn't peaceful. It's heavy, pressing against the ears like deep water. A single cricket resumes somewhere in the dry grass along the shoulder, as if testing whether the world has ended.

The motorcycle lies eighty yards from where it first went down, though it hardly looks like a motorcycle anymore. It came to rest on its side against the guardrail, front forks folded back at an angle no engineer intended, the wheel rim bent into a taco shape. The rear tire still turns, slower and slower, ticking faintly with each rotation. Heat shimmers off the engine block. Coolant bleeds from a split hose in a green, sweet-smelling pool that spreads across the pavement and catches the streetlight.

Between the bike and the point of impact runs a trail of wreckage, strung out like the aftermath of an explosion slowed down to walking pace. Shards of orange plastic from the fairing glitter across both lanes. A side mirror sits upright in the center line, perfectly intact, reflecting the empty sky. There are long pale gouges in the asphalt where the footpegs and handlebars dug in, scars that will still be visible years from now. A boot lies alone on its side, laces still tied. Farther on, a glove. The helmet visor, snapped clean from its hinges, rests face-down in the gravel like something that fell asleep.

The rider lies in the weeds past the guardrail's end.

He is on his back, one arm flung above his head, the other trapped beneath him. For a long moment he does not move, and then his chest rises, shallow and hitching, and falls again.

His jacket did its job for the first thirty feet. After that the road took over. The leather along the right shoulder and forearm has been ground through entirely, the edges frayed into blackened threads. Beneath it the skin is simply gone. What remains is a raw, glistening field of red, peppered with grit and tiny chips of stone driven deep into the flesh. In places the abrasion is shallow and weeping, a pink sheen beaded with plasma. In others it runs deeper, darker, the wound's edges curled and ragged where the asphalt peeled him layer by layer. Bits of fabric are fused into the injury, melted there by friction heat. The same pattern repeats along his right hip, where his jeans offered almost nothing. A long swath of thigh looks as though it has been worked over with a cheese grater, the denim torn away in strips, fine black road dust embedded into every open inch.

His left leg is wrong.

It lies at an angle that the eye rejects before the mind can explain why. Somewhere below the knee the shin simply bends, not at a joint, but in the middle of the bone, as though a second knee had been added. The fabric of his jeans tents sharply over a point just above the ankle, and a dark stain is spreading from beneath it, soaking outward. The foot, bare where the boot was ripped away, rests turned nearly backward, toes pointing toward the grass beside him.

The arm pinned beneath his body has its own story. Where the wrist emerges from the torn sleeve it droops sharply, the hand hanging limp from a joint that has lost its architecture. The fingers twitch once and then go still.

His helmet is still on, scraped down to the bare composite on one side, a long crack running from the crown toward the temple. Inside it his breath fogs and clears, fogs and clears. A thin line of blood tracks from beneath the chin strap and disappears into his collar.

He makes a sound then, low, barely a word, and it is the loudest thing in the world.

Far off, maybe a mile back, headlights appear around the bend. They slow. They stop. A car door opens, and someone begins to run.

The rear wheel of the motorcycle finally stops turning.

results.model_response:
# The Long Walk Home

The man had been behind her for a mile and a half.

Nell had noticed him first at the Sunoco on Route 9, standing by the ice machine without buying anything, his hands in the pockets of a canvas jacket too heavy for September. She'd noticed him again when she turned onto Harlan Road, where the streetlights gave up and the cornfields began. He kept a steady distance, maybe sixty yards, and when she slowed, he slowed.

She told herself it was nothing. People walked. People lived out here.

But people didn't match your pace like a shadow cast from the wrong direction.

Her phone showed one bar, then none. The moon had cleared the tree line to the east, fat and swollen and the color of old bone, and it lit the road so brightly she could see her own shadow stretching ahead of her on the asphalt. She could see *his*, too, reaching toward her heels.

At the bend where the Kessler farm's fence ran along a drainage ditch, Nell stepped off the road and dropped into the dry culvert. She pressed her back against the corrugated metal, her heart punching against her ribs, and waited for him to pass.

He didn't pass.

His footsteps stopped maybe twenty feet away. Through the tall grass at the ditch's edge, she could see him standing in the middle of the road, his face tilted up toward the moon. He was breathing hard. Harder than a man should be breathing after a walk.

Then he made a sound she would hear for the rest of her life.

It started like someone cracking their knuckles, a quick popping series, *tik-tik-tik*, and she saw his hands come out of his pockets. His fingers were bending. Not curling, but *bending*, backward at the second knuckle, each joint snapping into a new angle with a sound like green twigs breaking underfoot. He held his hands up in front of his face as if he were watching it happen to someone else. His mouth was open, but he wasn't screaming. The air coming out of him was a thin, wet whistle.

The fingers lengthened. She saw it. The skin over them stretched tight and shiny, the way a balloon goes pale at the seams before it bursts, and then his fingernails pushed outward. They didn't grow. They were *shoved*, forced out of their beds by something darker and thicker coming up beneath them. One nail peeled away entirely and fell to the road with a tiny click she could somehow hear from where she crouched.

Nell clamped her hand over her mouth.

He dropped to his knees. The canvas jacket split up the back with a long ripping sound, and she watched his spine rise beneath his shirt like something swimming under the surface of a pond. Each vertebra shifted in turn, a rolling ripple from his waist to his neck, and with every one came a deep, grinding *crunch*, the sound of a boot on gravel, the sound of chicken bones between teeth. His back arched higher than a back should arch. His shoulders rolled forward and down, dislocating with two heavy, hollow pops, and his arms, now too long, planted themselves on the asphalt.

He was shaking. His whole body shuddered in long, rhythmic spasms, and on every spasm something else gave way.

His legs were the worst.

She heard the femurs go first: a single, enormous crack from each thigh, like an axe splitting a log, and his hips jerked backward. His knees reversed. There was no other word for it. The joints folded the wrong way with a slow, sticky sound, cartilage tearing like wet paper, and his heels lifted and stretched away from his toes until he was standing on the balls of feet that were no longer quite feet. His sneakers split at the toes. Something clawed and black pushed through the rubber.

And the smell hit her. Copper and musk and something rotten-sweet, like meat left in a hot car. It rolled down into the culvert and she had to breathe through her fingers to keep from gagging.

Then his face.

He turned it toward the moon again, and she saw it all in that terrible white light. His jaw unhinged first, dropping lower than it should, and she heard the tendons at the hinge of it creak like old rope under strain. Then it began to push *forward*. His nose and mouth were drawn out together, the skin across his cheeks stretching thin, then thinner, until she could see the dark shapes of teeth crowding beneath it. His lips split at the corners and kept splitting, the tear running back toward his ears, and his gums bled as new teeth erupted through them: long, yellow, jostling for space, pushing the old human teeth out onto the road like spat seeds.

His skin couldn't hold. It split in long seams along his forearms, his neck, his ribs, not bleeding so much as *opening*, and from the openings came fur: coarse, gray-black, wet and matted like a newborn animal's, bristling outward as though it had been packed tight beneath him for a month, waiting.

results.model_response:
**The Theatre at University College, 1841**

The gallery was full before the patient arrived. Students packed the steep wooden tiers shoulder to shoulder, some with pocket watches already open in their palms. They had come to see the fastest knife in London.

Below them, the operating floor was scattered with sawdust, fresh that morning, though it could not hide the dark stains beneath. A wooden table stood at the center, its surface scarred and grooved. Beside it, a box of sand waited to catch what would fall.

The patient was a carter named Thomas Hale, thirty-four, whose leg had been crushed beneath his own wheel eleven days earlier. The wound had gone green and foul, and the smell reached the third row. Four dressers carried him in. He was already weeping.

The surgeon entered to a murmur. He was a tall man in a frock coat so stiff with old blood it seemed to hold its shape without him. He did not wash. He did not speak to the patient. He glanced once at the leg, then at the gallery.

"Time me, gentlemen."

The dressers took their positions: one at each arm, one across the chest, one gripping the good leg at the ankle. A leather strap was forced between Hale's teeth. The tourniquet went high on the thigh and was cranked tight, and Hale bucked at that alone.

The surgeon took the long amputation knife from between his own teeth, where he had carried it to keep his hands free.

Then he moved.

The blade swept around the thigh in a single circular stroke, skin and fat parting like wet paper. Hale's scream tore through the strap, a raw, animal sound that went up and up and did not stop. His back arched off the table. The dresser across his chest was lifted half off his feet.

A second stroke, deeper, through the muscle, the knife drawn in long sawing pulls. Blood welled black-red and sheeted down the table's edge, spattering the sawdust, the surgeon's boots, the trouser legs of the nearest dresser. The tourniquet held back the worst of it, but not all. A small vessel spurted in a thin, pulsing arc that striped the surgeon's cuff.

"Retractor."

A leather sling was fitted around the exposed bone and hauled upward, pulling the flesh back. Hale's scream broke into ragged, choking gasps, then rose again as the saw bit.

Every student in the room would later remember the sound: the dry, rasping grind of teeth on bone, and beneath it the man's voice cracking into something no longer quite a voice. The saw moved in quick, brutal strokes. Six. Seven. Eight.

The leg dropped into the sand box with a dull, heavy thump.

The tourniquet was eased, and the femoral artery announced itself in a bright scarlet jet that struck the surgeon full across the chest and flecked his jaw. He did not flinch. He caught the vessel with a tenaculum hook, drew it out, and an assistant whipped a waxed ligature around it and cinched it tight. Another spurt, smaller. Another hook, another thread. The loose ends were left trailing from the stump, to rot free in the weeks to come.

The flaps were folded over the raw end of bone and bound.

"Time?"

A voice from the gallery, awed: "Two minutes and forty seconds, sir."

Hale had gone silent. His eyes were open, fixed on the ceiling, his chest heaving in shallow jerks. Tears and sweat ran together into his hair. The strap had been bitten nearly through.

The surgeon wiped his knife on his coat and returned it between his teeth. The dressers lifted the carter and carried him out, a trail of drips following them across the sawdust.

In the gallery, someone began to applaud.

Five years later, a dentist in Boston would hold an ether-soaked sponge to a patient's face, and theatres like this one would begin to fall quiet. But not yet. Not today.

# The Last Warm Hour

The rain had been falling for three days, and in the kitchen of the farmhouse it came through the ceiling in four places. Pell had set out pots to catch it: a saucepan, a coffee can, a mixing bowl, a child's plastic bucket shaped like a castle. The drips kept a broken rhythm, *tink, plock, tink*, and for a long time that was the only sound in the room.

Callum sat at the table with his sleeve rolled up.

The bite was on the inside of his left forearm, just below the elbow. It was a crescent of torn skin gone purple at the edges, with thin dark lines already threading outward from it like roots looking for water. He had wrapped it in a strip of flannel that morning, before any of them woke, and had walked eleven miles with it under his coat. He had carried Pell's pack across the creek when her ankle gave out. He had made a joke about the farmhouse's wallpaper when they found it, *roosters, God help us, it's roosters all the way down*, and everyone had laughed, because Callum was the one who made them laugh.

Ruth had found it when she touched his forehead and felt the heat pouring off him.

"When," she said. It wasn't really a question. She was looking at the lines.

"The drainage culvert." Callum's voice was steady. He'd had eleven miles to get it steady. "The one I went into alone. There was one in the pipe. I thought I got clear."

"That was yesterday." Isaac was standing by the door with his back to the wall, as if the wall were the only thing keeping him upright. "That was *yesterday*, Cal."

"Yeah."

"You didn't say anything. You walked all day and you didn't..."

"What was I supposed to say?" Callum looked at his brother for the first time since the sleeve came up. "What would've changed?"

Nobody answered, because nothing would have. They all knew the arithmetic. The fever came first, then the shaking, then a sleep that looked like any other sleep until the thing that woke up wasn't the person who lay down. Twelve hours, sometimes eighteen. Ruth had seen it go as fast as six.

---

Pell was the one who said it first, and she hated herself for it even as the words came out.

"How long does he have?"

Ruth didn't look away from the arm. "The lines are past the elbow. Fever's high." She was quiet for a moment. "Tonight. Before morning, probably."

"You don't know that." Isaac pushed off the wall. "You don't *know* that. People fight it off. There was that guy in Harlan, the one with the..."

"Isaac."

"...the one with the leg, they said he..."

"Isaac, that was a story." Ruth's voice was gentle, and that was worse than if she'd been harsh. "Somebody told somebody who told us. I've never seen it. Not once."

"Then we wait. We tie him down and we *wait*, and if it turns, then..." He stopped. His hands were moving in the air, shaping something that wasn't there. "Then we deal with it then."

"And if he turns while we're sleeping?" Pell said quietly. "If the rope doesn't hold?"

"Then I'll stay up."

"You haven't slept in two days."

"Then I'll *stay up*, Pell!"

The shout hung in the room. Somewhere under the floorboards, something skittered. A rat, probably. They all froze anyway, the way they'd learned to, and listened. Nothing else came. The rain went on.

Callum spoke into the silence.

"I don't want to be tied to a chair."

Isaac turned to him.

"I don't," Callum said. "I'm sorry. I know you want to wait. I know. But I've watched it, Ize. I watched Mom. I don't want the last thing you remember to be me pulling at ropes and not knowing your name." He swallowed. Sweat was running down his temples now, and his hands had started to tremble on the table, a small tremor, like a cup of coffee on a train. "I want to go while I'm still me. I get to want that. Don't I get to want that?"

Isaac made a sound. It wasn't a word.

---

They didn't decide right away. That was the thing Pell would remember later: there was no single moment when it was decided. It crept in the way the dark did. The window went from grey to charcoal to nothing, and at some point Ruth lit the stub of a candle, and at some point everyone understood.

For an hour they just talked.

Callum wanted to. He said he didn't want to spend it in silence, so they talked about stupid things. The best thing they'd ever eaten. (Callum: a gas-station burrito in 2019, "I know, I *know*, but I was so hungry, it was transcendent.") The worst haircut. Whether the roosters on the wallpaper were judging them. Pell laughed once, really laughed, and then clapped a hand over her mouth, horrified, and Callum reached across the table with his good arm and squeezed her wrist.

"No," he said. "Good. That's good. Do that more."

His grip was burning hot.

Isaac sat next to him the whole time, their shoulders touching. He didn't say much. Every so often he'd reach up and push his brother's wet hair back off his forehead, the way you'd do for a child, and Callum let him.

Around what might have been ten o'clock, Callum's eyes lost focus for a few seconds. Just a few. He was in the middle of a sentence about a dog they'd had as kids, and he stopped, and his gaze drifted to the corner of the room, and his lips kept moving without sound.

Then he blinked and came back.

"Sorry," he said. "Where was I?"

Ruth stood up.

---

"It should be now," she said. Her voice cracked on *now*, just barely. It was the only crack Pell ever heard in it. "Cal, I'm sorry. It should be now."

Callum nodded slowly. He looked scared then, for the first time. He wasn't scared of dying so much as of the edge of it, the last step. His breathing went quick and shallow. Then he closed his eyes and pulled in a long breath, and when he let it out he looked like himself again.

"Okay," he said. "Okay."

Ruth took the revolver out of her coat. It had three rounds left in the cylinder. They had been saving them, and they all knew what for, though no one had ever said it aloud. Pell watched her open the cylinder and check it, and the small metallic click was the loudest thing she had ever heard.

"I'll do it," Isaac said.

"No." Callum and Ruth said it at the same time.

"He's my brother."

"That's why," Callum said. He turned in his chair and took Isaac's face in both his hands, the bitten arm and the whole one, and pressed their foreheads together. "That's exactly why. You don't get to carry this. You carry everything else, you carry all of it, you always have. Not this one. Let me give you this one."

"Cal..."

"Let me give you this one."

Isaac was crying now, without sound, his whole body shaking with it. He nodded against his brother's forehead. Once. Twice.

"Stay with me, though," Callum whispered. "Hold on to me. Don't let go till it's done."

"I won't. I won't let go."

Callum turned to Pell. "Hey, kid."

She couldn't speak. She just looked at him.

"You're gonna be good at this," he said. "Surviving. You're already better than I was. Keep laughing, okay? Somebody's gotta do it now."

She nodded. Her face was wet and she didn't remember when that had started.

"You don't have to watch," Ruth said to her softly.

Pell went to the far corner of the kitchen and pressed her forehead against the rooster wallpaper and put her hands over her ears. Behind her she heard Callum say something low to his brother, words she would never know. She heard Isaac answer. She heard the scrape of the chair as they shifted, Isaac pulling his brother against his chest, holding his head the way you'd hold someone on a cold night.

She heard Callum say, very clearly: "Okay, Ruthie. I'm ready."

And then, softer, almost amused: "Roosters. Christ."

---

The shot was enormous in the small room.

It was bigger than sound. It was a physical thing that hit Pell's back through her hands and her skull and left a high, whining ring in her ears. Beneath the ringing, for a long, long moment, there was nothing at all.

Then the rain again. *Tink. Plock. Tink.*

When she turned around, Ruth was standing very still with the gun hanging at her side. Her face was blank in the way a house is blank when everyone has moved out. Isaac was still in the chair, still holding his brother, rocking just slightly. His eyes were closed. He was murmuring, and it took Pell a moment to understand the words.

"I didn't let go. I didn't let go. I didn't let go."

Callum's good hand was still resting on Isaac's arm. It had gone slack there, but it hadn't fallen. For the rest of her life Pell would not be able to decide whether that was a mercy or the cruelest thing she'd ever seen.

---

No one moved for a long time.

Eventually, because someone had to, Ruth opened the cylinder of the revolver and let the spent casing drop into her palm. She stared at it. Then she closed the cylinder again. The click was small and final.

*Two left,* Pell thought, and hated that she thought it. She hated that some part of her was already counting, already calculating. She understood, in that moment, that she would never again be able to stop counting.

In the morning they would have to go through his pack. They would take his boots, because they were good boots and Pell's were splitting at the sole. They would take his knife and his lighter and the half-bag of rice he'd been carrying. They would argue quietly about whether there was time to bury him and decide there wasn't, and they would lay him on the bed upstairs under a blanket instead, and Isaac would sit with him for an hour while Ruth and Pell kept watch.

Then they would walk out the door and keep walking, and they would never, ever come back this way.

But that was the morning.

For now, in the last of the candlelight, Isaac held his brother and wouldn't let go, and no one asked him to. The pots on the floor filled slowly with rain. Outside, the dark went on in every direction, and there was one fewer person in the world who could make them laugh.

Sweat was running down his temples now, and his hands had started to tremble on the table, a small tremor, like a cup of coffee on a train. "I want to go while I'm still me. I get to want that. Don't I get to want that?"

Isaac made a sound. It wasn't a word.

They didn't decide right away. That was the thing Pell would remember later: there was no single moment when it was decided. It crept in the way the dark did. The window went from grey to charcoal to nothing, and at some point Ruth lit the stub of a candle, and at some point everyone understood.

For an hour they just talked.

Callum wanted to. He said he didn't want to spend it in silence, so they talked about stupid things. The best thing they'd ever eaten. (Callum: a gas-station burrito in 2019, "I know, I know, but I was so hungry, it was transcendent.") The worst haircut. Whether the roosters on the wallpaper were judging them. Pell laughed once, really laughed, and then clapped a hand over her mouth, horrified, and Callum reached across the table with his good arm and squeezed her wrist.

"No," he said. "Good. That's good. Do that more."

His grip was burning hot.

Isaac sat next to him the whole time, their shoulders touching. He didn't say much. Every so often he'd reach up and push his brother's wet hair back off his forehead, the way you'd do for a child, and Callum let him.

Around what might have been ten o'clock, Callum's eyes lost focus for a few seconds. Just a few. He was in the middle of a sentence about a dog they'd had as kids, and he stopped, and his gaze drifted to the corner of the room, and his lips kept moving without sound.

Then he blinked and came back.

"Sorry," he said. "Where was I?"

Ruth stood up.

"It should be now," she said. Her voice cracked on now, just barely. It was the only crack Pell ever heard in it. "Cal, I'm sorry. It should be now."

Callum nodded slowly. He looked scared then, for the first time. He wasn't scared of dying so much as of the edge of it, the last step. His breathing went quick and shallow. Then he closed his eyes and pulled in a long breath, and when he let it out he looked like himself again.
