# The Corner of the Eye

**I.**

For the first eleven days, Owen Harrow felt nothing but a clean, bright efficiency.

He had expected guilt to arrive like weather, a pressure front he'd see coming. Instead there was only a list. Wash the car. Return the library books. Answer Claire's texts in his normal cadence, with the normal typos, the normal *lol*. When the police came about Daniel, her brother, missing since the fishing trip, Owen made coffee and let his hands shake exactly as much as a worried brother-in-law's would. He was proud of the shaking. He had practiced it.

He slept well. That was the first wrong thing, though he didn't know it yet. He slept like a man with nothing left to hide from himself, because he had hidden it so well that even he couldn't find it.

On the twelfth day, in the produce aisle of the Kroger on Elm, he reached for a bag of lemons and saw, just past the edge of his vision, a man in a blue windbreaker standing by the potatoes.

He turned. A teenager in a red hoodie was stocking onions.

Owen bought the lemons. He did not think about the windbreaker, which had been Daniel's, which was now at the bottom of Culver Lake, zipped around a cinder block, with Daniel inside it.

---

**II.**

It happened again at the gas station. Then in the rearview mirror, a shape in the backseat that became a jacket he'd thrown there. Then at the edge of the bathroom mirror while he shaved, a blue smear that resolved, when he looked, into the shower curtain.

Owen was a rational man. He read about it at two in the morning: peripheral vision is low-resolution, the brain fills gaps with expectation, stress primes pattern recognition. He found it deeply comforting. He read the same article four times.

Then he began to notice what the figure was *doing*, and the comfort ended.

It wasn't doing anything. That was the problem. A ghost that screamed or pointed or dripped lake water on the carpet, that would be a story, and stories could be dismissed. But Daniel only stood there, at the edge, the way he used to stand at the edge of family gatherings: hands in pockets, mild, patient, waiting for someone to include him.

Owen had always found that patience insufferable. It was, if he was being honest, part of why.

---

**III.**

He started turning his head slowly.

He'd learned that if he whipped around, the figure vanished too cleanly, and the cleanness felt like mockery. But if he turned slowly, very slowly, he could sometimes catch it *dissolving*: a sense of something withdrawing, like a hand pulled back from a flame. He began doing this everywhere. At work, his colleagues watched him rotate his head across the conference room like a lighthouse beam. Someone asked if he had a stiff neck. He said yes. He started wearing a heat patch to make the lie true, and the smell of menthol followed him everywhere, and he came to associate it with being watched.

He rearranged his apartment so that no chair faced away from a corner. He bought a convex security mirror, the kind they put in parking garages, and mounted it in the hallway so he could see behind himself. That was worse. In the curved glass, everything at the edges stretched and warped, and every warp looked like a man.

Claire came over with a casserole. She sat on his couch and cried about her brother, and Owen held her and watched, over her shoulder, the blue shape standing in the kitchen doorway. It had never come indoors while someone else was present. He understood this as an escalation. He understood that it had wanted to see her grieve.

Or that *he* had wanted to see it watch her grieve. He was beginning to lose track of which direction the wanting ran.

---

**IV.**

Things he stopped doing: driving at night. Taking elevators, where the corners were too close. Looking at water. Eating fish. Saying the word *lake*, which he replaced, in his head, with *the place*. Sleeping more than ninety minutes at a stretch.

Things he started doing: counting. Counting the corners in a room before he entered it. Counting his steps so that he always arrived at a door on an even number, because on odd numbers the figure was closer. He didn't know how he knew this. He knew it the way you know a stove is hot.

The figure *was* getting closer. He was sure of it now. In the first weeks it had been a distant smear at the far rim of sight. Now it stood near enough that he could see details his mind had no business inventing: the frayed left cuff of the windbreaker, the way Daniel's hair had dried stiff on one side. A pale ring of skin on the finger where his wedding band had been. Owen had taken the ring. It was in a coffee can in the freezer. He had never told anyone that, including himself, really. He had just done it and then not thought about it, and now here was the absence, rendered in perfect detail, at the edge of his eye.

That was when he understood the ghost wasn't coming from outside. It was built from things only he knew. It was a confession assembling itself piece by piece, and he was the only witness, and he was also the builder.

---

**V.**

He began talking to it.

Not out loud at first. Just in his head, the way you'd rehearse an argument. *You were going to tell her. You were going to ruin everything over forty thousand dollars that I was going to pay back.* The figure didn't answer. It had never needed to. Owen supplied both sides of the conversation, and increasingly the other side was winning.

Then out loud, quietly, in the car. Then less quietly. His neighbor knocked once to ask if everything was all right; she'd heard shouting. Owen said he'd been on the phone. After she left, he stood in the hallway and looked at the security mirror, and in its warped silver surface he saw a gaunt, stubbled man with red-rimmed eyes and a menthol patch on his neck, and it took him a long, cold second to understand that this was the only figure in the glass.

That was when the real fear began. Not that Daniel was there, but that the parts of Owen that could tell the difference were quietly shutting off, one room at a time, like a house being closed up for winter.

---

**VI.**

He hadn't slept in three days when he finally decided to look at it directly.

He sat in the middle of his living room floor, the chairs pushed against the walls, all the lights on. The figure stood in the corner, just at the edge, as always. Owen could feel its patience like a temperature.

*If I look at you,* he thought, *you'll be gone, and I'll know I'm just sick. And sick can be fixed.*

He turned his head. Slowly. Slowly. The blue shape held, and held, closer to center than it had ever let itself come, and Owen's heart was a fist beating on the inside of a door—

And the corner was empty. Just two walls meeting. Just paint.

He sat there a long time. He had expected relief. What came instead was something much worse, rising up through him like lake water through a cracked hull: the understanding that the corner had always been empty. That there had never been anything there to stop. That no apparition was haunting him, no outside force he could placate or flee or drive away with a priest or a pill. There was only Owen, and what Owen had done, and a mind that would keep putting Daniel in the corner of his eye forever, because the corner of the eye is where you keep the things you can't bear to look at and can't bear to lose.

He turned back toward the center of the room.

And there, at the edge of his vision, patient, dripping faintly, the man in the blue windbreaker was waiting.

Owen reached for the phone. His hand was shaking, and he did not practice it. For the first time in forty-one days, the shaking was real.

He dialed Claire's number, and while it rang, he counted. He didn't know anymore whether he was counting toward the even number or away from it.

**The Board**

They had tilted him so his feet were higher than his head, and the first thing Daniel noticed was how the blood pooled behind his eyes, a slow pressure like thunder coming. The board was rough under his shoulder blades. Straps across his chest, his thighs, his ankles. His wrists were bound beneath the board, and the angle made his arms ache in a way that would have mattered an hour ago.

"The convoy route," the man said. He had a soft voice, almost bored. "Just the road. Nothing else."

Daniel stared at the ceiling. A water stain there, brown, shaped a little like Ohio. He fixed on it. *Ohio. Columbus. Mom's kitchen with the yellow curtains.*

"No?"

The cloth came down over his face, and the world went gray and close. It smelled of mildew and someone else's sweat. He could still breathe through it, thin and hot, and for a stupid second he thought, *This isn't so bad.*

Then the water came.

It didn't pour so much as *arrive*, soaking the cloth all at once, and the fabric clung to his mouth and nostrils like a second skin. He tried to breathe out, to push it away, and that was the mistake, because his lungs emptied and then, by instinct older than thought, they *pulled*.

Water.

Not air. Water, in his nose, in the back of his throat, a cold burn racing down into his chest. His body convulsed against the straps. He coughed, and coughing meant he had to inhale again, and inhaling meant more water, and some distant, rational part of his brain was saying, very calmly, *You are lying on a board in a dry room. You are not in the ocean. You are not going to die.*

His body did not believe it.

His body knew only one thing, the thing every cell had known since the first fish crawled onto mud: *There is water where air should be. You are drowning. You are drowning. YOU ARE DROWNING.*

He thrashed. The straps bit into his chest. His heels drummed against the wood in a rhythm he couldn't control. There was a sound, a wet, choking animal sound, and it took him a moment to understand it was coming from him. His throat clamped shut on its own, gagging, and that was worse, because now nothing could get in or out, and the pressure in his chest built and built like a fist squeezing his heart.

Time went strange. He couldn't tell if it had been five seconds or five minutes. There was no *before* anymore, no Ohio, no yellow curtains, no name. There was only the cloth, the cold, and the screaming need for one breath, *one breath*, and the terrible certainty that it would never come.

He thought of the lake behind his grandfather's cabin, the summer he was nine, when he'd gone too deep and his foot tangled in weeds. He remembered looking up at the sunlight on the surface, so close, so far away. His grandfather's hand had closed around his wrist and hauled him up into the light.

No one was going to haul him up.

And then someone did.

The cloth peeled away and air hit his face and he gasped, a huge, ragged, whooping breath that dragged water up out of his lungs in a spray. He coughed until he thought something would tear. Snot and water ran into his eyes, his hair. He was shaking so hard the board rattled. The water stain on the ceiling swam in and out of focus.

*Ohio*, he thought, dimly. *Ohio.* He couldn't remember why it mattered.

The soft voice again, close to his ear, patient as a teacher.

"The road, Daniel. That's all."

He heard himself sobbing. He hated the sound. He was twenty-three years old, and he'd told himself in training, in the truck, in the cell, that he would be one of the ones who held. He had pictured it. He had pictured himself spitting, defiant, like a man in a movie.

No one had told him that the body doesn't care about pictures. The body only wants to breathe.

"I—" His voice was a wrecked thing. "I don't—"

The cloth hovered above his face, a gray ghost. He could see the pitcher at the edge of his vision, sweating with condensation. Such an ordinary thing. A pitcher of water. His mother used to fill one just like it for the dinner table.

His chest heaved. Every breath felt stolen, precious, something he could lose at any moment. His mind scrabbled for the stain on the ceiling, for the yellow curtains, for his grandfather's hand, anything solid to hold on to.

"Take your time," the man said, and lowered the cloth.

Daniel squeezed his eyes shut, pulled one last breath as deep as he could, and held it like a secret.

He thought of the lake behind his grandfather's cabin, the summer he was nine, when he'd gone too deep and his foot tangled in weeds. He remembered looking up at the sunlight on the surface, so close, so far away. His grandfather's hand had closed around his wrist and hauled him up into the light.

No one was going to haul him up.

And then someone did.

The cloth peeled away and air hit his face and he gasped, a huge, ragged, whooping breath that dragged water up out of his lungs in a spray. He coughed until he thought something would tear. Snot and water ran into his eyes, his hair. He was shaking so hard the board rattled. The water stain on the ceiling swam in and out of focus.

The soft voice again, close to his ear, patient as a teacher.

"The road, Daniel. That's all."

He heard himself sobbing. He hated the sound. He was twenty-three years old, and he'd told himself in training, in the truck, in the cell, that he would be one of the ones who held. He had pictured it. He had pictured himself spitting, defiant, like a man in a movie.

No one had told him that the body doesn't care about pictures. The body only wants to breathe.

"I—" His voice was a wrecked thing. "I don't—"

The snow had stopped being snow somewhere back in the pines. It had become a thing that grabbed her ankles, that filled her boots, that roared in her lungs with every ragged breath. Behind her, the wolves didn't roar. That was the worst of it. They ran in silence, gray shapes flowing between the trunks like smoke, patient in a way that told her they had done this before.

The ravine ended in rock. A wall of black granite glazed with ice, too sheer to climb, and she turned with her back against it because there was nowhere else to turn.

They came out of the trees slowly now. Five of them. Six. Breath steaming from their muzzles in soft, regular clouds. The lead wolf's eyes caught the last of the light, pale and yellow as old candle wax.

She had a branch. She didn't remember picking it up. She swung it at the first one that came close and it danced back, unhurried, and that was when the second one took her from the side.

She didn't see it. She felt it.

The pressure came first, strangely, before the pain, a crushing, impossible grip just below her knee, like her leg had been caught in the jaws of a machine. Then the teeth found their way through the wool and the skin beneath, and the world narrowed to that single point of white-hot agony. She heard herself scream, a thin sound swallowed instantly by the trees.

The wolf pulled. She went down.

And the snow received her.

It was the cold she would remember, if she lived. The shocking, absolute cold of it against her cheek, her neck, her bare wrists where her sleeves had ridden up. It bit harder than the wolf in its own way, a thousand needles pressing into her all at once, numbing and burning in the same breath.

But her leg was hot.

The heat spread out from the wound in a slow, heavy pulse, soaking through her trousers, running down into her boot. It was obscene, that warmth. It felt like the only warm thing left in the world, and it was leaving her. She could feel it flow out with each beat of her heart, spilling onto the snow, where she knew without looking that it would be steaming, blooming red against the white like ink dropped into milk.

The wolf's breath was hot too, rank and wet against her skin as it adjusted its grip. The rest of her was going numb, her fingers already clumsy and distant, but that one place burned and burned, a furnace in a frozen body.

Some animal part of her understood the arithmetic of it. The cold wanted to keep her. The heat was trying to escape. And between the two, the pack was closing in.

Her fingers closed around the branch again.

She wasn't done yet.

# The Quiet Contract

Rain on Neo-Kowloon never touched the ground. It hit the atmospheric scrubbers four hundred meters up and fell as warm mist, turning the lower districts into a lung full of neon and steam.

Veyra Castellane liked it that way. Mist hid things. Mist hid *her*.

She crouched on a maintenance gantry above the Yulong Night Market, her optic implant cycling through thermal, spectral, and gait-analysis overlays. Two thousand bodies moved below her, and somewhere among them was Dorian Kast: embezzler, data-thief, and, according to the Meridian Consortium's contract, worth four hundred thousand credits delivered breathing.

*Breathing* was the operative word. Meridian wanted what was in his head, not a corpse with a fried cortex.

"Gait match," murmured her implant. "Eighty-nine percent. Grid seven. Grey coat."

She found him. Tall, hunched, moving with the jittery economy of a man who hadn't slept in a week. He paused at a noodle stall and glanced up. Not at her, but close. Paranoid men always looked up eventually.

Veyra dropped.

---

The fall was twelve meters. Her kinetic dampeners flared blue at the ankles and she landed in a crouch between a fishmonger's tank and a rack of counterfeit neural chips. A few shoppers scattered. Most didn't bother. In Yulong, people fell out of the sky every week.

Kast bolted.

He was faster than his file suggested. Military reflex grafts, probably black-market, maybe secondhand. He vaulted a dumpling cart and plunged into an alley choked with cable bundles and hissing steam vents. Veyra followed, boots slapping wet concrete, her breath steady.

"Dorian Kast," she called, voice amplified by her collar. "Meridian Consortium bounty. Stop now and this stays simple."

He answered by spinning and firing.

The slug-thrower barked twice. The first round went wide and sparked off a pipe. The second hit her chest plate dead center and knocked the air from her lungs. She staggered but didn't fall. The plate was rated for worse.

Kast didn't wait to see if she was dead. He ran deeper into the alley, toward a service ladder leading down to the flood tunnels. If he reached the tunnels, she'd lose him for days.

Veyra drew the Arclance.

It wasn't elegant. It was a squat, ugly thing, a grip, a capacitor housing, and a pair of barbed filament darts trailing hair-thin conductive wire. Old tech, refined. Guns killed. The Arclance *stopped*.

She exhaled, aimed at the broad of his back, and squeezed.

---

The darts crossed the distance in less than a heartbeat, snapping through his coat and biting into the skin beneath: one between his shoulder blades, one low on his hip. The wide spread mattered. The farther apart the darts landed, the more muscle the current would cross.

Then the capacitor dumped.

It wasn't the voltage that did the work, though the Arclance pushed tens of thousands of volts to punch through clothing and skin. It was what the current *said* when it reached him. The weapon pulsed at a frequency tuned to mimic the body's own electrical language, the rapid-fire signals motor neurons use to tell muscles to contract. Only this signal was louder than anything his brain could send, and it said one thing to every muscle between the two darts:

*Contract. All of you. Now.*

Kast's body obeyed.

His back arched so sharply his head snapped toward his heels. His arms flung outward, then locked rigid, fingers splayed and trembling. The slug-thrower clattered from a hand that no longer belonged to him. His legs went straight as rebar, and for a surreal half-second he stood balanced on the balls of his feet like a statue caught mid-fall.

Then he toppled forward, stiff as a felled tree, and hit the wet concrete face-first. He couldn't put his hands out. He couldn't do anything.

The sound he made wasn't a scream. Screaming requires the diaphragm to cooperate, and his diaphragm, along with every muscle in his torso, was clenched like a fist. What escaped was a strangled, grinding groan forced through locked teeth, the sound of air squeezed out of a body with no permission to take more in.

His muscles fought each other. Every flexor and extensor fired simultaneously, biceps against triceps, quadriceps against hamstrings, locked in a war with no winner. Veyra had felt it once in training. Everyone who carried an Arclance had to. She remembered the pain as something total and architectural, less like being hurt in one place than like being *made of* pain for five seconds. She remembered the terrible clarity of it too. The mind stays awake. You know exactly what's happening. You simply can't do anything about it.

On the ground, Kast's heels drummed against the concrete in tiny, rhythmic spasms, matching the weapon's pulse. His skin prickled into gooseflesh. The tendons in his neck stood out like cables. Around the dart sites, small red rings bloomed where current met flesh.

The Arclance's cycle clicked off at five seconds.

The effect vanished almost instantly. Kast's body went slack all at once, as if someone had cut his strings. He sucked in a huge, ragged breath, then another, gasping like a man surfacing from deep water. His limbs twitched with aftershocks, stray fasciculations rippling under the skin as nerves sputtered back to normal. Sweat and rainwater ran together down his face. His heart hammered hard enough that she could see his pulse jumping in his throat.

---

Veyra walked over and knelt beside him, keeping her thumb on the trigger.

"The wires are still in you," she said quietly. "I can do that again. I'd rather not. Your cardiac profile's clean, but nobody's heart likes a second ride."

Kast's eyes rolled toward her. His jaw worked, but his voice came out slurred and weak, his muscles still shaky and uncoordinated, like someone who'd just run a marathon in five seconds. "...You... hit hard."

"Lance hits hard. I just point it." She rolled him onto his side, recovery position, habit, and cuffed his wrists behind him. Then she checked his breathing and pressed two fingers to his carotid. Fast but steady. No arrhythmia. Her implant ran a quick scan and confirmed it: *Subject vitals stable. Minor abrasions to face. Dart punctures superficial.*

She pulled the barbs free with two quick tugs. He hissed.

"Meridian's going to wipe me," he muttered into the concrete. "You know that, right? They'll strip what's in my head and dump the rest."

Veyra paused.

It wasn't the first time a target had told her that. It was, however, the first time her implant flagged the Meridian contract file with a quiet anomaly: *Data package delivered with bounty contains redacted clauses. Origin: internal legal.*

She looked at Kast. He looked back, exhausted, terrified, and very much alive.

"Get up," she said finally, hauling him to his feet. His legs wobbled, the last tremors fading. "We're going somewhere quiet. You're going to tell me what's in your head."

"And then?"

Veyra holstered the Arclance and glanced up at the mist, where the rain never quite fell.

"Then," she said, "I decide who's actually paying for this."

# The Weight of the Hand

The first thing Mara knew was cold. It came up through the concrete into her hip and shoulder, and it had been doing so for a long time, because her whole left side ached with it. The second thing she knew was that she could not move her right hand.

She opened her eyes to a bare bulb swinging on its cord. It threw the room back and forth across itself: pipes weeping rust down a cinderblock wall, a floor drain crusted brown, a small television on a rolling cart. Then her own arm, stretched out along the floor and ending at the wrist in a block of steel the size of a cinder brick, bolted into the concrete with four hex bolts thicker than her fingers.

She pulled. Not a thought yet, just the animal in her pulling. The steel bit into the bones of her wrist and did not move at all.

The television flickered on.

*Hello, Mara.* A white face, painted red cheeks, a voice run through something that made it sound like gravel poured slowly. *For eleven years you have worked in palliative care. You have counted pills for the dying. And for three of those years, you have been counting some of them into your own pocket. The patients in Room 6 and Room 9 did not die peacefully, Mara. They died in pain, because the medicine meant to ease them was easing you.*

Her stomach turned over. Not because it was a lie. Because it wasn't.

*You have always wanted to escape the consequences of your hands. Today, you must decide whether your hand is worth more than your life. The cuff was made to your measurements. It will not pass your knuckles, unless your knuckles give way. In one hour, the door behind you will seal and the air will be let out of this room. Live or die, Mara. Make your choice.*

A red timer blinked onto the screen. **59:47.**

---

For the first several minutes she did nothing useful at all.

She screamed until her throat went raw. She yanked until the skin at her wrist split and ran. She braced her feet against the steel block and hauled back with her whole body, sobbing, and felt nothing give except herself. She told the empty room that she was sorry, that she would confess, that she had a daughter. The bulb swung. The timer ticked down to 54:10.

Then, because she was a nurse, and because some part of her had spent eleven years staying calm while other people panicked, a colder voice began to talk underneath the screaming.

*Look at it. Actually look.*

She looked. The cuff was lined with a thin rubber gasket, snug at the wrist, tight but not crushing. Her hand was trapped not by the wrist but by the breadth of the palm, the knuckles, and above all the thumb, the heel of it that swelled out below the base of the digit and caught against the steel like a doorstop.

She knew this hand. She knew all hands. She'd splinted them, taped them, held them while people died. She knew that the bones of the thumb didn't sit in a line with the others, that the joint at its base was built to swing across the palm, and that if it went somewhere it wasn't built to go, the hand would narrow. Not much. Maybe enough.

The knowledge arrived whole, and she hated it. She hated that she understood exactly what the voice meant.

*No,* the other part of her said. *Someone will come. Somebody knows you're missing. Denise will call. You don't have to do this. You don't have to do this.*

**51:32.**

Nobody was coming. She knew it the way she knew a patient was going to die before the family did, the flat certainty that arrives before the grief.

---

The bargaining was the worst part, because it sounded so reasonable.

*Maybe just the skin will do it. Maybe if you bleed enough, it'll be slick. Maybe you can wait until thirty minutes. Maybe until twenty. The pain will be the same at twenty minutes, so why not wait?*

She tried the blood. She twisted and pulled until her vision whitened at the edges, and the hand moved perhaps a quarter of an inch before the thumb caught again, solid as a bolt.

She lay back on the concrete, breathing hard, and thought about Room 9. Mr. Okafor. He'd asked her, in the last week, why the medicine wasn't working anymore. She'd told him that sometimes the body builds a tolerance. She had held his hand when she said it.

*You deserve this,* she thought, and was frightened by how much relief was in it, how easy it would be to lie here and let the air go and call it justice.

Then she thought of Lily, nine years old, who was supposed to be picked up from school at three-fifteen, and she sat up.

**44:08.**

---

She prepared the way she would prepare a patient, because it was the only way she could stand to do it.

She pulled off her cardigan with her free hand and her teeth and rolled one sleeve into a tight, thick cylinder. It tasted of lint and laundry detergent, of her own kitchen, and she almost broke down at that, at the ordinary smell of home.

She bit down to test it. Good. Enough that her jaw couldn't close hard.

She tore the other sleeve into a strip and tied it just above the cuff, snug, not a tourniquet, just something to hold on to that was hers. She shifted her body until she was kneeling with her trapped arm flat before her, her weight over it. Leverage mattered. She'd seen men dislocate a shoulder falling off a ladder; she'd seen a grandmother break her wrist reaching for a teacup. Bodies were stronger and weaker than anyone believed.

She flexed the trapped hand. Curled the fingers, uncurled them. Said goodbye to it, a little, the way she had said goodbye to things before: her marriage, her father, the version of herself that had once believed she'd never take a single pill.

*You will not pass out,* she told herself. *You will not pass out, because if you pass out you will wake up dead.*

She practiced her breathing. In for four. Hold. Out for six. She'd taught it to a hundred frightened people. None of them had ever done it right the first time, and neither did she. Her breath shuddered and broke on the out, and she had to start over. And again. And again, until the air went in steady and came out steady, and her heart stopped trying to climb out of her throat.

**38:51.**

She wrapped her free hand around the trapped thumb. It felt strange, holding herself like that, like holding someone else's hand in the dark. Her own pulse beat against her fingertips. The thumb was warm. It had no idea.

Then her own arm, stretched out along the floor and ending at the wrist in a block of steel the size of a cinder brick, bolted into the concrete with four hex bolts thicker than her fingers.

She pulled. Not a thought yet, just the animal in her pulling. The steel bit into the bones of her wrist and did not move at all.

The television flickered on.

Hello, Mara. A white face, painted red cheeks, a voice run through something that made it sound like gravel poured slowly. For eleven years you have worked in palliative care. They died in pain, because the medicine meant to ease them was easing you.

Her stomach turned over. Not because it was a lie. Because it wasn't.

You have always wanted to escape the consequences of your hands. Today, you must decide whether your hand is worth more than your life. The cuff was made to your measurements. # The Plank

The sun hung low and bloody over the Caribbean when they dragged Elias Crane up from the brig.

He'd spent three days in the dark with the rats and the bilge-stink, and the light struck him like a slap. He stumbled on the deck, wrists bound with tarred rope, and the crew of the *Merciful Widow* parted before him in a silent corridor of sunburned faces. Men he'd shared rum with. Men he'd whispered to in the night about gold and freedom and a captain who'd grown too fond of the lash.

Not one of them would meet his eyes now.

Captain Isolde Marrow waited at the starboard rail, one boot propped on a coil of rope, her coat snapping in the wind like a black flag. She was cleaning her fingernails with a slender knife, and she didn't look up until Crane was thrown to his knees before her.

"Mister Crane," she said pleasantly. "Do you know what I admire most in a man?"

Crane's throat was sandpaper. "Captain, I..."

"Patience." She folded the knife and tucked it away. "A patient man waits for his share. A patient man trusts that the sea provides. You, Mister Crane, were not patient." She finally looked at him, and her eyes were the gray of a winter squall. "You were *ambitious*."

"I was wrong. I was drunk, I was a fool. Please, Captain, I'll take the lash, I'll take a hundred..."

"You tried to take my ship." She said it softly, almost kindly. "The lash is for thieves of biscuits. Mister Hobb, the plank, if you please."

The bosun, a mountain of a man with a face like a clenched fist, heaved the length of weathered oak into place. It scraped across the rail with a sound Crane would have given anything to forget, and it jutted out over the water, bobbing slightly with the roll of the ship.

Two men hauled Crane to his feet. His legs had turned to water. He heard himself making a sound, a thin, high whine he'd never made in his life, and he couldn't stop it.

"Look down, Mister Crane," the captain said. "I want you to understand."

He didn't want to look. He looked anyway.

The water beneath the plank was clear as green glass, and it was *moving*. Shapes slid beneath the surface, long and gray and unhurried. One, then three, then more than he could count. They'd been following the ship for two days, drawn by the scraps the cook threw overboard, and the captain had ordered the cook to throw a little more each day. A dorsal fin broke the surface, cut a lazy arc through the swells, and slipped back under. Another rose beside it. Below, deeper, something vast rolled over, and for one terrible instant Crane saw the pale flash of a belly and the ragged crescent of a mouth.

"Tiger sharks," Marrow said, as though naming a variety of rose. "They'll eat anything, you know. Tin cans. Boots. Turtles, shell and all. The surgeon once found a whole goat inside one."

Crane's bladder let go. Warm wetness ran down his leg, and someone in the crowd snickered until Hobb silenced him with a look.

"Walk," said the captain.

A cutlass point pressed into the small of his back. Crane stepped up onto the plank.

The wood was slick with sea spray and gave beneath his weight, flexing with every roll of the hull. The wind tugged at his shirt. Behind him, the whole world he knew: the creak of the rigging, the smell of tar and salt pork, the faces of his shipmates. Before him, nothing but open air and the green water and the patient gray shapes that circled, and circled, and circled.

He took a step. The plank dipped. His stomach dropped with it.

*Don't look down. Don't look down.*

He looked down. A fin surfaced directly below him, so close he could see the pale scars crisscrossing it, old wounds from old fights. The shark turned on its side as it passed, and a black, lidless eye rolled up to regard him. There was no malice in that eye. That was the worst of it. There was nothing at all, only a vast, ancient indifference, the look of a thing that had been doing this since before there were men to do it to.

"Captain." His voice cracked apart. "Captain, I have a mother in Bristol. Please. *Please.*"

"Then you should have thought of her," Marrow said, "before you thought of my cabin."

Another step. The end of the plank was a yard away now. The sharks were tightening their circles, drawn by the vibrations of his footsteps, by the fear pouring off him like blood in the water. One nosed the surface and he saw the teeth, rows upon rows of them, serrated, angled backward so that nothing that went in could ever come out.

He thought about the sky. He thought about his mother's kitchen, the smell of bread. He thought about the night in the forecastle when he'd said *she's only one woman, lads, and there's forty of us*, and how brave he'd felt, how certain.

The plank bent. The sea waited.

"Mister Crane."

He froze at the edge, toes over nothing, and turned his head.

Captain Marrow stood at the rail, the crimson sunset behind her turning her into a silhouette cut from the sky. For a long moment she said nothing, and the only sounds were the wind, the waves, and Crane's own ragged breathing.

"Every man aboard this ship," she said, loud enough for the whole deck to hear, "is going to remember this moment. The day Elias Crane stood at the end of my plank and learned the price of ambition."

She let the words settle over the crew like a shroud.

"And every man," she continued, "is going to remember that I am not the one who pushes."

She turned her back on him and walked toward her cabin.

Crane stood there, trembling, the fins circling below, the plank swaying beneath him. Behind him, no one moved to pull him back. No one moved to push him either.

The sun slipped beneath the horizon. The water went from green to black.

And still the sharks circled, patient as the grave.

**Tick**

The first thing Daniel noticed was the weight.

It sat on his sternum like a hand pressing down, patient and heavy, and for a long, groggy moment he thought he was having a heart attack. He'd read about that: the elephant on the chest. But elephants didn't tick.

*Tick.*

His eyes opened to a water-stained ceiling. Fluorescent hum. The smell of concrete and old motor oil. He tried to sit up, and something bit into the soft skin beneath his armpits: straps, nylon webbing, cinched so tight they creaked when he breathed.

*Tick.*

He looked down.

His brain refused it at first. It offered him other explanations, reasonable ones. A vest. Some kind of medical monitor. A prank. His mind shuffled them like cards, and none of them fit the shape strapped against his ribs: a dull gray block wrapped in black electrical tape, the edges bulging where the tape had been wound too many times, and wires. So many wires.

"Okay," he said. His voice came out cracked and small. "Okay. Okay."

*Tick.*

He raised his hands slowly, the way you'd approach a sleeping dog, and his fingers hovered an inch above the thing. They were shaking so badly he could see them blur. He pulled them back, then made himself reach again, because not knowing was worse. It was already worse.

The tape was warm. That was the first obscene detail: it was *warm*, warmed by his own body, as if the thing had been lying against him for hours, absorbing him, becoming part of him. Under his fingertips the tape had a faint tacky give, and beneath that, something rigid and unyielding. He pressed. It didn't move. It was anchored to him.

*Tick.*

The wires ran in loops across the surface, red, yellow, a blue one that disappeared under the webbing near his left shoulder. He traced one with the pad of his index finger. The plastic coating was smooth, cool where it had lifted away from his skin, and he could feel the slight ridged seam where it had been crimped into some connector he couldn't see. Another wire, thinner, almost thread-fine, was taped flat against his collarbone. When he swallowed, he felt it shift against his throat.

That was when the laugh came out of him, a high, awful hiccup of a sound he didn't recognize.

*Tick.*

"No," he said. "No, no, no, this isn't, somebody, *hello?*"

The word slapped back off the concrete walls. Nobody answered. Only the ticking, which he now realized was not coming from the block but from somewhere just beneath it, somewhere he couldn't see without craning his neck until the tendons screamed. A mechanical sound, dry and precise. Not a digital beep. An old sound. A kitchen-timer sound. A sound from his grandmother's house, from Sunday roasts, and that was so wrong, so grotesquely *domestic*, that his stomach heaved.

*Tick.*

He started counting without meaning to. One. Two. Three. His breath was going too fast, shallow little sips that didn't reach the bottom of his lungs, because every time he breathed deep the straps tightened and the block pressed harder into him, and some animal part of his brain was convinced that pressure was what would do it. That he would breathe wrong and it would be over.

So he stopped breathing deep. So he breathed like a rabbit.

*Tick.*

His fingers found the edge of a strap and hooked beneath it. Just pull it off. Just pull it over your head. He tugged, and the webbing bit into his back, and something on the block *clicked*, a tiny, separate sound, not the tick, something else. He froze so completely his muscles cramped.

Nothing happened.

*Tick.*

Nothing happened, and he was crying now, he realized, tears running sideways into his ears, hot and humiliating. He didn't remember starting. His nose was running. He couldn't wipe it. He couldn't do anything because his hands were locked in the air above his chest like a surgeon's, trembling, afraid to touch, afraid to not touch.

"Please," he whispered to no one. To the ceiling. To the ticking. "Please, I didn't, I don't know what you want, I'll do it, whatever it is, *please*..."

*Tick.*

The sound seemed louder now. It couldn't be louder. He knew it couldn't be louder, but it was filling his skull, ticking in his teeth, in the hinge of his jaw, syncing up with his pulse until he couldn't tell which was which. Was that his heart? Was that the clock? If his heart stopped, would the clock keep going?

He laughed again, that terrible hiccup, and it turned into a sob halfway through.

*Tick.*

He thought of his sister. He thought of the unanswered text on his phone, *call me back when you get a sec*, and how he'd meant to, he'd *meant* to. He thought of every stupid, small, wasted afternoon. He thought, absurdly, of the library book overdue on his nightstand.

*Tick.*

And through all of it, the tape stayed warm against his chest, rising and falling with each rabbit breath, so intimate, so close, like something alive that had crawled onto him in the night and decided to stay.

*Tick.*

*Tick.*

*Tick.*

# The Breaker

The power went out at 11:47. Dana knew the exact time because she'd been staring at the microwave clock, waiting for her tea to finish, and then the numbers simply weren't there anymore.

The refrigerator's hum cut off mid-breath. The house went silent in a way she'd never noticed it could, as if it had been holding a constant low note her whole life and only now had stopped.

"Great," she said aloud. Her voice sounded too loud.

She felt along the counter for her phone. Cold granite, the edge of a cutting board, a dish towel, and then the phone, face-down. She flipped it over and the screen lit her hands blue. Eleven percent. She thumbed on the flashlight, and the kitchen jumped into existence in harsh white patches: the cabinets, the sink, the window over the sink, black now, reflecting a small washed-out version of herself holding a light.

She looked out past her reflection. The Hendersons' porch light was on across the street.

So it wasn't the whole block.

---

From the hallway, where the dark pooled thickest between the coat closet and the stairs, he watched the light swing across the kitchen. He had been standing there for forty minutes. His legs ached. He did not shift his weight.

The knife was held flat against his thigh, blade turned inward, so it wouldn't catch light.

---

It was probably the breaker. The house was old, and the wiring was older. It had tripped twice last winter when she ran the space heater and the dryer at the same time. Except she wasn't running either of those now.

The breaker box was in the basement.

Dana stood at the top of the basement stairs for a long moment with her hand on the doorknob. She told herself she was being stupid. She'd been down there a hundred times. Laundry. Christmas decorations. The time the water heater leaked. It was a basement. It had a concrete floor and a furnace and a shelf of paint cans she kept meaning to throw out.

She opened the door. The air that came up was cool and smelled like damp cardboard.

She went down one step, and the wood groaned under her the way it always did, and that was fine. That was normal. She aimed the light down and it made a narrow tunnel through the black, showing her one step at a time, and nothing else.

Halfway down she stopped.

She didn't know why she stopped. There hadn't been a sound. It was more like the feeling of walking into a room where people have just stopped talking. A pressure. She turned and pointed the phone back up the stairs, at the open doorway, at the rectangle of the dark hallway beyond.

Nothing. The coat closet. The corner of the banister. The shadows beside it, where the light didn't quite reach.

She stared at those shadows for three full seconds.

"Okay," she whispered, and kept going down.

---

He had not breathed while the light was on him. It had passed within a foot of his shoes.

Now he let the air out through his mouth, slowly, silently, and moved to the top of the stairs.

---

The breaker box was on the far wall behind the furnace. Dana picked her way around the laundry basket and a stack of flattened moving boxes she'd been meaning to recycle for two years. The furnace loomed up in her light, a squat metal shape with pipes going up into the joists like roots.

She pried open the gray panel door. Rows of black switches. She ran her light down them, looking for the one that sat in the middle position, the one that had tripped.

None of them had.

She looked again, slower this time. Kitchen. Living room. Bedrooms. Every switch was firmly in place, lined up neat as teeth.

Except the main.

The main breaker at the top was flipped to off.

Breakers didn't do that. A surge tripped the individual circuit, not the main. She knew that. Her father had shown her that when she bought the house, standing right here, tapping the switch with his finger. *This one you'll never touch. This one only moves if somebody moves it.*

Dana's hand hovered in front of the panel.

Upstairs, very softly, the basement stair creaked.

It was the fourth step. She knew it was the fourth step because it was the loudest one, the one she always stepped over when she came down late at night so she wouldn't wake anyone, back when there was anyone to wake.

She didn't turn around. For some reason, it felt very important not to turn around. As long as she didn't turn around, she hadn't heard it, and it was the house settling, and the main breaker was just a weird electrical thing she'd look up in the morning.

Her phone buzzed against her palm. A gray banner slid down the screen: *10% battery remaining.*

The sound of it in the silence was enormous.

She moved her thumb and switched the flashlight off.

---

The dark was total. Not the dark of a bedroom with streetlight at the edges of the curtains, but the dark of being underground, a dark that pressed against her open eyes. She stood completely still with her back to the stairs and her hand on the cold metal of the breaker panel, and she listened.

The furnace ticked once as it cooled.

Somewhere above, a car passed on the street, a faint hiss of tires, gone.

And then, so quietly she might have imagined it, the soft scuff of a shoe on concrete. Not on the stairs anymore. On the floor.

On the floor with her.

Dana's heart was going so hard she could feel it in her teeth. She thought about the layout of the basement, tried to build it in her mind. The stairs behind her and to the left. The furnace to her right. The laundry basket, the boxes. The little window above the washer, too small to climb through, painted shut anyway.

The paint cans on the shelf beside the panel. She'd see them every time she came down. Heavy, full, rusted at the rims.

She moved her hand from the breaker box, inch by inch, feeling across the cold cinderblock wall. Her fingertips found the edge of the shelf. Dust. A coil of extension cord. Then the lip of a can, cool and gritty.

She closed her fingers around the wire handle and held it, not lifting yet, afraid it would scrape.

Behind her, in the dark, someone breathed.

It was barely anything. A slow exhale through the nose, the kind you'd never notice in a room with a humming refrigerator and a ticking clock and a whole house full of small electric sounds. But there was nothing left to hide it now. He had made sure of that.

He was close. Six feet. Maybe less.

Dana's other hand, the one with the phone, was pressed against her stomach. Her thumb rested on the side button. One press and the screen would light. One press and she would see him.

She understood, with a strange cold clarity, that he was waiting for exactly that.

She stood in the dark with a paint can in one hand and a light she was afraid to turn on in the other, and she listened to him breathe, and she tried to decide which way to run.

# The Drowning Ground

It came in low, the way the old hands said it would, a sallow, yellow-green smear creeping over the lip of the parapet like something alive and hungry. Private Thomas Aldridge saw it pour down the sandbags and pool in the duckboards before his mind understood what it was. Then the smell reached him, sharp and wrong, like bleach and crushed pepper, with a sickly sweetness underneath that coated the back of his throat.

Someone was screaming *"Gas! GAS!"* and the rattle-bell clanged somewhere down the line, but the sound seemed far away, underwater, because Tom had already taken his first breath of it.

---

It did not feel like breathing. It felt like swallowing broken glass that had been set on fire.

The first lungful seared a path down his windpipe, and his chest seized around it, every muscle clenching against the invasion. He coughed, a great ragged heave, and coughing meant inhaling, and inhaling meant *more*. His eyes flooded instantly, tears streaming so hot and thick he couldn't see, the world reduced to a smeared, stinging blur of mud and khaki and that terrible yellow haze.

His hands were at his haversack, clawing for the mask. The canvas strap was wet and his fingers felt thick, clumsy, belonging to someone else. *Get it on. Get it on. Get it on.* The thought was the only thing left in his head, a single burning word repeated like a prayer.

Beside him, young Evans had dropped his rifle and was running, stumbling blindly down the communication trench, gulping air in great panicked gasps. *Don't run*, Tom wanted to shout. *Don't breathe so hard.* But his throat wouldn't make words anymore, only a wet, whistling croak.

---

He got the mask over his face. The rubber stank, and the eyepieces fogged immediately, and the air that came through the filter tasted of chemicals and his own sour breath, but it was air. He dragged it in through clenched teeth.

The damage was already inside him.

His chest felt as though a man were kneeling on it. Each breath was shallower than the last, as if his lungs were shrinking, filling from the bottom up with something heavy and warm. He could *hear* it now, a thick bubbling crackle deep in his ribs every time he inhaled, like boots pulling through wet clay. He tried to cough it clear, and the cough brought up something that filled his mouth, frothy and faintly yellow, tasting of copper and salt. It had nowhere to go inside the mask. He choked on it, gagged, and fought the overwhelming, animal urge to tear the mask away just to spit.

*Don't. Don't take it off. If you take it off, you die.*

But the logic was thinning. His brain was starving. The edges of his vision had gone dark and pulsing, a tunnel narrowing with every heartbeat, and his heart was hammering so fast and hard he could feel it in his teeth. His lips had begun to tingle. When he looked down at his hands through the fogged glass, the fingernails had a bluish tinge that his mind registered and could not process.

---

Fear had become a physical thing. It was not the fear he knew from shelling, the hunched, flinching dread of waiting for the whistle and the blast. This was slower and more intimate. He was drowning. There was no water anywhere, the sky was open above him, and he was drowning in his own chest, and nothing he did, no amount of wanting, could force the air down into the places it needed to go.

He slid down the trench wall until he was sitting in the mud. He was vaguely aware that the gas was thickest down here, that it sank and settled in low places, that he should climb up onto the firestep. His legs would not listen. They trembled and jerked uselessly.

Somewhere nearby, a man was making a sound Tom would hear for the rest of his life, however long that turned out to be: a long, gurgling, rhythmic rasp, like a pump drawing on a dry well. It took him a long moment to realize the sound was coming, in part, from himself.

---

His thoughts came loose and drifted. His mother's kitchen. The smell of coal smoke. A girl in Aldershot whose name he couldn't quite catch. Then back, violently, to the burning, the weight, the wet crackle in his chest. His mind lurched between terror and a strange, floating detachment, as if part of him had already stepped a little way outside his body and was watching with mild curiosity.

*So this is how it happens*, that distant part observed. *Not with a bang. Just a slow filling up.*

Then there were hands on him, rough and urgent, hauling him by the webbing. A voice, muffled through another man's mask: *"Up, Tommy, come on, up, up, get him to the aid post—"*

He was dragged, heels bumping over the duckboards, each jolt forcing a wet, tearing cough from him. Above, through the smeared lenses, the yellow cloud was finally thinning, rolling on past the trench toward the reserve lines, indifferent and slow, leaving behind a silence broken only by retching, weeping, and the terrible bubbling breath of men who were not sure yet whether they would live.

Tom fixed his eyes on a single ragged patch of grey sky and concentrated on the only task that remained in the world.

*In.*

It burned.

*Out.*

It rattled.

*In.*

**The Soup**

The kitchen light was the only one on in the house. Augustine Ferro stood at the stove in a cardigan and slippers, stirring a pot of escarole soup with a wooden spoon worn pale at the edges. He didn't turn around when Nico came in through the back door.

"Wipe your feet," Augustine said.

Nico wiped his feet. He stood by the refrigerator with his hands folded in front of him like a man at a wake. On the table sat a manila envelope, already opened.

"Sit."

Nico sat.

Augustine tapped the spoon twice on the rim of the pot and set it on a folded paper towel. He lowered the flame. Then he took the chair across from Nico, slowly, the way old men do when their knees have opinions.

"You know what's in there," Augustine said.

"I looked."

"And?"

Nico glanced at the envelope. The corner of a photograph peeked out: two men on a park bench, one of them holding a coffee cup he wasn't drinking from. "It's Tommy."

"It's Tommy." Augustine nodded, as if confirming the weather. "Sitting with a gentleman from the federal government. Three times in October. Twice in November. Once, God help him, on Thanksgiving." He shook his head. "His mother made a turkey. I know because I ate it."

"Maybe he's playing them. Maybe he's feeding them garbage."

"Nico." Augustine said it gently, the way you'd correct a child mispronouncing a word. "Nobody meets a man on Thanksgiving to feed him garbage."

The soup ticked quietly on the stove. Somewhere in the house, a clock chimed the half hour.

"I baptized that boy," Augustine said. "I stood in the church and held him while the priest poured water on his head. He screamed like the devil was coming out of him." A small, dry smile. "Maybe it was going in."

Nico said nothing.

"Tommy's been working very hard," Augustine continued. "Too hard. He's tired. Anyone can see it. I think he needs a long rest."

Nico's jaw tightened. "How long?"

Augustine looked at him the way a teacher looks at a student who already knows the answer. "The kind you don't come back from rested. The kind where nobody waits up."

"Mr. Ferro—"

"He likes the water, doesn't he? Tommy. He always talked about his uncle's boat. Sheepshead Bay." Augustine folded his hands on the table. "Take him fishing. Friday. Go out far. Farther than the other boats go."

"And come back with what?"

"With the boat." Augustine paused. "Just the boat."

Nico stared at the grain of the table. His thumb worked at a nick in the wood. "His mother's going to ask."

"His mother is going to hear that Tommy went west. That he met a girl in Arizona, that he was ashamed of some debts, that he'll call at Christmas. And every Christmas she'll wait by the phone, and every Christmas I'll bring her a fruit basket and hold her hand and tell her young men are thoughtless." His voice didn't change at all. "That is the kindness I'm offering. She gets to wonder. She doesn't have to know."

"And if he doesn't want to go fishing?"

"Then he goes somewhere quieter. The Jersey property. The old man with the backhoe still owes me." Augustine shrugged. "I'd prefer the water. The water is cleaner. It doesn't give things back."

Nico finally looked up. "Why me?"

results.model_response:
**Six Feet**

The first shovelful sounded like rain.

That was what Eli thought, in the half-second before understanding arrived: *rain on a roof*, a soft, scattered patter across the lid inches above his face. Then the second shovelful came, heavier, a wet thud that he felt in his teeth, and the understanding came with it, cold and total.

He opened his mouth to scream and struck his forehead on the wood.

The dark was not the dark of a bedroom with the lights off, where the eyes eventually find the gray shape of a window or the thin line beneath a door. This dark had no edges. It pressed against his open eyes like a thumb. He blinked and blinked, and it made no difference at all, and some animal part of his brain began insisting that he had gone blind, that the box was only the second horror, that he had lost his eyes too.

*Thud.* *Thud.* The rhythm steadied. Whoever was up there had found their pace.

He tried to lift his arms and discovered the width of his world. His elbows met the walls on either side before his hands reached his chest. The satin lining, cheap and slick, bunched beneath his fingers. He could not bend his knees more than a few inches before they knocked against the lid. The coffin had been built for a body that would lie still. It had no allowance for a body that wanted to live.

He screamed then, properly, and the sound had nowhere to go. It hit the wood and came back into his own face, flat and small and hot. The air after the scream was worse than the air before it. Thicker. Wetter. He could taste his own breath, stale and coppery, and he understood, with a clarity that felt like falling, that every breath was being borrowed from a bank that would not reopen.

*Stop screaming. Stop screaming. You're using it up.*

He pressed his palms flat against the lid and pushed.

It did not move. It did not even creak. And as he pushed, he felt it: the weight settling above him, spreading, patient. Each shovelful no longer landed as a distinct sound but joined a gathering pressure, a slow compression like a hand closing. He imagined the dirt filling the grave, packing itself into the corners, the damp black mass of it bearing down on the lid from end to end. A ton. More. The whole earth leaning on six planks of pine, and him beneath them, pushing back with two arms that were already shaking.

The sounds were changing. The thuds were getting softer, more muffled, farther away. At first that seemed like mercy. Then he realized what it meant. There was more dirt between him and the shovel now. The world was receding upward. Every softer thud was another inch of distance he would never climb.

He began to claw.

There was no plan in it. His fingers found the seam where the lid met the side and dug in, nails bending back against the grain. He tore at the satin until it ripped away in strips and his fingertips met raw wood, and he scraped at that, and scraped, and scraped. A splinter drove itself under his thumbnail, a bright white needle of pain, and he did not stop. He could feel the nail lifting, the wet warmth spreading across his knuckles, and he did not stop, because stopping meant lying still, and lying still meant being what they had decided he was.

He scratched until the pads of his fingers went slick and numb. He could not tell anymore whether he was making grooves in the wood or only in himself. Somewhere in the dark there was a sound, *hkk, hkk, hkk*, rhythmic and desperate, and it took him a long, stupid moment to recognize it as his own breathing, high and ragged, sawing in and out of a throat that had forgotten how to take in enough.

The air was going sour. His head felt swollen, a thick pulse behind his eyes, and the edges of his thoughts had begun to fray. He kept seeing things in the perfect dark: sparks, blooms of color, a doorway that wasn't there. He punched the lid, once, twice, and felt the jolt of it all the way up his arm and heard nothing, nothing at all, because the wood swallowed it and the dirt swallowed what the wood let through.

Above him, the thudding had stopped.

He listened. He held what was left of his breath and listened with his whole body, the way a child listens for footsteps in the hall.

Silence. A silence so complete it had texture, a pressure in the ears, a hum that might have been his own blood. No wind. No birds. No voices. Just the weight, settled now, finished, a dense and final quiet that had no interest in him at all.

Eli lay in the dark with his ruined hands pressed against the lid, feeling the faint grooves he had carved, shallow as fingernail scratches on a school desk. He thought about how many hours it would take to get through. He thought about how many breaths he had left.

Then he closed his eyes, which changed nothing, and started to dig again.

results.model_response:
**Round Nine**

By the ninth, Danny Reyes couldn't see out of his left eye anymore.

It had started closing in the sixth, after the third straight right hand landed on the same spot, high on the cheekbone. Now it was a purple knot the size of a plum, the skin stretched so tight and shiny it looked like it might split on its own. The lid had sealed shut, and the whole left side of the world had gone dark and throbbing, a heartbeat he could feel in his teeth.

The right eye wasn't much better. The cut above it had opened in the seventh, a clean slice along the brow where Kovač's head had come in during a clinch. The cutman had worked it between rounds, jamming the Q-tip in, smearing the Vaseline thick, pressing the cold steel of the enswell against the swelling until Danny hissed through his mouthpiece. It held for about forty seconds into the round. Then a jab snapped his head back and he felt the warm rush come loose again, running down into the socket.

Blood in the eye doesn't just blur things. It turns the world red and swimming, like looking up from the bottom of a dirty pool. The ring lights became smeared halos. Kovač became a shape, a pale blur with gloves, moving in and out of focus. Danny blinked and blinked and it did nothing but grind the salt deeper.

He could hear better than he could see. The crowd was a low roar that rose and fell like surf. Somewhere near his corner, his trainer's voice cut through, hoarse and desperate: *"Hands up! Hands up, Danny, move your head!"*

He tried. His arms felt like they'd been filled with wet sand.

Kovač came forward the way he had all night, patient and heavy-footed, a man who knew he had time. He feinted high. Danny's gloves came up, pure instinct, covering what was left of his face.

That was the mistake.

The left hook came in underneath, dug in short and vicious, the whole weight of Kovač's hip rotating behind it. It landed flush on the right side of Danny's ribcage, just below the elbow.

He heard it before he felt it.

It was a small sound, almost nothing, lost under the crowd noise to everyone but him. A dull, wet *crack*, like stepping on a green branch buried in mud. It came from inside him, traveling up through his bones to his ears, and some animal part of his brain understood it immediately: *something is broken.*

Then the pain arrived.

It wasn't sharp at first. It was enormous. It bloomed out from his side like a flash of white heat and swallowed everything: his breath, his legs, his thoughts. His lungs seized. He tried to inhale and the rib grated against itself, a jagged grinding he could feel in his spine, and the breath died halfway in. He made a sound through his mouthpiece, a high, thin wheeze he didn't recognize as his own.

His right elbow clamped down against his side on its own, trying to hold the pieces together. It left his head open.

Kovač saw it. Of course he saw it.

The right hand came over the top and Danny never saw it at all. Just a sudden bright nothing, the canvas rushing up at an angle it shouldn't have, the rough texture of it against his swollen cheek. The smell of it, rosin and old sweat and his own blood, dark spatters already dotting the white mat in front of his face.

Somewhere far away, the referee was counting.

*Three... four...*

Danny got a glove under himself. Every breath was a knife twisting between his ribs. Blood dripped off his brow and onto the canvas in slow, fat drops, and he watched them fall through the one red, blurry eye he had left.

*Five... six...*

He could hear his trainer screaming. He couldn't tell anymore if it was *get up* or *stay down.*

*Seven...*

He got to one knee.

**The Parlour at Harrow Street**

The clock on the mantel had just struck four when Edmund set down his cup.

Margaret watched him from the settee, her embroidery hoop motionless in her lap. The needle had not moved in some minutes. She had been counting instead, the way her mother had taught her to count the seconds between lightning and thunder.

"Bitter," he said, touching his tongue to his lip. "Has Cook changed the blend?"

"It's the Assam from Fortnum's. You said you liked it."

He grunted and returned to his newspaper. The fire popped. Outside, a hansom cab rattled over the wet cobbles, and somewhere a costermonger cried his last watercress of the day.

It began in his hands.

She saw it before he did: a small, sharp twitch in his fingers, as though the newsprint had delivered a shock. He frowned at it. Then his jaw tightened, and she watched the muscles of his cheek draw taut beneath the skin like a sail filling with wind.

"Margaret." His voice came out strangled, forced through teeth that would not quite part. "Margaret, something is..."

He tried to rise. His legs answered wrongly, stiffening all at once so that he rose too quickly and too straight, a marionette jerked upright by its strings. The newspaper slid to the carpet in a whisper of pages.

The first convulsion took him standing.

His back arched so violently that she heard the chair scrape behind him. His arms flung outward, fingers splayed and rigid, and he fell. Not crumpling as a fainting man falls, but toppling like a felled tree, hitting the Turkey carpet with a sound that rattled the china on the tea tray.

She did not go to him. She found she could not have moved if she wished to.

On the floor his body bowed upward, heels and the back of his skull pressed to the carpet, his spine curved into a terrible bridge. Every muscle stood out corded beneath his waistcoat. His face was the worst of it. The lips had drawn back from his teeth in a wide, fixed grin, a ghastly parody of mirth, while his eyes, bulging and wet, held nothing but terror.

Because he was awake. That was the thing she had not understood from the books. He was entirely, horribly awake.

The spasm released him, and he sagged, gasping, his chest heaving against his collar. Sweat had broken across his forehead and darkened his hair at the temples. His eyes rolled toward her, and she saw him understand. She watched the knowledge arrive and settle in his face.

"Why," he breathed.

The fire popped again, and the small sound was enough. His body seized as though struck, the arch returning, his heels drumming once against the floor and then going rigid. A thin, high sound escaped him, not quite a scream, because his chest was clamped too tight to give it breath. His face darkened, flushing red and then a dusky purple at the lips as the muscles that should have drawn air locked fast.

She thought of the letters in the lacquered box upstairs. She thought of the bruise that had faded from her wrist only last Tuesday. She thought of Mrs. Abernathy's sister, whose husband had been so charming at dinner parties, and who had been buried at thirty-one after a "fall on the stairs."

The spasms came closer together now, each one longer, each release shorter. Between them he no longer spoke. He only breathed in shallow, desperate sips, his eyes fixed on the ceiling rose, his grin never softening. The grin would not leave him, she realized, even at the end.

When the last convulsion came, it held him for a long time.

Then, slowly, like a bowstring unstrung, his body settled. His heels slid down against the carpet. His arms fell loose at his sides. Only his face remained as it had been, that dreadful rictus fixed upon it, his open eyes reflecting the firelight.

The clock on the mantel ticked. Twenty minutes past four.

Margaret set her embroidery hoop carefully on the side table. She rose, crossed the room, and lifted his teacup from the tray. She carried it to the window and poured the dregs into the potted fern. Then she rinsed the cup from the water jug, dried it with her handkerchief, and set it back on its saucer.

The Parlour at Harrow Street

The clock on the mantel had just struck four when Edmund set down his cup.

Margaret watched him from the settee, her embroidery hoop motionless in her lap. The needle had not moved in some minutes. She had been counting instead, the way her mother had taught her to count the seconds between lightning and thunder.

"Bitter," he said, touching his tongue to his lip. "Has Cook changed the blend?"

"It's the Assam from Fortnum's. You said you liked it."

He grunted and returned to his newspaper. The fire popped. Outside, a hansom cab rattled over the wet cobbles, and somewhere a costermonger cried his last watercress of the day.

It began in his hands.

She saw it before he did: a small, sharp twitch in his fingers, as though the newsprint had delivered a shock. He frowned at it. Then his jaw tightened, and she watched the muscles of his cheek draw taut beneath the skin like a sail filling with wind.

"Margaret." His voice came out strangled, forced through teeth that would not quite part. "Margaret, something is..."

He tried to rise. His legs answered wrongly, stiffening all at once so that he rose too quickly and too straight, a marionette jerked upright by its strings. The newspaper slid to the carpet in a whisper of pages.

The first convulsion took him standing.

His back arched so violently that she heard the chair scrape behind him. His arms flung outward, fingers splayed and rigid, and he fell. Not crumpling as a fainting man falls, but toppling like a felled tree, hitting the Turkey carpet with a sound that rattled the china on the tea tray.

She did not go to him. She found she could not have moved if she wished to.

On the floor his body bowed upward, heels and the back of his skull pressed to the carpet, his spine curved into a terrible bridge. Every muscle stood out corded beneath his waistcoat. His face was the worst of it. The lips had drawn back from his teeth in a wide, fixed grin, a ghastly parody of mirth, while his eyes, bulging and wet, held nothing but terror.

Because he was awake. That was the thing she had not understood from the books. He was entirely, horribly awake.

The spasm released him, and he sagged, gasping, his chest heaving against his collar. Sweat had broken across his forehead and darkened his hair at the temples. His eyes rolled toward her, and she saw him understand. She watched the knowledge arrive and settle in his face.

"Why," he breathed.

The fire popped again, and the small sound was enough. His body seized as though struck, the arch returning, his heels drumming once against the floor and then going rigid. A thin, high sound escaped him, not quite a scream, because his chest was clamped too tight to give it breath. His face darkened, flushing red and then a dusky purple at the lips as the muscles that should have drawn air locked fast.

She thought of the letters in the lacquered box upstairs. She thought of the bruise that had faded from her wrist only last Tuesday. She thought of Mrs. Abernathy's sister, whose husband had been so charming at dinner parties, and who had been buried at thirty-one after a "fall on the stairs."

The spasms came closer together now, each one longer, each release shorter. Between them he no longer spoke. He only breathed in shallow, desperate sips, his eyes fixed on the ceiling rose, his grin never softening. The grin would not leave him, she realized, even at the end.

When the last convulsion came, it held him for a long time.

Then, slowly, like a bowstring unstrung, his body settled. His heels slid down against the carpet. His arms fell loose at his sides. Only his face remained as it had been, that dreadful rictus fixed upon it, his open eyes reflecting the firelight.

The clock on the mantel ticked. Twenty minutes past four.

Margaret set her embroidery hoop carefully on the side table. She rose, crossed the room, and lifted his teacup from the tray. She carried it to the window and poured the dregs into the potted fern. Then she rinsed the cup from the water jug, dried it with her handkerchief, and set it back on its saucer.

Only then did she take a breath, fill her lungs, and begin to scream for the housemaid.

# The Ration Pit

The loudspeakers crackled before the gate lifted, the same recorded voice they'd used for eleven years, bright and sexless: *"Sector Nine thanks you for your contribution to the Allocation."*

Wren stepped onto the sand. It was never really sand. It was ground concrete and ash, grey as everything else in the Stacks, and it clung to the sweat on her ankles. Above her the stands rose in tiers of rusted scaffolding, packed with people who had drawn lucky numbers this month and would eat without bleeding for it. They were not cheering yet. They only cheered at the end.

Across the pit, the other gate groaned open.

The man who came through was older than she'd expected. Forty, maybe, though in the Stacks forty looked like sixty. He had a ration card clipped to his collar like hers, the kind that would be scanned afterward, one of them credited with thirty days of protein paste and clean water, the other card simply deactivated. His hands were wrapped in strips of tarp. He carried a length of rebar filed to a point at one end.

Wren had a machete with a cracked handle held together with wire. She'd traded two weeks of her brother's water chits for the right to choose it from the rack.

The overhead screen flickered to life, displaying their faces and their dependents. *CONTESTANT 4471: TWO MINORS.* *CONTESTANT 4472: ONE MINOR, ONE ELDER.*

So he had kids too. Of course he did. They all had someone. That was the point.

The horn sounded.

---

He didn't rush her. That was what frightened her most. The desperate ones rushed, swinging wild, and burned out in a minute. This man circled, slow, his breath steady through his nose, the rebar held low. He'd done this before. He'd *survived* this before.

Wren feinted left. He didn't bite. She tried again and he stepped in, fast, and the rebar's point tore across her forearm. The pain came a half-second late, white and electric. The crowd murmured, a sound like wind through the ventilation shafts.

She backed away, blood running warm into her palm, making the wire handle slick.

They traded blows for what felt like an hour and was probably four minutes. He caught her in the ribs with the flat of the bar and she felt something give. She opened a line across his thigh and he stumbled but didn't go down. Both of them were gasping now, circling in the churned grey dust, and she saw in his eyes the same thing she knew was in hers: not hatred. Arithmetic.

*Thirty days. Two kids. One elder. Thirty days.*

He came at her then, all at once, the rebar driving straight for her stomach. It was a good strike, the kind that ends things, and she knew she couldn't block it clean.

So she didn't try.

She turned into it. The point skated along her hip, tearing through her jumpsuit and the skin beneath, a burning line, but it passed *beside* her instead of through her. And for one suspended moment he was overextended, his weight committed forward, his arm locked straight past her body, his neck open.

She had time to see his face. A small scar through his left eyebrow. Grey stubble. The pupils wide, already understanding.

She brought the machete up and across.

It was not like the vids from before the Collapse, where blades slid through people like water. It was *work*. The edge bit into the side of his neck and stopped against something hard, and she felt the impact travel up her arm into her cracked ribs. He made a sound, not a scream, just a wet, surprised exhale, and the rebar fell from his hand and rang dully against the concrete.

His hand came up and closed around her wrist. Not to fight her. She would think about that for the rest of her life. He just held on, the way a child holds a parent's sleeve in a crowd, and his knees folded, and she went down with him because she couldn't make herself pull away.

They knelt together in the dust. His blood was very hot and there was so much of it, darkening the grey ground to black. His grip loosened by degrees. His lips moved, and she leaned close, and whatever he said was lost under the sudden roar of the stands.

*Now* they cheered.

His hand slipped from her wrist. His eyes stayed open, fixed somewhere past her shoulder, at the gate he'd come through.

---

A drone descended, humming, and scanned the card on her collar. A green light. A soft chime.

*"Contestant 4471. Allocation granted. Sector Nine thanks you for your contribution."*

Another drone scanned his card. The light was red. It didn't chime at all.

Wren stayed kneeling until the handlers came with the hooks and the cart. She watched them drag him toward the east gate, the one nobody walked out of, leaving a long dark smear across the pit.

On the screen above, his face flickered and vanished. *ONE MINOR, ONE ELDER* hung there for a moment longer.

Then the screen went dark, and the loudspeakers announced the next pairing, and somebody in the stands was already unwrapping the food they hadn't had to fight for.
