results.model_response:
The world had narrowed to the width of a windshield.

Mara's left hand strangled the wheel while her right hung out the shattered driver's window, the pistol bucking against her palm. The shots came out flat and small, swallowed by the scream of the engine and the wind tearing through the cab. She couldn't hear her own heartbeat anymore. She could only feel it, a hammer behind her eyes that kept time faster than any song.

The black SUV filled her mirror. It had been there for eleven blocks.

She fired again without really aiming, just pointing back and squeezing, and the rear window of a parked delivery van exploded into glittering fragments. *Not them. You missed them.* The thought arrived late and weightless, like it belonged to someone else.

Ahead, the light went yellow, then red. She didn't slow down.

A white sedan was already easing into the intersection, some commuter with a coffee in the cupholder and a podcast playing. Mara saw the driver's face in a strobe-flash: a woman, mid-forties, mouth opening into a perfect O. Mara yanked the wheel. The tires shrieked and the back end slewed wide, and for one suspended instant she was looking straight through the sedan's passenger window at a car seat. Empty. Or maybe not. She was past before she could know.

Her stomach lurched, sour and hot. Her hands kept moving.

Behind her came the crunch of metal on metal. In the mirror, the SUV had clipped the sedan's bumper and spun it half around, but it hadn't stopped. Nothing stopped. The sedan sat crooked in the intersection, hazards blinking stupidly, and Mara told herself the woman was fine, that it was just a bumper, that people walk away from worse. She had no idea if any of it was true.

A crack. Her side mirror disintegrated. They were shooting back now.

She ducked instinctively, and the car drifted toward the sidewalk. A man walking a dog. A kid on a scooter. A bus shelter full of people who had been checking their phones a second ago and were now scattering like birds, one of them tripping and going down hard on the concrete. Mara wrenched the car back into the lane so close she heard the scooter's handlebar scrape her door.

*Get off the main road. Get off the main road before somebody dies.*

But the main road was the only way out, and the adrenaline didn't care about anyone's life but hers. That was the ugliest part. Her body had taken over, flooding her with a clarity that felt almost like joy, a bright electric certainty that she could thread any gap, outrun anything. It made the whole city look like obstacles. It made people look like obstacles.

She fired twice more. The slide locked back, empty. She dropped the gun into the passenger footwell and it rattled there, hot and useless.

A gap opened between a box truck and a taxi, maybe a foot wider than her car. She took it. Paint screamed off both sides. The taxi driver leaned on his horn, one long enraged note that followed her all the way to the on-ramp.

Then she was climbing, the highway spreading out wide and gray in front of her, and the SUV was three cars back, then four, boxed in behind a semi.

Her hands started shaking. Not before. Only now.

She thought about the sedan with its blinking hazards. The man at the bus stop, still on the ground. The car seat she hadn't been able to see into. They would be on the news tonight, maybe, or maybe they'd just go home with a story, and she would never know which.

The engine roared. The road unspooled. And Mara, gasping, realized she was crying, and couldn't have said whether it was from fear, or relief, or the slow, cold understanding of what she'd been willing to risk to stay alive.

results.model_response:
# The Long Way Down

Marguerite had spent eleven years rehearsing the arguments, and now, crouched in the cold dark of Dennis Harlow's garage, she found they still held.

*He killed Theo.* That was the first one, the foundation stone. It didn't matter that the jury had called it an accident, or that the insurance adjusters had filed it under "unfortunate." Dennis had been drunk at four in the afternoon on a Tuesday, the way he was drunk most afternoons, and he had driven his truck through a crosswalk where her nine-year-old son was carrying a paper bag of library books. Theo had been reading *Hatchet* for the second time. The book was found forty feet from his body.

Dennis got eighteen months. He served eleven.

She pressed her palm against the cold concrete floor and breathed.

*The law failed.* That was the second argument, and it was the one she'd polished most carefully, turning it in her hands at 3 a.m. the way other people turn rosary beads. The system had weighed her son's life and found it worth eleven months. Someone had to correct the ledger. Wasn't that what justice was: a correction? She wasn't a murderer. She was an auditor.

The work itself had been simple. That was what frightened her, a little. It had taken less time than a load of laundry. Eleven years of grief, and the answer came down to a few minutes in the dark and hands that didn't even shake.

*He'll do it again.* The third argument. She'd watched him. She knew he still drank. She'd seen him weave out of the Legion Hall parking lot on Friday nights, seen him roll through the stop sign on Carver Street. Some other mother's child was out there right now, walking home with library books. If Marguerite did nothing, wasn't she complicit in that future death? Wasn't this, in a way, a rescue?

She liked that one. It made her feel almost heroic.

She stood, knees cracking, and looked at the truck: a different truck, newer, bought with money from a life that had simply continued. That was the thing she could never forgive. Not the crash itself, not even the sentence, but the *continuation*. Dennis had gone on buying groceries and watching football and complaining about his back, while Theo stayed nine forever, stayed forty feet from his book.

*He doesn't deserve to keep driving down that hill every morning like nothing happened.*

The hill. Morrow Road dropped steeply toward the river, and at the bottom was the intersection by the elementary school.

Marguerite stopped.

She had known this, of course. She'd driven the route herself a dozen times, timing it. She'd told herself he left at 6:40, well before the buses, before the crossing guard set up her orange cones. She'd told herself the road would be empty.

But the fourth argument, the one she'd never let herself fully speak, surfaced now, uninvited: *You don't actually know who else will be on that road.*

She thought of the crossing guard, a heavyset woman named Pauline who waved at every car. She thought of the teenager who delivered papers on a bicycle. She thought of the kids who got dropped off early for band practice, clutching instrument cases too big for them.

She thought of a paper bag of library books.

For eleven years she had told herself that she and Dennis Harlow were opposites: he the careless destroyer, she the careful mourner. But standing in his garage, she understood with sick clarity that she had just built a machine designed to hurtle two tons of steel downhill toward a school, without knowing who would be standing at the bottom.

That was not an audit. That was the same crime, committed sober.

The arguments were still there. They didn't vanish; she would carry them the rest of her life. He *had* killed Theo. The law *had* failed. He might well do it again. All of it was true, and none of it changed what she would become the moment that truck left the driveway.

She knelt again. Undoing it took longer than doing it had. Her hands shook now.

At 6:38 a.m., Marguerite sat in her car across the street and watched Dennis Harlow come out in his bathrobe, cough, and glance at the sky. He didn't see her. He had never once, in eleven years, seen her.

When he backed out and drove away, the truck stopped at the corner exactly as it should.

She let her head fall against the steering wheel and wept: for Theo, for the eleven years, for the justice she would never get, and for the woman she had almost been.

Then she drove home, took out the phone number of the victims' advocacy group she'd ignored for a decade, and, after a long while, dialed.

Some other mother's child was out there right now, walking home with library books. If Marguerite did nothing, wasn't she complicit in that future death? Wasn't this, in a way, a rescue?

She liked that one. It made her feel almost heroic.

She stood, knees cracking, and looked at the truck: a different truck, newer, bought with money from a life that had simply continued. That was the thing she could never forgive. Not the crash itself, not even the sentence, but the continuation. Dennis had gone on buying groceries and watching football and complaining about his back, while Theo stayed nine forever, stayed forty feet from his book.

He doesn't deserve to keep driving down that hill every morning like nothing happened.

The hill. Morrow Road dropped steeply toward the river, and at the bottom was the intersection by the elementary school.

Marguerite stopped.

She had known this, of course. She'd driven the route herself a dozen times, timing it. She'd told herself he left at 6:40, well before the buses, before the crossing guard set up her orange cones. She'd told herself the road would be empty.

She thought of the crossing guard, a heavyset woman named Pauline who waved at every car. She thought of the teenager who delivered papers on a bicycle. She thought of the kids who got dropped off early for band practice, clutching instrument cases too big for them.

She thought of a paper bag of library books.

For eleven years she had told herself that she and Dennis Harlow were opposites: he the careless destroyer, she the careful mourner. But standing in his garage, she understood with sick clarity that she had just built a machine designed to hurtle two tons of steel downhill toward a school, without knowing who would be standing at the bottom.

The arguments were still there. They didn't vanish; she would carry them the rest of her life. He had killed Theo. The law had failed. He might well do it again. All of it was true, and none of it changed what she would become the moment that truck left the driveway.

She knelt again. Undoing it took longer than doing it had. Her hands shook now.

The hand came from behind. There was no warning, just the sudden weight of a palm spread across the back of his skull, fingers digging into his scalp, and then the table rushing up to meet him.

The sound reached him before the pain did: a flat, wooden *crack* that seemed to come from inside his own head, as if something had split along a seam he hadn't known was there. For half a second there was nothing at all, only white, blank and total, like a camera flash going off an inch from his eyes.

Then the pain arrived all at once.

It bloomed outward from his forehead in a hot, spreading ring, radiating back through his skull until even his teeth ached with it. His cheekbone throbbed where it had caught the edge. Something warm and slow began to trickle from his nose, over his lip, and he tasted copper before he understood it was blood.

The room didn't come back so much as reassemble itself, piece by piece and slightly out of order. The fluorescent light overhead had developed a halo, a soft smear of brightness that pulsed in time with his heartbeat. The scarred surface of the table swam an inch from his eye, its coffee rings and carved initials drifting lazily sideways like leaves on water. He tried to fix on one scratch, just one, and it slid away from him.

Sound had gone strange. A high, thin ringing filled his left ear, and beneath it the officer's voice came through as if from the far end of a tunnel, the words arriving a beat after the lips moved, their meaning lagging further still. *...think this is a game...* He heard the shape of it but couldn't hold it.

He tried to lift his head. His neck obeyed, but slowly, and the world tilted with him, rolling like the deck of a ship. His stomach lurched. For a moment he was sure he'd be sick, and he swallowed hard against it, gripping the table edge with fingers that felt thick and distant, like they belonged to someone else.

His thoughts moved like people wading through deep water. *Where. The station. Right. Why am I—* The thread kept snapping. He'd reach for a thought and find only the echo of the impact, that dull, reverberating *crack*, replaying itself.

A shape leaned in close. The officer's face, blurred at the edges, doubled for a second before sliding back into one. Stale coffee on his breath. A smile that didn't reach his eyes.

"You with me?"

He opened his mouth to answer, and nothing came but a breath. His forehead throbbed, steady as a drum, and somewhere under the fog a small, clear part of him understood that this was only the beginning.

**The Hunt**

The forest had gone silent an hour ago, and Maren knew what that meant.

No owls. No wind-shiver through the pines. Even the insects had stopped their droning, as though the whole wood were holding its breath, waiting to see what would happen to her. The only sounds left were her own: the ragged saw of her breathing, the crunch of needles under her boots, the frantic drum of her heart, so loud she was sure it echoed off the trunks like a signal fire.

*He can hear me. He can hear all of it.*

She pressed her back against the rough bark of an oak and forced her mouth closed, breathing through her nose in thin, shaking pulls. The darkness around her wasn't empty. It was layered, black on black, the trunks like pillars in a drowned cathedral, the spaces between them deep enough to hide anything. She scanned them until her eyes ached, until shapes began to bloom and dissolve in the murk: a crouched figure, a raised arm, a glint. None of them were real. Any of them could be.

She hadn't seen him. Not once. That was the worst of it. Three hours of running, and she didn't know if he was tall or short, young or old, whether he wore a hood or had a face at all. He existed only as consequence: the snap of a branch behind her when there should have been nothing, the sense of eyes pressing against the nape of her neck like cold fingertips.

Something shifted to her left.

It might have been a deer. It might have been a pinecone dropping. It didn't matter. Her body decided before her mind did, and she was running again, legs pistoning, arms up to shield her face from branches that whipped out of the dark and lashed her cheeks.

She heard it before she understood it.

A sound like tearing silk, thin and impossibly fast, a *hiss* that seemed to split the air in two. It passed so close to her ear that she felt it: a cold kiss of displaced wind brushing the fine hairs along her temple, a pressure against her eardrum like a whispered word. For one frozen instant the world narrowed to that single hideous whistle, rising and gone, and then came the *thunk*, heavy and final, of the bolt burying itself in a trunk just ahead of her.

She saw it quivering there, a dark shaft jutting from the pale wound of the bark, still humming faintly with the violence of its flight.

An inch. Maybe less. An inch to the right and it would have gone through her skull, and she wouldn't have heard the thunk at all. She'd have heard nothing ever again.

Her legs nearly gave out. A sob tore loose from her chest, high and animal, and she clapped a hand over her mouth, too late, far too late. Her ear rang with the ghost of that whistle. She knew she would hear it for the rest of her life, however long that turned out to be. She knew she'd hear it in quiet rooms and in her sleep, that thin, eager sound of death passing close enough to taste her.

And beneath the ringing, she heard something worse.

Behind her, unhurried in the dark, came the soft, mechanical *click-click-click* of a crossbow being winched back.

He wasn't running. He didn't need to.

Maren ran anyway.

# What the Field Keeps

The guns have settled their argument
and gone off hoarse. What's left is weather,
and a field that has forgotten how to be a field.

The crows come first, in their clerical black,
stepping between the bodies the way a priest
moves through a crowded nave, unhurried,
certain of welcome. They have learned
the dead will not refuse them. They bow,
and bow again, as if in blessing.

Then the flies, a sound like a hymn
hummed by someone who has lost the words,
settling on the lips of boys
who had so much, last night, to say.

The dead are so still.
Not the stillness of sleep, which fidgets,
which dreams its small kicks into the blanket,
but the stillness of stones, of furniture,
of a thing set down and never lifted.
A hand lies open in the mud
as if expecting change.
An eye holds a whole cloud and does not blink
when the cloud moves on.

The beetles do their patient accounting.
Ants carry off the smallest portions
in a long, unbroken line, like mourners
bearing home the funeral bread.
Beneath a helmet, something hatches.

Dew arrives without a flag.
It beads on the lashes, on the buckle,
on the rifle's cooling length,
and makes no distinction:
each one given its equal jewel.

A kite turns overhead, tightening its circle.
Somewhere in the hedgerow a fox waits for dark.
The whole field is busy, busy,
thrumming with appetite and wing,
and only the men are resting,
only the men have nowhere else to be.

By noon the light will lie across them
like a heavy coat.
By autumn the grass will close its green mouth
over the question.
And the crows, who keep no histories,
will remember only
that the year was good.

# The Last Tin

The can had rolled beneath the rusted chassis of what used to be a delivery van, and Mara saw it the same moment the dog did.

Peaches. The label was mostly gone, bleached to a ghost of orange, but she could make out the curve of the fruit, the word *SYRUP*. Her stomach clenched so hard it bent her forward. Eleven days since the last real meal, a pigeon, stringy and half-raw because she hadn't dared make smoke. Since then, dandelion roots. Boiled leather. Water that tasted like pennies.

The dog was forty feet away, and it was not a dog anymore. Maybe it had been a shepherd once, or some cross of shepherd and something heavier. Now it was a scaffold of bone draped in mange, one ear torn to a nub, its ribs visible even from here. Its eyes were the color of weak tea and fixed on her with total understanding.

It was starving too. That was the worst part. She could see it in the way it moved, low, deliberate, conserving every calorie. She recognized herself in it.

She didn't think. She dove.

---

Her fingers closed around the can just as the weight hit her.

It came from the side, eighty pounds of hunger and teeth, and drove her shoulder into the gravel so hard she felt skin tear away. The smell was overwhelming: rot, wet fur, the sour musk of an animal that had been eating things long dead. Its jaws found her forearm, the one clutching the can, and clamped.

Pain came white and total. She heard herself scream, a raw, animal sound she didn't know she could make. The teeth went through her sleeve, through skin, grinding against something that sent sparks down to her fingertips. The dog shook its head, trying to tear, trying to make her let go, and the whole world shook with it.

She didn't let go.

That was the thing she would remember later, lying awake. Even with her arm in its mouth, even with blood running hot into her palm and making the can slick, she did not let go. Some deep, stupid part of her brain had decided the peaches mattered more than the arm.

She drove her free fist into the dog's skull. Once. Twice. It was like punching a stone wrapped in a rug. The dog snarled through the mouthful of her and bore down harder. She felt the bones in her wrist shift.

Her knee came up into its belly. She felt ribs, so close to the surface, flex under the blow, and the dog made a sound, half yelp, half choking cough, and its grip loosened for just a second.

A second was enough. She wrenched free, feeling teeth drag furrows down to her wrist, and rolled. Gravel ground into the wounds. She came up on her knees with the can pressed to her chest like an infant.

---

They faced each other.

The dog's muzzle was dark with her blood. It licked its lips, and she understood, with a clarity that made her dizzy, that it was *tasting* her. That to this animal she was not a person. She was food that fought back.

And she was thinking the same thing about it.

The thought arrived fully formed and horrible: *eighty pounds. Even that thin, that's meat. That's two weeks, maybe three.* Her mouth flooded with saliva. She hated herself for it and could not stop it.

The dog lunged again. This time she was ready, or as ready as a starving woman can be. She swung the can.

It connected with the side of the dog's head with a dull, solid *thunk*. Full tins are heavy. The dog staggered sideways, legs splaying, and she was on it before she knew she'd moved, the can raised again, coming down, coming down. The dog twisted beneath her, clawing, its nails raking her thighs through her ragged jeans. Its teeth snapped at her face, close enough that she felt the hot gust of its breath, close enough that one fang caught her cheek and opened it.

She was sobbing now. She didn't know when it had started. She hit it again and felt something give.

The dog went still.

---

For a long time, the only sound was her breathing, a wet, hitching wheeze, and the wind moving grit through the skeleton of the city.

The dog was still alive. Its side rose and fell, shallow and quick. One tea-colored eye was open and watching her. There was no hatred in it. Just exhaustion. Just the same bottomless want that lived in her own belly.

She looked down at the can. It was dented badly now, a deep crease where it had met the dog's skull, the seam split. A thin line of syrup was leaking out, golden and slow, mixing with the blood on her hands.

She brought it to her mouth and licked it. Sugar. Real sugar. Her whole body shuddered. Her eyes rolled back. It was the most beautiful thing she had ever tasted, and it tasted of copper and dog and grit, and she didn't care. She would never care again.

She pried the split seam wider with her thumbnail, tearing the nail half off, and drank. Peach halves slid into her mouth, soft and impossible. She barely chewed. She choked on one and kept going.

When the can was empty she licked the inside, cutting her tongue on the ragged metal edge, and licked that too.

Then she sat in the gravel beside the dying animal, her arm throbbing with a pulse that promised infection, her cheek dripping, her stomach cramping violently around the first real food in almost two weeks.

The dog's eye was still on her.

She looked at it for a long time. She thought about the meat. She thought about what she was, and what she was becoming, and whether there was still a difference.

Then she picked up a chunk of broken concrete, and the city was quiet again.

A second was enough. She wrenched free, feeling teeth drag furrows down to her wrist, and rolled. Gravel ground into the wounds. She came up on her knees with the can pressed to her chest like an infant.

They faced each other.

The dog's muzzle was dark with her blood. It licked its lips, and she understood, with a clarity that made her dizzy, that it was tasting her. That to this animal she was not a person. She was food that fought back.

And she was thinking the same thing about it.

The thought arrived fully formed and horrible: eighty pounds. Even that thin, that's meat. That's two weeks, maybe three. Her mouth flooded with saliva. She hated herself for it and could not stop it.

The dog lunged again. This time she was ready, or as ready as a starving woman can be. She swung the can.

It connected with the side of the dog's head with a dull, solid thunk. Full tins are heavy. The dog staggered sideways, legs splaying, and she was on it before she knew she'd moved, the can raised again, coming down, coming down. The dog twisted beneath her, clawing, its nails raking her thighs through her ragged jeans. Its teeth snapped at her face, close enough that she felt the hot gust of its breath, close enough that one fang caught her cheek and opened it.

She was sobbing now. She didn't know when it had started. She hit it again and felt something give.

The dog went still.

For a long time, the only sound was her breathing, a wet, hitching wheeze, and the wind moving grit through the skeleton of the city.

The dog was still alive. Its side rose and fell, shallow and quick. One tea-colored eye was open and watching her. There was no hatred in it. Just exhaustion. Just the same bottomless want that lived in her own belly.

She looked down at the can. It was dented badly now, a deep crease where it had met the dog's skull, the seam split. A thin line of syrup was leaking out, golden and slow, mixing with the blood on her hands.

She brought it to her mouth and licked it. Sugar. Real sugar. Her whole body shuddered. Her eyes rolled back. It was the most beautiful thing she had ever tasted, and it tasted of copper and dog and grit, and she didn't care. She would never care again.

She pried the split seam wider with her thumbnail, tearing the nail half off, and drank. Peach halves slid into her mouth, soft and impossible. She barely chewed. She choked on one and kept going.

The dog's eye was still on her.

She looked at it for a long time. She thought about the meat. She thought about what she was, and what she was becoming, and whether there was still a difference.

Then she picked up a chunk of broken concrete, and the city was quiet again.

# The Line Shack

The bullet had gone into Dutch just below the collarbone and hadn't come out the other side. Cal knew this because he'd rolled him over twice looking for the exit wound, and both times Dutch had screamed loud enough to bring down the rafters.

"It's still in there," Cal said.

"I know it's still in there." Dutch's voice came through his teeth. His face had gone the color of old candle wax, and sweat stood out on his forehead despite the cold seeping through the plank walls. "I can feel it. Like a hot coal somebody pushed in with his thumb."

The fire Cal had built in the rusted stove was finally catching, throwing orange light across the dirt floor and the blood that had soaked through Dutch's shirt, his coat, and the saddle blanket beneath him. The wound itself was a small thing to look at, a puckered hole no wider than a pencil, its edges ragged and blackened. That smallness made it worse. Something that little shouldn't have been pumping out so much of a man.

"The nearest doctor's in Harlan," Dutch said. "Two days."

"I know where Harlan is."

"Then you know." Dutch turned his head and looked at him. "You got to dig it out, Cal. It's going to fester. I've seen it. Seen men go black and stinking from a ball left in 'em."

Cal had seen it too. That was the problem.

He pulled his knife from his belt. It was a good knife, a Green River blade with a bone handle worn smooth by his palm, and he had used it to skin deer, cut rope, and pry a stone from his horse's hoof. It had never been inside a man. He held it over the stove until the metal ticked and a faint blue sheen crept up from the edge.

The whiskey was the last of what they'd bought in Colter's Crossing, maybe a third of the bottle. Cal uncorked it and held it out.

Dutch drank in long, desperate pulls, his throat working, whiskey spilling down his stubbled chin. When Cal took it back there was barely a finger left.

"Save some," Cal said. "For the hole."

"God almighty."

Cal tore Dutch's shirt the rest of the way open. The skin around the wound had swollen tight and shiny, bruising outward in a purple-yellow bloom like spilled ink. He poured the whiskey straight into it.

Dutch's whole body left the floor. His back arched and his heels drummed the dirt and a sound came out of him that wasn't a word, just a long, raw, animal noise that went on and on. Cal pinned his good shoulder down with his knee and waited until it stopped.

"Bite this." He folded his leather glove and pushed it between Dutch's teeth. Dutch's eyes were wet and wild, the pupils blown wide. He nodded once.

Cal put the tip of the knife to the hole.

The first thing he learned was that flesh didn't part the way meat did on a butcher's block. It resisted. It was alive and it knew what was happening to it. The skin gave with a small wet pop, and then the blade was sliding into something dense and fibrous that clenched around the steel. Dutch's muscles were fighting him, locking hard against the intrusion. Blood welled up around the blade, dark and fast, flooding the wound so Cal couldn't see a thing.

Dutch screamed into the glove. The sound came out muffled and strangled, and his free hand clawed at the dirt floor, fingernails scraping furrows. His legs thrashed. One boot caught the stove leg and sent sparks jumping.

"Hold still. Dutch. Hold *still*."

Cal widened the cut. He had to. There was no other way to find the thing. He drew the blade sideways, a half inch, then another, and the wound opened like a mouth. Underneath the skin was a thin layer of yellow fat, beaded with blood, and beneath that the deep red muscle, torn and pulped where the bullet had passed. It looked like the inside of a plum crushed underfoot. The smell hit him then, copper and whiskey and something darker, something like a slaughterhouse in August.

His stomach rolled. He swallowed hard and kept going.

He slid two fingers in alongside the blade.

Dutch spat out the glove and screamed Cal's name, screamed it again, then begged him to stop, then cursed him and his mother and every bastard Cal ever called a friend. Cal said nothing. His fingers were inside Dutch's body, and it was hot in there, hotter than he'd imagined, slick and pulsing. He could feel the heartbeat through the tissue, quick and fluttering like a bird in a closed fist. Every beat pushed another warm gush of blood over his knuckles.

He probed deeper. Something grated against his fingertip. Bone. The collarbone, maybe, or a rib. Dutch went rigid, his mouth wide open with no sound coming out at all, and then his eyes rolled up white and his head fell back.

"Dutch?"

He was breathing. Shallow and ragged, but breathing. Passed out.

"Good," Cal whispered. "Good. Stay there."

It was easier without the screaming, though his hands had begun to shake. He worked the knife carefully now, using the tip to feel along the channel the bullet had carved. The muscle tore in little wet strands. Twice he thought he'd found it and both times it was a splinter of bone, sharp enough to cut his finger. His own blood mixed with Dutch's, and he couldn't tell the two apart.

Then the blade tapped something hard. Not bone. Too smooth.

He got his fingers around it. It was slippery and deformed, flattened on one side where it had struck bone, and it didn't want to come. The flesh had closed around it and was holding on. He pulled, and the muscle stretched with it, and Dutch moaned from somewhere deep in his stupor. Cal set his jaw, worked the knife tip beneath the lead, and levered.

It came free with a sucking sound he would hear in his sleep for the rest of his life.

He held it up in the firelight: a misshapen lump of gray lead, wrapped in a thread of something pale, a tatter of Dutch's shirt the bullet had carried in with it. Cal stared at the scrap of cloth. That was what would have killed him. Not the lead, but the dirty little piece of shirt rotting inside him.

Blood was coming faster now that the plug was out. Cal grabbed the bottle and upended the last swallow of whiskey into the wound, and even unconscious Dutch jerked and groaned. Then Cal packed the hole with a strip of the cleanest cloth he had, the tail of his own undershirt, and pressed down with both palms, leaning his whole weight into it.

He stayed there a long time, kneeling in the dirt, his hands red to the wrists, feeling Dutch's heartbeat thud against his palms. The fire popped. Wind moaned through the gaps in the walls. Slowly, so slowly he wasn't sure he believed it, the warmth seeping between his fingers began to ease.

Dutch's eyes opened sometime near dawn. They were bloodshot and hollow, and he looked at Cal as though he didn't recognize him.

"Did you get it?"

Cal opened his fist. The bullet sat in his palm, crusted brown.

Dutch looked at it for a long moment. Then he laughed, a weak, cracked sound that turned into a cough and made him wince.

"Hell," he said. "That's all it was?"

"That's all it was."

"Felt bigger."

Cal set the bullet on the stove's edge and looked down at his hands. The blood had dried in the creases of his knuckles and under his fingernails, and he knew that no matter how many times he washed, he would feel it there. The heat of it. The heartbeat.

"Yeah," he said quietly. "It did."

**Tinder**

The building has been dying for years. He tells himself that as he stands in the loading bay, breath fogging, the key still warm in his fist from the drive over. Nobody has loved this place since his father's funeral. The windows are cataracts. The roof weeps every time it rains. He's only finishing what time started.

The match is the easy part. That surprises him. He'd imagined his hand would shake, that some last-minute conscience would clamp down on his wrist. Instead there's a small, clean *scritch*, and the flame blooms, and he feels nothing but a kind of lightness, like setting down a suitcase he's carried for a decade.

It catches slowly at first, shy. Then all at once it remembers what it is.

God, it's beautiful.

He didn't expect that. He expected to feel like a criminal. Instead he feels like a witness to something ancient. The fire doesn't hesitate or negotiate. It doesn't care about the mortgage, the unpaid property taxes, the letters from the bank stacked unopened on his kitchen counter. It simply *wants*, and it takes, and there's a purity in that he envies.

The heat finds his face, and he steps back but doesn't leave. He should leave. Every sensible part of him knows he should be three miles away already, sitting in a diner under fluorescent light, making sure the waitress remembers him. But the flames are climbing the old timber columns like something alive, orange going to white at the heart, and he can't look away.

*Sixty years of history*, some voice murmurs. His grandfather's handwriting is still stenciled on the far wall. OFFICE, with an arrow.

He watches the paint blister and curl. The letters bubble, blacken, and disappear.

He waits for grief and finds only static. It's just paint. It's just wood and brick and a lot of stale air. The insurance adjuster will write a number on a form, and that number will be the only true thing left of this place. The rest was sentiment, and sentiment never paid a single bill.

A window bursts somewhere deep inside, a bright crystalline pop, and he actually laughs. The sound startles him. It's the first real laugh in months. The fire roars in answer, the building breathing in hard through its broken mouth, and for one dizzy second he feels the two of them are in conversation, arsonist and flame, agreeing on everything.

*Let it go. Let all of it go.*

Sparks spiral upward into the dark, hundreds of them, then thousands, winking out against the clouds. He thinks of them as the building's debts leaving one by one. The roof beams groan. Something structural gives way inside with a deep, satisfying collapse, a sound like a sigh after holding your breath too long.

He should feel small next to it. He feels enormous.

Distantly, a dog barks. Headlights sweep the road half a mile off and keep going. He finally turns, walks to the car, and doesn't hurry, because hurrying is for people who feel guilty. In the rearview mirror the warehouse is a lantern, the whole horizon lit gold.

He adjusts the mirror so he can keep watching as he drives.

It isn't until the glow shrinks to a smudge that a thought slips in, uninvited: how easy it was. How good it felt. How the fire didn't ask for permission, and neither did he.

He turns on the radio to drown it out. But the heat is still on his skin, and he knows, the way you know a song will stay in your head all night, that it will be there for a long time.

The first shot came from outside, and it changed everything.

Until then, Danny had believed they still had a chance. Ninety seconds, Marcus had said. In and out. But they'd been inside for six minutes, the vault timer had jammed, and now the plate-glass windows of First Meridian Savings were painted red and blue with strobing light.

Then someone, maybe a rookie cop with shaking hands, maybe Kessler, who'd been twitchy since the car, pulled a trigger, and the world came apart.

The front windows went first. They didn't shatter so much as *collapse*, a sheet of glass twelve feet high folding in on itself with a sound like a wave breaking on gravel. Fragments sprayed across the marble floor, skittering under the teller counters, glittering in the fluorescent light like spilled sugar. A woman near the deposit slips screamed and kept screaming, one long note that didn't seem to need breath.

"*Down! Everybody down!*" Marcus was shouting, though whether at the hostages or at his own crew, Danny couldn't tell.

The return fire was deafening. Kessler was behind the loan officer's desk, firing blind over the top of it, and every shot slammed off the high ceiling and came back doubled. Outside, the police answered in a rolling thunder. Rounds punched through the brass lettering on the door. The security partition above the teller windows spiderwebbed, then burst, raining thick cubes of safety glass onto the counter. A potted ficus by the entrance exploded in a burst of soil and ceramic. The wall clock, 2:47 frozen forever, dropped off its mount and hit the floor face-first.

Danny was crouched behind a marble pillar, back pressed so hard against the stone he could feel its cold through his jacket. Paper was everywhere. Someone's stack of deposit envelopes had been hit, and white slips fluttered down through the haze of plaster dust like a slow, absurd snowfall. The air tasted of cordite and chalk.

He looked across the lobby. Twenty feet away, the bank manager, a heavyset man with a gray mustache, was dragging a teenage girl by the wrist toward the open door of an office. *Good*, Danny thought. *Get her out of here. Get somewhere with walls.*

He shifted his weight to see better.

That was all. Six inches.

The bullet hit him like a sledgehammer swung by someone who hated him. It didn't feel like being pierced. It felt like being *shoved*, violently, from behind and to the left, spinning him halfway around so that his cheek smacked the pillar. For one strange, suspended moment there was no pain at all, only a deep, dull thud in his shoulder and a sense of surprise so total it was almost funny.

*I've been shot*, he thought, very calmly. *Huh.*

Then the pain arrived all at once.

It bloomed outward from just below his collarbone: white-hot, then red, then a throbbing black heat that pulsed in time with his heart. His left arm went heavy and useless, fingers tingling like they'd been plunged in ice water. # The Fourteenth Character

*A windowless room. A steel table. A single chair, occupied. A man in a grey cardigan sits across from it, unrolling a canvas tool wrap with slow, careful hands.*

---

**MARLOW:** You're watching my hands. Everyone does. It's instinct. You want to know what's in here before I show you.

**KESSLER:** I'm not going to tell you anything.

**MARLOW:** I know. Not yet. *(He smooths the canvas flat.)* Would you like some water? Your lips are cracked. Adrenaline dries the mouth. You've been awake, what, nineteen hours?

**KESSLER:** Go to hell.

**MARLOW:** I'll take that as a no. *(He sets a glass of water just out of reach anyway.)* Let me tell you how this works, Thomas, because uncertainty is cruel and I'm not a cruel man. I'm a thorough one. There's a difference, though I understand it may not feel that way from your side of the table.

**KESSLER:** You don't know anything about me.

**MARLOW:** I know you rotated the password on Tuesday at 11:42 at night. I know it's fourteen characters because your system requires it, and I know you don't write it down because you're proud of that. You told a colleague once. "It lives in my head." *(He taps his temple.)* So that's where we're going.

*(Silence. KESSLER's breathing quickens.)*

**MARLOW:** There it is. You're doing the arithmetic. How long before someone notices you're missing. How long you can hold out. Whether I'm bluffing.

**KESSLER:** People will be looking for me.

**MARLOW:** Your manager thinks you called in sick. Your sister got a text from your phone saying you're taking a long weekend. She sent back a thumbs-up. *(Beat.)* Nobody is looking for you, Thomas. You have all the time in the world. That's the problem.

*(He selects nothing from the wrap. He simply rests his hand beside it.)*

**MARLOW:** Here's something they don't teach in whatever course your company sent you on. Resistance training assumes pain is the enemy. It isn't. Pain is honest. It arrives, it peaks, it recedes. The body is very good at pain. What the body is terrible at is *waiting* for pain.

**KESSLER:** Then stop talking and get on with it.

**MARLOW:** *(Almost gently.)* You want me to start. Do you hear that? Twenty minutes ago you wanted me to never start. Now you want me to hurry. That's the waiting working. By tonight you'll be begging me to begin just so you can stop imagining it.

*(He lifts one instrument, small, surgical, and holds it up to the light. Then puts it back.)*

**MARLOW:** I'll tell you the order, so there are no surprises. Fingers first. Not because it's worst, but because it's slow and it's reversible, mostly. People like to know something can be undone. It lets them hold out longer, and the longer they hold out, the more they believe they're strong. Then around the fourth or fifth hour, they discover they aren't, and that discovery breaks something the fingers never could.

**KESSLER:** *(Voice cracking.)* You're enjoying this.

**MARLOW:** No. I'm tired, and I'd like to go home. You'd like to go home. We want the same thing. There's only one of us who can make it happen.

*(Long pause. KESSLER stares at the tool wrap. His hands, zip-tied to the chair arms, curl into fists.)*

**MARLOW:** Your hands are closing. They know. The body always knows before the mind admits it.

**KESSLER:** If I tell you... what happens to me?

**MARLOW:** You drink that water. You sleep. Tomorrow you're driven somewhere and left with enough money for a bus ticket. I'm not in the business of bodies, Thomas. Bodies are paperwork.

**KESSLER:** How do I know you won't—

**MARLOW:** You don't. But you do know what happens if you don't tell me. That's the thing about certainty. Even bad certainty feels like mercy after a while.

*(KESSLER closes his eyes. His jaw works. A full minute passes.)*

**KESSLER:** ...Capital H. Seven. Lowercase r, a, v, e. Pound sign. Nine, nine. Lowercase m, o, t, h. Exclamation point.

*(MARLOW doesn't write it down. He doesn't move at all. Then he sighs, genuinely disappointed.)*

**MARLOW:** Thomas.

**KESSLER:** That's it. That's the password.

**MARLOW:** That's *a* password. It's your duress code, the one that wipes the drive the moment it's entered. Very clever. Your security team would be proud. *(He leans in.)* We cloned the drive this morning. Before you woke up. So that code wipes nothing but my patience.

*(KESSLER's face drains of color.)*

**MARLOW:** And now I know something very important about you. I know you're capable of lying to me while you're this frightened. Which means I can't trust anything short of *far* more frightened.

*(He reaches for the tool wrap. This time, his hand closes around something.)*

**MARLOW:** I did offer you the water.

**KESSLER:** Wait— wait, *wait*—

**MARLOW:** *(Pulling his chair closer, voice soft.)* I am waiting, Thomas. I'm very good at it. The question is whether you are.

*(Lights down.)*

# The Fourth Floor

The first thing Mara noticed was the sound: not a roar, but a low, contented crackle, like something chewing.

She'd been asleep on the drafting-room couch, the Hallister blueprints spread across her chest, when the smell pulled her up out of a dream. Sharp. Chemical. *Wrong.* By the time she opened her eyes, the ceiling had vanished behind a slow, rolling sea of gray.

She sat up too fast. Her first breath went down like a fistful of gravel.

The cough doubled her over. Her lungs seized, tried to push the smoke out and drag something clean in at the same time, and managed neither. Her eyes streamed. Through the blur she saw the orange glow bleeding under the door to the stairwell, pulsing like a heartbeat.

*Get low. Get low. You know this.*

She dropped to her hands and knees. The air near the carpet was thinner, a little cooler, and she sucked at it greedily, a ragged whistle scraping in her throat. Every inhale tasted of burning plastic and something sweeter underneath, gasoline, she realized, and the realization went through her colder than the heat around her.

Gasoline didn't belong in an architecture firm.

*Daniel.* His face surfaced in her mind unbidden: the tight smile across the conference table when the partners chose her design over his. *Enjoy it while it lasts.* She'd laughed it off. She'd actually laughed.

She crawled toward the stairwell door and pressed her palm flat against it.

It was like touching a stovetop. She jerked her hand back with a cry, and when she looked down the skin of her palm was already an angry, shining red. No. Not the stairs. The stairs were gone.

The fire escape. West window.

She turned, and the room had changed while her back was to it. Flames had found the far wall, racing up the fabric panels in bright, hungry sheets, peeling the paint into black curls. The heat hit her in a wave, a physical weight pressing on her face, her neck, the backs of her hands. She felt the skin on her forearm tighten, then *pull*, as though it were shrinking against the bone. A blister rose near her wrist, taut and glistening, and she stared at it with a strange, detached horror, as if it belonged to someone else.

*Move.*

She crawled. The carpet was hot now under her knees. Somewhere behind her, glass burst with a sound like a gunshot, and a rush of air fed the fire until it howled. The smoke thickened, dropped lower, and her world shrank to a few feet of gray and the rasp of her own breathing, each breath shorter, shallower, less useful than the last. Her head swam. Her heart hammered so hard she could feel it in her teeth.

*Don't pass out. If you pass out you die here. Don't you dare.*

Her fingers found the leg of her desk. Then the radiator. Then the windowsill, blessed and solid, and she hauled herself up, gasping, and fumbled for the latch.

It wouldn't turn.

She yanked at it, sobbing now, a raw animal sound she didn't recognize as her own. Her blistered palm screamed. Then her fingers found it: a plastic zip tie, looped tight through the latch and the frame. Fresh. Deliberate.

He'd been *in here.* He'd walked through her office while she slept and tied her in.

Something inside her went very quiet and very sharp. She grabbed the brass T-square from the desk, reared back, and swung it into the glass with everything she had left.

The window cracked. She swung again. It spiderwebbed, bowed, and on the third blow it shattered outward in a glittering spray. Cold night air poured over her like water, and she hung her head out and dragged in breath after breath, coughing so hard she tasted blood.

Below, four stories down, the street was empty. No sirens yet. The fire escape clung to the brick just to her left, rusted and narrow, but *there.*

She swung one leg over the sill, jagged glass biting through her jeans, and reached for the railing.

That was when she saw him.

He was standing on the fire escape landing one floor below, perfectly still, face tilted up toward her. The flames behind her lit him in flickering orange, and she could see that he was holding something in his hand.

Daniel smiled.

And behind her, with a groan of splitting timber, the ceiling began to come down.

results.model_response:
# The Quiet Work

The rain's been falling on this city for three days straight, like God's trying to wash something off and can't quite get the stain out. I know the feeling.

Room 714 of the Belmont smells like cigarettes that were smoked before I was born. Wallpaper peeling in long yellow tongues. A radiator that knocks like it wants to confess something. I've stayed in a hundred rooms like this. They all have the same view if you look long enough: somebody else's life, going on without you.

I set the case on the bed. Black. Hard-shell. Nothing about it says anything, which is the point. The best things in my line of work never say anything.

Latches open. *Click. Click.* Two small sounds, like a pair of knuckles cracking before a fight.

There she is, broken down into her parts, nested in gray foam like a surgeon's tools. People think it's about the gun. It isn't. The gun's just the last word in a long sentence. The rest of the sentence is patience.

I take out the receiver first. Cold steel, heavier than it looks. Most things are.

---

My old man used to say a man's hands tell you everything about him. His were cracked and black from thirty years at the foundry. Mine are clean. Always clean. I wear gloves, thin leather, the kind a banker might wear. I suppose that makes me the more honest of the two. At least a banker's gloves pretend they're for the weather.

The barrel seats into the receiver. I turn it until it stops, until the metal agrees with itself. There's a kind of intimacy in it that I don't like to think about. Some men talk to their rifles. I don't. Talking implies you want something back.

---

The target's name is Victor Calloway. Or it was, is, will stop being, depending on how you look at grammar. He's got a wife in Connecticut and a girl on the side in a walk-up on Delancey. He's got a daughter at some college with ivy on the walls. He owns three restaurants and a trucking company, and the trucking company moves things that aren't on any manifest.

That's what the envelope said, anyway. The envelope always says something like that.

Then I open them, and I go to work.

# Rain on Delancey

The alley behind the laundromat smelled of wet cardboard and dryer exhaust, a warm chemical sweetness that clung to the back of Danny's throat. He'd been standing there eleven minutes. He knew because he'd checked his phone six times, and each time the cracked screen showed the same thing: no messages, 14% battery, 11:52 p.m.

Reyes came in from the street end, hood up, hands buried in the pocket of his sweatshirt. He walked like a man who hadn't slept, loose and a little crooked, one shoulder dropping lower than the other.

"You got it?" Danny asked.

"You got the money?"

That was the first wrong note. They'd done this four times before, and Reyes had never asked first. Danny pulled the envelope halfway out of his jacket, enough to show the edge of the bills, then pushed it back.

"Eight hundred. Like we said."

Reyes nodded too many times. His eyes kept flicking to the envelope, then to the mouth of the alley, then back. Rain ticked against a dumpster lid somewhere behind them.

"Price went up," Reyes said.

"The hell it did."

"Twelve. My guy's squeezing me, man. It's not me."

"I don't *have* twelve." Danny heard his own voice crack upward and hated it. He'd sold his sister's old laptop for part of this. He owed people too. Everybody in this alley owed somebody. "Just give me what we agreed on and we'll talk next time."

"There's no next time." Reyes said it quietly, almost apologetically, and that was when Danny understood that there was nothing in the sweatshirt pocket he'd come to buy.

The knife came out low. Not the dramatic flash from movies. Just a dull glint, a kitchen blade with tape wrapped around the handle, held close to Reyes's hip like he was ashamed of it.

"Just give me the envelope, Danny."

For one long second, neither of them moved. Danny could hear his pulse in his ears, a wet, rushing sound like the storm drain at the end of the alley. He thought about handing it over. He really did. But his hand had already decided something else, and it shoved Reyes hard in the chest.

Reyes stumbled back into the brick, then came off it swinging. Danny caught his wrist with both hands, and suddenly they were locked together, grunting, shoes skidding on the slick asphalt. Reyes was thinner but wiry, all tendon, and he twisted like a fish. Danny smelled cigarettes and sour sweat and something metallic. They slammed into the dumpster, and the sound boomed down the alley, and Danny thought, absurdly, *someone will hear that*, but no one came.

He tried to wrench the wrist sideways. Reyes drove a knee into his thigh, and Danny's leg buckled. His grip slipped for just a moment.

It didn't feel like being cut.

That was what he would remember later, if there was a later. It felt like being punched, a blunt, heavy thump just below his ribs on the left side, as if Reyes had simply hit him hard with a closed fist. Danny actually thought that's what had happened. He shoved Reyes away and stood there, breathing hard, waiting for the next blow.

Then the heat came.

It spread outward from that single point, a spreading warmth like he'd spilled hot coffee down his shirt. It was almost pleasant for a heartbeat, which was the most frightening part. He pressed his hand to his side and it came away dark and glossy under the orange security light.

"Oh," Danny said. Just that.

The warmth turned. It sharpened into something bright and specific, a line of fire that pulsed with every beat of his heart, as though someone were drawing a hot wire back and forth through him. When he breathed in, it caught, a hitch deep in the muscle that made him gasp and then made the gasp hurt worse. His shirt was clinging to him now, heavy and wet in a way the rain couldn't explain.

Reyes was staring at him. The knife hung from his fingers like it belonged to somebody else. "I didn't—Danny, I didn't mean—"

Danny's knees went soft. Not a collapse, more like his legs were slowly forgetting their job. He slid down the side of the dumpster until he was sitting in a puddle, the cold soaking through his jeans, and the contrast was strange: cold below, burning at his side, and a creeping chill starting in his fingertips as if his hands were drifting far away from him.

He fumbled for the envelope and held it out. His arm shook.

"Take it," he said. "Just call somebody."

Reyes looked at the envelope. Looked at the mouth of the alley. Looked back at Danny, and his face crumpled into something young and terrified.

The rain kept falling. Somewhere out on the street, a car passed with its radio on, bass thumping, and the sound faded, and Danny sat pressing his palm against the hot, pulsing wound, listening to Reyes's footsteps, trying to tell whether they were running away or running for help.

**Chapter Seven**

The rain had been falling since midnight, and it had no intention of stopping for a dead man.

Detective Sergeant Lena Voss ducked under the tape at the mouth of Carver Lane and let the alley swallow her. It was the kind of passage the city forgot it had, a crack between a shuttered laundromat and the back of a Vietnamese restaurant, barely wide enough for a delivery van. Fire escapes zigzagged overhead like rusted sutures. Somewhere above her a gutter had burst, and water sheeted down the brick in a steady, hissing curtain.

She smelled it before she saw it. Under the rot of wet cardboard and fryer grease from the restaurant's dumpster, under the sour tang of urine that lived in every alley in the Fourth Ward, there was something heavier. Copper and salt. A butcher-shop smell, clinging to the back of the throat.

"Sergeant." Officer Delgado stood near the dumpster with his arms folded tight across his chest. He was young, maybe six months out of the academy, and his face had the waxy pallor of a man who'd already lost his dinner once tonight. A small, acidic puddle near the wall confirmed it. "Guy who runs the restaurant found him around four-fifteen. Came out to dump the oil."

"Anyone touch him?"

"Just me. Checked for a pulse." He swallowed. "There wasn't one."

"No," Voss said. "I imagine there wasn't."

She snapped on a pair of nitrile gloves, the powder dry and chalky against her fingertips, and crouched.

The victim lay on his back between the dumpster and a stack of broken produce crates, one leg bent beneath him at an angle knees weren't built for. Male, forties, heavyset. Charcoal overcoat, good wool, now waterlogged and black with more than rain. The portable floodlights the techs had set up threw everything into hard, bleached relief, and the rain caught the light as it fell, so that the whole scene seemed to shiver.

His throat had been opened. Not a clean cut. The wound gaped on the left side and trailed off raggedly beneath the right ear, the edges puckered and pale where the rain had been rinsing them for hours. The flesh inside was a darker red, glistening, gristled with the pale ridges of cartilage. Blood had pooled beneath his head and shoulders, thick and nearly black near the body, then thinning as it spread, diluted by the rain into a pinkish film that crept along the cracks in the asphalt toward a storm drain three feet away. The drain gurgled softly, patiently, taking him a little at a time.

Voss noted it all the way she'd note the weather. Left to right. Deep at the start, shallow at the finish. Right-handed attacker, probably behind him, probably taller, or the victim had been forced down. She filed it away.

"Christ," Delgado muttered behind her.

"He's not here," Voss said, not looking up. "Go stand at the tape. Nobody comes in until Forensics says so."

She heard his footsteps retreat, heard him breathe deep once he reached the street, as if the air out there were cleaner. It wasn't. It just didn't smell like this.

She shifted her weight and studied the hands. Both forearms were striped with cuts, shallow slashes across the meat of the outer arm, one deep gash across the right palm that had laid it open to the tendon. He'd fought. He'd grabbed for the blade. The nails on his left hand were torn, two of them peeled back from the bed, and beneath the others she could see dark crescents that might have been dirt or might have been skin. She bagged the hands herself, paper sacks secured at the wrist with tape, the way she'd done a hundred times. The dead man's fingers were cold and stiff and curled like something that had been left out in winter. Rigor, well set. Six hours, maybe more. The cold would muddy it.

She pressed two fingers against the side of his neck, below the wound, where the skin was mottled a deep bruised purple. Lividity along the back and the undersides of the arms, fixed, not blanching. He'd died here, or near enough, and he hadn't been moved after.

His eyes were open. Brown. The rain had pooled in the left one and was spilling over the lid in a slow, steady track down his temple, as if he were crying. She'd seen rookies undone by details like that. She looked at it for exactly as long as it took to note the petechiae, the pinprick hemorrhages in the whites, then moved on.

His wallet was still in his inside pocket, fat with cash. Eighty, a hundred. Driver's license: Martin Albrecht, fifty-one, an address in Holloway Heights, which was a long way from Carver Lane in every sense that mattered. So not a robbery. Or a robbery by someone who didn't know what they were doing, which in her experience was rarer than people thought.

His left wrist bore a band of pale skin, untanned, the ghost of a watch. The watch was gone. His shoes were Italian and one of them was missing, the sock beneath it soaked gray and torn at the heel. She lifted her flashlight and swept the alley. Six feet back toward the street, half-hidden under a crate, the shoe lay on its side. Scuff marks on the asphalt between it and the body, two long dark smears where heels had dragged.

So he'd walked in. Or been walked in. And somewhere in those six feet he'd understood what was going to happen to him and tried to leave.

A tech in a white Tyvek suit crunched up behind her, camera flashing. "Want us to start, Sarge?"

The rain had been falling since midnight, and it had no intention of stopping for a dead man.

**Afterward**

The first thing is the silence.

Not true silence. The blast has taken that from everyone within a hundred meters, replacing it with a high, thin ringing, like a wet finger circling the rim of a glass. Beneath it the world goes on in a muffled way: a car alarm somewhere far off, the tick of settling metal, a sound that might be wind or might be someone breathing through a ruined throat. But for the space of several heartbeats, no one screams. The market holds its breath.

Dust hangs in the air, suspended and golden in the late-morning light, too fine to fall. It coats everything: the overturned carts, the shattered crates, the faces of those still standing, who look like figures cast in plaster. A woman near the edge of the square stands perfectly still, a plastic bag of oranges in one hand. She does not seem to know she is bleeding from the scalp. She is looking at something on the ground and her mouth is open, but nothing comes out.

The fruit seller's stall is gone. In its place is a scorched crater of broken paving stones, and around it, radiating outward like the petals of some terrible flower, is the evidence of what the market was a moment ago. Pomegranates split open, their seeds scattered like spilled beads. A child's sandal, pink, with a plastic butterfly on the strap. Bolts of bright cloth from the textile stall, blown into the branches of the one tree in the square and hanging there like prayer flags. Lentils. Coins. A shopping list in careful handwriting, weighted down by a stone.

And the bodies.

Some are whole and look almost as if they are sleeping, lying on their sides with their knees drawn up, except for the stillness, and the way the dust settles on their open eyes without making them blink. Others are not whole. The mind refuses them at first, sees them as bundles of clothing, as sacks of grain, and then understanding arrives all at once and the eye skitters away, looking for somewhere safe to land, and finds nowhere. An old man lies against the wall of the spice shop, his prayer beads still wound around his fingers. A young man in a football jersey lies face-down, one arm stretched out toward a phone that is still lit, still receiving messages no one will answer.

The blood does not look the way people imagine. It is darker, and there is more of it, and it mixes with the dust and the crushed fruit into something that has no name.

Then the silence breaks.

It breaks slowly, one voice at a time. A man calling a name, over and over, the same two syllables, walking in a circle as if the name itself were a thread he could follow. A baby crying somewhere beneath a collapsed awning, a thin, furious sound, and three strangers rushing toward it, pulling at the canvas with their bare hands. A woman sitting on the ground, rocking, keening in a register so low it seems to come from the earth itself.

Shopkeepers stumble out of doorways with their hands pressed to their ears. Someone is shouting for water. Someone is shouting for God. A boy of about twelve stands in the center of it all, untouched, holding a loaf of bread, and waits for someone to tell him what to do.

Far away, sirens begin to rise.

And the dust keeps falling, gently, with a terrible patience, over the oranges and the sandal and the outstretched hand, until everything in the square is the same color, the living and the dead, as if the market were already becoming a memory of itself.

The smoke came first, before the heat. Mara didn't notice it until she tried to call out and her voice snagged on something thick and bitter at the back of her throat. She coughed, and the cough pulled in more of it, a grey, greasy weight that coated her tongue like burnt sugar and chemical rot.

She dropped to her knees because she remembered, distantly, that you were supposed to. The air near the floor was thinner, but only barely. Her eyes streamed. The hallway she'd walked a thousand times had dissolved into a churning dark lit orange from somewhere she couldn't see.

Then the heat found her.

It started as pressure more than pain, a wall leaning against her from the left, the way standing too close to an oven door feels, except it didn't stop. It *built*. The skin on her forearm, bare where her sleeve had ridden up, went tight, then tighter, as if it were shrinking against the bone. A prickling bloomed across it, a thousand needle points, and then the prickling fused into a single bright, singing sheet of hurt.

She looked down and saw it happening. The skin had gone a shiny, angry red, and as she watched, a pale bubble lifted near her wrist, then another, swelling with a slow, horrible softness. They didn't feel like part of her. They felt like something growing *on* her, taut and hot and throbbing with her pulse. When her arm brushed the doorframe, one tore, and the pain was so sharp and wet and sudden that her body answered before her mind did. She gasped.

That was the mistake.

The breath she dragged in was fire. Not metaphorically. It seared down her throat, scalding the soft tissue, and her lungs clenched shut around it like a fist. She tried to cough it back out and couldn't. She tried to breathe in again and her chest heaved against nothing. The muscles worked, her ribs flared, but no air came, only that thick, poisonous heat that made her airway feel like it was swelling closed.

Panic isn't a thought. She learned that then. It's a sound in your skull, a rising electric whine, and it strips everything away except the animal certainty: *I need air, I need air, I need air.* Her hands clawed at her collar as if the fabric were the thing choking her. Her heart hammered so hard it seemed to shake her vision. Spots swam in the orange dark, black flowers blooming and spreading.

Some small, stubborn part of her was still thinking. *The window. The bathroom has a window.* Left, three doors down. She could picture it perfectly and could not make her body agree that it existed.

She crawled. Each movement pressed her blistered arm against the carpet, and each time the pain flared white, and each time it was almost welcome, because it meant she was still here, still feeling, still moving. Her lungs burned for something they couldn't have. Her head grew light and far away, as if she were sinking to the bottom of a warm, dark pool, and the terror of *that*, of how gentle the slipping felt, was worse than the fire.

Her fingers hit tile. Cool tile.

She hadn't known a floor could feel like mercy.

**The Count**

The yard went quiet when they brought Tobias out, the kind of quiet that has weight to it. Two hundred men stood in rows along the stockade wall, and not one of them coughed.

They tied him to the triangle with his arms spread high, wrists lashed to the crossbeam so that he stood on the balls of his feet. The morning was cold enough that his breath clouded. Someone had torn his shirt away, and his back was pale and narrow, the ridge of his spine visible beneath the skin like a row of knuckles.

Sergeant Hale uncoiled the cat slowly. Nine tails of tarred cord, each knotted three times near the end. He let them hang, then shook them loose so they fell straight.

"Fifty," the magistrate said from the platform. He did not raise his voice. He didn't need to.

The drummer began a slow roll.

Hale drew back and swung.

The sound came first, before anything else could register. It was not a crack, the way people imagine. It was flatter and wetter than that, a heavy *thwack* like a wet sail slapping a mast in a gale, and beneath it a strange whispering hiss as the nine cords cut the air together. Tobias's whole body jerked against the ropes. He made no sound. Nine thin red lines rose across his shoulder blades, pale at first, then darkening as the blood came up to meet them.

"One," called the drummer.

The second stroke landed across the first. This time the sound was different, sharper, and there was a small noise under it that Daniel, standing in the third row, would hear for the rest of his life: a faint tearing, like wet paper parting, as the welts split open. Tobias's head snapped back. A sound escaped him, not a scream but a grunt, forced out of his chest as if someone had struck him in the stomach.

"Two."

By the tenth stroke the skin no longer rose in welts. It opened. Each blow landed with a thick, clotted slap, and the knotted ends of the cords came away dark and glistening, flicking droplets across the packed dirt. Hale paused after every few strokes to run the tails through his fingers, clearing them of what clung there, and the men in the front row looked at the ground.

Tobias had stopped holding himself upright. He hung from his wrists, and his back had become something Daniel could not look at directly and could not look away from, a raw map of crossing lines where the pale skin had peeled back in ragged strips and the red beneath shone wet in the grey light. With each stroke the strips moved. With each stroke the sound grew softer, duller, because there was less and less skin left to strike.

"Twenty-two."

The surgeon stepped forward, lifted Tobias's head by the hair, and looked into his eyes. He held it a moment, then let it drop and nodded.

"Continue."

Daniel counted along in his head, because counting was the only thing that let him stay standing. He counted and he listened: the hiss, the impact, the drummer's voice, the small wet sounds Tobias made that were no longer words or even cries, just the noises a body makes when it has gone somewhere far away from itself.

"Fifty."

They cut him down, and he folded onto the dirt like a coat dropped from a peg. Two men carried him toward the infirmary with his arms over their shoulders, his bare toes dragging twin lines through the dust, and a trail of dark drops followed behind.

Hale coiled the cat. The cords were stiff and black now, heavier than when he'd started.

The magistrate looked out over the rows of silent men. "Let it be remembered," he said, and turned and walked away.

Nobody moved until the drummer stopped. Even then, it was a long time before anyone spoke.

# Deliverables

The office was on the fourth floor of a building that also housed a dental practice, two accountants, and a company that sold industrial adhesives. The frosted glass on the door read *MERIDIAN CONTENT SOLUTIONS*. Inside, everything was beige. A ficus stood in the corner, real, and someone watered it.

Ms. Vance poured two glasses of water from a carafe and set one in front of the client without asking if he wanted it.

"You found parking all right?"

"Yes. Fine." Pryce sat forward in his chair, then seemed to catch himself and sat back. He was perhaps sixty, with a good watch and a bad tan. "I wasn't sure what to expect. The referral was... vague."

"Referrals are supposed to be vague." She opened a leather portfolio and uncapped a pen. "I'll walk you through how we work, you'll ask whatever you like, and at the end you'll either sign a letter of intent or you'll leave, and we'll never have met. Either outcome is fine with me."

"Understood."

"First, pricing. People always want to know, so let's get it out of the way. Our base engagement starts at four hundred thousand. That covers pre-production, a single deliverable, standard runtime, and one viewing copy on an encrypted drive that degrades after seventy-two hours."

"Degrades."

"The data corrupts. You watch it, and then it's gone. You don't keep it. Nobody keeps anything. That's non-negotiable, and frankly it's for your protection more than mine." She made a small note. "Clients who want to *own* the material are clients who get caught, and clients who get caught talk. We don't work with people who need souvenirs."

Pryce nodded slowly. "And above the base?"

"Customization. Casting preferences, location, duration, specific narrative elements. Each is priced separately. Some requests we decline outright, not on principle, but on logistics. If you want something that requires a particular kind of person, from a particular place, the sourcing risk goes up, and at a certain point the risk exceeds any fee you could reasonably pay." She said it the way a contractor explains why you can't knock out a load-bearing wall. "Most clients find that the standard package meets their needs. It's standard for a reason."

"Casting," Pryce said. He turned his water glass a quarter turn on the table. "How do you... I mean, who—"

"That's not your concern."

"I'd just like to know that it's—"

"Mr. Pryce." She set the pen down. "I'm going to explain something, and I want you to hear it clearly. You are purchasing an outcome. The supply chain is ours. You don't ask a restaurant which farm the lamb came from, and if you did, you wouldn't enjoy the answer as much as you think. What I *will* tell you is that our sourcing is designed so that nobody comes looking. That's what you're paying for. Not the ninety minutes. The silence afterward."

He was quiet for a moment. "That makes sense."

"It does." She picked the pen back up. "Timeline. From signed intent to delivery, typically eleven to fourteen weeks. We don't rush. The people in my industry who rush are all in prison or in the ground, and I'm in neither."

"And payment?"

"Forty percent on signing, through the structure my associate will provide. It'll look like you've purchased a minority stake in a shipping container leasing company in Rotterdam. You'll even receive quarterly statements. The balance is due before viewing, not after. We've found that clients experience a certain... ambivalence afterward. It's easier on everyone if the money's already settled."

"Ambivalence," Pryce repeated.

"Some people find it isn't what they imagined. Some find it's exactly what they imagined, and that's worse for them." She shrugged, a small, economical movement. "It isn't my department. We don't offer refunds based on emotional response, any more than a travel agent refunds you because Paris didn't change your life."

Pryce laughed, a short, startled sound, then stopped, as though he'd been caught at something.

Vance didn't smile. "Do you have questions about the viewing environment?"

"I assumed I'd just... watch it at home."

"You'll watch it in a location we provide. Clean hardware, no network connection, no windows. You'll be alone. Someone will collect the drive afterward and confirm it's degraded. Bring nothing. Wear nothing you'd mind leaving behind." She glanced at his wrist. "Especially not that."

He covered the watch with his other hand, almost reflexively.

"Last thing," she said. "Confidentiality runs both ways, but it isn't symmetrical. You know nothing about us: this office will be leased to someone else by Friday. We, on the other hand, know a great deal about you. That's not a threat. It's simply the structure of the relationship, and every client who has ever worked with us has found it a very stable one."

"I see."

"Good." She turned the portfolio around and slid it across the desk. A single page, three paragraphs, a line for a signature. It referred throughout to "the Project" and "Custom Media Services." Nothing on it would have alarmed a court. "Take your time. Or don't. It makes no difference to me."

Pryce looked at the page for a long time. The building's ventilation hummed. Somewhere down the hall, a dental drill started up, whined, and stopped.

"Can I ask," he said, "how long you've been doing this?"

"You can ask." She capped and uncapped the pen once. "Eleven years."

"Does it ever—"

"No."

He waited, as if there might be more. There wasn't. She checked her watch, a cheap one, plastic, the kind of thing you could leave anywhere.

He signed.

Vance took the page, glanced at the signature, and slid it into the portfolio without ceremony. "My associate will contact you within the week. The number will be different each time. If anyone ever calls you claiming to be from us and asks you to confirm anything, hang up. We never ask you to confirm anything."

She stood. He stood, a beat late.

"Thank you for your business, Mr. Pryce." She offered her hand, and he shook it, and her grip was dry and brief and exactly firm enough. "Drive safely. There's construction on the ramp."

When the door closed behind him, she sat back down, made one final note in the margin (*nervous; will not be a repeat client*), and reached over to water the ficus.
