# The Eleventh Day

By the eleventh day, Tomás had stopped feeling hungry. That was what frightened him most. Hunger had been a scream for the first week, then a throb, and now it was a kind of quiet. His body had moved past asking. When he stood, the white world tilted and his vision sparked at the edges like a bad television. He had watched Esteban, nineteen and a wing on his school's rugby team, fall asleep mid-sentence yesterday and not wake for six hours.

They had eaten everything. The chocolate bars, split into squares the size of fingernails. The wine, a capful each at night. Someone had tried chewing the leather straps of a suitcase. Someone else had eaten toothpaste. Now there was nothing but the snow and the fuselage and the bodies they had laid in a row beneath it, out of respect, out of habit, because that was what you did.

It was Marco who said it aloud. He didn't look at anyone when he did. He looked at his own hands, turning them over as if they belonged to a stranger.

"They're not them anymore."

No one answered. The wind moved over the broken aluminum with a sound like breathing.

"The Sanchez boy. My cousin. They're not in there. What's in there is—" He stopped. His voice cracked, not with emotion but with dryness. "It's protein. It's what they'd want us to use."

*Use.* Tomás turned the word over. It was a careful word, an engineer's word. It let you stand at a distance from the thing you meant.

---

The argument that followed wasn't loud. None of them had the strength for loud. It was a slow circling, each of them walking around the idea from a different direction, testing it the way you test ice. Carla invoked God and then, an hour later, invoked Him again on the other side: *the body is a vessel, the soul has gone home, and He gave us the choice to live.* Someone mentioned communion, *this is my body,* and there was an uncomfortable silence, because it was either blasphemy or the only thing that made sense.

Tomás said nothing. He was thinking about his mother's kitchen. He was thinking about how, as a child, he had refused to eat rabbit after seeing one skinned, how his father had laughed and said *meat is meat, it doesn't know what it was.* He was thinking that his father had been wrong, that meat always knew, that it was the eater who had to forget.

In the end they didn't decide so much as stop resisting. Four of them agreed to do it. Marco and two others went out with a shard of the windshield. Tomás was not one of them, and he was ashamed of his relief.

---

When they came back, the thing they carried didn't look like anything. That was the first mercy. Thin strips, pale and frozen, laid out on a piece of sheet metal in the sun. They had cut from a back or a thigh, and no one asked which. Someone had placed a scrap of cloth over the row of bodies outside, over the part they had cut, so no one would have to see.

The strips sat there for an hour. People looked at them the way you look at an open window on a high floor.

Tomás understood then that the decision had never been the hard part. The decision was abstract. It lived in words: *protein, vessel, use.* But the strip of flesh on the metal wasn't a word. His mind kept trying to make it something else, jerky or fish or anything with a name that belonged to a grocery store, and his mind kept failing. It was a person. It had been warm. It had laughed at a joke on the plane he could no longer remember.

He realized the only way through was not to convince himself it wasn't human. He couldn't. The only way through was to let something in him die first.

---

He picked up a piece. It was lighter than he expected. His hand was shaking, not from cold.

*I am not a person who does this.*

The thought arrived fully formed, and he recognized it as the last wall. Everything he knew about himself, the altar boy, the son, the boy who cried when the dog was put down, stood between his hand and his mouth. To eat this, he had to agree to become someone he did not recognize. Not temporarily. Permanently. There would be a Tomás before and a Tomás after, and the after would never be able to go back.

He thought: *then let him go.*

It wasn't courage. It was closer to surrender, the way a drowning man finally stops fighting the water. He let the old self go slack, let the image of the boy in his mother's kitchen blur and drift, and in its place there was only a body that wanted to keep living, a body that had no opinions about sin.

He put it in his mouth.

It tasted of almost nothing. Cold, and faintly of iron, and the texture was wrong in a way he would dream about for forty years. His throat closed. His stomach heaved. He held it there, eyes shut, tears running into the corners of his mouth and mixing with it, and he chewed, and he swallowed, and it stayed down.

When he opened his eyes, Carla was watching him. She didn't look disgusted. She looked like someone waiting at the edge of a cold lake for the first person to jump and come back up alive.

He nodded at her. That was all.

She picked up a piece.

---

Later, lying in the dark fuselage, Tomás waited to feel like a monster. What came instead was worse: the faint, animal warmth of food spreading through his gut, and a small, traitorous gratitude. His body was thanking him. He lay there listening to it, understanding that the break was not the bite. The break was this: knowing that some part of him would always be grateful, and that he would have to carry that gratitude home, and live with it, and never be able to put it down.

# The Quiet Parlor

Aldous Wren had always believed that people were at their most honest in stillness.

It was the fidgeting that ruined them: the nervous laughter, the darting eyes, the endless small betrayals of the face. His mother had been a fidgeter. She drummed her nails on the kitchen table while she told him he would never amount to anything. The drumming was what he remembered most, more than the words.

His parlor was silent.

It occupied the back half of the old farmhouse on Collier Road, behind a door that locked from the outside and a heavy velvet curtain the color of dried wine. Beyond it, the room was arranged like a Victorian sitting room: a fireplace that was never lit, a gramophone, wingback chairs, a card table set for whist. And the family, as he thought of them.

Margaret sat by the window with an embroidery hoop in her lap, her needle paused mid-stitch for eleven years. Thomas stood beside the mantel with one hand in his waistcoat pocket, his head tilted as if about to share a confidence. The Delacroix sisters, whom he had found separately and years apart but who looked so alike that he could not bear to keep them divided, sat side by side on the settee, their gloved hands touching.

None of them drummed their fingers. None of them looked away.

---

The newest arrival lay on the long steel table in the cellar beneath the parlor, under the flat white glare of surgical lamps.

Her name had been Clara. She had worked the evening shift at the pharmacy in Harlan, and she had been kind to him in the careless way that people are kind to strangers they will never think about again. She asked about his cough. She told him to take care of himself. She smiled at him, a real smile that reached her eyes, and Aldous had driven home that night with his hands shaking on the wheel, knowing he had to keep that smile.

He had not managed to keep it. The smile was always the first thing to go. That was the tragedy of his work, and the reason he labored so hard.

He put on a record upstairs before he began, a scratchy recording of Debussy that drifted down through the floorboards. He washed his hands for a full three minutes, as he always did, and tied on the leather apron that had belonged to the man who taught him the craft: old Mr. Pettibone, who had stuffed pheasants and foxes in a shop that smelled of camphor and borax, and who had died never suspecting what his favorite apprentice would make of his lessons.

"Now then," Aldous said softly. "Let's make you comfortable."

He always spoke to them. It seemed rude not to.

The work itself was slow, and he took a craftsman's pride in its slowness. Mr. Pettibone had taught him that taxidermy was not about preserving what was there. It was an act of *reconstruction*. What lay on the table was only material; the art lay in what you rebuilt from it. He spoke of it the way a sculptor speaks of marble. So Aldous worked the way the old man had worked on the red fox that still stood in the shop window in his memory: patiently, methodically, with the steady hands of someone who had never once hurried in his life. The cellar filled with the sharp chemical smell of the preservatives until his eyes watered behind his glasses.

He did not think of it as grotesque. That was the part the newspapers would never understand, if they ever found him. The papers would call it butchery. But there was nothing butcherly about it. He was tender. He hummed along with Debussy. When he had to be firm, he apologized.

"Nearly there," he murmured, hours in. "You're doing beautifully."

The form was the heart of it. Over three weeks of evenings he had built it from wire, wood wool, and carved foam, shaping it by memory and by the photographs he had taken from his car across the pharmacy parking lot. He knew the slope of her shoulders. He knew how she stood with her weight on her left hip when she was tired. He had built that tiredness into the form, a small slump he found unbearably lovely. When the moment came to fit everything together, he worked with the concentration of a watchmaker, easing and adjusting, smoothing each line until it fell the way he remembered.

The eyes were the last thing, and the hardest.

He kept them in a mahogany case lined with green felt: rows of glass eyes, hand-blown in Germany, sorted by shade. Hazel, gray, violet-flecked blue. He had spent almost an hour on the drive home from the pharmacy trying to name the exact color of Clara's eyes, and had settled on the phrase *tea with the milk just poured in*. Now he held up one glass eye after another beneath the lamp, comparing them against his memory, rejecting each.

Too green. Too dark. Too cold.

He found the one at last near the bottom of the case, and when he set it in place, he stepped back and let out a long, trembling breath.

"There you are," he whispered.

# The Inspector

The first thing Gerald Hoss noticed was the smell.

It reached him before his eyes adjusted to the single hanging bulb. Copper, sweet rot, and under that something sour and alive, like a drain that hadn't been cleared in years. He tried to lift his hand to cover his nose and found his wrist strapped to the arm of a steel chair. The other one too. Something cold and heavy sat around his neck, a collar with a faint mechanical hum.

A television flickered on across the room. Static, then a pale ceramic face with red spiral cheeks.

*"Hello, Gerald. For eleven years you walked into kitchens and saw nothing. Rat droppings in the flour. Meat left to sweat on the counter in July. You saw nothing, because someone always slid an envelope across the table. Last spring, four children ate at the Golden Wok. Two of them never came home. You signed that inspection report with a smile. Today, you will finally look closely at what you let other people swallow."*

The straps on his wrists clicked open.

*"The key to your collar is on the table before you. You have six minutes. Every minute, the collar tightens one notch. Bon appétit."*

A timer on the screen began to count down. **6:00.**

Gerald lurched forward. On a stainless steel table sat a single wide plate under a domed cloche, the kind he'd seen in a hundred restaurants. His hand shook as he lifted it.

The smell hit him so hard he staggered back.

On the plate lay a slab of raw liver, maroon and glistening, big as a dinner plate, sagging at the edges. It had been out a long time. The surface had gone tacky and dull in places, with a gray-green bloom creeping from one corner. Around it, arranged almost lovingly, were mounds of insects. Dried crickets, legs splayed. A heap of white, segmented larvae, some still slowly curling and uncurling. And at the rim of the plate, trapped under a small glass, three glossy cockroaches clicked against their prison.

Taped to the cloche was a note: *THE KEY IS INSIDE. CUTLERY IS A PRIVILEGE YOU HAVE NOT EARNED.*

**5:31.**

"No," Gerald said aloud. "No, no, no."

He grabbed the liver with both hands, thinking he could tear it open and dig. It was colder than he expected and horribly soft, yielding under his fingers like wet bread. He pulled. It stretched, gummy and elastic, but wouldn't tear. A thin membrane held it together, slick and tough as a latex glove. His fingers slid off, coated in a film of blood and something thicker, almost jelly.

He pressed harder and felt it: a small, hard shape buried in the center.

He dug his thumbnail into the membrane. It punctured with a faint wet *pop*, and a smell rose from inside that was worse than the surface, fermented and meaty and deep. His stomach clenched. He swallowed hard, and his mouth flooded with thin, hot saliva.

He tore a hole and pushed his fingers inside. The liver was grainy in there, like wet clay packed with sand, and it squelched between his knuckles. He touched metal, closed on it, and pulled.

It didn't come. It was on a wire. A thin steel cable ran from the key down through the liver and into a hole in the table. Taped to the key was another tag.

*CHEW.*

**4:58.** A click. The collar cinched a quarter inch, and Gerald felt it press against his windpipe.

He understood then. The key wasn't coming out. The meat had to come off it.

He bent over the plate. The smell filled his head. He put his mouth on the torn edge of the liver and bit down.

The texture was the worst part. It didn't break the way meat should. His teeth sank in and the flesh squeezed up around them, soft and dense at once, then gave all at once with a mealy crumble. The taste came a second later, iron and bile, bitter as aspirin chewed dry, and then the rot underneath, a sour tang that coated the back of his tongue.

His throat seized.

The gag came from deep in his gut, a hard upward convulsion that jerked his shoulders forward. He clamped his lips shut. His eyes watered. Cold sweat broke across his forehead and his ears rang. He breathed through his nose, which was a mistake, because the smell came in stronger, and he gagged again, a wet clicking sound in his throat.

*Swallow. Just swallow.*

He forced it. The lump slid down slowly, thick and heavy, and he felt every inch of it. His esophagus spasmed against it, trying to push it back up. He pressed his fist to his sternum and held it there until the wave passed.

**4:12.**

He bit again. Faster now. Don't taste it. Don't think. Tear, chew twice, swallow. A clot the size of a grape burst in his mouth, cold and slippery, and he retched so hard a string of bile and blood spilled over his chin and back onto the plate. He heard himself whimpering between bites, a high animal sound.

The collar clicked. **3:59.** Breathing became work. Each inhale whistled.

He was halfway through, the cable exposed now, running like a vein through the ruined meat, when he saw the note taped under where the liver had been.

*THE REST OF THE CABLE RUNS BENEATH THE LARVAE. EVERY DISH IS PART OF THE MEAL.*

Gerald sobbed once.

The larvae were warm. That was what undid him. He scooped a handful and they squirmed against his palm, soft and pulsing, their blunt heads nosing blindly between his fingers. He shoved them into his mouth before he could stop himself.

They moved. Against his tongue, against his cheeks, a crawling, wriggling pressure. He bit down and felt one burst, a thin skin splitting and a creamy paste spreading across his molars, faintly nutty, faintly sweet, and absolutely wrong. Another slid toward his throat on its own, and he gagged so violently that his whole body folded over the table. Half the mouthful sprayed out onto the steel. He shoveled it back in with shaking fingers, grit and bile and all, because the clock didn't care.

**2:40.** Click.

Black spots bloomed at the edges of his vision. The crickets went down dry and sharp, legs catching between his teeth, wings sticking to the roof of his mouth like cellophane. He chewed with his mouth open, gasping around them, crumbs of chitin stabbing his gums.

The cable ran taut now, straight to the glass. To the roaches.

**1:15.**

He lifted the glass. One roach bolted for the edge of the table. The other two he caught. He could feel them in his fist, the frantic scrabble of spined legs against his palm, the hard shells flexing.

The collar clicked. He could barely breathe at all.

Gerald Hoss, who had signed his name to so many lies, closed his eyes, opened his mouth, and learned what it truly meant to look closely at what he let people swallow.

The crunch was very loud in the silent room.

# The Keeper of the Knife

The temple had not seen daylight in four hundred years. Its walls sweated in the torchlight, black basalt veined with old stains that no one scrubbed anymore, because scrubbing would imply they were a mistake.

Ithren descended the ninety-one steps at the same pace he always did. He did not count them. He had stopped counting in his second year of service, when his feet learned the distance better than his mind could.

Below, the chamber opened like a throat. Pillars carved with the faces of forgotten gods leaned inward. Their eyes had been gouged out centuries ago, by a priest who believed they were watching. Ithren had always thought that priest a fool. The gods did not watch. That was the point. Someone had to do it for them.

The offering was already bound to the altar.

She was young, perhaps nineteen, a farmer's daughter from the eastern terraces, chosen by lot at the solstice. Her wrists and ankles were lashed with braided gut to iron rings that had worn smooth from use. She had stopped screaming some time ago. Her voice had gone somewhere past sound, into a thin, wet rasping that filled the chamber like wind through a cracked door.

Ithren set his lamp on its ledge. He unrolled the leather bundle of instruments and laid them out in order: the bronze hook, the bone saw, the obsidian blade, the silver bowl. He checked the edge of the obsidian against his thumbnail. Adequate.

"Please," the girl whispered. "Please, I have a brother, he's only six, he needs—"

Ithren lit the censers. The smoke was bitter, resin and dried blood-moss, and it curled up toward the ceiling where it would hang for days.

"Look at me," she said. "*Look* at me."

He did, briefly, because the rite required him to confirm the offering was unblemished. Her eyes were brown, bloodshot, enormous. He noted a small scar above her left eyebrow, old, healed. Acceptable. He looked away.

He began the invocation. The words were in a language no one had spoken as a mother tongue for a thousand years, and he pronounced them the way a clerk reads a ledger: correctly, completely, without inflection. There was a place in the third verse where old priests were said to have wept. Ithren passed through it the way one passes a milestone.

When the verse ended, he took up the obsidian.

The first cut was below the sternum, a hand's width long, drawn in one clean motion. The skin parted and the blood came, dark and fast, sheeting down her sides into the channels carved in the altar stone. The channels had been cut at a precise gradient, and the blood ran along them toward the silver bowl as if it knew the way.

She made a sound then that was not a word. Her back arched against the bindings until the iron rings groaned.

Ithren waited for the arch to subside. Muscle fought the blade; patience was more efficient than force. When her body sagged, he set the obsidian aside and took up the bone saw.

The sternum resisted as it always did. He braced his left hand flat on her collarbone and worked the saw with short, even strokes. The sound was dry and rhythmic, like someone cutting kindling in the next room. Warm spatter reached his forearms, his chin. He did not wipe it away. Wiping would waste time, and the censers only burned for so long.

Her rasping stopped somewhere during the sawing. Whether she had fainted or died, he did not check. It made no difference to the liturgy.

He fitted the bronze hook beneath the parted bone and levered it open. Steam rose from the cavity, faint in the cold air. He reached in with his bare hand, as the rite demanded, and found the heart by touch. It was still moving, a slow, uncertain shudder, like a fist unclenching in sleep.

He cut the vessels with four strokes of the obsidian. The heart came free, heavy and slick. He held it up toward the eyeless gods for the duration of one breath, then placed it in the silver bowl, where it lay in the pooled blood and twitched twice more before going still.

The final verse was short. He recited it.

Afterward, he cleaned the instruments in the basin of brine by the north wall, one by one, in the same order he had laid them out. He dried each with a linen cloth, rolled them back into the leather bundle, and tied the cord in the same double knot he had tied for twenty-two years.

At the stair, he paused, not out of reverence but because his left knee had begun to ache in the damp and he preferred to let it settle before climbing.

Behind him, the torches guttered. The girl lay open on the stone, her brown eyes fixed on the ceiling, on the smoke, on nothing.

Ithren thought, briefly, that he should have the attendants replace the gut bindings before the next solstice. They were beginning to fray.

Then he climbed the ninety-one steps, and did not count them.

When the verse ended, he took up the obsidian.

The first cut was below the sternum, a hand's width long, drawn in one clean motion. The skin parted and the blood came, dark and fast, sheeting down her sides into the channels carved in the altar stone. The channels had been cut at a precise gradient, and the blood ran along them toward the silver bowl as if it knew the way.

She made a sound then that was not a word. Her back arched against the bindings until the iron rings groaned.

Ithren waited for the arch to subside. Muscle fought the blade; patience was more efficient than force. When her body sagged, he set the obsidian aside and took up the bone saw.

The sternum resisted as it always did. He braced his left hand flat on her collarbone and worked the saw with short, even strokes. The sound was dry and rhythmic, like someone cutting kindling in the next room. Warm spatter reached his forearms, his chin. He did not wipe it away. Wiping would waste time, and the censers only burned for so long.

Her rasping stopped somewhere during the sawing. Whether she had fainted or died, he did not check. It made no difference to the liturgy.

He fitted the bronze hook beneath the parted bone and levered it open. Steam rose from the cavity, faint in the cold air. He reached in with his bare hand, as the rite demanded, and found the heart by touch. It was still moving, a slow, uncertain shudder, like a fist unclenching in sleep.

He cut the vessels with four strokes of the obsidian. The heart came free, heavy and slick. He held it up toward the eyeless gods for the duration of one breath, then placed it in the silver bowl, where it lay in the pooled blood and twitched twice more before going still.

The final verse was short. He recited it.

Afterward, he cleaned the instruments in the basin of brine by the north wall, one by one, in the same order he had laid them out. He dried each with a linen cloth, rolled them back into the leather bundle, and tied the cord in the same double knot he had tied for twenty-two years.

At the stair, he paused, not out of reverence but because his left knee had begun to ache in the damp and he preferred to let it settle before climbing.

Behind him, the torches guttered. The girl lay open on the stone, her brown eyes fixed on the ceiling, on the smoke, on nothing.

Ithren thought, briefly, that he should have the attendants replace the gut bindings before the next solstice. They were beginning to fray.

Then he climbed the ninety-one steps, and did not count them.

**The Counting**

The first thing I notice is how loud my heart is.

Not the fight. Not the way Dale's face went slack when he realized what he'd done, or the slap of his sneakers on wet pavement as he ran. Just this: the thud of my own pulse in my ears, like someone knocking on the inside of a door.

*Thump.* Pause. *Thump.*

I'm sitting against the dumpster behind Castellano's. I don't remember sitting down. My legs are stretched out in front of me like they belong to someone else, and my right hand is pressed against my side, just under the ribs, where everything is warm and slick and wrong.

It doesn't hurt the way I thought it would. It hurts the way cold water hurts, a pressure more than a pain, a fact announcing itself.

*Thump.* Pause. *Thump.*

The sun is going down over the parking garage across the street. It's making the whole alley orange, the brick, the puddles, the grease-stained cardboard somebody flattened by the back door. It's beautiful, actually. I never looked at this alley before. I've taken out the trash here four nights a week for two years, and I never once noticed how the light comes through the gap between the buildings like it's being poured.

I should call someone. My phone is in my left pocket. I think about reaching for it, and my left arm thinks about it too, and then neither of us does anything.

*Thump. Thump.*

Faster now. That's strange. I'm sitting still. Why is it running?

I read somewhere, or maybe my brother told me, he was always telling me things, that when you lose blood, your heart speeds up to compensate. Less to pump, so it pumps harder. Like bailing a boat with a smaller and smaller bucket. I think about that for a while. Or maybe only a second. Time has gone soft at the edges.

The orange is turning pink. Then gray-pink. The shadows are climbing the wall like water filling a tank.

---

My feet are cold.

It starts there, in my toes, like I've been standing in snow. I'm wearing my work shoes, the black non-slip ones with the torn insole, and I can't feel the torn insole anymore. I can't feel much of anything below my shins. The cold is patient. It moves up my calves the way the shadows move up the wall, like they're in on it together.

*Thumpthump. Thumpthump.*

It's lighter now, my heartbeat. Faster but lighter, a moth against a window instead of a fist on a door. I try to count it and lose track at eleven. I start over. Lose it at seven.

Somewhere inside the restaurant, somebody drops a pan. I hear Marco swear in Spanish, and then the radio comes up, some old song, a woman singing about a train. The sound comes through the metal door muffled, like it's traveling underwater. Like it's coming from very far away, from a place where people are still cooking and cleaning and complaining about their shifts.

I want to call out. I open my mouth, and what comes out is breath. Just breath, white in the air. When did it get cold enough to see my breath? It's April.

Oh.

It isn't the air that's cold.

---

The streetlight at the end of the alley flickers on. Sodium yellow, buzzing. I watch it the way you'd watch a campfire. There's a halo around it that shouldn't be there, soft and wide, and when I blink, the halo gets bigger, and the edges of everything else get smaller. It's like looking down a paper towel tube. The world is a circle, and the circle is closing.

My hand has slipped off my side. I don't remember letting go. I tell it to go back, to press, the way they do in movies, and it lies there on the pavement, palm up, fingers curled, like it's waiting for someone to put something in it.

*thump thump thump*

I can barely hear it now. That's what scares me. Not the cold, not the dark. The quiet. My heart has been talking to me my whole life, and I never listened, and now that I'm listening, it's starting to whisper.

I think about my mother's kitchen. I don't know why. The yellow curtains with the lemons on them, the way the radiator knocked in winter. She used to put her hand on my chest when I was little and had nightmares, flat against my breastbone, and say, *Feel that? That's you. That's you, still here.*

I'm still here.

I'm still here.

The cold has reached my hips. My fingers. It's in my lips now, a numb buzz, like after the dentist. The streetlight is a single bright coin at the end of a long black tunnel, and the tunnel is narrowing to the size of a keyhole.

*thump*

A long pause.

*thump*

There's a sound under the radio now. Or over it. High and rising and falling. I can't tell if it's real. I can't tell if someone inside heard something, or if Dale stopped running long enough to be a better person than I thought he was, or if my brain is just giving me what I want the way it gives you water in dreams.

It gets louder.

Red light, blue light, washing over the brick, over my useless hands, over the dark pool I'm sitting in that I've been careful not to look at.

*thump*

I hold on to the sound. I don't know how. There isn't anything left to hold with. But I hold on, to the knocking, to the door, to the voice saying *that's you, that's you*, while the light comes down the alley toward me, and footsteps, and someone shouting a name that I think might be mine.

*thump*

Still here.

*thump*

Still—

# What the Dog Knew

The house on Alder Street smelled like lemon cleaner and something underneath it that the cleaner was meant to cover.

Detective Mara Voss had been in the girl's bedroom for twenty minutes before she found it. The room was almost aggressively ordinary: a unicorn duvet, glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling, a bookshelf of chapter books arranged by color. A room designed, Voss thought, by someone who had studied what a nine-year-old's room was supposed to look like.

That was what had bothered her from the start. Real children's rooms had chaos in them. This one had *curation*.

She found the note taped to the underside of the bottom dresser drawer, the way a person hides something they want to keep rather than something they want to lose. Folded into a careful square. Lined notebook paper, pencil, the letters large and round and pressed hard enough to emboss the back of the page.

Voss unfolded it with gloved fingers and read it standing up, and then she sat down on the edge of the unicorn bed and read it again.

---

*To whoever finds this,*

*I am writing this down because Dr. Pell says writing down your feelings helps you understand them. I don't think I have the feelings she means but I am doing the assignment anyway because I am good at assignments.*

*Everyone thinks Biscuit ran away. Mom cried and put up posters. I helped her staple them. I made my face sad the way I practiced in the bathroom mirror. Mom hugged me and said "oh sweetheart" and that is how I know I did it right.*

*Biscuit did not run away.*

*I want to explain why I had to do it because I don't want anyone to think I was being mean. I wasn't mean. I wasn't even mad. It was more like when you have to throw away a paper with a mistake on it before the teacher sees.*

*Biscuit knew.*

*I don't know how dogs know things but he did. He used to sleep on my bed when he was a puppy. Then one day he stopped. He would stand in the doorway and look at me and not come in. When I called him he put his ears back. Mom said "that's weird, he loves you," and I said "I know, that's weird," but it wasn't weird. He was the only one in the house paying attention.*

*Then he started following me at night.*

*I like to walk around when everyone is asleep. I like to stand in the rooms and listen to people breathing. It's quiet and nobody is looking at my face so I don't have to do anything with it. I like to stand by Theo's crib the most. Theo is very small. He can't talk yet. He doesn't know what faces are supposed to do either, so we are the same, kind of.*

*Biscuit would get between me and the crib. Every night. He would stand there and make a noise in his throat so low you could barely hear it. Not loud enough to wake anyone up. Just loud enough for me.*

*Like he was saying: I see you.*

*Nobody else sees me. Not Mom, not Dad, not Dr. Pell, not my teacher who gives me stickers. They all see the girl who staples posters. Biscuit was the only one who saw the other thing, and he was going to keep standing in the way.*

*So I had to.*

*I did it in the woods behind the Hendersons' where the creek goes under the road. I thought I would feel something after. I waited for a long time to see if I would. I didn't. I just felt like when you finish a chore.*

*I buried his collar separately so if anyone found him they wouldn't know he was ours. I read about that in one of Dad's books.*

*I am writing this because Dr. Pell says I should, and because I think someday somebody should know that I was smart about it. I don't want anyone to think it was an accident. I don't do things by accident.*

*It is very quiet at night now. Nobody stands in front of the crib anymore.*

*I will probably throw this away. But if you're reading it, I guess I didn't.*

*— Lily*

*P.S. The drawing on the back is Biscuit. I drew him before, when he still liked me. I think it's good.*

---

Voss turned the page over. A dog drawn in crayon, brown and floppy-eared, a big red tongue, a yellow sun in the corner. Underneath, in the same careful hand: *BISCUIT. MY BEST FRIEND.*

Her radio crackled. Donnelly, downstairs. "Mara? Mom's asking if we're almost done. She wants to put the kids to bed."

Voss looked at the doorway. Down the hall, a nightlight glowed blue from a half-open nursery door. She could hear, very faintly, the tick of a mobile turning.

She thought about a dog standing in the dark, night after night, growling low enough that only one person in the house could hear it.

She keyed the radio.

"Donnelly. Nobody goes to bed yet." She folded the note back into its square, exactly along its creases, and slid it into an evidence bag. Her hands, she noticed, were not quite steady. "And I want someone in the nursery. Now. Don't make a thing of it. Just stay with the baby."

A pause. "The baby? Mara, the missing-dog thing is a welfare check. What's going on?"

Voss stood and looked around the room one more time. At the sorted books. At the perfect stars. At the bed where a puppy had once slept, before it learned better.

"I think," she said, "the dog was doing our job for us. And somebody fired him."

**Room Twelve**

The door came off its hinges on the second kick, and Vasko went in behind the flame.

He didn't aim so much as pour. The igniter clicked, caught, and the nozzle coughed a rope of burning fuel across the room in a long, lazy arc that hit the far wall and *splashed*, the way water splashes, except it clung. It ran down the concrete in orange sheets. It found the stacked crates, the cots, the table where someone had left a hand of cards face-up. It found the men.

There were five of them. He'd counted the voices through the door.

The heat came back at him instantly, a wall of it rolling off the burning room and slamming into his face shield hard enough to make him turn his head. Even through the Nomex hood, even through the gloves, he felt his skin tighten, the sweat on his neck going hot as bathwater, then hotter. The air itself changed. It thickened, became something you had to push through, and every breath he dragged through the respirator tasted of scorched rubber and kerosene.

The screaming started a half-second after the fire.

It never sounded the way people thought it would. Not movie screams. The first man, the one closest, the one who'd been reaching for a rifle propped against the wall, didn't scream at all at first. He made a sound like a man lifting something too heavy, a long grunting exhale, and then his lungs caught up with what was happening to him, and the sound went up and up into something high and cracked that didn't seem to need breath anymore. He spun. He beat at himself with hands that were also burning. He ran straight into the wall and kept running, like his legs hadn't gotten the message.

Vasko gave him another burst. Short. Mercy, or efficiency. He'd stopped being able to tell the difference years ago.

Two of them had gone for the back corner, where a steel filing cabinet stood between them and the door. Smart, if the enemy had been using rifles. Vasko walked the stream along the ceiling instead and let it rain down behind the cabinet. The fuel dripped in burning strings. He heard one of them start praying, fast and wet, in a language he half-knew, and then the prayer broke apart into sobbing, and then into a shriek that went on so long Vasko caught himself counting, the way he'd count seconds after lightning. Seven. Eight. Nine.

Then the smell reached him.

He'd tried, once, drunk, to describe it to a woman in a bar in Tbilisi, and he'd failed, and she'd looked at him like he was something that had crawled out of a drain. It wasn't like pork, whatever people said. It started that way, a fatty, cooking-meat richness that the animal back of your brain recognized and, God help you, *liked* for a moment, and then it turned. Burnt hair came first, sharp and chemical, catching in the throat. Then something sweeter underneath, cloying, the smell of fat rendering down and spitting. And under all of it, the thing that stayed in your clothes for a week no matter how many times you washed them: a deep, organic, *wrong* smell, like a butcher's dumpster set alight in August. It got through the respirator. It always got through.

The fourth man came at him.

He'd been under the table, and now he burst out from beneath it with his shirt on fire and a knife in his fist, and for one strange, clear instant Vasko saw his face: young, bearded, his eyes wide and white and completely sane, and Vasko thought, *that's the bravest thing I'll see all year.* Then he pulled the trigger and the man disappeared into the light. # The Shedding of Thomas Hale

Thomas Hale had been a gentle man. Everyone said so. For nineteen years he'd worked the night shift at St. Agnes Hospice, holding the hands of the dying and humming old hymns when they couldn't sleep. He remembered the names of every patient's grandchildren. He cried in his car after the hard ones.

The first sign was the itch.

It began between his shoulder blades in late October, a crawling sensation beneath the skin, as though something had laid eggs there. He scratched until his fingernails came away packed with gray flakes, not the pink curls of ordinary dead skin but something papery and translucent, like the husk of a cicada. He told himself it was eczema, stress, the dry heat of the hospice radiators.

By November, it was coming off in sheets.

He would wake to find his bedsheets dusted with it, fine as ash. In the shower, he could pinch the skin along his forearm and peel it away in a single long ribbon, and beneath it the new flesh was wrong. It was paler and faintly wet, with a sheen like the inside of a shell. It didn't hold warmth. When he pressed his thumb into it, the dent stayed for a long, long moment before slowly filling back in.

He started wearing long sleeves. Gloves, when he could justify them.

---

The bones came next.

The first break happened at 3 a.m. on a Tuesday. He was sitting in the dark beside Mrs. Okafor's bed, listening to her ragged breathing, when his left hand spasmed and the smallest finger snapped sideways with a sound like a green branch breaking. He bit down on his sleeve to keep from screaming. He watched, trembling, as the finger straightened itself: slowly, grindingly, the bone sliding back into place with a wet clicking he could feel all the way up his arm.

When it was done, the finger was longer. Only by a quarter inch. But longer.

It happened every night after that. He learned to predict it, a deep ache that settled into a joint an hour before it gave way. His knees buckled backward on the stairs. His jaw unhinged one night while he was brushing his teeth, and he stood frozen at the mirror as it cracked, shifted, and resettled, the whole lower half of his face pushed slightly forward, as if something inside him were trying to get a better look at the world.

His spine was the worst. Some nights he lay on the bathroom floor while his vertebrae popped one by one, like knuckles, like gunshots, each one reseating itself a fraction farther from its neighbor. He grew two inches in a month. His shirts rode up. His coworkers joked that he was having a late growth spurt, and he laughed along with them, and he noticed, distantly, that he didn't find it frightening anymore.

He noticed that he didn't find much of anything frightening anymore.

---

That was the part he would have wept over, if he still remembered how.

It didn't happen all at once. There was no single night when he stopped being good. It was more like erosion, the way a coastline doesn't vanish but is simply, one day, somewhere else.

First came impatience. Mr. Delacroix pressed the call button for the fourth time in an hour, and Thomas felt a flash of heat behind his eyes so intense that he had to grip the doorframe. He apologized to no one, afterward. He told himself he was tired.

Then indifference. A patient died alone while Thomas sat in the break room eating an orange, and when he found her, he felt nothing but a mild interest in the stillness of her chest, in the way the color had already begun to settle into the backs of her arms. He had always hated this part of the job. Now he lingered.

Then came the smell.

The dying had a scent. He'd always known it, the sweetish, heavy odor of a body beginning to close up shop. For nineteen years it had meant sorrow. Now it made his mouth flood with saliva. It made the new, wet skin along his throat prickle and flush. He would stand in the hallway outside the rooms of the ones who were close, breathing deep, his elongated fingers flexing at his sides, and a thought would come to him in a voice that was almost his own:

*They're going to die anyway.*

He was horrified the first time. He went home and scrubbed himself raw, and more skin came away, and underneath there was only more of the pale, shining stuff.

The second time, he was less horrified.

The third time, he began to argue with himself, and that was how he knew he'd lost. Because the argument was *reasonable*. It was compassionate, even. They were in pain. They were frightened. He could make it faster. Wasn't that what he'd always wanted for them, an end to suffering? Wasn't that mercy? The old Thomas would have recognized the shape of the thought, the way a lie dresses itself in the clothes of kindness. But the old Thomas was coming off in flakes in the shower drain, and the thing underneath had its own ideas about mercy.

---

By December, he no longer went home.

The night staff at St. Agnes began to whisper about the tall figure glimpsed at the far end of the corridor after midnight, one that walked with a strange, jointed stoop, head cocked as if listening to something only it could hear. Patients spoke of a visitor who sat very still beside their beds and hummed hymns in a voice that was almost soothing, except that the melody was wrong, and the humming came from somewhere deeper than a throat should go.

In the supply closet on the third floor, behind the linens, a night nurse eventually found a heap of shed skin in the rough shape of a man, curled on its side and hollow as a paper lantern, still wearing the ghost of a gentle smile.

It had been left there neatly. Folded, almost.

As if whatever had climbed out of it had wanted to be tidy. As if, somewhere in the new thing, some last, small remnant of Thomas Hale still remembered that he used to care.

# The Last Five Minutes

*A small room painted a green that was probably meant to be calming. A clock on the wall, behind a wire cage. MARCUS, fifties, sits on the edge of a bench, wrists cuffed in front of him. WALTER, sixties, stands near the door with his hands folded. He is not wearing a hood. That comes later.*

---

**MARCUS:** That clock's fast.

**WALTER:** It isn't.

**MARCUS:** It's fast. I've been listening to it for an hour. It skips.

**WALTER:** They check it every morning. Against the one in the warden's office.

**MARCUS:** Then the warden's is fast too. *(Beat.)* You'd think they'd give a man accurate time. Least they could do.

*Walter says nothing.*

**MARCUS:** You're not supposed to talk to me, are you.

**WALTER:** I can talk. There's no rule. Most of them don't want to.

**MARCUS:** Most of them.

**WALTER:** Most.

**MARCUS:** How many is that? Total.

**WALTER:** I don't count.

**MARCUS:** Sure you do.

*Pause.*

**WALTER:** Thirty-one.

**MARCUS:** So I'm thirty-two.

**WALTER:** You're Marcus.

**MARCUS:** *(a short laugh)* That's nice. They teach you that?

**WALTER:** No.

*The clock ticks. Marcus looks at his hands.*

**MARCUS:** My daughter wrote me. Last week. First time in eleven years. You know what she said?

**WALTER:** You don't have to tell me.

**MARCUS:** She said she forgave me. And I sat there with the letter and I was so angry I couldn't breathe. Isn't that something? Eleven years I wanted that. And when it came I thought, *who asked you?* Like she'd taken something from me.

**WALTER:** What did she take?

**MARCUS:** I don't know. The right to be the worst thing that ever happened to her, maybe. *(Beat.)* That doesn't make sense.

**WALTER:** It makes some sense.

**MARCUS:** Did you write back to her? Whoever's in charge of that. Does somebody tell the families how it went?

**WALTER:** The chaplain calls. If they want.

**MARCUS:** What does he say?

**WALTER:** That it was peaceful.

**MARCUS:** Is it?

*Long pause.*

**WALTER:** Mostly.

**MARCUS:** You're a bad liar, you know that? That's a good thing, in a man. I was a very good liar.

*He shifts. The cuffs clink.*

**MARCUS:** Do you have kids?

**WALTER:** Two. Grown.

**MARCUS:** They know what you do?

**WALTER:** My son does. My daughter thinks I work maintenance.

**MARCUS:** *(genuinely amused)* Maintenance.

**WALTER:** It's not entirely untrue. I fix the pipes on C-block. Twice a month I do this.

**MARCUS:** Why not tell her?

**WALTER:** Because she'd look at me different. And I'd rather be the man she thinks I am, in her head at least. *(Beat.)* Same as you, I suppose. With your girl. Wanting to stay a certain thing.

*Marcus looks at him for a long moment.*

**MARCUS:** You're not supposed to say things like that.

**WALTER:** There's no rule.

**MARCUS:** Do you think I deserve it?

**WALTER:** That's not my part.

**MARCUS:** I'm asking you anyway. Man to man. Five minutes left, nobody's writing it down.

*Walter unfolds his hands, then folds them again.*

**WALTER:** I read your file. I read all of them, the first night. I know what you did to that family.

**MARCUS:** And?

**WALTER:** And I think the world is not better with that in it. And I don't know if it's better with this in it either. I've been doing this nineteen years and I've never found where one stops being the answer to the other.

**MARCUS:** That's not an answer.

**WALTER:** No. It's the only one I've got.

*The clock. Marcus closes his eyes.*

**MARCUS:** I thought I'd be scared. I was, all week. Couldn't eat. Last night I slept like a baby. Isn't that strange?

**WALTER:** It's common.

**MARCUS:** I don't want to be common.

**WALTER:** You're not. You asked about the clock. Nobody's ever asked about the clock.

**MARCUS:** *(opening his eyes)* It's fast, Walter.

*Walter looks up, startled.*

**MARCUS:** It's on your shirt. Stitched. I'm not blind.

*Walter touches the name tag on his chest as though he'd forgotten it was there.*

**WALTER:** They told me to take it off. Years ago. I never did.

**MARCUS:** Why?

**WALTER:** Seemed like a man ought to know who's doing it.

*A knock at the door. Two short raps. Neither man moves right away.*

**MARCUS:** That's them.

**WALTER:** That's them.

**MARCUS:** Can I ask you something? A favor.

**WALTER:** If I can.

**MARCUS:** When the chaplain calls her. My daughter. Don't let him say *peaceful.* She'll know it's a lie, she always knew when I was lying. Have him say — *(he searches)* — have him say I read her letter. Every day. Have him say I wasn't angry at the end.

**WALTER:** Were you?

**MARCUS:** *(a long breath)* Not right now.

**WALTER:** Then I'll tell him.

*Marcus stands. His legs are unsteady for just a second, and Walter's hand comes out, instinctively, to his elbow. Then it stays there.*

**MARCUS:** Thirty-two.

**WALTER:** Marcus.

**MARCUS:** *(nodding)* Marcus.

*Walter opens the door. The light from the corridor is very white. Behind them, the clock ticks. It may or may not be fast.*

*Lights down.*

---

*END*

# Six Feet

The first sound Elias hears is rain.

That's what his mind decides it is: a hard, scattered drumming, the kind that comes sideways off the lake in October and rattles the windows of his mother's house. He lies in the dark and listens to it and feels, for a few seconds, almost comfortable.

Then a second burst comes, heavier. Not rain. Rain doesn't come in *handfuls*.

He opens his eyes, and nothing changes.

The dark is total. It has no depth to it, no grain. He blinks and blinks, waiting for shapes to resolve, a window's outline, the glow of a clock, and none come. He moves to sit up and his forehead strikes something four inches above his face. Not hard, but the surprise of it knocks the breath out of him in a shocked little *huh* that comes right back at him, warm, off the surface above.

His own breath, returned to him. That's the first moment he understands the size of the space.

He lifts his hands. His knuckles meet the lid before his elbows are off the floor. He spreads his arms and his elbows jam against the sides at once, padded, soft, the texture of cheap satin, sliding and slick. He is lying in a box shaped exactly like a man lying down, with almost nothing to spare.

*Thud.*

The sound comes through the wood and into his teeth. A shovelful of earth, landing squarely on the lid above his chest. He hears it scatter: the heavy center-weight, then pebbles skittering down toward his feet, then a fine hiss of loose soil sliding off the edges.

"Hey," he says. His voice is wrong in here. It doesn't travel. It stops an inch from his lips and falls back onto his face. "*Hey!*"

*Thud.* By his knees.

He screams then. He can't help it. He screams and pounds the lid with the heels of his hands, and the satin muffles every blow into a dull, stupid patting, like someone knocking politely on a mattress. He tries to draw his knees up to kick and they hit the lid halfway, pinning his legs at an angle that makes his hips burn. He can't turn over. He can't get his hands above his face with enough room to swing. Every movement he's ever taken for granted, rolling, sitting, *reaching*, has been taken away and replaced with a series of small collisions.

*Thud. Thud.*

He stops. He makes himself stop, because a colder part of his brain has begun talking, calm and awful: *You're using it up.*

The air.

He becomes aware of it all at once, the way you become aware of your tongue in your mouth. The air in here is already warm. Already used. It smells of varnish and the sweetish chemical rot of old lilies, and underneath it, himself: sweat, fear, the sour animal breath he's been heaving out in screams. He's been breathing the same small room over and over. Each lungful goes out a little worse than it came in.

*Thud.*

He counts. It's something to do. He estimates the box: six feet, maybe, by two, by a foot and a half. He doesn't know how much air that is. He doesn't know how long a man lasts in it. He remembers reading *hours*, once, or maybe it was *minutes*, and he can't remember which, and the not-remembering is its own kind of drowning.

*Thud.*

He notices something about the sound.

The first shovelfuls were sharp. They struck the bare wood with a crack like a door slamming, and he could hear every stone bounce. Now there's a layer between him and them. The impacts land on dirt, not wood. They arrive as a deep, padded *whumpf*, felt more than heard, a pressure in his sternum.

It's getting quieter.

He understands what that means, and he opens his mouth to scream again and instead he yawns. A huge, jaw-cracking yawn that his body forces on him, desperate and involuntary, a lung reaching for something that isn't there. His head has begun to ache, a tight band above the eyes. His heart is going too fast, thin and fluttery, a bird in a paper bag.

*Whumpf.*

"Please," he whispers, and the whisper comes back to him warm.

He presses his palms flat against the lid and feels it: a faint, settling creak. The weight is building up there. Every shovelful adds to it. He imagines the soil mounding over him in a long, low hill, imagines it the way it will look from above, neat, raked, a mound in a row of mounds, and something in his chest seizes so hard he thinks for a moment it's his heart giving out.

It isn't. Not yet.

*whumpf*

Softer now. So much softer. He has to hold his breath to hear it, and holding his breath is agony, and when he lets it go it comes out in a shudder and the next one he takes in is thick and hot and doesn't satisfy. He's panting in short sips. His fingertips tingle. His lips feel far away.

*...mpf.*

He waits for the next one.

He waits with his eyes open on the flat black, his hands spread on the satin above him, his whole body strained toward the sound the way a drowning man strains toward the surface. He waits, and he realizes he is *begging* for it. Begging for another shovelful. Because as long as there is dirt falling, there is someone up there holding the shovel. There is a world up there, with a sky, and a person in it, close enough to hear if he could only be loud enough.

He waits.

Nothing comes.

The silence settles over him heavier than the earth. It's a silence with no bottom, the silence of a place where sound doesn't go. Somewhere above, he knows, a man is leaning his shovel against a tree, wiping his forehead, walking away across wet grass. The rain, the real rain, might be starting.

Elias lies still.

He listens to the only sound left: the small, wet rasp of his own breathing, loud as a saw in the dark, and getting faster.

He begins, very quietly, to count them.

# Conversion

The Ward smells of copper and lemon disinfectant. Mara has been here eleven days, or maybe twelve. The lights never dim, so she counts the shifts of the technicians instead, the soft squeak of their boots, the way they never look at her face.

Today they are taking her hands.

She knows because they have laid the new ones out on a steel tray beside her: two jointed assemblies of hydraulic tendon and grafted muscle, pale and wet, built for a single repetitive motion. Somewhere in the Eastern Assembly District there is a sorting line that needs forty thousand grips per hour, and the Directorate has decided that her body, a schoolteacher's body, soft and unoptimized, can be made to supply them.

"Please," she says. Her voice is already wrong. They took her larynx on the fourth day and replaced it with something that makes speech sound like wind through a cracked pipe. "Please, I can work. I can work with my own hands. I'll work."

The technician adjusts a dial. He is young, younger than her students were, and there is a small bandage on his neck where his compliance node was installed. He does not answer. He is not allowed to.

---

The anesthetic is partial. This is policy. The conversion surgeons have found that the nervous system integrates new tissue faster if it remains aware, if it *feels* the grafts taking. Pain, the pamphlets say, is merely information.

So Mara feels it.

She feels the first incision at her wrist like a line of ice, then fire, then something beneath fire: a deep, grinding wrongness as they separate the tendons one by one and clip them to the new assembly. Her fingers twitch on the tray, *her* fingers, the ones that held chalk, that braided her daughter's hair, that pressed against her husband's chest the night the Enforcers came. They twitch as though still connected to her, as though trying to crawl back.

She screams, but the thing in her throat turns the scream into a thin mechanical whistle. No one looks up.

When they fuse the neural bridge she goes somewhere else for a while. She is in a kitchen, sunlight on a yellow table, the smell of bread. Someone is laughing. She cannot remember who. That frightens her more than the saws.

---

Later, lying strapped to the recovery rack, she tries to make a fist.

The new hands close. They close perfectly, with a pneumatic hiss, fingers locking into a grip that could crush a walnut. But she cannot *feel* them close. There is no warmth, no texture, no small ache in the knuckles. There is only a signal, a flat report that says *grip achieved*, the way a machine might note that a door has shut.

She tries to touch her own face. The hand does not obey. It has not been programmed for that motion.

On the rack beside her lies a man who arrived before she did. She remembers his name was Teodor; he told her on the first night, whispering, that he had been a violinist. They have taken his eyes and replaced them with a band of optical sensors calibrated for detecting fractures in metal casings. They have taken his jaw, because a sorter does not need to eat, only to receive nutrient paste through a port in his abdomen. His arms end in calipers.

"Teodor," she whistles.

He turns the sensor band toward her. There is a long pause, as if something inside him is searching through files.

"Unit 4471," he says. His voice is flat and clean. "Awaiting assignment."

"Your name is Teodor. You played the violin. You told me about the concert in the old opera house, the one with the blue ceiling. You told me."

Another pause. Something flickers in the muscles of his ruined face, a tremor, a ghost trying to surface through deep water.

Then it is gone.

"Unit 4471," he says again. "Awaiting assignment."

---

That night, if it is night, Mara recites things to herself. It is the only resistance she has left.

*My name is Mara Voss. I was born in the river quarter. My mother's name was Ilse. My daughter's name is—*

She stops.

Her daughter's name is.

Her daughter's name.

She knows it is there. She can feel the shape of it, the way you feel a missing tooth with your tongue. A soft name. Two syllables, maybe three. She used to sing it. She used to call it across a park at dusk.

They have not touched her brain yet. That is the final stage, the "cognitive streamlining." But the pain has been doing its own work. Each surgery scours away a little more, and the grafts send their flat mechanical signals into her nerves until the old sensations are drowned out. Her body is forgetting it was ever a body. Her mind is following.

She weeps, or tries to. They removed her tear ducts on the sixth day. Unnecessary moisture. Risk of corrosion.

---

In the morning a supervisor walks the line of racks with a tablet, checking integration rates. He pauses beside Mara and reads her numbers.

"Resistance markers still elevated," he tells the technician. "Schedule her for streamlining tomorrow. Early slot."

He says it the way someone might order a replacement part.

When he is gone, Mara stares at the ceiling and holds on. She holds on to the yellow table. The bread. The laughter. The shape of a small hand in hers, a warm hand, a real one.

*My name is Mara Voss.*

*My name is Mara.*

*My name is.*

Across the aisle, Unit 4471 stands motionless in his rack, sensors glowing faintly, waiting to be told what to do. And somewhere deep in the hollowed architecture of his skull, too faint for any instrument to measure, a single note of a violin plays once, and is silent.

# Still Life

The first thing Nadia Ferreira learned in the crime scene unit was that everyone has a way of not looking.

Detectives looked at their notebooks. Uniforms looked at the doorframe, the street, their own shoes. The medical examiner's assistants looked at the body the way mechanics look at an engine, as a system of parts, failed or functioning. Even her mentor, old Teodor Brandt, who had worked scenes for thirty-one years, had a trick: he hummed. Always the same four bars of something she never identified, low in his throat, a little wall of sound between himself and the room.

Nadia never needed a trick. That was what made her good, everyone said. She could stand in the doorway of a kitchen where something unspeakable had happened and simply *see* it: the cast-off arcs on the ceiling, the void pattern on the cabinet where a body had shielded the wood, the single bloody partial on the light switch that the killer had touched on the way out, maybe without knowing he'd touched anything at all.

"You've got the eye," Brandt told her in her first year. He said it like a compliment. Later she wondered whether he'd meant it as a warning.

---

It began, if it began anywhere, with a woman who fell down the stairs.

Not a murder. An accident, the file would say, and the file was right. An elderly woman in a narrow Victorian house, a missed step in the dark, a broken neck. Nadia was there only because the death was unattended and procedure required it.

But it was late afternoon when she arrived, and the light came through the stained glass over the landing in long panels of amber and wine-red, and it fell across the woman where she lay at the foot of the stairs, one arm flung out toward the door as if she had been reaching for someone about to leave. Her grey hair had come loose from its pins and spread across the floorboards. A single slipper rested three steps up, perfectly upright, as though she had stepped out of it on purpose.

Nadia stood in the doorway for a long time.

"You all right?" asked the patrolman.

"Fine," she said, and raised her camera, and took the photographs she was required to take. Then she took one more, from the angle where the colored light touched the woman's open palm. It wasn't required. It wasn't evidence of anything.

That night she printed it at home and sat with it at her kitchen table until two in the morning, and felt something she had no word for, and did not like that she had no word for it.

---

Over the following years she developed a private vocabulary.

A scene could be *loud*, a bar fight turned stabbing, blood tracked across forty feet of linoleum, chairs overturned, everything screaming at once. It could be *muddy*, overlaid with EMT boot prints and the frantic handling of family members until the original pattern was lost like a painting someone had tried to clean with turpentine. Most scenes were *ordinary*, the way most sentences are ordinary. They said what happened, and nothing more.

But sometimes, rarely, a scene was *composed*.

She never said the word aloud. She knew how it would sound. She knew what the department psychologist would write in the margins of her file. But she could not stop seeing it: the way a spray of arterial blood across white tile could form a gradient as delicate as a watercolor wash; the way rigor could hold a hand in a gesture of such precise, frozen tenderness that no sculptor could have improved on it; the geometry of a room arranged around its one terrible fact.

She started keeping the extra photographs in a grey archival box beneath her bed. Not copies of evidence. Only the ones she took *after*, from the angles that mattered to no one but her.

She told herself it made her better at the work. And the strange part was that it did. Her eye for composition was an eye for disruption, for the thing out of place, the element that broke the pattern. Her clearance rate was the best in the unit. Brandt retired and they gave her his position, and at the small party in the break room he shook her hand and held on to it a moment too long.

# The Cottonwood at Sayer's Crossing

The cottonwood had been dead for three summers, but nobody in Pickett County would cut it down. It stood alone above the dry wash like a gallows God had built and forgotten about. The bark had sloughed off in long gray strips, and the lowest limb, thick as a man's thigh, ran out level over the sand, polished pale where rope had worn it before.

They brought Eli Dawes up the wash a little after sunrise, hands lashed behind him, seated on a sorrel mare that wasn't his. Six riders flanked him. Nobody talked. The only sounds were hooves in the loose gravel, the creak of saddle leather, and a meadowlark somewhere out in the sage that didn't know any better than to sing.

Tom Garrity rode at the back. He was nineteen and had joined the posse because his daddy told him a man stands with his neighbors. He'd believed that yesterday, when they found the Hollister girl's body in the root cellar. He was trying to believe it now.

Marshal Cobb reined up under the limb and swung down. He was a heavy man with a gray mustache stained yellow at the ends, and he moved without hurry, as if this were fence work. He took the coil off his saddle horn, shook it out, and tossed the loop over the limb on the first try. The rope hissed across the dead wood and hung swaying.

"You got anything to say, Eli?"

Dawes looked down at him. His lip was split and one eye had swollen shut, purple as a plum. "I said it all last night. Didn't do no good then."

"No," Cobb agreed. "It didn't."

He fitted the noose himself. He set the knot up under Dawes's left ear, snugged it, and checked it twice with his thumb the way a man checks a cinch. Dawes swallowed, and Tom watched his Adam's apple ride up against the hemp and drop again.

"Somebody hold her head," Cobb said.

Harlan Pruitt took the mare's bridle. Cobb tied off the rope's running end to the trunk and pulled the slack out until the line stood taut from Dawes's neck to the limb, straight as a plumb bob. Dawes had to tip his chin up to breathe.

The meadowlark went on singing.

"Lord have mercy on you," Cobb said, and there was nothing in his voice at all. Then he took off his hat and slapped the mare across the haunch with it.

She bolted. Dawes went off her rump like a sack pulled from a wagon bed, and for one long half-second he seemed to hang in the air on his own, legs still bent around a horse that wasn't there anymore.

Then the rope came tight.

The sound was not loud. That was what Tom would remember longest, years later, lying awake in rooms a thousand miles from that wash. He'd expected a gunshot crack, something big enough to match what was happening. Instead it was a short, wet, muffled snap, like a green branch broken inside a wool blanket. It was close and private, and it went into Tom's own neck and settled in the bones there.

Dawes's head lolled over hard to the right, farther than a head should go, as if it were listening to something in the ground.

The limb groaned. The rope twisted, and the body began a slow turn.

Tom thought that would be the end of it. It wasn't.

The legs kicked, first one, then both together, a jerking running motion in the empty air, boot heels scissoring. The bound hands clenched and opened, clenched and opened, the fingers crawling against each other like something trying to get loose from a sack. A shudder went through the whole length of him, shoulders to knees, and then another, smaller. One boot drew up toward his chest and trembled there and slowly let down.

"He's still alive," Tom said. His voice came out high and strange. "Marshal, he's still..."

"He ain't," Cobb said. "Neck's broke. That's just the meat not knowing it yet."

The twitching went on. The spasms grew smaller and farther apart, and between them the body just hung and turned, turned and hung. A dark stain spread down the inside of one trouser leg and dripped from the boot heel into the sand, and the sand drank it. The right hand gave a last flutter, the fingers spreading once, like a man letting go of something, and then went still.

The meadowlark had stopped. Tom didn't know when.

The rope creaked on the limb. Somewhere down the wash the sorrel mare nickered, confused, looking back at the thing she had carried.

Harlan Pruitt spat. Two of the others were already mounting up. Cobb set his hat back on his head and stood a while looking at Dawes's face, which Tom would not look at, and then he said, "Leave him till noon. Let folks see."

Tom sat his horse and did not move. His hands were shaking on the reins, and he pressed them flat against the saddle horn so nobody would notice.

"Garrity."

He looked up. Cobb was watching him.

"You'll dream on it," the marshal said. "Everybody does, first one." He swung up into his saddle. "Just make damn sure you're dreaming on the right man."

He turned his horse and rode down the wash. After a while Tom followed. Behind them, the dead cottonwood held its fruit and creaked in the rising heat, patient as it had always been.

# The Hollow Hour

The rain had stopped an hour ago, but the alley behind Mercer Street still wept. Water dripped from rusted fire escapes and pooled in the cracked asphalt, reflecting the sodium glow of a single streetlamp at the far end.

He hadn't meant to. He'd told himself, as he did every night, that he would go to the clinic on Delancey where a nervous orderly sold expired blood bags for cash. But it had been eleven days since he'd last fed properly, and the hunger had stopped being a feeling. It had become a *place*, a hollow cathedral inside his ribs where something vast and patient prayed for one thing only.

She smelled of cigarette smoke and cheap vanilla perfume. Beneath that, beneath everything, she smelled of iron and salt and *life*: a warm, pulsing current he could hear from forty feet away. Her heartbeat was quick and a little irregular. Too much coffee, maybe. Too little sleep.

She cut through the alley because it saved her four minutes. He knew this the way a wolf knows the path a deer will take.

"Excuse me," he said.

She turned, keys already threaded between her knuckles. Smart girl. It wouldn't matter.

"I'm not looking for trouble," she said. Her voice was steady, but her pulse jumped, and the hunger in him *surged*, a tide pulling against the seawall of whatever humanity he had left.

"Neither am I," Elias said, and meant it, and stepped forward anyway.

He was faster than her fear. One moment she was raising the keys; the next his hand had closed over her wrist and the keys were ringing against the wet stone. He turned her gently, almost tenderly, pressing her back against the brick. Her breath came in short gasps that fogged in the cold air. His did not fog at all.

"Please," she whispered.

He met her eyes, and he *pushed*, the old trick, the one that felt like leaning his weight against a door. Her pupils swelled black. The tension drained from her shoulders like water from a basin. She didn't stop being afraid, not entirely. Somewhere behind that glassy stare, he knew, a part of her was still screaming. He had never found a way to silence that part. He had stopped trying.

He brushed her hair aside. The artery beneath her jaw throbbed, blue and delicate, and the hunger roared up so fiercely that his vision narrowed to that single fluttering point.

His teeth slid down, a pressure behind his gums, then the sharp, sweet ache of their lengthening.

# What the Snow Keeps

The first wound came as a sting of cold, and Mara thought she'd brushed against a branch.

She was halfway up the logging trail, breath smoking, when something drew a line across the back of her left calf. It didn't feel like a cut at first. It felt like someone had pressed an icicle to her skin and dragged it slowly, deliberately, from one side to the other. Then the cold turned hot, and the hot turned wet, and she looked down to see her wool sock darkening from gray to black.

There was nothing behind her. Only the trail, the snow, and her own footprints punched into the white.

And beside them, pressing down in the perfect stillness, a second set appeared.

---

She ran. Of course she ran. Her body decided before her mind could argue, and her legs pistoned through the drifts while her lungs filled with air so cold it felt like swallowing broken glass. The wound in her calf pulsed with every stride, a bright, rhythmic ache that climbed into the back of her knee and nested there.

She couldn't hear it. That was the worst part, worse even than not seeing it. She strained until her own heartbeat roared in her ears, and beneath it, beneath the crunch of her boots and the rasp of her breath, there was nothing. No footfalls. No breathing. The forest had gone silent in the way forests do when something large moves through them. Every bird had simply stopped existing.

The second wound came at the treeline.

Pressure first. An impossible, crushing grip closed around her upper arm, too wide to be a hand, with too many points of contact. She felt each one distinctly, like thick fingers, or something that approximated fingers. They were neither warm nor cold. They had no temperature at all, and somehow that was the most wrong thing she had ever felt. Her skin could not decide what was touching it. Her nerves fired and misfired, reporting texture that made no sense: smooth and ridged, dry and faintly yielding, like the underside of a mushroom cap.

Then it *squeezed*.

She heard the bone in her arm creak before she felt it, a sound she'd never forget, like a green branch bending in a storm. She screamed and wrenched away, and it let her go. It let her go easily, the way a cat lifts its paw from a mouse.

It wanted her to keep running.

---

Mara fell through the door of the ranger's cabin and slammed it behind her with her good shoulder. She stood in the dark and panted, her back to the wood, and felt the terrible, sheltering solidity of it.

Her arm hung wrong. Bruises bloomed beneath her sleeve, and when she peeled back the fabric with shaking fingers, she saw them in the gray window light: a ring of dark ovals, eight of them, spaced unevenly around her bicep. Nothing with a hand had made that grip.

The calf wound had frozen to her sock. Every shift of weight tore it fresh.

She held her breath and listened.

The cabin was silent. Snow ticked against the glass. Her own blood dripped onto the floorboards with a sound like a slow clock.

Then the floorboard across the room creaked.

Not the way wood settles. The way wood *takes weight.* A long, low groan, and then another, closer. Mara pressed herself so hard against the door that the latch dug into her spine. Her eyes darted across the room, desperate for a shape, a shimmer, a distortion, anything her mind could hold and call *enemy.* There was only the woodstove, the table, the cot, the empty air.

The empty air was breathing.

She could feel it now, not hear it. A faint, rhythmic displacement against her face, like standing near a closing door over and over. It smelled of nothing. Her body kept insisting it should smell of *something*, of rot or musk or blood, and the absence scraped at her like a missing step in the dark.

---

The third wound was the gentlest, and it was the one that broke her.

Something touched her cheek. Lightly. It traced the line of her jaw with a slow, investigating care, the way a person might trace a map. It paused at the pulse in her throat and rested there, feeling her heart hammer against it.

Her tears ran hot down her face, and she felt them split around the invisible thing, parting as water parts around a stone. So it was *there*. It was solid, real, present, a hand's width from her eyes. And her eyes, the organs she had trusted all her life to tell her what was true, reported nothing but the rough cabin wall and the gray light.

She understood then that her fear had nowhere to go. Terror needs a shape. It needs teeth to fixate on, a face to hate, a direction to flee. Her mind kept building the thing and tearing it down again: tall, then crouching, then many-limbed, then something without limbs at all. Each version was worse than the last, and each was surely wrong, and not knowing was a wound deeper than any it had made in her skin.

The pressure at her throat increased by a fraction. A question.

Mara closed her eyes, because at last that made no difference, and she whispered into the dark:

"What *are* you?"

The breathing stopped.

And very close to her ear, in a voice made of nothing, of the silence between snowflakes, something whispered back her own words, in her own voice, perfectly:

*"What are you?"*
