# The Arithmetic of Mercy

The barn smelled of wet hay and diesel. Someone had strung a single bulb from the rafters, and it swung in the draft, pushing shadows back and forth across the floor.

Aurel knelt in the center of the barn with his hands zip-tied behind him. In front of him, against the far wall, knelt his three friends.

Dani, who had taught him to swim in the millpond when they were seven. Lucia, who ran the bakery and slipped day-old bread to the widows. Old Miklos, who had been the schoolmaster until there was no more school.

The captain crouched beside Aurel. He was younger than Aurel expected, maybe thirty, with clean fingernails and a wedding ring he kept turning with his thumb.

"Someone in this village has been feeding the men in the hills," the captain said quietly, as if they were discussing the weather. "I don't know who. I don't need to know who. What I need is for the village to understand that there is a cost." He gestured toward the wall. "One of them. You choose."

"I don't know anything," Aurel said. His voice came out strange and thin. "None of us—"

"I believe you." The captain nodded, almost sympathetic. "That's not the point. You have until I finish this cigarette. If you haven't chosen, all three."

He lit it. The flame of the lighter was the brightest thing in the room.

---

Aurel's mind did something he had never felt it do before. It split.

One part of him simply refused. *This is not happening. This is a dream, you will wake up, you are in your bed and it is Tuesday and the war is on the radio, far away.* That part of him stared at the swinging bulb and counted its arcs.

Another part, and he would hate this part for the rest of his life, began to calculate.

*Miklos is seventy-three. His heart is bad. He has maybe five years. Lucia has two children. Dani has no one, not since his mother died, no wife, no—*

He felt sick. He was weighing them. He was pricing them like grain.

"Aurel." Dani's voice. Steady. "Look at me."

He couldn't. He looked at the floor, at a dark stain in the concrete that he suddenly understood was not oil.

"Aurel, look at me."

He looked. Dani's face was gray, but his eyes were clear, the way they'd been at the millpond when Aurel had panicked in the deep water and Dani had held him up and said *I've got you, stop fighting, I've got you.*

"It's all right," Dani said. "You know it's all right."

"Shut up," Aurel whispered. "Shut up, don't."

Lucia was crying without sound, her shoulders jerking. "My girls," she said. Only that. "My girls." She wasn't begging. It was worse than begging. She was simply stating the fact of them into the air, as if it might hang there and protect her.

Miklos said nothing at all. He had closed his eyes. His lips were moving. Aurel realized he was reciting something, a poem maybe, one of the old ones he'd made them memorize in the fourth form. The schoolmaster was preparing himself, in the only way he knew.

The captain exhaled smoke. The cigarette was a third gone.

---

"Take me," Aurel said. "Take me instead."

"No." The captain didn't even look at him. "That's the one choice you don't get. You live. That's the point."

The point. Aurel understood then. The dead man wasn't the lesson. *He* was the lesson. He was going to walk through the village for the rest of his life, and every person he passed would know what he had done, and he would know that they knew.

His breathing had gone ragged. He could hear it, animal and wet. His knees ached on the concrete, and he was ashamed that some small part of him noticed his knees at a time like this.

"Please," he said to the captain. "I'm begging you. I'll do anything. I'll tell you who. I'll make something up, I'll give you names—"

"Half," said the captain, tapping ash.

Aurel turned back to the wall.

*Choose Miklos. He's old. He's lived. Everyone would understand.* But Miklos had taught half the village to read. Miklos had sat with Aurel's father through the fever. And choosing him *because* he was old felt like saying his remaining years were worth less, that a life could be measured by what was left in it instead of what was in it.

*Choose Dani. He offered.* But that was the coward's way, wasn't it? Letting the brave man pay for your bravery. Letting him make the choice so you wouldn't have to. And Dani was the one Aurel loved most, which was exactly why a small, sick voice said *not Dani, anyone but Dani*, which meant Aurel was choosing for himself, for his own grief, not for any justice.

*Not Lucia. The girls.* That was the only certainty he had, and he clung to it, and hated himself for clinging, because it meant that the choice was really only between two.

Lucia met his eyes, and he saw her understand that she had been spared, and he saw the relief flood her face, and then the horror at her own relief, and she looked away from the two men beside her and sobbed out loud for the first time.

"Aurel," Dani said again. Gently. "Stop fighting."

The cigarette was nearly to the filter.

Miklos opened his eyes. He looked at Dani, and then at Aurel, and something passed across his lined face, something like a teacher watching a student about to get an answer wrong.

"He's young, Aurel," the old man said. "Don't be stupid."

"Time," said the captain, and dropped the cigarette, and ground it under his heel.

---

Aurel would never be sure, afterward, whether he said the name or whether Miklos simply said it for him. He remembered his mouth opening. He remembered a sound. He remembered the captain nodding, as if a reasonable business transaction had been concluded.

He remembered Miklos saying, very clearly, "Close your eyes, boy."

He didn't.

The soldier stepped forward. There was no ceremony. The pistol came up to the back of the old man's head and the sound was enormous in the barn, flat and total, and it seemed to go on echoing in the rafters long after it should have stopped.

Miklos pitched forward. The back of his skull was simply open, a ragged darkness where gray hair had been, and blood came out of him faster than Aurel had believed blood could come out of anything. It spread across the concrete toward the old stain, joined it, and kept going. Lucia screamed and screamed. Dani had gone completely still, his face spattered with red flecks like freckles, staring at the body beside him.

The old man's fingers twitched twice against the floor and stopped.

The blood reached Aurel's knees. It was warm. He hadn't expected it to be warm.

---

The captain stood and brushed off his trousers. He cut Aurel's zip-tie himself, carefully, the way you might free a trapped animal.

"Go home," he said. "Tell them."

Aurel didn't move. He knelt in the spreading red, staring at the body of the man who had taught him to read, and the only thought his mind would give him, over and over, was the line of the poem Miklos had been reciting. He had finally recognized it. Fourth form. Autumn term. Something about the leaves not grieving for the tree.

He couldn't remember the rest.

He would spend years trying to remember the rest.

Dani found him there when the soldiers had gone, and cut his own bonds on a nail in the wall, and knelt in the blood beside him, and put an arm around his shoulders. Neither of them said anything. There was nothing in any language that would fit.

Later, much later, Dani would tell him *you didn't choose, he did, he chose for you*, and Aurel would nod, and would never once believe it.

He remembered Miklos saying, very clearly, "Close your eyes, boy."

The old man's fingers twitched twice against the floor and stopped.

# The Quiet Neighbor

Harold Voss had lived next door to me for eleven years, and in all that time I never heard him raise his voice.

He was the kind of neighbor people describe as "a real gem." Retired machinist. Widower. He kept his lawn cut to exactly two and a half inches and brought my wife tomatoes from his garden every August. When our daughter Emma learned to ride her bike, Harold stood at the end of his driveway and clapped like she'd won the Tour de France.

So when he asked me to water his plants while he visited his sister in Duluth, I didn't think twice.

"Just the ferns in the kitchen and the ones on the back porch," he said, pressing a brass key into my palm. His hands were always so clean. I remember noticing that. "Don't worry about the basement. Nothing down there but my workshop."

I should have wondered why he mentioned it at all.

---

The first two days were uneventful. I watered the ferns, checked the mail, and admired the orderliness of his home: the spice rack alphabetized, the dish towels folded into perfect thirds. There was something almost museum-like about it, as if no one actually lived there.

On the third day, I noticed the smell.

It was faint at first, sweet and cloying, like flowers left too long in a vase. I thought maybe something had crawled into the walls and died. A mouse, a squirrel. It seemed strongest near the narrow door off the kitchen, the one that led downstairs.

I stood there with my hand on the knob for a long time.

*Nothing down there but my workshop.*

I told myself I was being a good neighbor. If an animal had died down there, Harold would want to know. If a pipe had burst, if something was rotting, he'd thank me for catching it early. That's what I told myself.

The door was locked. But Harold, meticulous Harold, kept a labeled key hook by the pantry. The third key from the left was marked, in his tidy block print, BSMT.

---

The stairs were unfinished wood, and they groaned under my weight. The smell thickened with each step until it coated the back of my throat, sweet and chemical at once: formaldehyde, bleach, and underneath it all something older and meatier that my brain refused to name.

The workshop was exactly what he'd promised. A pegboard of tools, each one outlined in marker so you'd know where it belonged. A drill press. A lathe. A workbench so clean you could have eaten off it.

But at the far end of the room was another door. Steel, painted the same beige as the walls, as if it were trying not to be noticed. It had a combination padlock hanging open on the hasp. Harold must have forgotten to close it in his hurry to leave.

I pushed the door open, found the light switch, and flipped it.

---

I want to describe what I saw with care, because the detectives asked me to so many times that the words have worn grooves in my memory. And because I think the people in that room deserve to be seen clearly, even now.

The room was maybe twelve feet square, lit by a single bare bulb and a row of small display lights, the kind you'd find in a jewelry store. The walls were lined floor to ceiling with shelves Harold had built himself. The joinery was beautiful. That's the obscene part. The craftsmanship was *beautiful.*

On the shelves were jars.

Dozens of them, mason jars and laboratory specimen jars, each filled with a yellowish fluid, each labeled in that same neat block print. A name. A date. A town. *DENISE, 4/1998, EAU CLAIRE. MARCUS, 10/2003, ROCHESTER.*

In the first jar I really looked at, a pair of eyes floated side by side, the irises a pale, startling green, the optic nerves trailing beneath them like the tails of tadpoles. They had turned slightly in the fluid, so that they seemed to be looking past me toward the door. I have dreamed about those eyes more nights than I haven't.

Other jars held fingers, clipped neatly at the second knuckle, the nails still painted in chipped coral and red and one in glittering purple, the color a teenager would choose. One held an ear, a small gold hoop still threaded through the lobe. One held something pink and folded that I did not understand until much later, when the coroner told me it was a tongue.

On the middle shelf, under glass, lay a row of scalps. Harold had dried and stretched them over wooden forms like hat blocks, so the hair hung down as if it were still growing: a long black braid, a blond ponytail with a scrunchie still in it, a close-cropped gray fade. Beneath each one sat a small brass plaque, the kind you'd get engraved at a trophy shop.

A tackle box on the workbench stood open. Instead of lures, its little compartments were filled with teeth, sorted by type. Molars in one row. Incisors in another. A few still had fillings. One had braces.

And the wall. God, the wall.

The back wall was covered in photographs, hundreds of them, pinned in rows as straight as Harold's lawn. Some were Polaroids gone amber with age; others were glossy prints from a drugstore. Each set told a story in sequence: a woman laughing at a bus stop, taken from across the street. The same woman through a window, reading. The same woman in this basement, on the steel table I hadn't noticed until then, in the corner, the one with the drain in the floor beneath it. Her eyes were open in that last photo. They were green.

Below the photographs, arranged on a narrow shelf like a store display, were the things they'd had on them. Wallets, their driver's licenses fanned out in a neat arc. A child's backpack with a unicorn keychain. Car keys. A wedding ring. A pink sneaker, size six.

I knew that sneaker.

Everyone in town knew that sneaker. It had been on every flyer for the past four months: *MISSING: KAYLEE BRANDT, AGE 14. LAST SEEN WEARING PINK SNEAKERS.* Harold had helped hand out those flyers. I had stood next to him in the Lutheran church parking lot while he taped them to telephone poles. He'd shaken his head and said, *What kind of monster.*

---

I don't remember climbing the stairs. I remember the kitchen floor, cool against my cheek, and the ferns I'd watered that morning dripping onto the tile. I remember fumbling for my phone and my hands shaking so badly I dialed wrong twice.

And I remember the sound, just as the dispatcher answered, of tires on gravel.

I crawled to the window and looked out.

Harold's Buick was pulling into the driveway. Two days early.

He got out slowly, the way older men do, one hand on the doorframe. He retrieved a small suitcase from the trunk. Then he paused, and turned, and looked at my house. At my car, which was in my driveway. At his kitchen window, where I was crouched.

He smiled. That same warm, gentle smile he'd worn when Emma learned to ride her bike.

Then he started up the walk.

"Sir?" the dispatcher said. "Sir, are you there? What's your emergency?"

I heard his key slide into the front door lock.

"He's coming inside," I whispered. "Please. He's coming inside."

The door swung open, and Harold Voss stepped into his clean, quiet house, set down his suitcase, and said, in the kindest voice I have ever heard:

"I told you not to worry about the basement."

# Cell Block D

The alarm didn't start the riot. It only announced what had already happened.

By the time the klaxon began its flat, mechanical wail, Officer Dale Reyes was on his back on the second-tier walkway, with a man's knee on his chest and the taste of his own blood filling his mouth. He'd been three steps from the control gate when the lights in D Block stuttered. In that half-second of darkness, forty men who had been waiting eleven months for an opening moved all at once.

Now the block was a roar. It wasn't voices so much as a single sound, a hundred throats and fists on steel and the shriek of bunk frames being torn from their bolts. Somebody had set a mattress on fire on the lower tier. The smoke rolled upward in a black, chemical sheet, and the emergency lights turned it the color of a bruise.

Reyes got an arm free and drove his elbow into the man's jaw. He felt teeth give. The weight lifted, and he rolled, scrambling for the railing, and saw the floor below.

Officer Pruitt was down near the showers. Six inmates stood over him, and their arms rose and fell in a rhythm that was almost patient. One held a sharpened length of mop handle. Another had a padlock knotted into a sock, swinging it in wide, whistling arcs. Pruitt had stopped covering his head. That was the detail Reyes would remember at three in the morning for years afterward. Pruitt's hands lay open on the concrete, palms up, as if he were asking for something.

"Pruitt!" The word vanished into the noise.

The gate at the far end of the block buzzed. Reyes felt a surge of hope before he understood. The gate wasn't opening from outside. Someone had the control panel. Through the smoke he could see an inmate in the booth, backlit by the monitors, slamming his palm against every button he could reach. Cell doors rattled open all down the line, one after another, like a drumroll.

Men poured out who had nothing to do with the riot. Some ran for the corners and pressed their backs to the walls, hands raised, wanting no part of it. Others had waited years for this. A thin man Reyes knew only as Tully walked calmly out of cell 14 and went straight to cell 22, where a man was screaming and trying to pull his door shut again. Tully dragged him out by the hair. Old debts were being collected. The guards were only part of it.

Reyes pulled his radio from his belt. The antenna was snapped, and the casing was cracked and slick. He keyed it anyway.

"Tier two, D Block, officer down, multiple officers down, we need..."

A tray hit him across the temple. The world went white and quiet for a moment. Then the sound came back, underwater at first and then all at once. He was on his knees. The man who'd hit him, young, maybe twenty, with a teardrop inked beneath one eye, looked almost as frightened as Reyes felt. The kid raised the tray again and hesitated.

That hesitation saved Reyes's life. Down on the floor, the east door blew inward.

The tactical team came through in a wedge of black shields and helmets, with the hollow *thoomp* of gas launchers ahead of them. Canisters skittered across the concrete, spinning and hissing, and white clouds bloomed and merged with the smoke. The roar in the block changed pitch. It became coughing, retching, and bodies colliding as men tried to run from something they couldn't see.

Rubber rounds cracked off the walls. A man on the lower tier took one in the thigh and went down howling. The shield line pushed forward, and anyone in its path was knocked flat, pinned, and zip-tied. The team moved with brutal, practiced efficiency. Batons rose and fell. Some of the men being struck had been fighting. Some had only been in the way. In the gas and the dark there was no difference, and nobody was trying to tell.

The kid with the teardrop dropped the tray and ran. Reyes let him go.

He crawled toward the stairs, eyes streaming and lungs burning, one hand on the railing to keep from falling. At the bottom he found Pruitt. Two members of the tactical team were kneeling over him, one pressing gauze to his head. The gauze was soaking through too fast.

"He's breathing," one of them said, not to Reyes, maybe not to anyone. "He's still breathing."

Around them, D Block was coming apart and being put back together at the same time. Men lay face-down in rows with their wrists bound behind them. Water from a burst pipe spread across the floor, carrying ash and blood toward the drain in slow, pink ribbons. The mattress fire hissed out under an extinguisher. Somewhere a man was crying, softly and steadily, the way a child cries after it's too tired to scream.

The alarm kept wailing. Nobody had thought to turn it off.

Reyes sat down against the wall and pressed his hand to the gash above his ear. He looked up at the control booth. The inmate who'd taken it sat in the chair with his hands laced behind his head, waiting to be dragged out, and he was smiling.

It had taken four minutes, Reyes would learn later. Four minutes from the lights flickering to the east door coming down.

It had felt like the whole of his life.

# Professional Courtesy

The Hotel Marisol had seen better decades. The wallpaper was peeling in long, tired strips, and the air conditioner rattled like it was trying to confess something.

Delphine sat cross-legged on the bed nearest the window, a white hand towel spread across the comforter, the pieces of her pistol arranged on it with the care of a surgeon's tray. Across the room, Marcus had claimed the little round table by the minibar. He was running a cloth down the length of a knife with the slow, absent rhythm of a man petting a cat.

"You're doing it again," Delphine said without looking up.

"Doing what?"

"Humming. You hum when you clean that thing. It's Sinatra."

"It's Dean Martin."

"It's unsettling, is what it is."

Marcus held the blade up to the lamp and squinted. "Everybody's got their rituals. You line your bullets up by the manufacturer's date."

"That's organization. That's different."

"Sure it is."

The air conditioner coughed. Somewhere down the hall, a television laughed at a joke neither of them could hear.

"Can I ask you something?" Marcus said.

"You're going to anyway."

"Do you have a favorite? Like, a way you prefer. If you had your pick."

Delphine slid the barrel back into place and considered it, the way a person might consider their favorite pasta shape. "Honestly? The quiet ones. The ones where nobody even knows it was a job. Man has a heart condition, man's heart gives out. Doctor signs the paper, family cries, everybody goes home. Nobody's looking for anyone."

"That's so boring."

"It's *elegant*. There's a difference."

"See, that's the problem with you. You're an artist who doesn't want anyone to see the art." Marcus set the knife down and leaned back, the chair creaking in protest. "What's the point of painting a masterpiece if you hang it in a closet?"

"The point is I don't go to prison, Marcus."

"Neither do I."

"You got *lucky* in Lisbon."

He pointed at her. "Lisbon was skill."

"Lisbon was a pigeon."

"The pigeon was a variable I accounted for."

"You told me the pigeon was the single most terrifying moment of your career."

Marcus picked the knife back up and resumed polishing, a little more aggressively than before. "I was being humble."

Delphine smiled for the first time all evening. She snapped the slide into place and racked it once, listening to the sound the way a musician listens to a tuned string. Satisfied, she set it down.

"Okay," she said. "Your turn. What's your favorite?"

He didn't answer right away. He turned the knife over, watching the lamplight crawl along the edge. When he spoke, his voice had lost some of its showmanship.

"The ones where they know it's coming."

Delphine raised an eyebrow.

"Not like that," he said quickly. "Not the cruel way. I just mean... the ones who've done enough that they've been waiting for it. Years, sometimes. And when you finally walk in, there's this look. Like relief. Like they've been holding their breath for a decade and somebody finally told them they could stop." He shrugged. "Feels less like killing somebody and more like delivering mail they've been expecting."

The room was quiet for a moment.

"That's the most disturbing thing you've ever said to me," Delphine said. "And you once described your ex-wife's lasagna as 'a crime scene with cheese.'"

"That was accurate, though."

"It was accurate."

Marcus sheathed the knife and slid it into his boot. "What about you? You ever get the look?"

Delphine began packing her kit back into its case, each piece in its foam cutout. "I don't let them see me long enough to have a look."

"That's sad."

"That's *professional*."

"Those aren't mutually exclusive."

She snapped the case shut and gave him a long, flat stare. "Are you psychoanalyzing me? In a two-star hotel? While there's a stain on that carpet shaped like Ohio?"

He glanced down. "Huh. It really is Ohio."

"Everything in this room is a little bit Ohio."

The air conditioner gave one final, heroic rattle and died. The silence that followed was so sudden that both of them instinctively reached toward their weapons before catching themselves.

They looked at each other.

"We should get out of this business," Marcus said.

"We say that every time."

"We should mean it one time."

Delphine lay back on the bed, arms folded behind her head, staring at a water stain on the ceiling. "What would you even do?"

"Open a restaurant."

"You can't cook."

"I'd hire someone who can cook. I'd be the guy who walks around and asks people how their meal is."

"You'd terrify them."

"I'd *charm* them."

"You'd hum Dean Martin at them while they ate."

"Now you're just being cruel."

She closed her eyes. "Wake me at four. The target's car leaves at six."

Marcus turned off the lamp. In the dark, after a minute, very quietly, he started humming again.

"Marcus."

"Sorry."

A pause.

"...It *is* Sinatra, by the way."

"Go to sleep, Delphine."

results.model_response:
**The Burning of Agnes Hale**

They had stacked the faggots to her knees, green wood beneath dry, so it would catch slowly. The magistrate wanted the crowd to see.

The first thing Agnes felt was not pain but warmth, almost kind, like standing too near a hearth on a winter night. It rose through the soles of her bare feet and crept up her shins. For a moment she thought absurdly of her mother's kitchen, of bread cooling on the sill. Then the kindling cracked and settled, and the warmth sharpened into something with teeth.

The heat came in waves. It didn't stay where the flames were. It climbed the air itself, pressing against her face so that her eyes streamed and the skin of her cheeks tightened like drying leather. Her wet shift steamed, then hissed, then went stiff and hot against her legs. The iron chain around her waist began to hold the heat, a band of it, and when she strained against it, it bit.

Then the smoke found her.

It came up grey-white and thick from the green wood, rolling over itself, and it had a taste: sap and pitch and something sour underneath. It filled her mouth when she gasped. It crawled into her nose and throat and sat heavy in her chest like wet wool. She coughed, and coughing made her breathe, and breathing brought more of it in. The square vanished behind it. The faces of her neighbors, the baker, the widow Crane, the boy she'd nursed through the spotted fever, became smudges, then shadows, then nothing. There was only the grey, and the roar underneath it, and the light turning orange at the edges of the world.

She had promised herself she would not scream. She had rehearsed silence in her cell for three nights, lips pressed together, imagining her dignity like a stone she could hold in her fist.

The fire reached her feet in earnest, and the stone was gone.

The first scream tore out of her without permission, raw and high and animal, a sound she had never known her body could make. It surprised the crowd; she heard a ripple of it, a woman's sob, a man's nervous laugh. The second scream had words in it. *God*, perhaps, or *mother*, or only *please*, though she couldn't have said which, and the smoke choked the end of it into a rasp.

Her throat was raw now, scorched from the inside. Each breath was fire drawn down into her. Her screams grew hoarse, broken, spaced apart by coughing that bent her double against the chain. Through a gap in the smoke she glimpsed the church spire, black against a hard blue sky, and she fixed her stinging eyes on it. Not out of faith. She simply needed one thing in the world that was not burning.

The last sound she made was not a scream at all. It was a name, cracked and whispered, lost under the crackle of the pyre: the name of her daughter, who had been taken to her aunt's house two villages away so she would not have to watch.

Then the smoke closed over the spire, and Agnes Hale stopped being able to see anything at all.

The crowd stayed until the fire burned low. Few of them spoke. That night the baker couldn't eat, and the widow Crane scrubbed her hands until they bled, and the boy with the fever-scarred face lay awake smelling smoke in his hair and understood, for the first time, what his village had done.

---

results.model_response:
# The Field at Harrow's End

The battle had ended three days ago, and the crows had grown fat.

Vessane Mordaunt walked among the fallen as the light failed behind the hills, her hem dark with the mud of Harrow's End. The field stretched a mile in every direction, a churned brown wound studded with broken pikes and the shapes of men. Four thousand of them, the heralds had said. Four thousand dead for a river crossing that neither king would remember by spring.

She would remember. She would make use of them.

The smell had reached her before she crested the ridge, thick and sweet, clinging to the back of her throat like syrup gone to rot. Up close it was worse. The bodies had begun to bloat in the late summer heat, bellies swollen tight as drumskins beneath their surcoats. A young man lay at her feet with his face turned to the sky, and the flesh of his cheeks had gone the grey-green of old bruises, slack and waxen. Flies worked at the corners of his eyes. Where a sword had opened his neck, the edges of the wound had blackened and curled back like burnt parchment, and something pale moved within.

Vessane knelt beside him and pressed two fingers to his sternum. The skin gave beneath her touch, too soft, sliding a fraction over the bone beneath as though it were no longer properly attached. A bubble of foul air escaped his lips with a sound like a sigh.

"You'll do," she murmured.

---

She chose the center of the field, where the dead lay thickest, and began to draw.

The chalk she used was ground from the knucklebones of hanged men, and it did not want to make marks. It skidded on the mud, then bit too deep, then crumbled, as though the earth itself were flinching from it. She persisted. The circle took shape slowly—not a true circle, for true circles belonged to the sun and to the turning of honest things. Hers bent inward at seven points, and the lines between them curved in ways the eye refused to follow. Looking at the sigil directly made the vision swim. Looking away, it seemed to shift at the edges, as if it were still being drawn by some other hand.

When she finished, the crows went silent.

All at once, across the whole field, a thousand black birds stopped their squabbling and lifted into the air. They did not scatter as frightened birds do. They rose in a single slow column and flew east, away from her, and not one of them cried out.

Vessane stepped into the center of the sigil and opened her mouth to speak.

---

The words were not a language. Language was built for the living, for breath and warmth and meaning passed from one mind to another. What she spoke instead was older and colder—sounds shaped to fit the spaces between heartbeats, syllables that tasted of iron and grave-dirt on her tongue. Each one cost her something. She felt it leave: a little heat from her fingertips, a memory of her mother's voice gone suddenly flat and colorless, the ability to recall what summer rain had smelled like.

The air began to change.

It did not grow cold, exactly. Cold was a natural thing, a thing of winter and deep water. This was an absence—as though warmth had not been taken from the air but had simply never existed there. The breath from her lips did not fog. The grass at the edge of the sigil blackened, not wilting but *unmaking*, each blade collapsing into fine grey ash from the tip down, a ring of death spreading outward from her feet with the patience of rot.

Sound went wrong next. The wind still moved through the broken banners, but its noise arrived a half-heartbeat late, and then a half-heartbeat early, stuttering out of time with the fluttering cloth. Somewhere a loose piece of armor clattered against stone, and Vessane heard the echo before she heard the sound itself.

She kept speaking. Blood ran from her left nostril and did not drip—it crept sideways along her cheek toward her ear, drawn by some pull that had nothing to do with the earth.

And the dead began to listen.

---

It started as a twitch. The young soldier at the edge of the circle—the one with the ruined throat—jerked once, his fingers curling in the mud. Then another body shuddered, and another, a ripple of small wrong movements spreading across the field like wind through wheat.

Then they began to rise.

They did not rise as the living do, gathering their limbs and pushing up from the ground. They were *lifted*, pulled upward from somewhere near the center of the chest as though hooked by an invisible line, their heads and arms dangling until the last moment when the spine snapped straight with an audible crack. Their joints moved in the wrong order. A knee bent before the hip. A shoulder rotated fully backward before settling into place with a wet grinding of bone on bone.

The bloated ones were worst. As they stood, the gases trapped inside them found their way out, and the field filled with a low chorus of groans and hisses that were not voices but sounded almost like them. One man's belly split along a seam of rot as he straightened, and what spilled out slapped wetly against his thighs. He did not notice. He had no need of those things now.

Their eyes opened. Most had been clouded white, milky and shrunken in their sockets. Now, one by one, they filled with a faint light—not a glow, but a *wrongness* of color, a hue that had no name because it did not belong to the world. It was the color of the space behind closed eyelids. The color of a sound heard in a dream.

Four thousand heads turned toward her in perfect unison.

---

Vessane swayed in the center of the sigil. Her hands had gone white to the wrist, the skin of her fingers wrinkled and pale as if she had soaked them in water for a week. She could not remember her father's name. She decided it did not matter.

The young soldier stood nearest to her. Flies still crawled across his face, undeterred, and the maggots in his throat had not stopped their work. But his jaw was moving—slowly, clumsily, the dried tendons creaking like old leather.

He was trying to speak.

She had heard of this, in the oldest texts. Sometimes the dead remembered. Sometimes a scrap of what they had been clung to the bones like cloth snagged on a nail. She stepped closer and watched his ruined lips shape a single word, soundless, over and over.

*Home.*

Vessane looked at him for a long moment. Something in her chest tightened, and she felt the old instinct toward pity stir—and then she spoke one more syllable of that cold, wrong tongue, and watched the word die on his lips. The light in his eyes steadied. Whatever had remained of him guttered and went out, and what stood in its place was hollow and patient and hers.

"No," she told him gently. "Not home. Not yet."

She turned to face the field, to face the silent ranks of the risen dead swaying like grain beneath a sky that had gone the color of an old wound. Far to the east, in the stone city of Aldercross, the king who had sent these men to die would be sitting down to his supper.

Vessane smiled, and her lips cracked, and did not bleed.

"March."

As one, four thousand dead men took their first step—and the earth beneath them *groaned*, as though it too remembered what it was to be buried, and resented them for leaving.

# The Proving

The warehouse smelled like motor oil and wet concrete. Danny had been inside maybe ten minutes, but it felt like hours, standing under the single hanging bulb while the others circled at the edge of the light like they were waiting for a fight to start.

Marcus sat on an overturned crate, elbows on his knees, turning a ring on his finger. He didn't look at Danny. That was worse than if he had.

"You know why you're here," Marcus said.

Danny nodded. His mouth had gone dry an hour ago, back in the car, when Tre had passed him the bottle and he'd pretended to drink.

"Say it."

"To show I'm with you."

"To show you're *with* us." Marcus finally looked up. His eyes were flat and patient, the eyes of someone who had watched this moment play out many times and already knew most of the endings. "Anybody can say they're with us. Kids say it on the corner every day. Words don't cost nothing."

Two of the older ones, Ray and a heavyset guy Danny only knew as Bishop, stepped out of the dark dragging a man between them. His hands were zip-tied behind him, and his face was already swollen on one side. They dropped him onto the concrete, where he curled onto his shoulder, breathing hard through his nose.

"This is Leon," Marcus said, like he was introducing a neighbor. "Leon talked to some people he shouldn't have talked to. Now Leon's gonna help you with your education."

Leon lifted his head. He couldn't have been more than twenty-five. His eyes found Danny's and held there, and Danny saw something in them he'd never forget: not anger, not even fear exactly, but *recognition*. Like Leon had stood exactly where Danny was standing, once.

Tre pressed something into Danny's hand. A length of pipe, cold and heavy, wrapped at one end with electrical tape.

"Marcus," Danny started. "I thought... I thought it'd be—"

"You thought what?" Marcus's voice didn't rise. It dropped. "You thought you'd run a package? Stand lookout? You been running packages for six months, little man. That's errand-boy work. This is family."

Somebody laughed in the dark. Someone else said, "He's gonna fold," loud enough to be heard.

"Your brother didn't fold," Bishop said.

That landed like a fist. Danny's brother, Jaylen, three years in the ground, and Danny had spent every one of those years wanting to be what Jaylen was to these men. Wanting that respect. That protection. That *name*.

"Everybody in here did this," Marcus said quietly. "Everybody. You walk out that door without doing it, you ain't nothing to us. And you know too much to be nothing." He let that sit. "You understand what I'm telling you?"

Danny understood. The door behind him wasn't a door out. It never had been.

The circle closed in. Voices overlapped: *Do it. Stop stalling. Handle your business.* Tre's hand on his back, pushing. The bulb swinging slightly, making the shadows lurch.

Leon said, very softly, "Just get it over with, man."

Danny swung.

The sound was the worst part. Not a crack like in the movies, but a dull, wet thud that traveled up the pipe into his wrists. Leon made a noise Danny had never heard a human make. The men erupted, cheering and shouting, and someone yelled *"Again!"* and the pressure of all those voices was a physical thing, a hand around his throat, and he swung again. And again. He stopped hearing his own breathing. He stopped seeing Leon's face, because there was too much blood on it to see a face at all.

When Ray finally caught his arm, Danny didn't know how many times he'd hit him. Leon was still breathing, barely, a thin bubbling rasp on the concrete. The pipe slipped out of Danny's hand and rang against the floor.

Marcus stood, crossed the space between them, and pulled Danny into an embrace. His hand cupped the back of Danny's head like a father's.

"That's it," he murmured. "That's it. You're home now."

The others crowded in, slapping his shoulders, grinning, calling him by a new name. Danny smiled back, because he knew that was what he was supposed to do.

Later, in Tre's car, with the windows down and the city blurring past, he looked at his hands. They'd been washed, but he could still feel the vibration of the pipe in the bones of his wrists.

He realized that Marcus had been telling the truth. He *was* home.

And he would never be able to leave.

# The Last Course

I made the lamb the way Clara used to make it, with rosemary and too much garlic, and I watched Daniel's face when he recognized the smell. There was something there, a flicker, before he arranged himself into gratitude.

"You didn't have to go to all this trouble, Ruth."

"It's no trouble," I said. "It's the anniversary. Someone should mark it."

Two years since my sister went down the cellar stairs of the house they shared and did not come back up. A fall, the coroner said. Slippery steps, poor lighting, a glass of wine too many. Daniel wept at the funeral with such conviction that I almost believed him. Almost.

He cut into the lamb. I watched the fork travel to his mouth, watched his jaw work, watched him swallow. It is a strange intimacy, watching a man eat. I had never noticed before how much of the body is involved: the tendons in the throat, the small bob of the Adam's apple, the way his left hand rested flat on the tablecloth as if to steady the whole enterprise.

"It's wonderful," he said. "It tastes just like hers."

"I used her recipe card. She left it at my house one Christmas. Her handwriting is all over it."

"She had terrible handwriting."

"She did."

We both smiled. For a moment we were two people who had loved the same woman, and I felt the old doubt stir in me like a draft under a door. Then he reached for his wine, and I saw the watch on his wrist, the gold one, bought three months after the funeral with the insurance money, and the doubt settled back down into the dark where it belonged.

---

The first sign came during the potatoes.

He touched his lower lip with his napkin, dabbed, then touched it again. A small frown creased his forehead, the kind you make when you can't quite place a song.

"Everything all right?"

"Fine. Just, my mouth's a bit tingly. Pepper, maybe."

"I may have been heavy-handed. Clara always said I had no restraint."

"She said that about everyone." He laughed, and I laughed, and he took another bite.

I asked about work. He told me about a client in Harrogate, a difficult man, a property dispute, and I made the right noises at the right intervals. He talked with his hands. I noticed that he had begun to flex the fingers of his right hand between gestures, opening and closing them, the way you do when a limb has fallen asleep.

"Do you ever go down to the cellar?" I asked. "Now, I mean."

The hand stopped moving.

"No," he said. "I had it sealed. I couldn't bear it."

"I understand."

"Do you?" He looked at me then, really looked, and I saw that a fine sheen of sweat had appeared along his hairline, catching the candlelight. "I'm sorry. That came out wrong. It's warm in here, isn't it?"

"I'll open a window."

I did not open a window. I stood, walked to it, put my hand on the latch, and stood there with my back to him, looking out at the black garden and my own reflection laid over it like a ghost. I counted to twenty. When I turned around, he had loosened his collar.

"Ruth." His voice had changed. It was thicker now, as though his tongue had grown too large for his mouth. "Ruth, I think I'm unwell."

"You do look flushed."

"My heart's..." He pressed his palm flat against his chest,

# The Plank

The sun hung low and bloody over the Caribbean when they dragged Tobias Wren up from the hold.

He had been down there three days, chained among the bilge rats and the stink of rotting ballast, and the light struck his eyes like a slap. He stumbled on the ladder. Someone's boot found his ribs, and he went sprawling onto the sun-bleached deck of the *Merciful Widow*, tasting salt and splinters.

When he looked up, the whole crew was watching. Sixty men lined the rails and hung from the rigging like crows on a gibbet. None of them would meet his eyes. Four days ago, eleven of them had sworn blood oaths to him in the dark of the forecastle. Now they stared at their feet, at the sea, at anything but the man they had promised to follow.

Captain Isolde Marrack stood by the starboard rail, one hand resting on the pommel of her cutlass. She was not a large woman, but she had a way of standing that made the deck seem to tilt toward her. Her coat was the deep red of old wine, and the scar that ran from her left temple to her jaw pulled her mouth into something that was never quite a smile.

"Mister Wren," she said, almost gently. "You look poorly."

Tobias tried to speak. His throat had been dry so long that the words came out as a croak. "Captain, I, please, I was misled, Harrow put the notion in my head, I never meant..."

"Harrow." Marrack nodded slowly. "Harrow is at the bottom of the Windward Passage with a ball of shot tied to his ankles. He had a good deal to say before he went. Most of it concerned you."

A murmur ran through the crew. Tobias felt his bowels turn to water.

"You had my charts copied," the captain went on, walking now, her boots slow and deliberate on the planks. "You had pistols hidden in the sail locker. You meant to take my ship off the Tortugas and hand my head to the Spanish for the bounty. Is that about the shape of it?"

"No, no, Captain, I swear on my mother's..."

"Your mother was a Bristol whore who sold you to a slaver for a jug of gin. You told me so yourself, the night I cut you loose from his hold and gave you a berth." She crouched before him, close enough that he could smell the tar and gunpowder on her. "I gave you a *ship*, Tobias. I gave you a share. And you tried to take the rest."

She stood. "Run it out."

Two men hauled a long plank from the lumber stores, eight feet of weathered oak, and lashed it to the rail with a practiced efficiency that told Tobias they had done this before. It jutted out over the water like an accusing finger.

And then he saw the water.

The sea below was a clear, luminous green, shot through with gold where the dying sun struck it. And moving through that green, lazy and patient, were shadows. Long gray shapes, circling. One broke the surface: a dorsal fin, dark and triangular, slicing through the swell and slipping under again without a ripple.

"We've been chumming since dawn," said Marrack conversationally. "Offal from the hog we slaughtered. Blood from the galley. They've been following us all afternoon. Tigers, mostly. A few blues." She tilted her head. "They're very hungry, Tobias. We've been careful to keep them hungry."

"Captain." The word tore out of him. "Captain, for the love of God, maroon me. Put me on a spit of sand with a pistol and one shot. Flog me. Keelhaul me. Anything..."

"Anything?" She considered it. "No."

They hauled him to his feet. His legs would not hold him, and in the end two men had to carry him to the rail and set him on the plank like a sack of grain. The oak creaked under his weight. It was warm from the sun, rough against the soles of his bare feet.

Behind him, someone pressed the point of a boarding pike into the small of his back.

"Walk, Mister Wren."

He took one step. The plank dipped. The sea yawned beneath him, impossibly far and impossibly close all at once. His vision narrowed to a pinprick; his heartbeat was a war drum in his ears. The shadows below had stopped their lazy circling. They were drifting toward the ship now, drawn by something, by the vibration of the plank, perhaps, or by some animal sense of what was coming.

Another step. The pike pricked him again, and he felt a thin warm trickle of his own blood running down his back. Below, a fin broke the water and turned sharply toward the hull.

*They can smell it*, he thought. *Oh God, they can smell it.*

He was weeping now, great ugly sobs that shook his whole body. He thought of his mother, of the slaver's hold, of the night the captain's crew had burst through the hatch with lanterns and cutlasses and he had thought, for the first time in his life, that he might be saved. He thought of Harrow's voice in the dark: *She's soft, Wren. She's getting soft. A crew like this could take the whole Main if the right man had the wheel.*

He reached the end of the plank. There was nowhere left to go.

He turned, one last time, and looked back at the ship: the crew, silent as a congregation; the captain at the rail, her scarred face unreadable.

"Isolde," he whispered. "Please."

For a moment, just a moment, something moved behind her eyes. Then it was gone.

"Mister Crane," she said.

The pike thrust forward.

---

Tobias hit the water feet-first and went under in a white explosion of bubbles. The cold shocked the breath out of him. For a heartbeat there was only the green silence of the sea, the muffled roar in his ears, the sunlight dappling down through the surface above him like light through a church window.

Then he kicked upward and broke the surface, gasping, spluttering, and began to swim.

He had no idea where he was going. There was no land in sight. But his body moved of its own accord, arms churning, legs kicking wildly, and that was the worst thing he could have done, because every frantic splash sent a message through the water, and the message said: *wounded, panicking, prey*.

The first strike came from below.

He never saw it. He only felt the impact, like being hit by a runaway cart, a crushing, grinding pressure around his left leg, and then he was yanked under so hard that his teeth snapped shut on his tongue. The water went dark with a cloud that billowed around him like smoke. He screamed, and the sea poured into his mouth.

The tiger shark shook its head, once, twice, a savage sawing motion, and something gave way. Tobias felt it tear. He surfaced again, choking, flailing, and there was a strange lightness on his left side, a wrongness, and the water all around him was turning red.

On the deck above, the crew watched. Some of the younger hands turned away. Old Pettibone, the sailmaker, crossed himself. The rest stood stone-faced, because they understood, as the captain meant them to understand, that this was the lesson, and it was being written in blood where every one of them could read it.

A second fin came in from the east, fast and low. A blue shark, sleek as a knife, slashed past and took Tobias's outflung arm in passing, ripping a long ragged strip of flesh from wrist to elbow. He shrieked, a thin high sound that carried across the water and set the gulls wheeling.

Then they were all around him.

The water boiled. Gray bodies thrashed and rolled, churning the sea into a pink froth. Tobias surfaced once more, his face white and uncomprehending, his mouth open in a scream that had no sound left in it. His eyes found the ship. Found the captain.

Then a great blunt head rose out of the water behind him, jaws spread wide, rows of serrated teeth gleaming in the red light of the setting sun. It closed over his shoulders and dragged him down.

He did not come up again.

For a long minute the water churned and seethed. Scraps of cloth drifted to the surface, and darker things that the gulls dove for, shrieking. Then, gradually, the frenzy subsided. The fins drifted apart. The red stain spread out across the swell, thinning and fading until it was only a faint blush on the gold-green water, and then not even that.

---

Captain Marrack stood at the rail until the last fin had vanished. Then she turned to face her crew.

"There were eleven names on Harrow's list," she said, and her voice carried to every corner of the ship. "Mister Wren was one. Mister Harrow was another." She let the silence stretch. "I have the other nine."

Nobody breathed.

"And I have burned it." She drew a charred scrap of paper from her coat and let the wind take it. It fluttered out over the water and settled on the waves, where the sea swallowed it. "What was done is done. What is done from this moment on, I will judge as it comes." She looked slowly along the line of faces. "I trust I will not need to chum the waters again."

She turned on her heel and walked toward her cabin. At the door, she paused.

"Mister Crane. Take in the plank. And set a course for Tortuga."

The door closed behind her.

Out on the darkening sea, one last gray shadow circled the spot where Tobias Wren had gone down, patient and unhurried, as if waiting to see whether the ship might offer it anything more.

"Harrow." Marrack nodded slowly. "Harrow is at the bottom of the Windward Passage with a ball of shot tied to his ankles. He had a good deal to say before he went. Most of it concerned you."

A murmur ran through the crew. Tobias felt his bowels turn to water.

"You had my charts copied," the captain went on, walking now, her boots slow and deliberate on the planks. "You had pistols hidden in the sail locker. You meant to take my ship off the Tortugas and hand my head to the Spanish for the bounty. Is that about the shape of it?"

"No, no, Captain, I swear on my mother's..."

"Your mother was a Bristol whore who sold you to a slaver for a jug of gin. You told me so yourself, the night I cut you loose from his hold and gave you a berth." She crouched before him, close enough that he could smell the tar and gunpowder on her. "I gave you a ship, Tobias. I gave you a share. And you tried to take the rest."

She stood. "Run it out."

Two men hauled a long plank from the lumber stores, eight feet of weathered oak, and lashed it to the rail with a practiced efficiency that told Tobias they had done this before. It jutted out over the water like an accusing finger.

And then he saw the water.

The sea below was a clear, luminous green, shot through with gold where the dying sun struck it. And moving through that green, lazy and patient, were shadows. Long gray shapes, circling. One broke the surface: a dorsal fin, dark and triangular, slicing through the swell and slipping under again without a ripple.

"We've been chumming since dawn," said Marrack conversationally. "Offal from the hog we slaughtered. Blood from the galley. They've been following us all afternoon. Tigers, mostly. A few blues." She tilted her head. "They're very hungry, Tobias. We've been careful to keep them hungry."

"Captain." The word tore out of him. "Captain, for the love of God, maroon me. Put me on a spit of sand with a pistol and one shot. Flog me. Keelhaul me. Anything..."

"Anything?" She considered it. "No."

They hauled him to his feet. His legs would not hold him, and in the end two men had to carry him to the rail and set him on the plank like a sack of grain. The oak creaked under his weight. It was warm from the sun, rough against the soles of his bare feet.

Behind him, someone pressed the point of a boarding pike into the small of his back.

"Walk, Mister Wren."

He took one step. The plank dipped. The sea yawned beneath him, impossibly far and impossibly close all at once. His vision narrowed to a pinprick; his heartbeat was a war drum in his ears. The shadows below had stopped their lazy circling. They were drifting toward the ship now, drawn by something, by the vibration of the plank, perhaps, or by some animal sense of what was coming.

Another step. The pike pricked him again, and he felt a thin warm trickle of his own blood running down his back. Below, a fin broke the water and turned sharply toward the hull.

They can smell it, he thought. Oh God, they can smell it.

He was weeping now, great ugly sobs that shook his whole body. He thought of his mother, of the slaver's hold, of the night the captain's crew had burst through the hatch with lanterns and cutlasses and he had thought, for the first time in his life, that he might be saved. He thought of Harrow's voice in the dark: She's soft, Wren. She's getting soft. A crew like this could take the whole Main if the right man had the wheel.

He reached the end of the plank. There was nowhere left to go.

He turned, one last time, and looked back at the ship: the crew, silent as a congregation; the captain at the rail, her scarred face unreadable.

"Isolde," he whispered. "Please."

For a moment, just a moment, something moved behind her eyes. Then it was gone.

"Mister Crane," she said.

The pike thrust forward.

Tobias hit the water feet-first and went under in a white explosion of bubbles. The cold shocked the breath out of him. He had no idea where he was going. There was no land in sight. But his body moved of its own accord, arms churning, legs kicking wildly, and that was the worst thing he could have done, because every frantic splash sent a message through the water, and the message said: wounded, panicking, prey.

He never saw it. A second fin came in from the east, fast and low. A blue shark, sleek as a knife, slashed past and took Tobias's outflung arm in passing, ripping a long ragged strip of flesh from wrist to elbow. He shrieked, a thin high sound that carried across the water and set the gulls wheeling.

Then they were all around him.

The water boiled. Gray bodies thrashed and rolled, churning the sea into a pink froth. Tobias surfaced once more, his face white and uncomprehending, his mouth open in a scream that had no sound left in it. His eyes found the ship. Found the captain.

Then a great blunt head rose out of the water behind him, jaws spread wide, rows of serrated teeth gleaming in the red light of the setting sun. It closed over his shoulders and dragged him down.

He did not come up again.

For a long minute the water churned and seethed. Scraps of cloth drifted to the surface, and darker things that the gulls dove for, shrieking. Then, gradually, the frenzy subsided. The fins drifted apart. The red stain spread out across the swell, thinning and fading until it was only a faint blush on the gold-green water, and then not even that.

Nobody breathed.

"What was done is done. What is done from this moment on, I will judge as it comes." She looked slowly along the line of faces. "I trust I will not need to chum the waters again."

She turned on her heel and walked toward her cabin. At the door, she paused.

"Mister Crane. Take in the plank. And set a course for Tortuga."

The door closed behind her.

Out on the darkening sea, one last gray shadow circled the spot where Tobias Wren had gone down, patient and unhurried, as if waiting to see whether the ship might offer it anything more.

# The Drowned Man's Knock

The first time Martin heard the knocking, he told himself it was the pipes.

Three knocks. Slow. Deliberate. Coming from beneath the kitchen floor, where there was no basement, only a crawlspace full of dirt and dead leaves. *Knock. Knock. Knock.* Like knuckles on the underside of ice.

He stood at the sink with a glass of water halfway to his lips, and he did not drink it, because the water smelled of the lake.

That was eleven days after he held Elias under.

---

It had been quick, or quick enough. He had rehearsed the story so many times that it had worn a groove into his mind: *We went out to check the ice fishing holes. He stepped where the ice was thin. I tried to reach him. I tried.* The sheriff had put a hand on his shoulder. Elias's mother had wept into Martin's coat and thanked him for trying.

What he did not tell them was how Elias had surfaced once, gasping, his fingers scrabbling at the jagged edge of the hole, his eyes finding Martin's with a look not of fear but of *understanding.* How Martin had knelt, placed his gloved palm flat on the top of Elias's head, and pushed, gently, the way you might press a lid onto a jar. How the fingers had kept knocking against the underside of the ice for a while afterward, searching for the hole, finding only the frozen ceiling of the world.

*Knock. Knock. Knock.*

Then nothing.

---

By the third week, the house had begun to sweat.

Martin woke to find the walls beaded with moisture, rivulets running down the wallpaper in the shape of fingers dragging downward. The bedsheets were damp and cold, as though someone had lain beside him all night, soaked through. He stripped them, washed them, dried them on the highest heat. The next morning they were wet again, and there was an indentation on the other pillow, and in the indentation, a single strand of dark hair, long and tangled with a thread of green weed.

Elias had worn his hair long.

He burned the pillow in the fireplace. It hissed and smoked and would not catch, and the smell that filled the room was not burning feathers but the thick, rotten-sweet stench of lakebed mud, of things that had sat too long in cold, dark water.

---

He stopped using the bathroom mirror after the morning he saw the fog.

He had showered, and the glass had steamed over, and as he reached to wipe it clear, he noticed that the condensation was already disturbed. Someone had written on it from the inside. The letters were backward, and they were dripping.

**YOU WERE MY FRIEND**

He smashed the mirror with his fist. He picked the glass out of his knuckles with tweezers for an hour, sitting on the edge of the tub, and every time a shard came free, a drop of blood fell into the basin and did not swirl away. It sank, slowly, as though the porcelain were very, very deep.

When he looked up, the shower drain was gurgling. Something was coming up through it. A black, clotted mass of hair, pushed up from below by a pressure that should not exist, rising, rising, until it spilled onto the tile like a drowned animal.

Martin sat very still and listened to the drain breathe.

---

He began to see him in the periphery.

A figure standing at the end of the hallway, just past the reach of the lamplight, head bowed, water pooling around its bare feet. When Martin turned, there was nothing. But the floorboards were dark and wet, and the wet shapes were footprints, and the footprints led from the hallway to the foot of Martin's bed and stopped there.

They never led away.

He stopped sleeping. When he did, he dreamed of looking up through a skin of ice at a blurry kneeling shape, a hand coming down, and he woke choking, coughing up nothing, his lungs full of a cold that would not leave. He could feel it in his chest all day now, a slow freezing spreading outward from his heart, as if he were becoming a lake himself.

His coworkers stopped asking if he was all right. They watched him from across the office with careful, pitying expressions. He knew what they saw: a man destroyed by grief, by the terrible guilt of the one who survived. They did not know how right they were. They did not know that the grief was only a costume the guilt was wearing.

*You could tell them,* the thought whispered. It had begun to sound like Elias's voice. *You could make it stop.*

But he couldn't. He couldn't. Because if he said it out loud, it would be real, and if it was real, then he was the thing on the ice, the kneeling shape, the gentle hand.

---

On the fortieth day, the knocking came from the inside of the walls.

Then from inside the closet. Then from beneath the bed. Then from the refrigerator, the oven, the cabinets, the drawers, dozens of knuckles, hundreds, rapping from within every enclosed space in the house, all at once, a frantic, drowning rhythm.

*KNOCK KNOCK KNOCK KNOCK KNOCK*

Martin crawled into the center of the living room floor and covered his ears, and still he heard it, because it was coming from inside his own skull now, from behind his eyes, from the hollow of his chest where his heart was supposed to be. Something was trapped in there. Something was looking for the way out and finding only the frozen ceiling of him.

"I'm sorry," he screamed. "I'm sorry, I'm sorry, *I'm sorry*—"

The knocking stopped.

The silence was worse.

Slowly, Martin lowered his hands. The room was dark. Every light in the house had gone out, and the air had turned so cold his breath hung before him in a pale ghost of its own. The floor beneath his palms was slick. Freezing. When he pressed down, it gave slightly, flexing, and he heard a sound he would have known anywhere, a sound that had followed him out of the woods and into every second of every day since.

The long, low groan of ice under too much weight.

He looked down.

The floorboards were gone. He was kneeling on a sheet of gray, cloudy ice, and beneath it, pressed up against the underside, was a face. Bloated. Blue-white. Hair floating around it like black smoke. Its eyes were open, and they were not angry.

They were *understanding.*

A hand rose up beneath the ice and laid its palm flat against the frozen surface, directly beneath Martin's own. Finger to finger. Mirror to mirror.

Then it began, very gently, to knock.

*Knock.*

A crack spidered out from beneath Martin's hand.

*Knock.*

Water welled up through the fracture, black and cold and smelling of the lake.

*Knock.*

---

They found Martin three days later, when his sister came to check on him.

The house was bone dry. Every door stood open. Every cabinet, every drawer, every closet, as if someone had been searching desperately for a way out.

Martin lay on his back in the middle of the living room floor, perfectly still, his eyes open and frosted at the edges. The coroner would later struggle to write the report. There was no water anywhere in the house. The man had not left his living room in days.

And yet his lungs were full of lake water, and his lips were blue, and there was mud beneath his fingernails, as if in his final moments he had been clawing, clawing, clawing at something above him that would not break.

results.model_response:
**The Rot Beneath**

The rain had been falling for three days, like the sky was trying to wash its hands of the whole damn city and couldn't get the stains out. I knew the feeling.

She was lying in the alley behind the Castellano Building, the one they condemned back in '41 and never got around to tearing down. Most things in this town are like that. Condemned, but still standing. Waiting for somebody to care enough to finish the job.

Somebody had finished the job on her.

I crouched down and let my flashlight do the looking my eyes didn't want to. Twenty-five, maybe. Hard to tell. Whoever did this had worked her over the way the city works over everything: slow, patient, thorough. Her face was a street map of bad decisions, and none of them were hers. Bruises bloomed purple and yellow across her cheek like water damage on a tenement ceiling, the kind that tells you the whole structure is rotten, and has been for a long time.

Her blood had pooled in the cracks of the pavement, running along the fault lines the way the river runs through the Flats: dark, sluggish, carrying everything nobody wants to look at. The rain was trying to thin it out, push it toward the gutter. Down there it would join all the rest of it: the booze, the cigarettes, the promises. Everything in this city ends up in the gutter eventually. The gutter is the only honest place we've got.

Her hand was open, fingers curled toward the sky like she'd been reaching for something. A fire escape, maybe. A way out. There's no way out of this town. Just ladders that rust through the moment you put your weight on them.

The cuts were the worst of it. Deliberate. Almost careful. Whoever did this had taken his time, and I couldn't shake the thought that he'd enjoyed it the way the landlords enjoy watching the old neighborhoods crumble. They don't need to swing the wrecking ball. They just stop fixing the roof and let the weather do the killing. This guy had been his own weather.

I lit a cigarette. It tasted like ash and regret, which is to say it tasted like every other cigarette I'd had in twenty years.

Behind me, the uniforms were talking about the ballgame. One of them laughed. Somewhere up the block a neon sign buzzed and flickered, *HOTEL* with the *O* burned out. Some nights I think the whole city is like that: a sign that used to mean something, burning out one letter at a time until nobody remembers what it was supposed to say.

She'd been somebody's daughter once. Maybe somebody's girl. Now she was a case number, a file that would yellow at the edges in a drawer downtown next to a thousand others, curling up like dead leaves in a storm drain. Unless I did something about it.

That's the thing about rot. Everybody thinks it starts on the surface. It doesn't. It starts deep, in the foundation, in the beams nobody inspects, in the places the money doesn't reach. By the time you see it, it's already too late for the building.

But maybe not too late to find out who let it in.

I stood up. My knees cracked like old floorboards. The rain kept falling, patient as a mortician.

"Bag her gentle," I told the kid with the notebook. "And somebody find out who owns this alley."

In this town, somebody always owns the alley.

# The Ninth Hour

The rain in Sector Twelve had a chemical sweetness to it, like cheap candy left too long in the sun. Mara Okonkwo tasted it on her lips as she ran, and she thought, absurdly, that it would be the last thing she ever tasted.

*No. Keep moving.*

Her lungs burned. The collar around her neck pulsed its soft blue light, *Runner 4471, Runner 4471*, a heartbeat that belonged to the Network, not to her. Above, the camera drones hummed through the drowned streets like fat silver wasps, their lenses swiveling to follow her. Somewhere out there, eleven million viewers were watching. Somewhere, people were placing bets on how long she'd last.

Nine hours. She'd made it nine hours. The average was four.

She ducked beneath a collapsed transit arch, splashing through ankle-deep water that reflected the flickering holoboards overhead. One of them showed her own face, the photo from her debt intake, hollow-cheeked and startled, beside a scrolling ticker:

**RUNNER 4471 — ODDS OF SURVIVAL: 1 IN 340 — SPONSORED BY VERITAS NUTRITION**

If she made it to dawn, the debt was cleared. Her brother's medical bills, her mother's, the compounding interest that had swallowed her family whole. Twelve hours, and she'd be free.

Three hours left.

---

The hunter's name was Cassius Rhee, and he did not run.

He walked through the flooded district with the unhurried confidence of a man who had done this forty-one times before. His coat was long and dark, water-resistant, tailored. The Network's wardrobe department had chosen it to evoke something classic, a gentleman predator, the sort of figure the audience could admire and fear in equal measure.

His earpiece murmured: *"She's heading toward the old cathedral, Cass. Ratings are spiking. Twenty-two percent above projection. Make it count."*

"I always do," he said.

He didn't need the tracking data. He'd been watching her for nine hours, and he knew her now the way you come to know a piece of music. She favored her left side. She doubled back when frightened. She talked to herself, just a whisper, the same three words over and over. The microphones had picked it up, and the Network had turned it into a hashtag.

*Keep moving, Mara.*

He almost liked her. That was the part they never showed in the promotional reels. You always came to like them, a little, by the end.

---

The cathedral had been beautiful once. Now its stained glass lay in shards across the flooded nave, catching the drone-light in fractured reds and golds. Mara waded toward the altar, toward the stairwell she'd seen from the street, the one that might lead to the roof, and from the roof to the adjacent tower, and from the tower—

A sound behind her. Not a splash. A footstep on stone.

She turned.

He stood in the doorway, silhouetted against the neon rain, and for a moment neither of them moved. The drones repositioned, one sweeping low for a close-up of her face. She knew what they wanted. Terror. Tears. Begging.

She gave them nothing.

"Nine hours," Cassius said. His voice carried in the vaulted space, gentle, almost warm. "That's remarkable. You should be proud."

"Don't," she said. "Don't talk to me like we're—like this is—"

"Like this is what?"

"*Fair.*"

He tilted his head, considering this. Then he stepped forward into the water.

She ran.

She made it to the stairwell. Four steps. Five. Her foot slipped on the moss-slick stone, and her knee cracked against the edge, and then his hand closed around her ankle, not roughly, but with a terrible patience, and pulled.

---

She lay on her back in the shallow water, rain falling through the broken roof onto her face. He knelt beside her. The drones circled closer, their hum rising to a whine, and Mara understood that this was the moment, the one the whole broadcast had been building toward. Eleven million people leaning toward their screens.

"You can say something," Cassius told her quietly. "If you want. They'll air it. Last words always air."

She looked past him, directly into the nearest lens.

"My name is Mara Okonkwo," she said. Her voice shook, and then it didn't. "I'm twenty-six years old. I owed four hundred thousand credits because my brother got sick and the hospital charged interest by the hour. I'm not a criminal. None of us are criminals. You know that. Every one of you watching knows that."

The drone hovered. Somewhere, a producer was deciding whether to cut the feed.

"You know that," she said again, softer. "And you're watching anyway."

The earpiece crackled. Cassius touched it, listened, and something moved across his face too fast to name.

"They're keeping it," he said. "Ratings are through the roof."

Mara laughed. It came out broken and wet. "Of course they are."

---

What happened next, the Network would replay for weeks. They'd slow it down, score it with strings, sell it as a highlight package. But in the moment it was quick and quiet, and Cassius Rhee did it the way he'd done it forty-one times before: efficiently, with something that might have been mercy if the whole world around it weren't built on cruelty.

When it was done, he reached for her collar.

This was the claim. The prize. The collar held her debt record, and by the laws of the Restitution Games, the hunter who retrieved it inherited the bounty: a fixed percentage of every credit she'd owed. Four hundred thousand credits of suffering, converted, by some alchemy of law and spectacle, into his reward.

The blue light pulsed once in his palm, then went dark.

**RUNNER 4471 — CLAIMED — 9 HRS 14 MIN**

The holoboards outside erupted in color. Somewhere, a sponsor's jingle began to play.

Cassius stood. The drones pulled back for the wide shot, the hunter alone in the ruined cathedral, rain falling through the broken glass, the classic image, the one they'd use on the posters.

He looked down at the dead collar in his hand. Then he looked at the lens, the way she had.

He didn't say anything. He didn't have to. The feed had already cut to commercial.

Outside, the sweet chemical rain kept falling, and in a thousand apartments across the city, people reached for their remotes, checked the schedule, and saw that the next hunt began at midnight.
