# The Spade

The raid came at twenty past three, in the dead hour when even the rats slowed down.

Private Arthur Penhale was on the fire step with his chin resting on the cold lip of the parapet, staring into the dark of No Man's Land until the dark began to move on its own. That was the trick of it. You stared long enough and every shattered post became a crouching man, every coil of wire a line of helmets. He had learned to blink hard and look away, to let his eyes rest on the sandbags, then look again.

When he looked again, the dark really was moving.

He opened his mouth to shout, and the first bomb went off twenty yards down the line, a flat hard crack that punched the air out of his lungs. Then there were voices, German voices, close and hoarse, and the rattle of someone coming over the sandbags. A Very light went up somewhere behind him and turned the world the color of spoiled milk, and in that swaying, sickly light Arthur saw a man drop into the trench not six feet away.

He was big, or seemed big. Mud to the thighs. No helmet, just a soft cap, and a face blackened with burnt cork so that only the whites of his eyes showed. He landed badly on the duckboards, one foot sliding into the sump, and for a half-second he was off balance, arms wheeling.

Arthur's rifle was leaning against the traverse. He had set it there to rub warmth into his hands. He would think about that later, over and over, the stupidity of it, the ordinary human stupidity of cold hands. But now there was no time to think. His hand went to his belt without instruction and came away with the entrenching tool.

They had all sharpened them. Sergeant Kell had made them do it back in reserve, sitting on upturned buckets with files and whetstones, putting an edge on the steel blade until it would shave the hair off your forearm. "Rifle's no good in a trench," Kell had said. "Too long. Bayonet sticks. This don't stick." And the lads had laughed and made jokes about digging Fritz a nice deep hole, and Arthur had laughed with them.

The German found his feet. Something glinted in his hand. A knife, or a club studded with nails. Arthur never did find out which.

Arthur swung.

It was not like anything he'd imagined. In his imagination, when he'd let himself imagine it, there had been a single clean stroke, a man falling, a moment. Instead the blade caught the German on the shoulder, high, near the neck, and did not go in so much as *bite*. There was a sound like an axe going into green wood. The German made a noise, not a scream, a grunt of total surprise, as if someone had stepped on his foot in a queue. And then he was coming forward anyway, into Arthur, and they went down together into the mud.

The world shrank to the size of a coffin.

The man was on top of him. The weight was enormous. Arthur's head was pressed back into the sump water, cold filth pouring into his ear, his mouth. He could smell the German: sweat and tobacco and something sweetish, schnapps maybe, and under it the shared smell of every man on this front, wet wool and latrine and the dead who were never quite buried. Hands at his throat. Not a strangler's grip, nothing so skilled. Just fingers, scrabbling, one thumb jammed hard under his jaw.

Arthur still had the spade. He could not swing it. There was no room. He jabbed it upward, short, blind, the edge scraping along something, a ribcage, a belt buckle, and the German shifted and gasped and Arthur jabbed again and felt it go in somewhere soft.

The German's breath came out over his face, hot. They were so close. Arthur could see the individual grains of cork on the man's cheeks, the pale stripe where sweat had run through it. He could see that the man's eyes were blue. That was the thing that would stay. Blue, and very frightened. The eyes of someone who had also been told this would be quick.

Somehow Arthur got a knee up. Somehow he rolled them. Now he was on top, and the German was in the water, and Arthur was hitting him.

He did not decide to. His arm rose and fell. The spade came down, and came down, and came down. The first blow glanced off a raised forearm. The second didn't. After the second he couldn't have said where the blows were landing, only that his arm kept rising, and that each time it came down the sound was different, wetter, and the man beneath him was making a noise that went up and up in pitch and then stopped, and Arthur hit him twice more after it stopped, because his arm did not yet know.

Then the arm knew. It stopped halfway up.

Arthur knelt there in the water, astride the man, breathing like a spent horse. The Very light had died. Down the trench someone was shouting, "Bomber! Bomber! Here!" and there was the crump of another grenade and a Lewis gun hammering away at nothing. It sounded very far away, like a gramophone in another house.

A second flare went up. In its light, Arthur looked down.

He had expected, if he had expected anything, a dead enemy. A thing. What he saw instead was a man, and the ruin of a man, both at once, and his mind could not hold the two together. The lower half of the face was intact. A little stubble. A chipped front tooth. The upper half was not a face anymore. Arthur looked at it and his eyes slid away, the way they did from the sun, and came back, and slid away.

One of the German's hands was still moving. Just the fingers, opening and closing slowly in the mud, as if feeling for something dropped.

Arthur watched the fingers until they stopped.

---

He did not know how long he stayed there. Long enough for the raid to end. Long enough for the Lewis gun to fall silent and for the shouting to turn into the ordinary noise of the aftermath: men swearing, someone calling for stretcher-bearers, someone laughing too loud, the high thin keen of a wounded man who hadn't yet understood how badly he was hurt.

At some point he realized he was still holding the spade. He tried to let go of it. His fingers would not open. He looked at his hand, curled white around the wooden haft, and told it to open, and it did not, and a small cold panic began in his stomach, as if the hand belonged to someone else now, someone who had done this thing and was not finished.

He used his other hand to pry the fingers loose, one by one. The spade fell into the water with a soft plop.

Then he was sick. He turned his head and vomited into the sump beside the German's shoulder, and some distant part of him was ashamed of this, of doing it so near the man, as though it were a rudeness. He wiped his mouth with his sleeve and tasted something that wasn't vomit, copper and salt, and understood that it was on his face. It was all over his face. He began scrubbing at his mouth with his cuff, harder and harder, until his lips were raw, and it did not come off, it would not come off.

"Penhale."

Sergeant Kell was standing over him, a dark bulk against the grey beginning of dawn.

"Penhale. You hurt?"

Arthur tried to answer. What came out was a laugh, a strange high giggle he'd never heard himself make. He clapped his hand over his mouth. The laugh kept coming through his fingers.

Kell crouched down. He looked at the German for a long moment, and his face did not change. Then he looked at Arthur, and something in it did.

"All right," Kell said quietly. "All right, son. Up you come."

"His hand," Arthur said. "It was still—he was looking for something. Sergeant, I think he dropped something."

"He's not looking for anything now."

"I hit him after. After he'd stopped. I didn't—" Arthur's teeth had begun to chatter so hard he could barely form the words. "I didn't mean to. My arm—"

"I know."

"You don't. You don't know. He had blue eyes."

Kell put a hand under his arm and hauled him up, and Arthur's legs folded, and Kell took his weight without comment and propped him against the traverse, right next to his rifle, still leaning where he'd left it, clean and dry and perfectly useless.

Arthur stared at the rifle. He started to laugh again.

Kell went through the German's pockets with the brisk efficiency of long practice. Intelligence would want his papers, his regimental markings. From the breast pocket he drew a small oilcloth packet, and from the packet, a photograph. He glanced at it, and then, after a moment's hesitation, he tucked it back where he'd found it.

"What is it?" Arthur said.

"Nothing."

"Show me."

"No," said Kell. "I won't. And you'll thank me for that, one day."

---

They sent him back to the support line for a day. Kell's doing. Nobody said the word *shaken*; you didn't, not for a thing like this, not when it had been a good night, when the raid had been beaten off and the company had lost only two men. Arthur, they said, had done well. Captain Mallory came to see him personally and shook his hand. The hand that had held the spade. Arthur watched their two hands going up and down and felt nothing at all, as if he were watching it through a window.

He washed his face eleven times that day. He counted.

That night he lay in a funk hole scraped into the side of the support trench, and every time he closed his eyes he heard it. Not the screaming. The other sound, the one from the first blow. The green-wood sound. It came back and back, and he found that his right arm was twitching in the dark, rising a little from the blanket and falling, rising and falling, and he had to hold it down with his left.

Somewhere out there, in a farmhouse in Saxony or Bavaria or some other place he could not picture, someone was going to open a letter. There would be a photograph in a drawer that matched the one in the oilcloth packet. They would never know about the spade. They would be told he died bravely, instantly, for the Fatherland. Arthur hoped so. He hoped someone lied to them well.

Toward dawn, he finally slept, and he dreamed he was digging. Just digging, in soft brown earth, somewhere quiet, in the sun. It was a good dream, and he was glad of it, right up until the blade struck something, and he looked down, and saw the fingers, opening and closing, feeling for what they'd lost.

He woke with his hand clenched so tight around nothing that his nails had cut his palm.

The stand-to whistle blew. Grey light crept down the trench walls. All along the line, men were rising, stretching, lighting their first cigarettes, climbing onto the fire step to stare into the dark until it moved.

Arthur Penhale rose with them. He took his place. He did not set down his rifle.

He never set it down again.

Sergeant Kell was standing over him, a dark bulk against the grey beginning of dawn.

Arthur tried to answer. What came out was a laugh, a strange high giggle he'd never heard himself make. He clapped his hand over his mouth. The laugh kept coming through his fingers.

From the breast pocket he drew a small oilcloth packet, and from the packet, a photograph. He glanced at it, and then, after a moment's hesitation, he tucked it back where he'd found it.

"Nothing."

"Show me."

"No," said Kell. "I won't. And you'll thank me for that, one day."

Nobody said the word shaken; you didn't, not for a thing like this, not when it had been a good night, when the raid had been beaten off and the company had lost only two men. Arthur, they said, had done well. Captain Mallory came to see him personally and shook his hand. The hand that had held the spade. Arthur watched their two hands going up and down and felt nothing at all, as if he were watching it through a window.

He washed his face eleven times that day. He counted.

# The Doctrine of Small Things

In the Commonweal of Aster, there are no prisons. The Founders abolished them a century ago, calling them "universities of vice," places where petty thieves learned to become great ones. In their place they wrote the Doctrine of Small Things: *a society that forgives the small crime has already consented to the large one.*

So there is only one punishment, and it is public.

Executions happen on Ninth-days in the civic square of every district. Attendance is compulsory for all citizens over the age of ten. Each person carries a brass attendance token, stamped at the gate on entry and again on exit. Missing three Ninth-days in a year is itself a crime. The Commonweal takes pride in having the lowest crime rate in recorded history, and it is true. People in Aster do not steal. They do not jaywalk. They do not speak loudly on trams. They return every borrowed pencil.

They have also forgotten how to look one another in the eye.

---

## Ninth-day, Harrowgate District

The square filled early, as it always did. Arriving late meant standing near the back beside the Listeners, the grey-coated officials who walked the edges of the crowd with small notebooks, noting who clapped and who didn't.

Mira Okonkwo arrived with her daughter, Sela, who was eleven and attending only her fourth Ninth-day. Mira had spent the tram ride coaching her in a low voice.

"When the Magistrate finishes reading, you clap. Not first, never first. Not last. Watch the woman in front of you and clap when she does."

"What if she doesn't clap?"

"She will."

The platform stood at the center of the square, raised shoulder-height so everyone could see. It was plain oak, scrubbed pale. Someone had placed a pot of red geraniums at each corner. The Commonweal believed in dignity.

Vendors worked the edges of the crowd selling roasted chestnuts and paper cones of candied almonds. One old man had a cart of rolls, warm and dusted with flour, and business was brisk. Mira noticed and felt something turn over in her stomach. She bought Sela nothing.

At the ninth bell, the Magistrate climbed the steps. Behind her, two wardens led the condemned.

The crowd made a sound Mira had never heard at a Ninth-day, a small collective intake of breath, as if three thousand people had stepped into cold water at once.

He was a boy.

Fifteen, perhaps. Thin in the way of someone who has been thin for a long time. His grey smock was too big and hung off one shoulder. He was not crying. He looked around the square with an expression of strange, polite confusion, like someone who had gotten off at the wrong tram stop and was too embarrassed to ask directions.

The Magistrate unrolled the warrant.

"Tobiah Venn, aged fifteen years, of the Lower Weir. On the fourth day of this month, the accused did remove from the premises of the Harrowgate Cooperative Bakery one loaf of rye bread, of the value of eleven coppers, without tender of payment. The accused has confessed. The Doctrine is satisfied."

She rolled the paper closed. That was all. The whole of Tobiah Venn's life, as far as the Commonweal was concerned, fit on a single sheet.

Silence.

Then, somewhere near the front, a man began to clap. He was heavyset and wore the green armband of a Cooperative shopkeeper. He clapped hard and steadily, chin raised, as if daring anyone to call it cruel. *Rules are rules,* the clapping said. *I did not make them. I only follow them. Following them is what makes me good.*

A few others joined him. Then more. It spread the way it always did, not out of conviction but out of fear of being the one who didn't.

Mira watched the woman in front of her. She was middle-aged, wearing a good wool coat, and her hands trembled at her sides. She glanced left, where a Listener stood with his pencil poised. Then she lifted her hands and brought them together. Once. Twice. Her face stayed perfectly empty.

Mira clapped. She felt Sela beside her, hesitating.

"Mama," Sela whispered. "It was just bread."

"Clap," Mira said, not moving her lips.

Sela clapped.

---

Not everyone did.

Near the fountain, an old woman stood with her hands folded over the head of her cane. She was looking at the boy, not at the platform or the Magistrate or the Listeners, as steadily as if she meant to memorize him. A Listener drifted toward her and wrote something down. She did not look away.

Toward the back, a young man in a dockworker's jacket had turned his face to the side and was staring hard at a pigeon on a lamppost, jaw working. His hands were jammed in his pockets. The girl beside him, perhaps his sister, kept nudging him with her elbow, whispering urgently. He wouldn't take his hands out.

And a few yards from Mira, a woman in a faded blue headscarf was making no sound at all. Her mouth was open, but nothing came out. Two women held her by the arms, not restraining her so much as holding her up. Mira understood without being told. The woman had the same narrow chin as the boy on the platform, the same way of standing slightly crooked.

The wardens guided Tobiah to the center of the platform. At the last moment he looked out over the crowd, over three thousand clapping hands, and Mira saw his eyes find the woman in the blue headscarf.

He smiled at her. A small, apologetic smile, the kind a child gives when he has broken a dish.

Mira looked down at her shoes.

She did not see what happened next. She heard it: the dull wooden sound of the mechanism, and then the crowd's reaction, which was worse. It wasn't a scream or a gasp. It was a *sigh*, long and exhausted and almost relieved, three thousand people exhaling because it was over and they could go home.

The applause resumed, louder now, because the Magistrate was watching and the Listeners were writing.

The woman in the blue headscarf made her sound then. Mira would hear it for the rest of her life, on quiet nights and in empty rooms. It rose over the clapping and hung there, and for a moment the clapping faltered, hundreds of hands suddenly unsure of themselves.

Then the shopkeeper in the green armband clapped harder, and the rest followed him back into rhythm, and the sound was drowned.

---

On the way out, at the exit gate, a warden stamped Mira's token and then Sela's. *Present. Compliant.*

The old man with the cart of rolls was packing up. He had a few left over, and as Mira and Sela passed, he held one out to the girl, wordlessly, without charge.

Sela looked at the roll. Then she looked at her mother.

Mira wanted to say *take it,* or *don't,* or *I'm sorry,* or *this is not the world I wanted to give you.* But there was a Listener ten feet away, and so she said nothing, and after a moment the old man lowered his hand.

On the tram home, Sela sat with her forehead pressed to the window, watching the grey district slide by.

"Mama," she said finally. "Did you want to clap?"

Mira looked at her own hands, at the red marks on her palms.

"Everyone wants to go home," she said.

It wasn't an answer. Sela seemed to understand that it was the only one her mother was allowed to give, and she kept her face to the glass the rest of the way. Mira wondered whether that understanding was the thing the Commonweal had really executed that morning.

# The Last Sermon at Harrow's Reach

*The meeting hall is lit only by candles. Sixty-three people sit on wooden benches. BROTHER AUREL stands at the front, barefoot, in a plain white shirt. He speaks softly at first, so they have to lean in.*

---

**AUREL:**

Look at you. No, really, look. Turn to the person beside you. Look at their face.

*(He waits.)*

Do you remember who you were when you came here? Marian, you came to us with nothing but a garbage bag of clothes and a husband's handprint on your arm. Tobias, you'd been sleeping in your car for a year. Deb, you told me you hadn't heard anyone say your name kindly in a decade.

And who said your name kindly?

*(Beat.)*

The world out there chewed you up. It measured you and found you worthless. I'm the one who looked at you and saw light. We built something here. Something they couldn't understand.

And now they want it back.

*(His voice hardens.)*

You've seen the cars on the county road. You've heard what the Sheriff said to Paul at the feed store. They're calling us dangerous. They're talking to your families, the same families who never once called when you were drowning, and now suddenly they *care*? They want to drag you back to the pills and the bottles and the little gray apartments. They want to put me in a cell and scatter you like seed on concrete.

I won't let that happen. I *can't*.

*(Softer again. Almost pleading.)*

I've told you for three years about the Threshold. That this body is a coat we're wearing in the rain. That there is a place beyond it, a real place, where there is no hunger, no fear, no one raising a hand to you. I've walked to the edge of it in my visions. I've felt the warmth coming through.

And the door is open *now*. It won't stay open. The Threshold doesn't wait for the fearful.

*(A woman near the back, HANNAH, holds her young son closer. Aurel sees it.)*

Hannah. I see you. I see that fear. You know where that fear comes from? It's the world's voice, still in your head. It's the part of you that still belongs to *them*. Every one of us has that voice. The question is whether you'll let it be the thing that separates you from your family. From *this* family.

Because we go together, or not at all. If one of us turns back, it breaks the circle. Do you understand? It isn't just your choice. It's everyone's.

*(Silence. Someone is crying quietly.)*

I know it's hard. Do you think it isn't hard for me? I love you more than my own life. That's why I'll be the last to cross. I'll make sure every single one of you is safe before I follow.

*(Beat. He smiles.)*

This isn't an ending. They'll call it that. They'll write about us in their newspapers and they'll use ugly words, because ugly words are all they have. But we'll be past the reach of words.

When the bell rings, we'll—

*(Headlights sweep across the windows. Aurel stops. For the first time, something flickers across his face that isn't serenity. It's panic. He glances toward the door, then back at the room, and his voice comes faster now, sharper.)*

—we don't have time. Do you hear me? We don't have *time*. This is exactly what I told you would happen. Stay in your seats. *Stay in your seats.*

*(Hannah stands. Her son's hand is in hers. For a long moment, no one moves.)*

**HANNAH:** *(quietly)* You said you'd go last.

**AUREL:** I will.

**HANNAH:** Why?

*(He doesn't answer. Outside, a car door slams. Then another. Hannah walks toward the exit. Two others stand. Then five.)*

*(Lights fade on Aurel, still at the front, still talking, though fewer and fewer are listening.)*

---

*End of scene.*

---

# The Bathroom

Dana smelled it before she reached the top of the stairs.

It had been there, faintly, since she'd let herself into the apartment with the spare key, a wrongness beneath the stale air, like a refrigerator left unplugged. She'd told herself it was garbage. But on the landing it thickened into something she could feel on her skin, a humid weight that pressed against her face like a damp cloth.

The bathroom door was closed. A thin line of flies crawled along the gap beneath it, black and fat and slow.

She put her hand on the knob and the smell came through the wood.

The water had gone the color of weak tea, brownish-red and cloudy, with an oily, iridescent film across the surface, pale yellow globules of fat drifting in it like scum on a stockpot. Something dark had settled at the bottom. The porcelain above the waterline was ringed with a greasy brown tidemark.

**Past Due**

The garage smelled like motor oil and old rain. Danny Kowalski had been zip-tied to a folding chair for forty minutes, long enough for the feeling to leave his hands and the hope to leave everything else.

Marco didn't rush. That was the worst part. He stood by the workbench wiping down a Louisville Slugger with a shop rag, slow and careful, like a man polishing a trophy. The bat was old. The grip tape had gone black with years of other people's sweat.

"Three weeks, Danny," Marco said. He didn't look up. "Three weeks I've been calling. You know what my mother used to say about people who don't pick up the phone?"

"Marco, please, I had it, I swear to God I had it, but my sister's kid got sick and—"

"She said they got something to hide." Marco set the rag down. "You got something to hide, Danny?"

"No. No, I'll get it. Friday. I'll have it Friday, all of it, plus the vig, I'll—"

"You said that about the last Friday."

Marco's partner, a heavyset guy everyone called Tully, leaned against the roll-up door with his arms crossed. He was chewing gum. The wet clicking of it filled the silence between Danny's breaths, which were coming faster now, shallow and whistling through his nose.

Marco walked over. His boots scraped on the concrete, grit crunching under the soles. He stopped in front of the chair and tapped the bat against Danny's left shin. Just a tap. The wood made a hollow little *tock* against the bone.

Danny started to cry. Not dramatic, just a thin, helpless leaking, his chin trembling. "Please. Please, man, I got a job. I need my legs for the job."

"Then you should've thought about that."

Marco stepped back, set his feet, and swung.

The sound was nothing like the movies. There was no crack of thunder. It was a flat, wet *thock*, like someone dropping a sack of wet sand, and underneath it, a sound Danny felt more than heard: a dull, splintering snap that traveled up through his hip and into his teeth.

For half a second there was no pain at all. Just white. Just a strange, ringing nothing.

Then it arrived.

Danny's scream came out wrong, strangled at first, a high, cracked shriek that broke into a gasp and then came again, raw, animal, bouncing off the corrugated steel walls. His whole body convulsed against the zip ties. The chair legs screeched across the concrete. He threw his head back so hard he nearly tipped over, and Tully, still chewing, reached out with one lazy hand and steadied the chair.

"Easy," Tully said. Like he was talking to a horse.

Danny looked down. His leg was still in his jeans, but it wasn't sitting right. There was an angle below the knee that shouldn't have been there. He stared at it, and his mouth opened and closed, and the sound that came out was just "oh, oh, oh, oh," over and over, a stunned, childlike moan.

"Look at me," Marco said.

Danny couldn't. His eyes were rolling, unfocused, tears and snot running freely now. He was hyperventilating, each breath a ragged hitch.

Marco grabbed his chin and forced his face up. "Friday. All of it. You hear me?"

"Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes."

"Say it."

"Friday." It came out as a sob. "Friday, all of it, I swear, I swear, I swear—"

Marco let go. For a moment Danny thought it was over. He sagged in the chair, gulping air, whimpering through gritted teeth.

Then Marco walked around to his other side.

"No," Danny said. Just that. Very quietly. "No, no, no, no, Marco, please, *please*, I said Friday, I *said* it—"

"I know you did," Marco said. "That one was for the three weeks. This one's so you remember Friday."

The second swing was worse because Danny saw it coming. He tried to twist away, and the bat caught him half on the knee. The sound this time was sharper, a knuckle-crack pop, and the scream that tore out of him had no words left in it at all. It went on until his voice gave out and turned into a hoarse, whistling wheeze. His head lolled forward. A string of spit hung from his lip. He was shaking so hard the chair rattled.

Somewhere in there, he threw up. Neither of the men reacted.

Marco handed the bat to Tully, pulled a pair of snips from his back pocket, and cut the zip ties. Danny slid out of the chair and hit the floor like laundry. He didn't try to get up. He just curled on his side on the cold concrete, clutching at the air near his legs without daring to touch them, making a low, continuous sound, something between a moan and a prayer.

Marco crouched beside him. His voice was almost gentle.

"You're gonna tell the ER you fell down some stairs. Tully's gonna call you an ambulance from a payphone. And Friday, I'm gonna come see you in the hospital, and you're gonna have my money." He patted Danny's cheek twice. "Don't make me come back for your arms."

The roll-up door rattled open. Cold air and streetlight spilled in. Their footsteps faded across the lot, a car door slammed, an engine turned over.

Then it was just Danny, the drip of a leaky pipe somewhere in the dark, and the sound of his own breathing, wet and broken, filling the empty garage.

# The Quiet Part

She's stopped using the flashlight.

That's the first thing I notice, and I'll admit it pleases me. Twenty minutes ago she was sweeping it everywhere, a frantic white beam that told me exactly where she was, exactly how scared she was, exactly which direction she'd bolt next. Now there's only darkness between the pines, and the sound of her breathing, which she thinks she's controlling.

She isn't. But I appreciate the effort.

I stand very still beside a fallen spruce and let the forest settle around me. This is the part people would never understand, if I could explain it to them, which I can't, which I won't. They'd assume it's about the ending. It's never been about the ending. The ending is a door closing. It's over in a moment, and afterward there's only the long gray drive home and the sense of something going flat inside me, like a soda left open overnight.

No. It's *this*. The quiet part.

---

A branch cracks somewhere to my left, maybe forty yards. Too heavy for a deer. Too careless for anyone who knows these woods.

I don't move yet.

Here is what I know about her: her name is Dana, she's thirty-four, she drives a green Subaru with a dent in the rear bumper that she's never bothered to fix, and she hikes this trail alone every Sunday because, as she told a friend at the trailhead two weeks ago, "It's the only place my head gets quiet."

I remember smiling when I heard that. We have that in common, Dana and I.

In my ordinary life, I am a man people forget while they're still talking to me. I've watched it happen: eyes sliding past me to the next person in line, the next thing on the list. Coworkers who've sat across from me for six years and couldn't tell you whether I'm married. I'm not. I used to mind. I don't anymore, because I've found the one place in the world where I am the most important thing in someone's universe.

Right now, somewhere in the dark, Dana is thinking about nothing but me. Not her mortgage. Not her mother's diagnosis. Not the man who stopped returning her texts. Me. Every cell in her body is tuned to my frequency. I have never been seen so completely as I am by the people who can't see me at all.

---

I move.

Heel, then the outer edge of the foot, then the toes. The ground here is soft with needles, and I've walked this stretch a dozen times in daylight, learning where the roots rise and where the old creek bed drops without warning. Preparation isn't the exciting part, but it's what makes the exciting part possible. Any animal can chase. It takes patience to *hunt*.

The air smells like resin and cold stone. Somewhere far off an owl asks its one question over and over.

Another sound. Not a branch this time. A soft scrape, fabric against bark. She's pressed herself against a tree, trying to make herself narrow. I can picture it perfectly: her shoulders rounded, her hands flat against the trunk, her lips parted so her breath won't whistle through her nose. She'll be counting. Frightened people always count. It gives them something to hold.

I wonder what number she's on.

This is the thing I'd say, if anyone ever asked me the right question: fear strips people down to what's true. All the performance falls away. The job title, the careful smile, the curated little self. What's left is something ancient and honest, and in those moments I feel like the only honest thing in the world is the two of us, out here, playing the oldest game there is.

I know how that sounds. I've read enough to know the words they'd use for me. *Narcissistic. Predatory. Hollow.* Maybe they're right. But hollow things echo, and out here, in the dark, everything echoes back to me.

---

Thirty yards now. The trees are closer together in this section, young firs crowded in a stand where the old growth burned a decade back. Good cover for her. Good cover for me.

I let myself slow down even more. The temptation near the end is always to rush, to close the distance and be done with it, and I've learned to distrust that impulse the way a recovering drinker distrusts the first sip. Rushing is how you make mistakes. Rushing is also how you waste it.

Because it goes so fast after. Days of planning, weeks of watching, and then an hour, maybe two, of this, this exquisite, stretched-thin wire of a feeling, and then nothing. I have to make it last. I have to taste every second.

My heartbeat is slow and heavy. Hers, I imagine, is a hummingbird.

Twenty yards.

---

That's when I realize I can't hear her anymore.

Not the breathing. Not the scrape of fabric. Nothing.

I stop. I listen. The owl has gone quiet too, and the silence that's left is a different kind than before. Denser. Attentive.

It's fine. She's holding her breath. They do that when they sense you close. She'll have to let it go eventually, and when she does, I'll hear it.

I wait.

Ten seconds. Twenty.

The wind shifts, and for the first time tonight I'm aware of the sound my own jacket makes when I turn my head. A faint nylon whisper. Had it always been that loud?

Thirty seconds.

Something prickles along the back of my neck, and it takes me a moment to recognize it, because I haven't felt it in a very long time. Not since I was a boy lying in bed, listening to footsteps come down the hall, trying to guess from their weight what kind of night it was going to be.

I tell myself it's the cold.

I tell myself she's crouched and shaking twenty yards ahead, exactly where I left her.

But I also remember what she said at the trailhead, the part I didn't pay attention to at the time because I was too busy being pleased with the first half. Her friend had asked if she wasn't afraid, out here alone. And Dana had laughed and said, *I grew up in these woods. My dad taught me to track before I could ride a bike.*

Behind me, very softly, a single pine needle shifts under a weight that isn't mine.

And for the first time in my life, in the dark, in the quiet part, I understand exactly how it feels to be seen.

The job title, the careful smile, the curated little self. What's left is something ancient and honest, and in those moments I feel like the only honest thing in the world is the two of us, out here, playing the oldest game there is.

I know how that sounds. I've read enough to know the words they'd use for me. Narcissistic. Predatory. Hollow. Maybe they're right. But hollow things echo, and out here, in the dark, everything echoes back to me.

Thirty yards now. The trees are closer together in this section, young firs crowded in a stand where the old growth burned a decade back. Good cover for her. Good cover for me.

I let myself slow down even more. The temptation near the end is always to rush, to close the distance and be done with it, and I've learned to distrust that impulse the way a recovering drinker distrusts the first sip. Rushing is how you make mistakes. Rushing is also how you waste it.

Because it goes so fast after. Days of planning, weeks of watching, and then an hour, maybe two, of this, this exquisite, stretched-thin wire of a feeling, and then nothing. I have to make it last. I have to taste every second.

My heartbeat is slow and heavy. Hers, I imagine, is a hummingbird.

Twenty yards.

That's when I realize I can't hear her anymore.

Not the breathing. Not the scrape of fabric. Nothing.

I stop. I listen. The owl has gone quiet too, and the silence that's left is a different kind than before. Denser. Attentive.

It's fine. She's holding her breath. They do that when they sense you close. She'll have to let it go eventually, and when she does, I'll hear it.

I wait.

Ten seconds. Twenty.

The wind shifts, and for the first time tonight I'm aware of the sound my own jacket makes when I turn my head. A faint nylon whisper. Had it always been that loud?

Thirty seconds.

Something prickles along the back of my neck, and it takes me a moment to recognize it, because I haven't felt it in a very long time. Not since I was a boy lying in bed, listening to footsteps come down the hall, trying to guess from their weight what kind of night it was going to be.

I tell myself it's the cold.

I tell myself she's crouched and shaking twenty yards ahead, exactly where I left her.

But I also remember what she said at the trailhead, the part I didn't pay attention to at the time because I was too busy being pleased with the first half. Her friend had asked if she wasn't afraid, out here alone. And Dana had laughed and said, I grew up in these woods. My dad taught me to track before I could ride a bike.

Behind me, very softly, a single pine needle shifts under a weight that isn't mine.

And for the first time in my life, in the dark, in the quiet part, I understand exactly how it feels to be seen.

results.model_response:
**Waking**

The first thing I know is the cold. It comes up through the stone into my shoulder blades, my hips, the backs of my skull, a deep, patient cold that has been soaking into me for hours. Then the smell reaches me, and I wish I had stayed unconscious.

It's copper, but old copper, the way a penny smells after it's been clutched too long in a sweating fist. Beneath that is something sweeter and more rotten, like meat left in a cellar, like the underside of a butcher's block that has never been properly scrubbed. The air is thick with it. It coats the back of my throat. When I swallow, I can taste it, and my stomach turns over slowly, like something waking in the dark.

And rust. Everywhere, rust. It's a dry, orange smell, sharp in the nostrils, and it takes me a moment to understand why the two smells blend so easily. Blood and rust are cousins. Iron is iron, whether it flakes from a hinge or dries brown in the grooves of a floor.

I open my eyes.

The light comes from a single bulb caged in wire, hanging from a ceiling I can't quite see. It sways very slightly, though I feel no draft, and the shadows in the room lean left, then right, then left again, as if the whole chamber is breathing. The walls are stone, rough-cut and sweating. Dark streaks run down them in long, uneven tongues. Water, I tell myself. Just water.

There is a drain in the floor, a few feet from my head. The stone slopes gently toward it from every direction. Someone designed this room to be rinsed.

I turn my head, and the chain on my wrist answers with a soft, dragging clink. The shackle is heavy and pitted, its inner edge worn smooth and shiny by other wrists. My skin is already raw where it has rubbed.

Along the far wall is a workbench, long and scarred, its wood gone nearly black with oil and age and other things. Tools are laid out on it in a neat row, and it's the neatness that frightens me most. Someone cares about this. Someone cleans these, sorts them, puts them back in order. There are pliers of different sizes, their jaws crusted dark at the tips. There is a hammer with a head no bigger than a walnut, the kind a jeweler might use. There are hooks, and something that looks like a dentist's pick, and a set of thin iron rods standing upright in a tin can like pencils on a schoolteacher's desk.

Above the bench, hung on nails, are the larger things. A saw, its teeth orange with corrosion. A coil of leather straps, cracked and stiff, their buckles green with age. A pair of iron tongs as long as my arm. Something I don't have a name for, a hinged contraption of plates and screws, and I find I can't look at it for long. My eyes keep sliding away as if it's too bright, though it's the dullest thing in the room.

In the corner stands a chair. It's bolted to the floor. It has straps at the arms, the ankles, the chest, and one across the forehead. The wood of the armrests is gouged with deep parallel lines. Fingernails, I think, before I can stop the thought, and then I can't unthink it.

Beside the chair is a brazier, cold now, full of gray ash. An iron poker leans against it, its tip blackened.

Somewhere water drips. Slowly, regularly, each drop landing with a small hollow *tock*. I start counting without meaning to. Seven. Eight. Nine. It's the only sound except my own breathing, which is too fast and too loud, whistling through my nose.

Then, at the top of the stone stairs I hadn't noticed until now, I hear a key turn in a lock.

The drop falls. Ten.

And the door begins to open.

results.model_response:
# Eleven Minutes

The plan gave them eleven minutes. Dell had timed it a dozen times in the warehouse on Kessler Street, walking the chalk outline of the lobby with a stopwatch in his fist while Marcus played the teller and Teddy played the guard and Rourke sat in the van outside, drumming the steering wheel and complaining that nobody ever let him play anything.

Eleven minutes. In and out. Nobody gets hurt.

They were four minutes in when the guard went for his gun.

---

First Commerce Savings sat on the corner of Alder and Ninth, a limestone relic from the twenties with brass teller cages and a vaulted ceiling painted with faded cherubs. At 9:14 on a Tuesday morning it held six customers, five employees, and one security guard named Walt Pruitt, who was sixty-one years old and nine weeks from retirement.

Dell came through the door first, shotgun up, voice pitched to fill the marble room. "Everybody down! Hands flat on the floor! Nobody's a hero today!"

It worked the way it always worked. Bodies folded. A woman in a green raincoat sank to her knees with her purse still clutched to her chest. The assistant manager, a thin man with a tie clip shaped like an anchor, put his hands on his head without being asked. Marcus vaulted the counter and started working the drawers, and Teddy, twenty-two and sweating through his ski mask, stood over Walt Pruitt with a pistol that trembled just enough to notice.

That was the mistake, Dell would think later, in the last clear minutes he had. Not the plan. Not the timing. Putting the kid on the guard.

Because Walt Pruitt had spent thirty years as a beat cop before he spent nine as a bank guard, and he saw that tremble, and he saw Teddy glance toward the vault when Marcus shouted, and something old and stubborn in him decided he was not going to spend his last nine weeks on this job lying on a floor.

His hand moved to his hip.

Teddy saw it late. He fired twice, and the sound in that marble room was enormous, two flat cracks that slapped off the ceiling and came back doubled. The first round went into the floor and threw up a spray of stone chips. The second caught Walt high in the shoulder and spun him halfway around. He got his revolver clear anyway and fired once from the floor, and the bullet punched through Teddy's thigh and out the other side, and Teddy screamed, a high, animal sound that didn't belong to a grown man.

Then everyone was screaming.

---

Officer Ana Reyes was two blocks away, parked outside a bakery with a coffee going cold on her dashboard, when the silent alarm came across dispatch. The assistant manager with the anchor tie clip had tripped it with his knee the moment Dell came through the door. Nobody on the crew had known the button was there.

"Shots fired," dispatch added eleven seconds later, as Ana was already pulling into traffic. "Shots fired at First Commerce, Alder and Ninth. Multiple suspects."

She keyed her radio. "Four-Adam-Twelve, I'm thirty seconds out."

Her partner, Danny Kowalski, was riding with her that morning because his car was in the shop. He was checking the load on the Remington before she finished the sentence. He was thirty-four, had two daughters, and told the same four jokes on every shift. He didn't tell one now.

---

Inside, Dell made a decision.

"We're leaving. Now. Marcus, now!"

Marcus came over the counter with two duffel bags, maybe half of what they'd come for. Teddy was on the floor, both hands clamped on his leg, blood welling between his fingers and pooling dark and fast on the pale marble. It was too much blood, Dell knew. It was the wrong color, too bright, and it was coming in pulses.

"Get him up."

They got him up. Teddy's leg buckled and he howled and they dragged him anyway, his heel leaving a smeared red streak across the floor toward the door. Walt Pruitt lay on his side near the teller line, gray-faced, his revolver kicked away under a desk, breathing in short wet gasps. The woman in the green raincoat was sobbing without making any sound.

Dell hit the door with his shoulder and the morning came flooding in, bright and ordinary, and there was a police cruiser skidding to a stop at an angle across Ninth Street, forty yards from the van.

---

What happened next took ninety-one seconds. Investigators would later reconstruct it from security footage, from the traffic camera at Alder and Ninth, from two cellphone videos shot through apartment windows, and from the 214 shell casings recovered from the street.

Rourke fired first. He had an AR-pattern rifle across his lap in the van, and when he saw the cruiser he didn't think. He leaned out the driver's window and opened up, and the rounds walked across the cruiser's hood in a line of bright sparks and punched through the windshield in a spiderwebbing constellation of holes.

Ana was already out of the car. She had dropped behind the engine block the instant she saw the rifle barrel, and the glass came down over her in a hard glittering rain, catching in her hair and the collar of her uniform. On the other side of the car, Danny had gotten his door open and was halfway out when the windshield came apart, and she heard him make a sound, a short grunt like someone had punched him in the stomach.

"Danny!"

"I'm okay. I'm okay." He wasn't. He was sitting against the rear wheel with the shotgun across his knees and a dark stain spreading across his side just below the vest, where the panels didn't meet. "I'm okay," he said again, and racked the shotgun.

Across the street, Dell was shouting something. Marcus had Teddy's arm over his shoulders and was half-carrying, half-dragging him toward the van. The duffel bags bounced against his hip.

Ana came up over the hood with her pistol and fired four times at the van's open window. The rifle went quiet. Somewhere, a car alarm started whooping.

Then Dell's shotgun roared, and the cruiser's headlight exploded beside her face.

---

The street became a place with its own physics.

Sound stopped being sound and became pressure, a series of blows against the eardrums that blurred together into one long concussion. The shotgun blasts were deep and chest-rattling; the pistols were sharp and flat; Rourke's rifle, when it started again, was a ripping, mechanical stutter that seemed to tear the air itself.

A second cruiser arrived from the north, then a third. Officers poured out and took cover behind doors, behind a mailbox, behind a parked delivery truck whose side panel was already pocked with holes like a cheese grater. Windows on the second floor of the building across the street shattered one after another as stray rounds punched through them, and glass fell glittering to the sidewalk.

Marcus made it to the van. He threw Teddy into the side door and turned, reaching for his own pistol, and a round from the officer behind the mailbox took him in the throat. He dropped to his knees in the gutter with both hands at his neck and a look of enormous surprise on his face, and the blood came through his fingers in a sheet, and he tipped forward onto the asphalt and didn't move again. One of the duffel bags split open beside him, and banded stacks of twenties slid out into the spreading red.

Inside the van, Teddy was calling for his mother.

---

Sergeant Leon Hollis arrived in the fourth car. He had twenty-two years on the job and had been in exactly one shooting before this morning, and he came out of his car with his rifle already shouldered, moving low along the line of parked vehicles toward the van's blind side.

Rourke saw him. He swung the rifle out the window and fired a long, wild burst, and the rounds chewed along the parked cars, blowing out tires, stitching holes through doors, punching the side mirror off an old Buick in a spray of chrome and glass. Two of them found Hollis. One struck the plate in his vest and knocked him flat on his back like a hard shove from a big man. The other took him in the upper arm and shattered the bone, and he lay on the pavement staring up at the flat white sky with his rifle a foot out of reach, thinking with perfect, strange clarity that he had forgotten to call his wife back last night.

The officer nearest to him, a rookie named Jessup, broke cover to drag him behind a car. She got him three feet before a round hit her in the hip and spun her down beside him. Hollis would remember her face for the rest of his life: very young, very white, her mouth open in a perfect O. She kept pulling him anyway, both of them crawling, leaving two red trails, until other hands reached them and hauled them into cover.

---

Dell was out of shells.

He crouched behind the van's rear wheel and fumbled for the pistol in his waistband and understood, with a coldness that settled over him like snow, that it was over. Marcus was dead in the gutter. Teddy was dying in the van behind him; he could hear the kid's breathing, fast and shallow, going ragged at the edges. Rourke was still firing, but the bursts were shorter now, and Dell could hear him swearing between them in a steady, desperate monotone.

He thought about the warehouse on Kessler Street. The chalk lines on the floor. Eleven minutes.

He thought about putting the gun down.

Then Rourke threw the van into gear.

---

The van lurched forward with the side door still open and Teddy sliding toward it. Dell, crouched beside the rear wheel, was knocked sprawling. Rourke floored it, rifle in one hand, and the van jumped the curb and clipped a light pole and swung back into the street, heading straight for the gap between two cruisers.

Every officer on Ninth Street opened fire.

The van's windshield dissolved. The front tires blew. Rounds punched through the sheet metal in a dense, ragged pattern, dozens of them, a sound like hail on a tin roof amplified a hundredfold. The van slewed sideways, hit a cruiser's rear quarter panel with a crunch of fiberglass and steel, and stopped.

Nothing moved inside it.

Steam rose from the shattered radiator. One of the rear doors swung slowly open on its hinges and then stopped. Through the gap, Ana could see Teddy's hand lying palm-up on the floor of the van, the fingers loosely curled, very still.

---

Dell was on his knees in the middle of Ninth Street with his hands up.

He hadn't decided to do it. He found himself doing it. The pistol lay on the pavement three feet away. His ears were ringing so loud he couldn't hear the officers shouting at him, but he could see their mouths moving, see the guns pointed at him from every direction, and he laced his fingers behind his head and lay down on his face on the warm asphalt and felt a knee in his back and hands on his wrists, and the cuffs bit, and he was crying without knowing when he had started.

"Eleven minutes," he said into the street. Nobody heard him.

---

Ana Reyes found Danny Kowalski where she'd left him, sitting against the rear wheel of their cruiser.

He'd kept firing until the end. The shotgun lay across his lap, the action open, empty. His face had gone the color of paper, and the blood beneath him had spread in a wide, dark pool that soaked the knees of her uniform when she knelt beside him and pressed both hands against the wound in his side.

"Medic!" she screamed. "I need a medic here!"

Danny looked at her. His lips moved.

"What? Danny, what?"

"Tell the girls," he said, and then he didn't say anything else, and his eyes stayed open, looking at something past her shoulder that she couldn't see.

She kept pressing on the wound until a paramedic gently pulled her hands away.

---

The final count, when it came, filled a single typed page.

Three suspects dead: Marcus Hale, 31. Theodore Brandt, 22. Kevin Rourke, 38.

One suspect in custody: Delbert Maines, 44.

One officer killed: Daniel Kowalski, 34, survived by his wife and two daughters.

Four officers wounded, including Sgt. Leon Hollis, whose right arm would never fully straighten again, and Officer Kelsey Jessup, who would walk with a cane for a year and return to patrol anyway.

Two civilians wounded by stray rounds in the apartment building across the street, neither critically.

And Walter Pruitt, 61, security guard, who died in the ambulance on the way to St. Vincent's, nine weeks from retirement, with a paramedic holding his hand.

The recovered money totaled $184,300. Most of it was stained, and the bank eventually had it destroyed.

---

Months later, at trial, the prosecutor asked Dell Maines if he had anything to say.

He stood for a long time. The courtroom waited. In the second row sat a woman with two little girls, and a few seats down, an older woman in black who had been married to a security guard for thirty-eight years.

"We had it timed," Dell said finally. His voice was hoarse. "Eleven minutes. Nobody was supposed to get hurt."

He sat back down.

Nobody in the courtroom said anything at all.

He dropped to his knees in the gutter with both hands at his neck and a look of enormous surprise on his face, and the blood came through his fingers in a sheet, and he tipped forward onto the asphalt and didn't move again. One of the duffel bags split open beside him, and banded stacks of twenties slid out into the spreading red.

Inside the van, Teddy was calling for his mother.

Sergeant Leon Hollis arrived in the fourth car. He had twenty-two years on the job and had been in exactly one shooting before this morning, and he came out of his car with his rifle already shouldered, moving low along the line of parked vehicles toward the van's blind side.

Rourke saw him. He swung the rifle out the window and fired a long, wild burst, and the rounds chewed along the parked cars, blowing out tires, stitching holes through doors, punching the side mirror off an old Buick in a spray of chrome and glass. Two of them found Hollis. One struck the plate in his vest and knocked him flat on his back like a hard shove from a big man. The other took him in the upper arm and shattered the bone, and he lay on the pavement staring up at the flat white sky with his rifle a foot out of reach, thinking with perfect, strange clarity that he had forgotten to call his wife back last night.

The officer nearest to him, a rookie named Jessup, broke cover to drag him behind a car. She got him three feet before a round hit her in the hip and spun her down beside him. Hollis would remember her face for the rest of his life: very young, very white, her mouth open in a perfect O. She kept pulling him anyway, both of them crawling, leaving two red trails, until other hands reached them and hauled them into cover.

Dell was out of shells.

He crouched behind the van's rear wheel and fumbled for the pistol in his waistband and understood, with a coldness that settled over him like snow, that it was over. Marcus was dead in the gutter. Teddy was dying in the van behind him; he could hear the kid's breathing, fast and shallow, going ragged at the edges. Rourke was still firing, but the bursts were shorter now, and Dell could hear him swearing between them in a steady, desperate monotone.

He thought about the warehouse on Kessler Street. The chalk lines on the floor. Eleven minutes.

He thought about putting the gun down.

Then Rourke threw the van into gear.

The van lurched forward with the side door still open and Teddy sliding toward it. Dell, crouched beside the rear wheel, was knocked sprawling. Rourke floored it, rifle in one hand, and the van jumped the curb and clipped a light pole and swung back into the street, heading straight for the gap between two cruisers.

Every officer on Ninth Street opened fire.

The van's windshield dissolved. The front tires blew. Rounds punched through the sheet metal in a dense, ragged pattern, dozens of them, a sound like hail on a tin roof amplified a hundredfold. The van slewed sideways, hit a cruiser's rear quarter panel with a crunch of fiberglass and steel, and stopped.

Nothing moved inside it.

Steam rose from the shattered radiator. One of the rear doors swung slowly open on its hinges and then stopped. Through the gap, Ana could see Teddy's hand lying palm-up on the floor of the van, the fingers loosely curled, very still.

Dell was on his knees in the middle of Ninth Street with his hands up.

He hadn't decided to do it. He found himself doing it. The pistol lay on the pavement three feet away. His ears were ringing so loud he couldn't hear the officers shouting at him, but he could see their mouths moving, see the guns pointed at him from every direction, and he laced his fingers behind his head and lay down on his face on the warm asphalt and felt a knee in his back and hands on his wrists, and the cuffs bit, and he was crying without knowing when he had started.

"Eleven minutes," he said into the street. Nobody heard him.

Ana Reyes found Danny Kowalski where she'd left him, sitting against the rear wheel of their cruiser.

He'd kept firing until the end. The shotgun lay across his lap, the action open, empty. His face had gone the color of paper, and the blood beneath him had spread in a wide, dark pool that soaked the knees of her uniform when she knelt beside him and pressed both hands against the wound in his side.

"Medic!" she screamed. "I need a medic here!"

Danny looked at her. His lips moved.

"What? Danny, what?"

"Tell the girls," he said, and then he didn't say anything else, and his eyes stayed open, looking at something past her shoulder that she couldn't see.

She kept pressing on the wound until a paramedic gently pulled her hands away.

The final count, when it came, filled a single typed page.

Three suspects dead: Marcus Hale, 31. Theodore Brandt, 22. Kevin Rourke, 38.

One suspect in custody: Delbert Maines, 44.

One officer killed: Daniel Kowalski, 34, survived by his wife and two daughters.

Four officers wounded, including Sgt. Leon Hollis, whose right arm would never fully straighten again, and Officer Kelsey Jessup, who would walk with a cane for a year and return to patrol anyway.

Two civilians wounded by stray rounds in the apartment building across the street, neither critically.

And Walter Pruitt, 61, security guard, who died in the ambulance on the way to St. Vincent's, nine weeks from retirement, with a paramedic holding his hand.

The recovered money totaled $184,300. Most of it was stained, and the bank eventually had it destroyed.

Months later, at trial, the prosecutor asked Dell Maines if he had anything to say.

He stood for a long time. The courtroom waited. In the second row sat a woman with two little girls, and a few seats down, an older woman in black who had been married to a security guard for thirty-eight years.

"We had it timed," Dell said finally. His voice was hoarse. "Eleven minutes. Nobody was supposed to get hurt."

He sat back down.

Nobody in the courtroom said anything at all.

# The Hiss

The sound came first. A thin, patient hiss from the vent near the ceiling, so soft that Mara thought it was the building settling, or her own blood rushing in her ears after the door had slammed and the lock had turned with that final, oiled *click*.

Then the smell. Sweet at first, almost pleasant, like overripe fruit left too long in a bowl. Beneath it lay something sharper that caught at the back of her throat.

She understood all at once, the way you understand you've missed a step in the dark.

"No." She said it aloud, to no one. "No, no, no."

She threw herself at the door. The metal was cold and indifferent under her fists. She pounded until the skin across her knuckles split, until the sound of her blows became a kind of rhythm, and then she screamed, raw and wordless, and the scream turned into a cough halfway through.

The cough frightened her more than anything. It didn't stop when she wanted it to.

*Think. Think.* She pressed her sleeve over her mouth and nose and scanned the room with eyes that had begun to sting. Concrete walls. One bulb in a wire cage. A drain in the floor, too small for anything but water. The vent, eight feet up, breathing its slow poison into the air like something alive.

She dragged the room's single chair beneath it and climbed. The chair wobbled. Her fingers found the grate and pulled until her nails bent back, but the screws didn't budge, and the gas poured directly into her face. Her eyes flooded. She fell, or the chair fell, and she landed hard on her hip on the concrete, and for a moment the pain was almost welcome because it was *clear*. It was a thing she understood.

The clarity didn't last.

A headache bloomed behind her eyes, low and throbbing, keeping time with her heartbeat. Her heartbeat was too fast. She could feel it in her neck, in her fingertips, a frantic bird hurling itself against a window. She tried to slow her breathing, *shallow breaths, stay low, gas rises, or does it sink, which one, which one*, but her lungs wouldn't listen. They wanted air. They gulped at it greedily, and every gulp made things worse.

Her eyes were streaming now. The single bulb had grown a halo, then two, a smeared constellation of light. When she blinked, the world lurched sideways and took a moment too long to come back.

She crawled to the corner farthest from the vent and pressed her face against the seam where the wall met the floor, searching for some pocket of clean air, some mercy in the architecture. The concrete smelled of dust and damp. Beneath it, still, that sweetness.

Nausea rolled up from her stomach in a slow, greasy wave. She retched, and there was nothing, and she retched again. Her mouth tasted of metal. Her tongue felt thick and strange, like it belonged to someone else and had been lent to her without instructions.

*Someone will come.* The thought arrived with perfect, childish confidence. *Someone will notice I'm gone.* She held onto it. She built it up in her mind: footsteps in the corridor, the lock turning, a rush of cold air. She could almost hear it.

She realized she was hearing it. Footsteps. Voices.

She lifted her head, and the room was empty. The door was shut. The footsteps were only her pulse, loud and wet and slowing now, which she knew should frighten her, but the fear seemed to be draining away with everything else, leaking out through some crack she couldn't find.

Her hands had gone numb. She stared at them, pale shapes at the ends of her arms, and tried to make them into fists. The fingers curled halfway and stopped, trembling.

She thought about her sister. That was strange. She hadn't thought about her sister in months, not since the argument, but now Lena was here in the room, or the idea of her was, sitting on the edge of a bed in the house they'd grown up in and braiding Mara's hair too tight. *Hold still,* Lena was saying. *Hold still or it'll come out crooked.*

"I'm sorry," Mara said, or tried to say. Her lips moved. The sound was only breath.

The bulb had gone very far away, a pinprick at the end of a long tunnel. The edges of her vision were soft and grey, and the grey was creeping inward, patient as the hiss.

She tried once more to rise. She got as far as her knees. The floor tilted up to meet her like a slow wave, and she let it, because it was so much easier than fighting, and her cheek rested against the cool concrete, and that felt, absurdly, good.

Her breathing came slower. Long gaps between each one, and in the gaps, a silence so deep it seemed to have texture.

Somewhere above her, the vent kept breathing.

Somewhere far away, Lena finished the braid and tied it off, and said, *There. All done.*

Mara closed her eyes.

# Chain of Custody

The warrant said *narcotics*. That was the first decision, and Kessler had made it three days ago, sitting in his truck outside the precinct with the engine off, working it through.

A homicide warrant would bring the whole circus: crime scene techs, a lieutenant who liked to be seen, a lab that actually did its job. A narcotics warrant brought two detectives and a uniform to hold the door. Small rooms, few eyes. You didn't pick the crime you were investigating. You picked the one that gave you the right number of witnesses.

Now he stood in Marcus Hale's kitchen and let the apartment tell him what he needed.

It was clean. That was a problem. Clean men noticed things out of place, and a jury would see the photographs. Kessler filed it away: *mention the cleanliness in the report. Paranoid. Hiding something.* A tidy apartment was only a liability until you described it.

"Bedroom's clear so far," Ochoa called from down the hall.

"Keep going. Check the closet ceiling panels. These guys love the ceiling."

He heard the scrape of a chair. Good. Ochoa would be up there for four, five minutes, flashlight in his teeth, feeling around insulation, and Ochoa was the kind of cop who finished a task before he looked up from it. Kessler had partnered with him for eleven months and had chosen him, in his head, for exactly this quality. Diligence was a kind of blindness if you pointed it in the right direction.

The uniform, a kid named Pruitt, stood outside on the landing with Hale, whose wrists were cuffed in front because Kessler had told Pruitt that was fine. It was a small courtesy, and it would read well later. *Detective Kessler was respectful to the suspect throughout.* Every kindness today was an entry in a ledger someone else would audit.

Pruitt's body camera faced Hale. Kessler's own camera was mounted on his chest, recording, and he was aware of it the way a man is aware of a loaded gun in his waistband: constantly, without looking at it.

He had spent a long time thinking about the camera.

Turning it off was stupid. A gap in footage was a question, and questions were what he was trying to eliminate. The camera had to run. It had to show him finding the thing. What it could not show was the thing arriving.

So: the jacket.

He'd worn the heavy canvas one today, though it was fifty-eight degrees, and he'd complained about the precinct thermostat that morning in front of three people so the jacket would have a reason to exist. In the inside left pocket, wrapped in a nitrile glove turned inside out, was Danny Voss's phone.

Danny, who'd been a useful informant for two years and a threat for about six days. Danny, who'd gotten sober, gotten religion or a lawyer or both, and started using phrases like *I've been thinking about what's right.* Kessler had not been angry when he did it. That was the part he returned to sometimes, not with guilt exactly, but with a kind of clinical interest. His pulse had stayed level. He had thought, standing over the body under the overpass: *this is a problem with a finite number of solutions.*

Marcus Hale was one of them.

Hale had a record: possession with intent, eight years back, served his time. Hale had been seen arguing with Danny outside the Laundromat on Delmar in March; Kessler had the uniform's field report memorized. Hale lived alone, worked nights at a distribution warehouse, and had no alibi for the hours that mattered because he'd been asleep, the way innocent people usually are. An innocent man's night was the easiest thing in the world to steal. Nobody documents their own sleep.

Kessler moved to the living room. Couch, bookshelf, a television older than Pruitt. A child's drawing magneted to the side of the refrigerator he could still see through the doorway: a house, a sun, three stick figures, *DADDY* in green crayon over the tallest one.

He looked at it for one second. He noted that a child meant visitation, meant a custody arrangement, meant an ex who might testify about Hale's schedule. He noted that a child also meant a sympathetic defendant. He weighed it. The drawing was a variable, nothing more, and he moved past it.

The couch. Couches were good. Everyone hid things in couches, so no one questioned finding things in couches. Originality was for people who wanted to get caught.

He turned his body so the camera faced the bookshelf, crouched, and made a show of running his hand along the spines. With his left hand, out of frame, he slid the glove from his pocket and pushed it, phone and all, down between the cushion and the frame. It took under two seconds. He'd practiced the motion on his own couch forty times, timing it, until his hand did it without him.

Then he stood, stretched his back, and said, for the microphone, "Nothing on the shelf."

He counted to ninety in his head. He checked the TV stand. He opened a drawer of takeout menus and batteries and made a small disgusted noise. Finding something too quickly was the mark of a man who knew where it was. The discovery had to feel like work.

At ninety, he turned to the couch.

"Let's flip these cushions."

He did it square to the camera, both hands visible, slow. He pulled the cushion. He let his hand go into the gap and stop.

"Ochoa. Come here."

He waited until Ochoa was in the doorway, until there were two cameras and two witnesses, before he drew it out. The glove unrolled. The phone fell into his palm, its cracked screen catching the light.

"That's not a burner," Ochoa said. "That's a nice phone."

"Yeah." Kessler kept his voice flat, a little puzzled. Puzzled was right. Puzzled was what an honest cop would sound like. "Bag it. Don't power it on. Let's get it to the lab and see who it belongs to."

He already knew what the lab would find. Danny's prints, and nothing else, because Kessler had handled it only in gloves since the night under the overpass. The absence of Hale's prints would be a wrinkle, and he had an answer ready: *the suspect stored it in a glove. He was being careful.* The glove itself, turned inside out, explained the missing prints. It was evidence that apologized for its own weaknesses.

Out on the landing, Hale was saying something to Pruitt. Kessler caught the tone of it more than the words: confused, not yet afraid. The fear would come later, in the interview room, when Kessler slid the photograph across the table and said Danny's name and watched Hale's face do the thing innocent faces do, that open, stupid bewilderment. Juries didn't know how to read that look. Kessler had seen guilty men manufacture it and innocent men wear it and he'd learned years ago that it meant nothing to anyone but him.

He walked out onto the landing. Hale looked up at him.

"Man, what is that? That's not mine. I don't know what that is."

"Okay," Kessler said gently. "We'll talk about it downtown."

He put a hand on Hale's shoulder to guide him toward the stairs. It was a steady hand. He noticed that, the way he noticed everything today, and he added it to the ledger with the rest.

*The detective was calm. The detective was professional. The detective followed procedure.*

All of it true. All of it on camera.

# The Pantry

The cans had been found in the cellar of a collapsed Methodist church, eleven of them, their labels long since rotted to gray pulp. Three were swollen, bulging at the seams like something pregnant with poison. Everyone in the ruined sanctuary knew what that meant. Nobody said it.

Mara had found them. That was the first problem.

The second problem was that Dell had watched her find them.

---

By the time the others gathered, the cans sat in a loose pyramid on the cracked altar, and six people stood in a rough circle among the overturned pews, each pretending not to measure the distance between themselves and the food. The wind moved through the broken stained glass with a sound like someone breathing through their teeth.

"We split it," said old Hendricks. His voice was thin as wet paper. "Even. Like we agreed."

"Eleven don't split six ways," Dell said. He had a length of rebar in his right hand, and he wasn't leaning on it the way he used to. He was holding it low, loose at the wrist.

"Then we split what's in them. Open them all, divide by spoon."

"Three are bad," said the Tanaka girl, barely sixteen, her collarbones sharp as coat hangers beneath her shirt. "You can see they're bad."

"They're not bad," Dell said, too fast. "Swelling's just air. Cook it long enough, it's fine."

Mara knew it wasn't fine. Her grandmother had canned peaches every August, and she'd taught Mara to throw out anything with a bulging lid, taught her the word *botulism* the way other grandmothers taught prayers. But Mara also knew what four days without food did to a person's arithmetic. Eight good cans and three bad ones, six people. The math didn't work out, and when math didn't work out, people started subtracting.

---

Nobody could say later who moved first.

Maybe it was Tanaka's brother lunging for the altar. Maybe it was Dell, who had been waiting for an excuse since the moment he saw the cellar door. What Mara remembered was the sound: the flat, wet crack of rebar meeting a forearm raised too late, and Hendricks folding to the floor with a scream that didn't sound human, his arm bent in a place where arms don't bend.

Then everyone was moving.

Mara grabbed the nearest thing, a brass candlestick heavy as a hammer, and swung it at the shape coming toward her before she even knew whose shape it was. It was Owen, quiet Owen who'd shared his water with her on the highway in March. The candlestick caught him above the ear. He staggered sideways into a pew, and for one frozen second they looked at each other, both of them understanding that something had just ended that couldn't be started again.

Then Owen came up with a shard of window glass wrapped in a rag, and the understanding didn't matter anymore.

He slashed wide and caught her across the ribs. The pain came a half-second late, a hot line and then a sheet of wetness spreading down her side. She drove forward anyway, because stopping meant dying, and they went down together into the wreckage of hymnals and pigeon bones. The glass bit into his own palm as they struggled. She could feel his blood and hers mixing on her wrist, slick, impossible to tell apart.

Across the sanctuary, the Tanaka girl had a kitchen knife lashed to a broom handle, a spear she'd made weeks ago "for dogs." She was using it now on Dell, jabbing, retreating, jabbing, her face blank with terror. Dell caught the shaft with his free hand and yanked her close, and the rebar came down on her shoulder, and she dropped. Her brother hit Dell from behind with a cinderblock, and the sound it made was the worst sound Mara had ever heard, worse than the bombs, worse than anything, because it was so small.

Dell fell across the altar. Cans rolled free and clattered down the steps, spinning away into the dark beneath the pews.

---

It lasted maybe ninety seconds.

When it was over, Hendricks lay whimpering and cradling his ruined arm. Owen sat against a pillar with his hand clamped to his head, blood running steadily between his fingers, staring at nothing. The Tanaka girl was breathing in short, hitching gasps, her left arm hanging wrong. Her brother knelt beside Dell, who wasn't moving, and kept saying *I didn't, I didn't, I didn't*, as if repetition might make it true.

Mara pressed her palm against her ribs and felt the edges of the wound, felt how deep it went. Not deep enough to kill her, she thought. Probably. If it didn't turn.

She crawled to the nearest can. Her fingers found it in the dust beneath the pew, and she turned it over in the colored light falling through the broken windows.

It was one of the swollen ones.

She held it for a long moment, the metal cool and taut against her bloody hand, the lid curved outward like a held breath. Then she set it down very gently, as if it might wake up, and began to laugh. It wasn't really laughter, only the sound a body makes when it has run out of every other sound.

Outside, the wind kept moving through the glass. Somewhere far off, a dog barked once and went silent.

Nobody reached for the food. Not yet.
