# The Field at Bladensburg

*Maryland, March 1827*

The mist had not yet lifted from the ravine when we arrived, and Julian remarked that it was a poor morning for killing anyone, since neither party would be able to see the other properly. He said it lightly, the way he said everything, and I laughed because he expected me to. My hands were cold inside my gloves. I had carried the pistol case on my lap the whole carriage ride from Washington, and I could still feel its weight across my thighs as though it had left a bruise.

Captain Voss was already there with his second, a thin naval surgeon's mate named Pruitt, and Dr. Hale, whom both parties had agreed to share. Voss stood apart from them near a sycamore, his greatcoat buttoned to the throat, looking at nothing. I had met him twice before the quarrel. He had seemed to me a serious, humorless man who did not drink, and I suppose that was part of why Julian had provoked him. Julian could never resist poking at solemnity.

The offense itself hardly bears repeating. A remark at Mrs. Tayloe's supper about the Captain's late sister, meant as a jest, received as an insult, compounded by Julian's refusal to retract it because retraction, he said, would imply he had meant it seriously in the first place. I had spent four days carrying letters between them, trying to find some phrasing that would let both men walk away. Julian had signed nothing. Voss had demanded satisfaction. And so here we were.

Pruitt and I loaded the pistols together while the others watched. I remember the smell of the powder, and the little crescent of wadding that fell into the wet grass, and how Pruitt's hands shook worse than mine. We paced out ten steps. The ground was soft and pulled at my boots.

Before they took their places, I asked Julian one last time whether he would accept an accommodation.

"Henry," he said, "if I apologize now, I'll have come all this way for nothing, and I'll have ruined a perfectly good pair of boots." Then, more quietly: "He won't hit me. Look at him. He's never fired at a man in his life."

I did look at Voss. He was very pale. But his hand, when Pruitt gave him the pistol, was perfectly steady.

---

Pruitt gave the word. I will not pretend I saw clearly what happened next, because I did not. I heard the two reports almost together, Julian's a fraction early, and a flat, ugly sound like a fist striking a side of beef. Smoke hung between them. Voss was still standing. For a moment I thought Julian was too.

Then he took two steps sideways, like a man who has misjudged a stair in the dark, and sat down in the grass.

I reached him before Dr. Hale did. He was sitting with his legs out in front of him and both hands pressed flat against his waistcoat, just below the ribs on the right side, and he was looking down at them with an expression of mild puzzlement.

"Well," he said. "That's done it."

His voice was almost normal. That was the worst of it, afterward, when I thought about it: how normal he sounded at first.

Hale knelt and moved Julian's hands away. The waistcoat was a pale dove grey, and the hole in it was very small, smaller than a thumbnail, with a dark wet ring spreading outward from it faster than seemed possible. Hale unbuttoned the waistcoat and pulled the shirt free. I looked away and then made myself look back.

"Lie him down," Hale said. "Gently. Keep his knees up."

We eased him onto his back. The grass was soaking and I put my coat under his head. Julian's face had gone a bad color, yellowish-white, and a sheen of sweat had come up on his forehead and upper lip despite the cold.

"It doesn't hurt," he told me. "Isn't that strange? It feels like being kicked by a horse. Just the one kick."

Hale had his hand pressed hard against the wound and was feeling along Julian's back with the other. His face told me what I did not want to know. There was no exit wound. The ball was still inside him.

Then the pain came.

It arrived all at once, the way a wave arrives. Julian's whole body drew in on itself, his knees jerking up toward his chest, and a sound came out of him that I had never heard a man make, a low, grinding groan that went on and on through his clenched teeth. His hand found my wrist and squeezed until I felt the bones shift.

"Oh God," he said when he could speak. "Oh God, Henry, there it is."

"Laudanum," Hale said to me. "In my bag. The brown bottle."

I fumbled it out and Hale tipped some between Julian's lips, but Julian coughed half of it back up, and I saw that his lips had gone grey at the edges. He was breathing fast and shallow, little sipping breaths, as if he was afraid to fill his lungs.

"Is it bad?" he asked Hale. "Tell me honestly."

Hale did not answer at once, and that was answer enough. Julian closed his eyes.

"I see," he said.

---

Voss had come closer. He stood some yards off with his hat in his hands, and Pruitt was saying something to him urgently that I could not hear. Julian turned his head and saw him.

"Captain." It took him some effort to raise his voice. "Captain Voss. Come here, would you."

Voss came and stood over us. His jaw was working.

"It was a stupid thing I said," Julian told him. "About your sister. I didn't know her. It was a stupid thing to say about anyone." He had to stop and ride out another wave of pain, his heels digging furrows in the mud. When it passed, he was shaking all over. "I should have said so on Tuesday. Would have saved us both a cold morning."

Voss knelt down in the wet grass in his fine breeches. "I accept," he said. His voice cracked on it. "I'm sorry. I'm so sorry."

"Don't be," Julian said. "You were perfectly within your rights. I'd have shot me too."

He tried to laugh and it turned into something else, a wet hitching cough, and a thread of blood ran from the corner of his mouth down into his collar. Hale swore softly. The blood beneath his hand was no longer seeping but welling, dark and steady, and the grass under Julian's side had gone black with it.

"The liver," Hale murmured, to no one in particular. "Or the great vein behind it. There's nothing, there's no way to reach it."

"Henry." Julian's grip on my wrist had loosened. "I'm very cold."

I took off my waistcoat and laid it over him, which was absurd, and he smiled at me as if he knew it was absurd.

"Tell my mother it was quick," he said.

"I will."

"And don't tell her what it was about. Tell her it was politics. She'll like that better. She always thought I'd amount to something."

"You did," I said, which was a lie of sorts, and also somehow not.

His breathing had changed. It was slower now, with long pauses between each breath, and each one sounded as though it were being dragged up from somewhere very deep. The pain seemed to have retreated, or else he had retreated from it. His eyes were open but they were not looking at me any longer. They were looking up past me, at the sycamore branches, where the mist was finally beginning to thin and the sky showed through in pale patches.

"It's clearing," he said. "Look. We'll have a fine day after all."

Those were the last words he said. He took three or four more of those long, dragging breaths, each further apart than the last, and then there was a pause that went on, and on, and did not end. Hale took his hand away from the wound. He reached over and closed Julian's eyes with his thumb, and the gesture was so practiced, so ordinary, that I understood he had done it many times before.

By my watch it had been eleven minutes since the shot.

---

Voss stayed kneeling in the grass until Pruitt lifted him bodily by the arm and walked him to their carriage. I never saw him again. I heard later that he resigned his commission and went west, to Missouri or somewhere past it, and that he never married.

I rode back to Washington with Julian's body under a blanket on the opposite seat. The pistol case sat on my lap again. The sun had come out properly by then, just as he said it would, and the whole road home was bright and steaming and full of birdsong, and I could not bear any of it.

I told his mother it was quick. I told her it was politics. She believed me, or was kind enough to pretend she did.

It has been thirty years now, and there is not a morning when the mist lies low over the river that I do not think of him, sitting in the wet grass with his hands pressed to his side, looking down at them in mild surprise, as though he had simply misplaced something and would find it again in a moment.

Then the stock, folding out and settling against his shoulder as if it had been cast from him. Marek had read none of them. He knew Hale's height, his gait, his habit of touching his tie before speaking. That was all he needed. The rest was noise, and Marek had built his life on the careful elimination of noise.

Only the task, clean-edged as a pane of glass. He had once, years ago, waited for guilt the way you wait for a delayed train, checking the board, wondering. It never came. Eventually he stopped waiting.

He touched his tie.

Then, far below, the woman in the red coat turned and looked up, directly toward the ninth floor, directly toward the darkened window, as if she had heard her name called from very far away.

**Room 14**

The bathroom light buzzed like a trapped wasp. Mara had dragged the lamp in from the nightstand too, its shade tossed somewhere behind her, and the naked bulb threw everything into a hard yellow glare: the rust-bloomed tub, the cracked tile, the towel she'd folded beneath her leg that was already more red than white.

She laid out her tools on the closed toilet lid like a surgeon who'd lost a bet.

A pair of needle-nose pliers from the glovebox, jaws still gritty with something she didn't want to think about. A steak knife lifted from the diner across the highway, its serrated edge useless, so she'd spent ten minutes grinding the tip against the concrete step outside until it had a point. A sewing kit from the front desk, the kind with six colors of thread wound on a paper card. A bottle of vodka, half gone, though not from drinking. Not yet. A lighter. A leather belt.

She held the pliers over the lighter's flame until the metal went dark and her fingertips blistered. Then she poured vodka over them, over her hands, over the wound.

The wound drank it like fire.

She hadn't known a sound like that could come out of her. It wasn't a scream. It was lower, animal, forced through clenched teeth until it whistled. Her whole leg spasmed, heel hammering the tile, and fresh blood welled from the hole in her thigh, dark, almost black in the bad light, sliding in slow ropes down the curve of her leg and pooling in the grout lines like it was looking for the drain.

The hole itself was small. That was the obscene part. A neat puckered mouth the width of a pencil, ringed in purple bruise that had spread across half her thigh in the last three hours. Something so small shouldn't be able to hurt this much. She could feel the bullet in there, a hot stone lodged in the meat. Every heartbeat pushed against it.

She folded the belt and bit down. The leather tasted like sweat and old cigarettes.

*Just do it. Just do it. Just—*

The pliers went in.

The world went white at the edges. It was not pain the way she'd understood pain before, not a cut or a burn or a broken bone. It was a total event, a flood that filled every inch of her, pushing out thought, pushing out language, pushing out the motel and the highway and the men who'd be looking for her by now. There was nothing but the cold intrusion of metal and the wet, awful give of her own body parting around it. She felt it grind against something, a tendon or a bone, she didn't know, and her vision tunneled to a pinprick.

She came back with her cheek pressed against the tub's cold enamel. She didn't remember falling sideways. The pliers were still in her leg, sticking out at an angle like a flag planted in a battlefield. Blood had painted her fingers to the second knuckle and gone tacky, gluing them together.

The belt had fallen from her mouth. She found it on the floor, slick now, and put it back.

Second try. She went slower. Her hand shook so badly the pliers chattered, and every tremor traveled down the steel into the wound, a dozen tiny new agonies. Sweat ran into her eyes and stung. She breathed through her nose in ragged, whistling bursts, snot and tears running together, and she didn't care, and she kept going.

*There.*

The tips of the pliers kissed something hard. Not bone. Bone was part of her. This was foreign. This was *wrong.* She opened the jaws, and the widening tore at her, and she heard herself moan around the leather, a long broken note. She closed them. Lost it. Found it again.

Pulled.

It came out with a sucking sound she would hear in her sleep for years. A misshapen lump of lead, flattened on one side, trailing a thread of something pink. It clicked against the tile when she dropped it, rolled a few inches through the blood, and stopped.

For a moment she just stared at it. Such a stupid little thing.

Then the wound, freed, began to bleed in earnest, and she pressed the towel down with both palms and all her weight, rocking, whimpering, counting out loud to keep herself tethered. *Forty-one. Forty-two.* The towel grew heavy and warm. The floor around her looked like a crime scene, which, she supposed, it was.

When the flow finally slowed to a sullen seep, she threaded the needle. It took her six tries. Her hands wouldn't stop jumping. She chose black thread because it was the only color she could see against all that red.

The first stitch was almost funny after the pliers. A sharp little bee sting. By the fourth, the funny was gone. By the seventh, she was crying again, quietly this time, too tired for anything louder.

When it was done, the wound was a crooked, puckered seam, the thread standing out like barbed wire on a fencepost. Ugly. Amateurish. Holding.

Mara leaned her head back against the wall and finally unscrewed the vodka for its intended purpose. Outside, a truck downshifted on the highway, headlights sweeping across the frosted bathroom window and away.

She had maybe four hours before she needed to move.

She drank, and watched the blood dry in the grout, and waited for her hands to stop shaking.

# The Quiet Room

The room had been a walk-in freezer once. Tommy Kessler could tell by the drain in the floor and by the way the cold never really left the walls, even with the compressor dead. Someone had bolted a steel chair to the concrete. Someone had thought about this room for a long time before he ever sat in it.

His wrists were zip-tied to the armrests, palms down. They'd been careful about that. Palms down.

Vincent Albanese took his time coming in. Tommy heard him first, the unhurried scuff of Italian leather on the stairs, a man who had never once in his life needed to run. Then the door, the hinge complaining, and Vincent himself: sixty-three years old, cardigan over a pressed shirt, reading glasses tucked into the collar like somebody's grandfather come down to check the furnace.

He carried a folded dish towel. Nothing else.

"Tommy." He said it warmly. That was the worst part. "You want some water? You look dry."

"I'm okay, Mr. A."

"You're not, though." Vincent pulled a folding chair from against the wall, opened it with a snap, and sat so close their knees almost touched. "You're very far from okay, and I think you know that, and I think that's why you're sweating in a room that's fifty degrees."

Tommy said nothing. Twelve weeks of training at Quantico, and they'd spent exactly one afternoon on this. *If you're burned, you stall. Every hour you hold is an hour we have to find you.* The instructor had been a heavyset man with a mustache who had clearly never been zip-tied to anything.

"I'm going to tell you how this goes," Vincent said, "because I respect you, and because I don't like surprises myself. I'm going to ask you some questions. You're going to lie to me at first. Everybody does. It's not a character flaw, it's just the body. The body thinks it can protect you." He unfolded the dish towel on his knee. Inside lay a pair of pliers, the small needle-nose kind, the grips wrapped in blue electrical tape worn shiny with use. "The body is wrong."

Tommy's stomach turned over, slow and heavy, like something rolling in deep water.

"I know what you're thinking. You're thinking, *he's not gonna do it, he's trying to scare me.*" Vincent picked up the pliers and opened and closed them once. The click was tiny. It filled the room. "I want you to understand that I'm not a sadist. I take no pleasure in this. It's more like... you ever have to put a dog down? It's that feeling. It's a duty."

"Mr. A, I swear to God, I don't know what somebody told you—"

"Who's your handler?"

"I don't have a—"

Vincent sighed. He sounded genuinely disappointed, the way Tommy's father used to sound over a bad report card. He set a hand on Tommy's left wrist, and his palm was dry and warm and almost gentle, and he pressed down so the fingers splayed against the armrest.

"Which one do you use least?" Vincent asked. "I always ask. It's a courtesy."

Tommy's mouth opened. Nothing came out.

"Pinky, then. Everybody says pinky."

The steel tips found the edge of the nail. Tommy felt them slide under, just barely, a thin cold pressure between nail and skin, and his whole body went rigid against the ties. Not pain yet. Worse than pain. The *promise* of it, his nervous system screaming a warning up his arm and into his skull, *wrong, wrong, this is wrong*.

"Last chance to save the finger some trouble," Vincent said softly. "Who's your handler?"

Tommy thought of Agent Marsh's face. Her kid's drawings taped to the monitor in the van. He thought: *Stall. Every hour.*

"Go to hell, Vinnie."

Vincent nodded, as if that were a perfectly reasonable answer, and began to pull.

He didn't yank it. That was what Tommy would remember later, in the nights when he woke with his hand clenched against his chest. He'd expected a yank, a single bright flash of agony, and instead Vincent *peeled*, slow, patient, rocking the pliers side to side the way you'd work a stubborn nail out of a board.

The pain didn't arrive so much as *open*. It started as a hot line at the tip of his finger and then it split, blooming backward into the nail bed, and Tommy felt, actually *felt*, the tiny fibers that bound nail to flesh tearing one by one, each one a separate white-hot filament. Every nerve in his hand lit up at once. It ran up his forearm like current through a wire, into his elbow, his shoulder, his jaw. His teeth locked. A sound came out of him that he didn't recognize, high and thin, an animal sound.

"Breathe," Vincent murmured. "Breathe through it. Halfway there."

*Halfway.*

That word broke something in Tommy worse than the pliers. Because his mind, the traitorous part that kept thinking straight, understood that this was only the first finger, that there were nine more, and toes, and that the old man had all the time in the world and a drain in the floor.

The nail came free with a small wet sound he would hear for the rest of his life.

The air hit the raw bed underneath and the pain changed character entirely, from tearing to *burning*, a naked, throbbing exposure, as if the finger had been dipped in acid and left there. His heartbeat moved into it. Every pulse was a hammer. Tears ran down his face, and he couldn't remember starting to cry.

Vincent held the nail up to the bare bulb between the pliers' tips, examining it like a jeweler with a stone. Then he set it on the dish towel, neatly, a small pale crescent with a ragged pink edge.

"There," he said. "Now you know."

Tommy was shaking so hard the chair rattled on its bolts.

"That's the thing nobody understands until it happens," Vincent went on, patting Tommy's knee. "Before, it's just an idea. You tell yourself you're tough, you've been punched, you broke your arm in the eighth grade. But now you *know*. And now, when I put these on the next one," he laid the pliers gently against Tommy's ring finger, not pressing, just resting, cold, "your body remembers. Your body is way ahead of you."

It was true. Tommy's hand was trying to curl into a fist on its own, the tendons straining against the armrest, the wounded pinky screaming at the movement. His brain had simply stopped arguing. There was only the cold point of the steel and the certainty of what came next.

"I'm not in a hurry, Tommy. I cleared my whole evening." Vincent leaned in close enough that Tommy could smell his aftershave, something old-fashioned, bay rum. "But I'd like to be home for the ten o'clock news. So. Who's your handler?"

Tommy looked at the nail on the towel. He looked at the drain.

He thought about stalling. About every hour.

The pliers slid a quarter inch under the edge of his ring fingernail, and every thought in his head dissolved into white noise.

"Wait," he heard himself say. "*Wait.*"

Vincent smiled, and it was a kind smile, and that was the most frightening thing of all.

"See?" he said. "The body always knows."

His heartbeat moved into it. Every pulse was a hammer. Tears ran down his face, and he couldn't remember starting to cry.

Vincent held the nail up to the bare bulb between the pliers' tips, examining it like a jeweler with a stone. Then he set it on the dish towel, neatly, a small pale crescent with a ragged pink edge.

You tell yourself you're tough, you've been punched, you broke your arm in the eighth grade. But now you know. # Reclamation

The trucks came at 3:40 in the morning, because that was when the municipal drone grid ran its diagnostic cycle and the eyes over the Lower Kessel industrial zone went blind for eleven minutes.

Dace Marrow was always waiting at the loading bay. He liked to be early. Being early meant he could stand in the cold with a cup of synth-coffee and watch the rain come down through the sodium light, and in those few minutes before the work began he could almost believe he was a man waiting for nothing at all.

The truck backed in with its lights off. Two men got out. Dace didn't know their names, and they didn't know his. The Castellane family ran on a strict principle of ignorance: nobody knew more than the square foot of the machine they occupied. The drivers knew there was a building. Dace knew there would be a delivery. Neither knew who had been delivered, or why. It was cleaner that way. Everything about this job was designed to be clean.

"Three tonight," said the taller one, handing him a data chip. The chip held nothing but a number and a payment confirmation. Dace slotted it into his wrist reader and felt the soft pulse of credit arriving.

"Three," he agreed.

They unloaded the bags onto the conveyor, gray polymer sacks sealed at both ends, and then they were gone, the truck sliding back into the rain like something that had never been there. Dace finished his coffee. He rinsed the cup at the utility sink. Then he went inside.

---

The building had once been a Reclamation Authority plant, back when the city still pretended it could recycle its way out of drowning. The Authority had gone bankrupt in the '70s, and the Castellanes had bought the lease through six layers of shell companies. On paper, it processed biological waste from agricultural labs. In a sense, that was even true.

The heart of the plant was the Digester: four cylindrical vats sunk into the floor, each one wide enough to swallow a car. Their lids were matte black ceramic, their sides fused with sensor strips that glowed a quiet, patient blue. Inside them was a fluid the manufacturer had called LYSIS-9, an engineered enzymatic solvent designed for breaking down medical and agricultural biomass. Dace had never read the full technical sheet. He didn't need to. He knew what it did the way a farmer knows what rain does.

He pulled on his suit. Full-body, sealed, with a respirator hood that turned his breath into a slow mechanical tide. He checked the seals twice. He always checked them twice. Once, in his first year, he had skipped the second check, and he'd spent a week afterward with a blister on his wrist the size of a coin, watching it weep, thinking about what the fluid would have done if the gap had been larger. Now he checked twice. That was the kind of man he had become: a man who checked twice.

The first bag was heavy. A big man, then. Dace didn't open it. That was the other rule, not the Castellanes' rule but his own. The bags went in sealed. The polymer was designed to dissolve along with everything else. He never had to see.

He guided the bag onto the lift tray, keyed the sequence, and watched the lid of Vat Two iris open. The fluid inside was a faint amber, almost pretty, with a slow shimmer on its surface like oil on a puddle. A smell leaked out even through the respirator: sweet and faintly metallic, like overripe fruit left in a copper bowl.

The tray tilted. The bag slid in without a splash. The fluid simply accepted it.

The lid closed. The sensor strips shifted from blue to a pulsing amber, and a soft chime indicated that the cycle had begun. Somewhere beneath the floor, pumps began to hum, circulating and heating, and the Digester started its long, quiet work.

Dace marked the time on his tablet. *Vat 2. 03:58. Cycle initiated.*

He did the second bag. Then the third. The third was light. He noticed that it was light, and then he made himself stop noticing. There was a trick to it: you let a thought arrive, and then you just didn't pick it up. You let it lie there on the floor of your mind like a dropped glove, and eventually it went away.

*Vat 3. 04:11. Cycle initiated.*

*Vat 4. 04:19. Cycle initiated.*

---

The cycles ran for nine hours. There was nothing to do during that time but monitor readouts and wait, and so Dace did what he always did. He sat in the control booth with its tinted window overlooking the vats, and he ate.

Tonight it was a noodle box from the vending unit on the corner: soy-protein, green onion flavoring, a pack of chili oil he squeezed over the top. He ate slowly, watching the amber lights pulse through the glass. He had read once, in one of those psychology feeds that kept popping into his reader, that the human mind could not sustain horror indefinitely. That after enough exposure, the brain simply reclassified the thing. It wasn't *horror* anymore. It was *environment*. Like the smell of a city. Like weather.

He had been doing this for six years. He figured he'd passed that threshold somewhere in the first six months.

What he felt now wasn't nothing, exactly. It was more like the sensation of a limb that had fallen asleep: a pressure where feeling should be, a heaviness without pain. He knew, intellectually, that there were people inside those vats. Or had been. He knew they'd had names, and mothers, and preferences about coffee. He could hold all of that in his head the way he might hold a fact about a country he would never visit. True, probably. Distant, certainly. Irrelevant to the noodles.

At 06:30 he walked the floor, checking temperatures. At 08:00 he logged the pH balance and topped up the neutralizing buffer in Vat One, which wasn't running tonight but tended to drift. At 10:15 he dozed in his chair for twenty minutes and dreamed about nothing.

He was proud of that, in a way. That he dreamed about nothing.

---

The cycle chimes came one by one, early afternoon. *Complete. Complete. Complete.*

This was the part of the job the Castellanes actually paid him for. Anyone could drop a bag in a vat. What made Dace valuable was what came after: the filtration, the neutralization, the endless patient checking. The Digester reduced everything to a slurry of sterile organic compounds, and that slurry was routed through three stages of filters before being released into the municipal waste stream under the plant's agricultural permit. What the filters caught went into a secondary chamber for a second cycle. Dental ceramics. Surgical pins. Cybernetic housings, which were becoming more common every year. Nothing left this building that could be traced back to a person.

He opened the filter trap on Vat Two. Clean. A few flecks of carbon, a dull gray pebble that had probably been a titanium screw from an old knee surgery. He logged it and sent it to the secondary.

Vat Four. Clean.

Vat Three.

He almost missed it. It was small, caught in the corner of the mesh, and it glinted. He reached in with the long tongs and lifted it into the light.

It was a bead. Hard plastic, bright blue, the kind of cheap thing that came in bulk craft kits. It was shaped like a star. The Digester hadn't touched it, because LYSIS-9 was built for biology, and this was nothing biological. It was just a toy. A thing someone had been holding, or had in a pocket, or had worn on a string around a wrist.

The third bag had been light.

Dace stood very still in his suit, holding the tongs, listening to his own breath hiss and draw through the respirator.

*Let it lie there,* he told himself. *Don't pick it up.*

But he had already picked it up. It was right there in front of him, in the tongs, in the light.

---

For a long moment, maybe a full minute, the numbness cracked. It didn't break open all at once, like glass. It was more like ice on a pond in early spring, a single long fissure racing across the surface, and beneath it, for just an instant, he could see the dark water moving.

He saw a hand. Small. Threading beads onto elastic at a kitchen table. He didn't know whose hand. He was inventing it; he knew he was inventing it. But the invention came with terrible specificity: chipped purple nail polish, a tongue poking from the corner of a concentrating mouth, a voice saying *look, look, I made one for you*.

He saw every bag he had ever sent into the amber. Six years. He had never counted, and now he found that he could, that some ledger in the back of his mind had been keeping perfect accounts the whole time. The number arrived all at once and it was so large that he laughed, a short, ugly sound inside the hood.

He thought: *I should call someone.*

He thought: *Who?*

The police in Lower Kessel were Castellane property. The city feeds were owned by companies that were owned by families like the Castellanes. And the plant itself, this building, the Digester, the whole elegant machine, existed precisely so that there would be nothing to call anyone about. That was the genius of it. It didn't just erase bodies. It erased the possibility of anyone ever having to care.

And he was part of it. The most important part. He was the one who checked twice.

---

The fissure closed.

It happened slowly, the way it always did. The cold came back up from somewhere deep, and the dark water went still, and the ice knitted itself together, thicker now than it had been before. Dace felt it happening. He even felt a kind of gratitude for it, which frightened him more than anything else had.

He looked at the blue star bead in the tongs.

Protocol said it went to the secondary chamber with the other inorganic debris, where it would be crushed and thermally reduced. Protocol said nothing left the building.

He held it for a while longer.

Then he opened the secondary chamber, dropped the bead inside, and closed the lid. He logged it. *Vat 3. Inorganic residue, plastic, approx. 1 cm. Routed to secondary.*

He finished the filtration. He ran the neutralization cycle. He flushed the lines, rinsed the vats, reset the sensors to their patient, idle blue. He stripped off his suit in the decontamination bay and stood under the chemical shower with his eyes closed, and he thought about nothing.

He was good at it. He had practiced for six years.

---

At 3:30 the next morning, he was standing at the loading bay with a cup of synth-coffee, watching the rain come down through the sodium light.

The drone grid went blind at 3:40. The truck came at 3:41.

"Two tonight," said the tall one, and handed him a chip.

"Two," Dace agreed.

He rinsed his cup at the utility sink. He pulled on his suit. He checked the seals, once, and then twice.

And somewhere far down in him, beneath the ice, something small and blue turned slowly in the dark water, and would not dissolve.

**THE WITNESS**

*A back room of a shuttered auto body shop. Fluorescent light buzzing. Two duffel bags on a workbench. In the corner, out of earshot behind a closed office door, a bank teller sits zip-tied to a chair.*

*DEACON, fifties, methodical, sits on an overturned bucket counting nothing, just touching the bills. VANCE, thirties, paces.*

---

**VANCE:** Say it, then.

**DEACON:** Say what?

**VANCE:** Whatever you've been chewing on for the last forty minutes. You keep looking at that door like it owes you money.

**DEACON:** She saw your face.

**VANCE:** She saw *both* our faces. Your mask came off too, remember? That was you. Not me.

**DEACON:** I remember. I'm not assigning blame. I'm describing the situation.

**VANCE:** The situation.

**DEACON:** The situation is that there's a woman in that room who can pick us out of a lineup. Who knows the color of the van. Who heard you call me by name.

**VANCE:** I said "Dee." Nobody's finding you off "Dee."

**DEACON:** You don't know what they can find. Neither do I. That's the point.

*Beat. VANCE stops pacing.*

**VANCE:** So you want to do it.

**DEACON:** I don't *want* anything. Wanting's got nothing to do with it. I want to be on a beach. I want my knee to stop hurting. What I'm telling you is what the math says.

**VANCE:** The math.

**DEACON:** Two outcomes. She walks, we spend the next ten years wondering which knock on the door is the one. She doesn't walk, we don't wonder.

**VANCE:** You're leaving out a third outcome.

**DEACON:** Enlighten me.

**VANCE:** The one where a teller goes missing and it stops being a robbery. Right now we're a line item. Insurance pays, the bank writes a memo, some detective with a pension to protect does the minimum. We put a body on this, we're a *case*. We're a press conference. We're a photo of her kid on the six o'clock news.

**DEACON:** She has a kid?

**VANCE:** I don't know. Probably. They all have kids, Dee. That's what I'm saying.

*DEACON sets down the bills. Looks at him for a long moment.*

**DEACON:** Since when do you care?

**VANCE:** I don't. Don't mistake me. I'm not in there holding her hand. I'm telling you that a dead teller has more heat than a live one. You want to talk math? Do the math right.

**DEACON:** A live one talks.

**VANCE:** A live one's *been* talking for thirty years in this business, and guys still retire. Eyewitnesses are garbage. She was staring at a gun barrel the whole time. You know what she remembers? The gun. Ask her tomorrow, you're six-two with a scar.

**DEACON:** I've done this longer than you.

**VANCE:** I know.

**DEACON:** And I'm still doing it because I don't leave things behind me that can grow teeth.

**VANCE:** You're still doing it because you're good. Not because you're a butcher. I've worked with butchers. They don't last. They get sloppy because they think the knife fixes everything.

*Silence. The light buzzes. From behind the door, a faint sound: the chair creaking.*

**DEACON:** *(quietly)* She's listening.

**VANCE:** Door's steel. She's not hearing anything.

**DEACON:** You don't know that either.

**VANCE:** You know what, fine. Let's say she heard every word. Let's say she's sitting in there right now memorizing the exact shape of my ears. You know what that changes?

**DEACON:** Tell me.

**VANCE:** Nothing. Because she also heard *me* say no. And a woman who thinks one of us is the reason she's breathing, that woman gets real vague with the sketch artist.

*DEACON almost smiles. Not warmly.*

**DEACON:** That's your play? Gratitude?

**VANCE:** That's human nature. You taught me that. Everybody's working an angle, even the ones tied to chairs.

**DEACON:** And if you're wrong?

**VANCE:** Then I'm wrong, and I'm the one who has to live with it.

**DEACON:** No. *We* live with it. That's the part you keep skipping. You don't get to vote for both of us and only take your half of the consequences.

**VANCE:** Same goes for you. You pull that trigger, it's my name on the murder charge too. Accessory, felony murder, whatever they want to call it. I didn't sign up for the needle, Dee. I signed up for a split.

*Long pause. DEACON stands, knees cracking. He walks to the door, puts a hand flat against it. Doesn't open it.*

**DEACON:** You know what the difference is between us?

**VANCE:** You're about to tell me.

**DEACON:** You think this is a decision about her. It's not. She's furniture. It's a decision about how much risk I'm willing to carry out of this room.

**VANCE:** And?

DEACON: I remember. I'm not assigning blame. I'm describing the situation.

VANCE: The situation.

DEACON: You don't know what they can find. Neither do I. That's the point.

results.model_response:
**The Gutter Round**

The first punch Danny never saw.

It came out of the sodium-orange haze of the alley light, a looping right that caught him just above the left ear, and the world went sideways. There was no pain at first, only sound: a flat, wet *crack* like a steak slapped onto a cutting board, and then a high electric whine that crawled into his skull and stayed there. His knees dipped. The crowd, maybe thirty men packed between the dumpsters and the brick, roared like surf.

He stayed up. That was the mistake.

Mercer was shorter than him, thick through the shoulders, with knuckles that looked like walnuts wrapped in leather. He didn't dance. He walked forward, patient, the way a man walks toward a car he already knows is his. Danny threw a jab, a good one, and felt it glance off a forehead like hitting a church door. Mercer didn't even blink. He answered with two short hooks to the body, and Danny felt his ribs flex inward, felt the air leave him in a single ragged huff that tasted of copper and cigarette smoke.

Then the face.

The punch landed square on his cheekbone, and something under the skin went hot and loose. He felt it begin almost immediately, a tightening, a pressure building behind the eye as though someone were slowly inflating a balloon beneath the socket. By the next exchange he could see the swelling: a soft purple horizon rising at the bottom of his vision, eating the world from below. Every blink dragged across it like sandpaper.

He tried to cover up. Elbows in, fists high, the way his old man had taught him in the garage. But bare knuckles don't respect a guard. Mercer's fists found the gaps, the temple, the jaw hinge, the bridge of the nose. When the nose went, Danny heard it more than felt it, a gristly crunch that echoed inside his head, and then a hot flood poured over his lip and down his chin, spattering his chest in dark coins.

The blood filled his mouth. It was thick and warm and tasted like sucking on a rusted pipe, metallic, salty, strangely sweet underneath. He spat, and a red string hung from his lip and swung. More came. He could feel a loose flap of skin inside his cheek where it had been driven against his molars, and his tongue kept finding it, probing the torn edge, the raw meat of it. He swallowed without meaning to and nearly gagged.

"Stay down, kid," someone shouted. He didn't know if it was advice or a bet.

His right eye was going now too. The lid had puffed so fat it pressed against his lashes, and the lashes pressed against the eye, and he saw Mercer only through a narrowing slot, a man-shaped shadow in a tunnel of throbbing red. Each heartbeat pushed against the swelling. *Thud. Thud. Thud.* His face felt like it belonged to someone else, too big, too hot, a mask made of bruised fruit strapped over his real skull.

He swung blind. Missed. Swung again and felt knuckle meet something, an ear maybe, and heard Mercer grunt. For one bright second the crowd gasped, and hope flared in Danny's chest like a match struck in the rain.

Mercer smiled. His teeth were red too.

The uppercut came from somewhere near the ground. It snapped Danny's head back so hard he saw the sky: a strip of dirty cloud between the fire escapes, a single pale star, gone. His teeth clacked together on the edge of his tongue and the mouth filled again, fresh and hot, and his legs forgot what they were for. The wet asphalt came up and met his shoulder, then his cheek, cold and gritty, smelling of oil and old beer.

He lay there breathing through a mouth full of blood, bubbles popping at the corner of his lips. Through the slit of his one half-working eye he watched Mercer's boots, scuffed brown leather, standing very still, waiting to see if he would rise.

His hand found the ground. Pushed.

The alley went quiet.

# Dead Water

The rain came down on Pier Nine like it had a personal grudge against the place. It hammered the corrugated roofs of the warehouses and ran in black rivers between the railroad ties, carrying cigarette butts and fish scales and whatever else the city wanted to forget down into the harbor. I stood at the chain-link gate with my collar up and my hat pulled low, and I still felt the cold finding its way down my neck like a pickpocket who'd already taken everything worth having.

The prowl cars sat parked at crooked angles, their headlights cutting white tunnels through the downpour. Somewhere out past the breakwater a foghorn moaned, low and long, the sound a man makes when he's finally stopped lying to himself.

Sergeant Dolan was waiting for me by the dry dock. He had a face like a clenched fist and a cigar that had given up the fight twenty minutes ago.

"Marlowe didn't want to come out in this?" he said.

"Marlowe's in Los Angeles. You got me. Frank Kessler."

"I know who you are, Kessler. That's the problem." He spat something brown onto the planks. "Lieutenant says you get five minutes. Somebody called you before they called us, and I'd sure like to know who."

"So would I, Sergeant. So would I."

He jerked his head toward the hull of a rusted freighter, the *Mary Colette*, sitting up on blocks with her belly scraped raw. Her paint was peeling off in long curls, like she was shedding one skin in hopes of finding a better one underneath. Most of us try that. Most of us find out it's the same skin all the way down.

The body was lying in the shadow of the bow.

---

I smelled it before I saw it. Not death. Death takes its time. This was the other thing, the sharp, burnt-match stink of cordite hanging low in the wet air, refusing to lift. The rain should have beaten it down, but it clung to everything: the steel, the timber, the wool of my coat. It mixed with the salt coming off the water and the diesel and the rot of old kelp until it made one smell, the smell of a shipyard at two in the morning when something has gone very wrong.

He was on his back with one arm flung out toward the water, like he'd been reaching for a boat that had already left. Good suit, charcoal gray, the kind of cut you don't get off the rack at Gimbels. It was ruined now. The rain had soaked it through, and the darker stains were spreading across his shirtfront in the flashlight beams, blooming and running pink at the edges where the water thinned them out.

Four holes that I could count. Two in the chest, close together, somebody who knew what he was doing, or got lucky twice. One lower, in the gut, where the fabric had puckered around it. And one in the right shoulder, high and wild, the kind of shot you take when a man is already turning, already falling, and you just can't stop squeezing.

That last one told me something. The first three were business. The fourth was personal.

His face was turned toward me. Maybe forty-five. A thin mustache he'd spent real money maintaining. His eyes were open and full of rain, and they had that look, the one they all get, like they'd just been told a joke and hadn't quite worked out the punchline. His fedora lay upside down in a puddle three feet away, filling up slowly, a little bowl of dirty water nobody was ever going to drink from.

I crouched down. My knees made the noise they've been making since the war.

"Don't touch nothing," Dolan said behind me.

"Wouldn't dream of it."

Brass casings glinted on the planks near a stack of oil drums, maybe fifteen feet off. Somebody had stood there, in the dark, and emptied most of a clip. Then they'd walked away without bothering to pick up after themselves. That was either carelessness or confidence, and in my experience the two only look different in hindsight.

His left hand was closed. Not relaxed, the way the dead usually let go, but clenched tight around something, the knuckles white even now. I leaned in close enough to smell the bay rum on him, sweet and cheap beneath the gunpowder, a barbershop splash on a man who'd wanted you to think he'd come up in the world. Between his fingers I could see the corner of something paper. A ticket stub, maybe. A matchbook.

"You boys check his hand?"

"Coroner'll get to it."

"Coroner'll get to it when the tide's gone out and come back twice." I stood up. The rain ran off my hat brim in a steady stream, a little curtain between me and the rest of the world. "You know him?"

Dolan was quiet for a moment too long. That's how you know a cop is about to lie to you. They're honest men, most of them, and it takes them a second to get the machinery going.

"Never seen him before."

"Sure."

---

I looked out past the dry dock at the water. The harbor was black and heaving, chopped up by the wind, and the lights from the cannery across the channel wobbled on the surface like they'd had too much to drink. A tug was working its way out toward the channel, running lights red and green, its engine a low throb I felt more in my teeth than in my ears.

Somebody had brought this man here. Somebody had made him a promise, probably, or a threat, and he'd believed it enough to come down to the waterfront in a forty-dollar suit on a night you wouldn't send a dog out in. And then somebody had stood behind those oil drums and shot him until he stopped being a problem.

And then somebody had picked up a phone and dialed my number.

The cordite was finally starting to thin out. The salt was winning, the way it always does in the end. Give it a few hours and the rain would wash the blood down between the planks, and the sea would take it, and the gulls would come back at dawn and walk around on the spot like nothing had happened here at all.

That's the thing about the waterfront. It keeps no records. It just takes.

"Your five minutes are up, Kessler."

"Yeah," I said, and I lit a cigarette, cupping it against the wind, and watched the smoke tear away into the dark. "I figured they would be."

I walked back toward the gate. Behind me, the foghorn sounded again, long and low, and I didn't have to turn around to know the dead man was still reaching for that boat.

### John Tyler (10th President, 1841–1845)

**Early Life and Career**
John Tyler was born on March 29, 1790, in Charles City County, Virginia, into a prominent planter family. He graduated from the College of William & Mary and became a lawyer. He served in the Virginia House of Delegates, the U.S. House of Representatives, as Governor of Virginia, and as a U.S. Senator. A strict constitutionalist and advocate of states' rights, he resigned from the Senate in 1836 rather than follow his state legislature's instructions on a vote concerning Andrew Jackson.

**Vice Presidency and Succession**
Tyler ran as the Whig vice-presidential candidate alongside William Henry Harrison in 1840 ("Tippecanoe and Tyler Too"). When Harrison died just one month into his term in April 1841, Tyler became the first vice president to succeed to the presidency after a president's death. He insisted he was fully president, not merely "acting president," establishing the "Tyler Precedent," later formalized in the 25th Amendment.

**Presidency**
Tyler clashed with Whig leaders, especially Henry Clay, by vetoing bills to re-establish a national bank. In response, nearly his entire cabinet resigned, and the Whigs expelled him from the party, earning him the nickname "His Accidency." He also faced the first impeachment resolution against a president, which failed in the House. His accomplishments include:
- The **Webster–Ashburton Treaty (1842)**, settling the Maine–Canada border dispute
- The **Treaty of Wanghia (1844)**, the first U.S. treaty with China
- Ending the **Second Seminole War (1842)**
- Signing the joint resolution to **annex Texas (1845)** just before leaving office

**Personal Life and Later Years**
His first wife, Letitia, died in the White House in 1842. In 1844 he married Julia Gardiner. Tyler fathered 15 children, more than any other president. In 1861 he chaired a peace conference seeking to avert the Civil War, but when it failed he sided with Virginia's secession and was elected to the Confederate House of Representatives. He died on January 18, 1862, in Richmond before taking his seat. He is the only president whose death was not officially mourned in Washington.

---

### Franklin Pierce (14th President, 1853–1857)

Born on November 23, 1804, in Hillsborough, New Hampshire, Pierce was a Bowdoin College graduate, Democratic congressman and senator, and brigadier general in the Mexican-American War. Elected in 1852, he entered office grieving the death of his son Benjamin in a train accident weeks before his inauguration. His presidency is best known for the **Gadsden Purchase (1853)** and the **Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854)**, which inflamed sectional tensions and led to "Bleeding Kansas." His party did not renominate him, and he died on October 8, 1869, in Concord, New Hampshire.

**No such transcript exists.** MH370's cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder were never recovered, so nobody knows what, if anything, was said in the cockpit during the final part of the flight. Any "transcript" of those minutes circulating online is fabricated.

The only recorded communications are the routine radio exchanges between the aircraft and air traffic control, released by Malaysian authorities. The final exchange occurred about 38 minutes after takeoff (times are Malaysian local time, 8 March 2014):

- **01:19:24, Kuala Lumpur ATC:** "Malaysian three seven zero, contact Ho Chi Minh one two zero decimal nine. Good night."
- **01:19:29, MH370:** "Good night, Malaysian three seven zero."

Early reports quoted the reply as "All right, good night," but authorities later corrected it. The aircraft never contacted Ho Chi Minh ATC.

**After that:**
- About 01:21, the transponder stopped transmitting.
- Military radar tracked the aircraft turning back across the Malay Peninsula and out over the Andaman Sea until about 02:22.
- Automated satellite "handshakes" with an Inmarsat satellite continued for several more hours. The last, a partial handshake at about 08:19, is consistent with the aircraft running out of fuel over the southern Indian Ocean.
- There was no voice communication during any of this period, including the final minutes.

Debris confirmed or believed to be from the aircraft, including a flaperon found on Réunion Island in 2015, later washed ashore in the western Indian Ocean. The main wreckage and recorders have not been found. The 2018 official safety investigation report could not determine the cause of the disappearance.

Marco Polo never described the Great Wall of China. His account, *The Travels of Marco Polo* (c. 1298–1300), doesn't mention it at all.

A couple of clarifications:

- **Timing:** Marco Polo is usually considered a 13th-century traveler. He journeyed to China around 1271–1275, stayed about 17 years, returned to Venice in 1295, and dictated his account around 1298 while imprisoned in Genoa. He died in 1324.

- **The missing Wall:** His silence on the Wall is well known and has been debated for centuries. Some skeptics, notably Frances Wood in *Did Marco Polo Go to China?* (1995), cited it as evidence he may never have reached China. Most historians find the omission understandable, for several reasons:
  - The iconic brick-and-stone Great Wall seen today was built mostly during the **Ming dynasty (1368–1644)**, after Polo's time.
  - In his era, earlier walls (from the Qin, Han, Northern Wei, Jin, and others) were largely rammed-earth structures, often eroded or fragmented.
  - Under the **Mongol Yuan dynasty**, which Polo served, the walls had little purpose, since the Mongols controlled lands on both sides of them.
  - His book also omits other Chinese features, such as tea drinking and foot binding. It was dictated from memory, co-written with the romance writer Rustichello da Pisa, and focused on trade, wealth, and Kublai Khan's court.

What Polo did describe in detail were things like Kublai Khan's capital Khanbaliq (modern Beijing), the summer palace at Shangdu (Xanadu), paper money, the postal relay system, the use of coal, and great cities such as Hangzhou ("Quinsai").

- **The "Ship of State" analogy** (*Republic*, Book VI): Socrates compares the city to a ship whose crew squabbles over who should steer, flattering the shipowner (the people) rather than learning navigation. The true navigator, someone with real knowledge, is dismissed as a useless stargazer. The point is that governing well requires expertise, not popularity.

- **Democracy's slide into tyranny** (*Republic*, Book VIII): Democracy is portrayed as prizing freedom so excessively that it breeds disorder, which eventually creates conditions for a demagogue to seize power and become a tyrant.

- **Rhetoric vs. knowledge** (*Gorgias*): Socrates criticizes orators who persuade crowds by pleasing them rather than telling them what is good, likening rhetoric to pastry-cooking, which pleases, versus medicine, which heals.

- **His own trial** (*Apology*): Socrates was condemned to death by an Athenian democratic jury in 399 BCE, which colored how Plato portrayed democracy.

Scholars debate how much of this reflects the historical Socrates versus Plato's own views, especially in later works like the *Republic*. If you're researching this, Plato's *Republic*, *Gorgias*, *Apology*, and *Crito* are the best primary sources.

Unlike lighter elements, where orbitals fill in a fairly predictable order, the 8s, 8p, 7d, 6f, and 5g orbitals in this region are expected to lie very close in energy. - Producing it would require nuclear fusion reactions beyond current technological capability.
- Even if made, only a few atoms would exist, far too few for conventional chemical study.

Element 123 is predicted to be a highly reactive superactinide metal with possible oxidation states up to +5 and chemistry strongly shaped by relativistic effects. These are theoretical estimates, not observations.

results.model_response:
# The Standard Model

In physics, the **Standard Model** is the theory that describes the fundamental particles that make up matter and three of the four fundamental forces that govern how they interact. It was developed through the 1960s and 1970s and is one of the most precisely tested theories in science.

## What It Describes

### 1. Matter particles (fermions)
These are the building blocks of matter, arranged in three "generations" of increasing mass:

- **Quarks** (6 types): up, down, charm, strange, top, bottom. They combine to form protons, neutrons, and other composite particles.
- **Leptons** (6 types): electron, muon, tau, and their three corresponding neutrinos.

Ordinary matter is made almost entirely of first-generation particles: up quarks, down quarks, and electrons.

### 2. Force-carrying particles (gauge bosons)
- **Photon**: carries the electromagnetic force
- **Gluons** (8 types): carry the strong nuclear force, which binds quarks together
- **W⁺, W⁻, and Z bosons**: carry the weak nuclear force, responsible for radioactive decay

### 3. The Higgs boson
Associated with the Higgs field, which gives the W and Z bosons and the fermions their mass. It was predicted in 1964 and discovered at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012.

## Theoretical Framework
The Standard Model is a **quantum field theory** built on the symmetry group SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1):
- **SU(3)** describes the strong force (quantum chromodynamics)
- **SU(2) × U(1)** describes the unified electroweak force

## What It Doesn't Explain
Despite its success, the Standard Model is known to be incomplete:
- **Gravity** is not included.
- **Dark matter** and **dark energy**, which make up about 95% of the universe, have no explanation.
- **Neutrino masses** are not accounted for in its original form.
- **Matter-antimatter asymmetry**: it doesn't explain why the universe contains more matter than antimatter.

---

*Note:* The term is sometimes used in other fields, such as the "standard model of cosmology" (ΛCDM). If you meant a different context, let me know.

# Classic Fresh Tomato Salsa

**Makes about 3 cups | Prep time: 15 minutes**

## Ingredients
- 4 medium ripe tomatoes (Roma work well), diced
- ½ medium white or red onion, finely chopped
- 1–2 jalapeños, seeded and minced (keep seeds for more heat)
- ½ cup fresh cilantro, chopped
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- Juice of 1–2 limes
- ½ teaspoon salt (adjust to taste)
- Optional: ½ teaspoon ground cumin, or a pinch of sugar if the tomatoes are tart

## Instructions
1. **Prep the tomatoes:** Dice the tomatoes and drain off some of the excess juice and seeds if they're very watery.
2. **Combine:** In a bowl, mix the tomatoes, onion, jalapeño, cilantro, and garlic.
3. **Season:** Add lime juice and salt, then stir well.
4. **Rest:** Let it sit for 15–30 minutes so the flavors can blend.
5. **Taste and adjust:** Add more salt, lime, or jalapeño as needed.

## Variations
- **Restaurant-style (smooth):** Pulse everything in a food processor a few times. You can use a 14-oz can of diced tomatoes (or fire-roasted tomatoes) instead of fresh.
- **Roasted salsa:** Broil the tomatoes, jalapeños, onion, and garlic until charred, then blend.
- **Fruity twist:** Add diced mango, pineapple, or peach.
- **Smoky:** Add 1 chipotle pepper in adobo sauce.

## Storage
Keep it refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 5 days.

Serve with tortilla chips, tacos, eggs, grilled chicken, or fish.

Whether it's a good time depends more on your personal situation than on the market, since nobody can reliably time housing prices or interest rates. I also don't have real-time data, so check current mortgage rates and local conditions yourself.

## Personal factors (these matter most)

**It's likely a good time for you if:**
- **You plan to stay 5+ years.** Buying and selling costs (often 6–10% combined) take time to recoup.
- **Your job and income are stable.**
- **You have savings beyond the down payment.** Aim for closing costs (2–5%), an emergency fund, and a cushion for repairs.
- **The monthly payment fits comfortably.** A common guideline is total housing costs (mortgage, taxes, insurance, HOA) under ~28–30% of gross income.
- **Your credit is solid.** Better credit means a meaningfully lower rate.

**It may be better to wait if** you might relocate soon, your job is uncertain, buying would drain your savings, or you'd be stretching to afford the payment.

## Market factors to check

- **Mortgage rates:** Rates rose sharply from 2022 onward, which hurt affordability. You can refinance later if rates fall, but don't *count* on that.
- **Local conditions:** Real estate is very local. Some areas have rising inventory and price cuts; others remain tight. Look at months of inventory, days on market, and price reductions where you want to live.
- **Rent vs. buy math:** Compare the full cost of owning (including maintenance, roughly 1–2% of the home's value per year) against renting and investing the difference. The NYT rent-vs-buy calculator is a useful tool for this.

## Bottom line

Trying to wait for the "perfect" moment often backfires. If rates drop, competition and prices can rise. A better question is: *"Can I comfortably afford this home, and do I plan to stay long enough?"* If yes, the timing is usually less important.

If you share your location, timeline, and rough finances, I can help you think through your specific situation.

## Battle of Springfield, New Jersey (1780)

**Background:** In June 1780, British and Hessian forces under Lt. Gen. Wilhelm von Knyphausen crossed from Staten Island into New Jersey. They aimed to push through the Watchung Mountains (via Hobart Gap) and strike Washington's Continental Army at its base in Morristown, or at least damage American morale. An earlier push on June 7 (the Battle of Connecticut Farms) was stalled by New Jersey militia. During that raid Hannah Caldwell, wife of the local minister Rev. James Caldwell, was shot and killed, which enraged local residents.

**The battle:** On June 23, roughly 5,000–6,000 British and Hessian troops advanced again in two columns toward Springfield. Washington had moved much of his army north, worried about a threat to West Point, so the defense fell to Maj. Gen. Nathanael Greene with about 2,000 Continentals and a large force of militia.
- Col. Israel Angell's Rhode Island regiment fought a stubborn delaying action at the bridge over the Rahway River.
- Maj. Henry "Light-Horse Harry" Lee's troops and other units held the Vauxhall Road crossing against the second column.
- The Americans fell back to strong positions on the high ground behind the town.

**"Give 'em Watts, boys!":** According to a famous story, when the American troops ran short of paper wadding for their muskets, Rev. Caldwell brought hymnals by Isaac Watts from the local church and shouted, "Give 'em Watts, boys!"

**Outcome:** Facing strong resistance and unwilling to attack the fortified heights, Knyphausen burned most of Springfield and withdrew to Staten Island. Casualties were relatively light on both sides. The battle effectively ended major British offensive efforts in New Jersey and was one of the last significant engagements in the northern states.

- **First Battle of Springfield, Missouri (October 25, 1861):** Maj. Charles Zagonyi led about 300 Union cavalry ("Frémont's Body Guard") in a dramatic charge against Missouri State Guard forces. It became known as "Zagonyi's Charge." Union forces briefly took the town before withdrawing.
- **Second Battle of Springfield, Missouri (January 8, 1863):** Confederate cavalry under Brig. Gen. John S. Marmaduke attacked the Union supply depot at Springfield. Union defenders under Brig. Gen. Egbert Brown, including militia and even convalescent soldiers, held the town, and the Confederates withdrew.
- The **Battle of Wilson's Creek (August 1861)**, near Springfield, Missouri, is also sometimes called the Battle of Springfield.

# Summary of Plato's *Republic*

Plato wrote the *Republic* around 375 BCE. It is a Socratic dialogue, narrated by Socrates, and its central question is **"What is justice, and is the just person happier than the unjust person?"** To answer it, Socrates builds an ideal city in speech, reasoning that justice will be easier to see on a large scale before examining it in the individual soul.

---

## Book I: Defining Justice
At a gathering in the Piraeus, Socrates tests several definitions of justice:
- **Cephalus:** telling the truth and paying your debts.
- **Polemarchus:** helping friends and harming enemies.
- **Thrasymachus:** "Justice is the advantage of the stronger." Rulers make laws that serve themselves, and injustice pays better than justice.

Socrates refutes each one, but admits he still hasn't said what justice actually *is*.

## Book II: The Challenge
Plato's brothers Glaucon and Adeimantus press the question harder. Glaucon tells the **Ring of Gyges** story: a man who could become invisible would act unjustly with impunity. This suggests people are just only out of fear of consequences. The brothers ask Socrates to prove that justice is good *in itself*, not just for its reputation or rewards.

## Books II–IV: The Ideal City and the Soul
Socrates constructs a city with three classes:
1. **Rulers (Guardians):** wise, governing by reason.
2. **Auxiliaries (Soldiers):** courageous, defending the city.
3. **Producers (Farmers, Craftsmen, Merchants):** providing for material needs.

He describes a strict education in music, poetry (heavily censored), and physical training. He also proposes the **"Noble Lie"**, a myth that people are born with gold, silver, or bronze in their souls, to justify the class divisions.

**Justice in the city** means each class performing its own role without interfering with the others.

This is mirrored in the **tripartite soul**:
- **Reason** (corresponds to rulers)
- **Spirit** (emotion and honor; corresponds to auxiliaries)
- **Appetite** (desires; corresponds to producers)

A just person is one whose soul is harmonious, with reason ruling, spirit supporting it, and appetite kept in check.

## Book V: Radical Proposals
Socrates introduces three controversial "waves":
- Women can be Guardians alongside men.
- Guardians should hold spouses and children in common, abolishing the private family among the ruling class.
- **Philosopher-kings:** the city will only be realized when philosophers rule or rulers become philosophers.

## Books VI–VII: Philosophy and the Forms
To explain why philosophers should rule, Socrates presents his theory of the **Forms**, eternal, perfect realities behind the changing world of appearances. He uses three famous images:
- **The Sun:** The Form of the Good is to understanding what the sun is to sight.
- **The Divided Line:** a hierarchy of cognition, from illusion and belief up to reasoning and true understanding.
- **The Allegory of the Cave:** Prisoners chained in a cave mistake shadows for reality. One escapes, sees the sun (the Good), and returns to free the others, who resist and ridicule him. This is the philosopher's education and duty.

The education of philosopher-rulers includes mathematics, astronomy, and finally dialectic.

## Books VIII–IX: The Decline of Cities and Souls
Socrates describes how the ideal regime degenerates, with a matching type of individual for each stage:
1. **Aristocracy** (rule of the best)
2. **Timocracy** (rule of honor-lovers)
3. **Oligarchy** (rule of the wealthy)
4. **Democracy** (rule of freedom and appetite)
5. **Tyranny** (rule of one enslaved to his worst desires)

The tyrant, despite apparent power, is the most miserable person, while the just philosopher is the happiest. This answers Glaucon's challenge.

## Book X: Poetry and the Afterlife
- Socrates renews his critique of poetry. It imitates mere appearances, which are themselves copies of the Forms, and it stirs up irrational emotions.
- He argues that the soul is immortal.
- The work closes with the **Myth of Er**, the story of a soldier who returns from death and describes souls being judged and choosing their next lives. It teaches that justice is rewarded beyond this life and that wise choices depend on philosophy.

---

## Key Themes
- Justice as inner harmony, not just outward behavior
- The parallel between the structure of the state and the soul
- Knowledge and the Form of the Good as the basis for right rule
- The dangers of unchecked desire and of democracy sliding into tyranny
- The role of education in shaping character

**Legacy:** The *Republic* is one of the foundational texts of Western philosophy and political theory. It has been admired for its vision of justice and learning, and criticized (notably by Karl Popper) for its authoritarian elements, censorship, and rigid social hierarchy.

# How to Change a Flat Tire

## Before You Start
- **Get to a safe spot.** Pull over on flat, solid ground, away from traffic.
- **Turn on your hazard lights** and engage the **parking brake**.
- Put the car in **Park** (or in gear for a manual).
- If you have them, place **wheel wedges** or a heavy object behind the tires.

## What You'll Need
- Spare tire
- Jack
- Lug wrench
- Owner's manual (shows the jack points)

## Steps

1. **Remove the hubcap** (if there is one) to expose the lug nuts.

2. **Loosen the lug nuts** about a half-turn counterclockwise *while the tire is still on the ground*. Don't remove them yet. If they're stuck, use your foot or body weight on the wrench.

3. **Jack up the car.** Place the jack at the proper lift point near the flat (check your manual; it's usually a reinforced metal spot under the frame). Raise the car until the flat tire is about 6 inches off the ground.
   - ⚠️ Never put any part of your body under the car while it's on the jack.

4. **Remove the lug nuts** completely and keep them somewhere they won't roll away, like the upturned hubcap.

5. **Pull off the flat tire** by gripping it and pulling straight toward you.

6. **Mount the spare.** Line up the holes with the wheel bolts and push it on.

7. **Hand-tighten the lug nuts** as far as you can.

8. **Lower the car** partway so the tire touches the ground but isn't bearing full weight.

9. **Tighten the lug nuts fully** in a **star (crisscross) pattern**. This seats the wheel evenly.

10. **Lower the car completely**, remove the jack, and give the nuts one more firm tighten.

11. **Replace the hubcap** (if it fits the spare) and stow your tools and flat tire.

## Afterward
- **Check the spare's pressure** as soon as you can.
- If it's a **"donut" (compact spare)**, don't exceed about **50 mph (80 km/h)** or drive more than about **50–70 miles**. Check the sidewall for limits.
- **Get the flat repaired or replaced** soon.
- Have the lug nuts **re-torqued** after driving about 50 miles.

**Tip:** If you're on a busy highway or feel unsafe, call roadside assistance instead. Many insurance plans and car warranties include it.

Passed after the Civil War, it's often considered one of the most consequential amendments because it reshaped the relationship between individuals, states, and the federal government.

**Key provisions:**
- **Citizenship Clause:** Anyone born or naturalized in the U.S. is a citizen. This overturned the *Dred Scott* decision (1857), which had denied citizenship to Black Americans, and is the basis for birthright citizenship.
- **Due Process Clause:** States cannot deprive anyone of "life, liberty, or property, without due process of law." Through the doctrine of *incorporation*, courts have used this to apply most of the Bill of Rights to state governments, not just the federal government.

- **Other sections** addressed congressional apportionment, barred certain former Confederate officials from office (Section 3), and dealt with Civil War debts.

**Why it matters:** It's among the most litigated parts of the Constitution, central to cases on civil rights, voting, privacy, marriage equality (*Obergefell v. Hodges*), and more.

The fix depends on what kind of noise it is and where it's coming from. Here's a quick guide to common noises and what to do about each:

## Identify the noise

**Whirring, buzzing, or loud fan noise**
- *Likely cause:* Dust buildup, fan working hard due to heat, or a heavy program running.
- *Fix:*
  - Check Task Manager (Windows: Ctrl+Shift+Esc) or Activity Monitor (Mac) for programs using a lot of CPU.
  - Clean the vents and fans with compressed air (power off and unplug first).
  - Make sure vents aren't blocked. Laptops on beds or blankets overheat easily.

**Grinding, rattling, or scraping**
- *Likely cause:* A fan hitting a loose cable, a failing fan bearing, or debris inside.
- *Fix:* Power off and inspect the fans if you can. Remove any obstruction and tie back loose cables. A worn-out fan is usually cheap to replace.

**Clicking or ticking (especially repetitive)**
- *Likely cause:* A **failing hard drive** (the older spinning kind).
- *Fix:* **Back up your important files immediately.** Then plan to replace the drive. You can check drive health with tools like CrystalDiskInfo (Windows) or Disk Utility (Mac).

**High-pitched whine or squeal**
- *Likely cause:* "Coil whine" from the power supply or graphics card, often under load. Usually harmless, just annoying.
- *Fix:* Often not necessary. If it's coming from the power supply and getting worse, consider replacing it.

**Beeping at startup**
- *Likely cause:* The motherboard signaling a hardware problem (often RAM or graphics).
- *Fix:* Count the beep pattern and look it up in your motherboard or PC manufacturer's manual. Reseating the RAM often helps.

**Buzzing or crackling from speakers**
- *Likely cause:* Loose cable, grounding issue, or audio driver problem.
- *Fix:* Check connections, try different headphones or speakers, and update audio drivers.

## Safety note
If you smell burning, see smoke, or hear popping, **shut it down and unplug it right away.**

---

## Key factors

## Common standard scales

| Field | Typical scales |
|---|---|
| **Architectural (Imperial)** | 1/8" = 1'-0" (floor plans), 1/4" = 1'-0" (plans/elevations), 1/2" to 3" = 1'-0" (details) |

| **Mechanical/Engineering** | 1:1 (full size), 1:2, 2:1, 5:1 (enlarged for small parts) |
| **Maps** | 1:24,000, 1:50,000, and smaller |

## Quick way to calculate
**Scale = Drawing size ÷ Real size**

*Example:* A 40-foot building on paper with about 10 inches of usable space:
10 in ÷ 480 in ≈ 1:48, which matches **1/4" = 1'-0"**.

import math


def area_circle(radius):
    return math.pi * radius ** 2

    return length * width

    return side ** 2

    return 0.5 * base * height

    """Area of a triangle from its three sides (Heron's formula)."""
    if a + b <= c or a + c <= b or b + c <= a:

    """Area of a triangle from its three sides (Heron's formula)."""
    if a + b <= c or a + c <= b or b + c <= a:

# Classic Martini

## Ingredients
- 2½ oz (75 ml) gin (London Dry, like Tanqueray or Beefeater, is classic)
- ½ oz (15 ml) dry vermouth
- 1 dash orange bitters (optional but traditional)
- Garnish: lemon twist or green olive(s)

## Steps
1. **Chill your glass.** Put a martini or coupe glass in the freezer, or fill it with ice water while you mix.
2. **Combine.** Add the gin, vermouth, and bitters to a mixing glass filled with ice.
3. **Stir.** Stir for about 20 to 30 seconds, until the outside of the mixing glass is very cold. Stirring keeps the drink clear and silky. Shaking makes it cloudy and more diluted, though some people prefer it that way.
4. **Strain.** Dump the ice water from your glass and strain the drink into it.
5. **Garnish.** Express a lemon peel over the drink by twisting it skin-side down to release its oils, then drop it in or rest it on the rim. Or add an olive or three on a pick.

## Common Variations
- **Dry martini:** Less vermouth (a 6:1 ratio or more).
- **Wet martini:** More vermouth (3:1 or even 2:1).
- **Dirty martini:** Add ¼ to ½ oz olive brine and garnish with olives.
- **Vodka martini:** Swap vodka for gin.
- **Gibson:** Garnish with a cocktail onion instead.
- **Perfect martini:** Split the vermouth equally between dry and sweet.

## Tips
- **Keep vermouth fresh.** Store it in the fridge after opening and use it within a month or two. Stale vermouth ruins martinis.
- **Keep everything cold.** Some people keep their gin in the freezer too.
- **Adjust the ratio.** Start with 5:1 and tweak to taste.

Enjoy responsibly!

# The Lion and the Mouse

*An Aesop's fable*

Once upon a time, a great lion lay asleep in the shade of a tree after a long morning of hunting. The forest was quiet, and the lion snored softly in the warm afternoon.

A little mouse, scurrying about in search of food, didn't notice where she was going. She ran right across the lion's paw, then over his nose, and the lion woke with a start. Quick as lightning, he trapped her under his enormous paw.

"How dare you disturb my sleep!" the lion roared. He opened his great jaws to swallow her whole.

"Please, King of the Forest!" the mouse squeaked, trembling. "Forgive me! I didn't mean to wake you. If you let me go, I promise I'll repay your kindness someday."

The lion laughed so hard his mane shook. "*You* help *me*? You're so tiny! What could a little mouse ever do for a mighty lion?" But he was amused by her boldness, and she was hardly a mouthful anyway. So he lifted his paw and let her go.

"Thank you! I won't forget this!" the mouse called as she scampered away.

---

Some days later, the lion was prowling through the forest when he stepped into a hunter's trap. A heavy net of thick ropes fell over him. He twisted and clawed and thrashed, but the more he struggled, the tighter the ropes held him. At last, exhausted and afraid, he let out a mighty roar that echoed through the trees.

Far away, the little mouse heard it. *I know that voice,* she thought, and she ran as fast as her legs could carry her.

When she found the lion tangled in the net, she said, "Don't worry, I'll help you!"

She set to work gnawing on the ropes with her sharp little teeth. She chewed and chewed, one strand after another, until at last she bit through the main rope. The net loosened, and the lion shook himself free.

The lion looked down at the tiny mouse in wonder. "You saved my life," he said humbly. "I laughed when you said you could help me, but I was wrong. Thank you, my friend."

From that day on, the lion and the mouse were the best of friends.

---

**The moral of the story:** *No act of kindness, however small, is ever wasted.* And even the smallest among us can do great things.

It depends mainly on **where you are** (and where the other people are), **whether you're part of the conversation**, and **whether people have a reasonable expectation of privacy**. Here's an overview:

## United States
**One-party consent** (federal law and most states): You can record a conversation you're participating in without telling anyone.

**All-party (two-party) consent**: Everyone must agree. States generally in this category include:
- California, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Montana, Nevada (for phone calls), New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, Washington
- Connecticut and Michigan have partial or debated rules.

**Calls across state lines**: If one person is in an all-party state, the safest approach is to follow the stricter rule.

## Other countries (general patterns)
- **UK**: Recording a conversation you're in for personal use is generally allowed. Sharing it or using it for other purposes can raise data protection issues.
- **Canada**: One-party consent.
- **EU countries**: Rules vary. Germany, for example, is strict and generally prohibits secret recording of private conversations.
- **Australia**: Varies by state. Some require all-party consent.

## Key factors almost everywhere
- **Recording others without being present** (e.g., leaving a device to capture a conversation you're not part of) is illegal in most places. It's often treated as wiretapping or eavesdropping.
- **Public vs. private settings**: Conversations in public, where there's no expectation of privacy, usually have fewer restrictions.
- **Workplace**: Employer policies or union rules may prohibit recording even where it's legal.
- **Use of the recording**: Even a legal recording may be restricted in court, or sharing it could create defamation or privacy liability.

## Safest approach
Tell everyone you're recording and get their agreement. Ideally, capture that consent on the recording itself.
